After a long time he reached into the cold ash with one hand and held it there — not doing anything with it, not performing anything, just the specific contact of a hand in the remains of something that had burned well and was finished burning. The ash was cold and fine and settled against his palm with the specific weight of things that had been something else before they were this.

He held it.

Then he withdrew his hand.

He stood.

He looked at the cabin — all of it, the ceiling he had looked at from the other side of a child's fever, the pan on the hook, the window with the clearing outside it, the door frame that was just a door frame.

He left.

The cabin stood empty in the forest north of Ordenmere with the cold ash in the fire pit and the specific silence of a place that had held something for a long time and was now simply itself again.

### **Part Three — The Summoning**

---

She had been back in the mortal world for six days when the void opened for her.

Not a request. The void simply became available in the way that doors became available when the thing on the other side decided to open them. She stepped through without hesitation — hesitation communicated things she didn't want to communicate — and the void received her the way the void received everything it summoned. Completely. Without ceremony.

She stood in the darkness.

*"You summoned me,"* she said.

To the space. Not to a point in the space — she had learned that lesson early, the specific lesson of addressing presences that were distributed rather than located, that occupied the area around you rather than a position within it. She addressed the darkness evenly. Professionally.

Silence.

The textured silence of something listening rather than absent. She waited.

*"What do you know,"* the voice said.

Dark. Serpentine in register — not hissing, nothing so crude, just the specific quality of something that moved in curves even when producing language, the sentences arriving along paths that weren't straight. She didn't know the voice. She was an envoy — significant within the Order, capable, experienced — but the hierarchy above the Order was not something she had direct access to. She knew it existed. She knew its shape in the abstract. She did not know this specific voice and she was smart enough to know that asking who was speaking was the wrong move.

She answered carefully.

*"Caen has a project,"* she said. *"Of sorts. I've been aware of it for some time. I can't determine what the result would be. I'm not certain the result is something I have a framework for."*

The darkness was very still.

*"Tell me,"* the voice said.

---

She had followed his trail the way she followed all trails — not directly, cosmic entities didn't follow each other directly, the awareness of being tracked was itself a confrontation and she wasn't ready for that confrontation with Caen. But a being of his scale left signatures in the fabric of things. The specific impression of significant intention moving through the world, readable to something with the right kind of awareness. She had followed the signature.

It led her to a forest south of a settlement called Ordenmere.

It led her to a cabin.

She arrived during one of his absences — she had timed this, waited until the signature indicated he was elsewhere, until the cabin's specific presence was unoccupied by anything of his magnitude. She approached. She assessed the exterior. Then she went still.

Because there was something in the clearing.

---

*Inside her mind — the week she spent watching —*

He was fourteen years old.

She knew this the way she knew everything about mortals she assessed — not from asking, not from documents, from reading. Life force had age in it the way trees had age in their rings. You could read it if you knew how. She read fourteen years in him and then she read everything else and the everything else required her to stop and recalibrate immediately.

She had been cultivating mortals for a long time. She understood exceptional. She had found exceptional before — mortals whose life force density exceeded their peers by margins that made them worth the extended cultivation timeline, worth the investment of presence and guidance and the specific work of honing something toward the quality that made it worth feeding to the Devourer. She knew what exceptional felt like when she read it.

This wasn't exceptional.

This was something she didn't have a word for.

She watched him hunt.

He moved through the forest the way the forest moved — not like something in it but like something of it, each step placed with an awareness of the terrain that had nothing to do with caution and everything to do with complete integration. She had watched mortals move through wilderness before. She had watched trained soldiers, skilled hunters, people whose entire lives had been spent in environments like this. They moved through the forest. He moved with it. The distinction was not small.

She read his life force while he moved.

Dense. Refined in a way that life force wasn't supposed to be refined at fourteen — at fourteen life force was developing, building, the specific accumulation of a thing still growing into itself. His wasn't developing. It was formed. Not finished — she could feel the ceiling of it somewhere above what she could currently read — but formed in the way that blades were formed, shaped under specific conditions toward a specific purpose, the randomness of natural development replaced by the intentionality of directed work.

She recalibrated.

She had never read life force that felt like this in someone this age.

She watched him for a day. Then another. Then another. She told herself she was being thorough. She was being thorough. She was also recalibrating every twelve hours and arriving at a higher reading every time.

She watched him butcher an elk on the fourth day.

He worked the carcass with the specific unhurried efficiency of someone for whom this was neither remarkable nor unpleasant — just the necessary conclusion of a successful hunt. She watched his hands. She had handled mortals for long enough to understand what the wolf hide on his shoulders meant without needing it explained — not a trophy, not decoration, something earned, something worn so long it had become part of the specific signature of him. She read the hide the way she read everything. He had killed whatever this animal was at a young age. He had worn it since. The life force of the animal was still faintly present in the hide, absorbed into his own signature over years of contact.

She thought about what kind of child killed a direwolf.

She read him again.

Recalibrated again.

On the fifth day she moved closer than she had moved to any mortal she was observing without their knowledge. Close enough that a normal mortal would have felt something — the specific atmospheric disturbance of a cosmic presence in proximity. He felt nothing. He was fourteen years old and he felt nothing and this communicated more about what Caen had built into his awareness than anything else she had observed. His senses were calibrated for what existed in the world. She didn't exist in the world in the way the world's senses were calibrated for.

She was close enough to read him completely.

She did.

She stood in the forest beside a fourteen year old child who didn't know she was there and she read his life force from close range with the full application of everything she knew how to do and she arrived at a number that she had never arrived at before in the assessment of a mortal.

She recalibrated.

She arrived at the same number.

She recalibrated again. Different approach. Same result.

She stayed for the sixth day. The seventh.

On the seventh day she watched him return to the cabin from a hunt. She watched him sit by the fire in the specific comfortable silence of someone who had been alone long enough that alone had become the default state rather than a condition. She watched him eat. She watched him look at the fire with the specific quality of someone who was not thinking about anything in particular and was completely present in the not thinking, the way animals were present — without the human tendency to be somewhere else in the mind while the body was somewhere else in the world.

She tried to find the ceiling of what she was reading.

She couldn't find it.

Not because it wasn't there — everything had a ceiling. Because the ceiling was above the range of what she could read from the outside. She would have needed to go inside the life force to find it and going inside required contact and contact required revealing herself and revealing herself to this particular mortal was not something she was willing to do without understanding considerably more about what she was looking at.

She left on the evening of the seventh day.

She left without touching anything.

She left with a number in her assessment that she had never arrived at before and a question she couldn't answer — not what was Caen building, she understood what he was building — but why. Envoys trained mortals. It was the work. You found life force worth developing and you developed it toward the harvest. You did this with adults because adults were efficient — the development timeline was manageable, the outcome predictable, the harvest clean.

Children were not efficient.

The development timeline for a child was years. The outcome was uncertain. The harvest was delayed by a margin that made no practical sense when adults were available.

Caen knew this better than anyone.

Which meant he had a reason.

She couldn't see the reason.

She kept quiet about it.

For years she kept quiet about it, telling herself that Caen knew what he was doing, that the calculation she couldn't see existed and was sufficient, that the report would come when he determined it was time.

Year after year.

No report.

So she spoke up.

---

*Back in the void —*

*"I went to the cabin during one of his absences,"* she said. *"I watched the boy for a week. He was fourteen. Right before—"* she paused, choosing the word carefully, *"a significant development in his training."*

*"What did you read,"* the voice said.

*"Something I don't have a framework for,"* she said. *"I've cultivated exceptional mortals. I know what exceptional reads like. This wasn't exceptional. The life force was formed in a way I've never encountered at that age. Refined. Directed. The ceiling of it was above my reading range — I couldn't find it from the outside."*

The darkness was very still.

*"I recalibrated seven times,"* she said. *"I arrived at the same reading seven times."*

*"What did you conclude,"* the voice said.

*"That it isn't for the Devourer,"* she said.

She said it flatly. The way you said things that were true and uncomfortable simultaneously — without emphasis, without apology, just the fact of it laid out cleanly.

*"Caen trains mortals because it's our work,"* she said. *"We all do. We hone life force toward the harvest. But you don't spend years on something you intend to feed to the Devourer. You spend the minimum necessary. You don't choose a child when adults are available. You don't go dark to the Order for years. You don't—"*

She stopped.

*"You don't,"* she said more quietly, *"build something with a ceiling you can't read."*

The void moved.

The specific movement of something large that had been still and found a reason to stop being still — not toward her, not threatening, just the natural motion of something that processed information by moving, that thought in the physical the way others thought in the abstract. She felt it circling — the great curved motion of it, passing around her in the darkness, the specific excitement of something that had received what it came for and was working out what to do with it.

Then the light caught.

Not much light — the void had no light source, nothing to catch from. But there was always something, the faint ambient luminescence of the boundary between dimensions, and when the thing circling her passed through it the scales caught it and threw it back and for a fraction of a second she saw.

Platinum.

Silver-platinum — the specific color of something ancient and cold and metallic, not the warmth of gold or the flatness of grey but the specific cold brilliance of a material that had been forged or had become rather than grown. The scales overlapping with a precision that wasn't biological — each one fitted to the next with the specific exactness of something that had been made rather than born, the edges of them catching the ambient light and scattering it in the specific way that sharp edges scattered light. Enormous — the dimensions of it available to her awareness in the fraction of a second before the light was past and the darkness reasserted itself, the specific enormity of something that didn't have a size in the conventional sense because the space around it adjusted rather than the other way around.

Moving in a curve.

Always in a curve.

Then the darkness was simply the darkness again.

She floated in it.

She waited.

*"Find the boy,"* the voice said. *"Observe. Report to me."*

Not to the Order. To him. Whoever him was — the voice in the darkness, the platinum scales moving in a curve, the thing that had summoned her without introduction and given her orders without authority she could name and that she was going to obey anyway because the alternative was refusing something she couldn't identify in a void she couldn't leave until it decided she could.

*"And Caen,"* she said.

A pause.

*"Signus,"* the voice said, *"Is not your concern."*

The presence withdrew.

She floated alone in the void.

She thought about the seven days in the forest. The number she had recalibrated seven times and arrived at seven times. The ceiling she couldn't find.

She thought about the white-haired child sitting by the fire with the wolf hide on his shoulders eating alone in the specific comfortable silence of someone who had never known anything else.

She thought about what she had just agreed to and who she had just agreed to do it for.

Then she left the void.

She had work to do.

# 9 \- The Edge of Things

### **Chapter Nine — The Edge of Things**

#### **Part One — The Walls**

---

The rocks were wrong.

This was the first thing — not the color, not the fog, not the specific purple-grey that bled across the horizon like a bruise that had been there long enough to stop hurting and start simply being. The rocks. He had been walking the corruption's edge long enough to have developed a specific literacy for it — the way you developed literacy for anything you lived beside for years, the way the corruption's particular wrongness communicated itself through everything it touched in ways that weren't always visible until you knew what you were looking at.

The rocks were wrong because they weren't entirely rocks anymore.

Not transformed — not yet, not fully, the transformation was a process not an event and these rocks were somewhere in the middle of it, which was worse than either end. A rock that was fully corrupted was at least finished. These were in between. The surface of them had taken on the specific texture of something that had been stone and was becoming something else and hadn't arrived yet — faintly veined with the purple that the corruption put into everything it moved through, the veins following the grain of the rock the way water followed low ground, finding the paths of least resistance through the material and changing them as it went. If you looked at them long enough they seemed to pulse.

He had been looking at them long enough.

He looked away.

The ground was worse. Whatever grew here — grass, the low scrub that populated the corruption's margins, the occasional tree that had been here before the spread reached it — grew with the specific vitality of something that was alive and not alive simultaneously. The grass was green in color and wrong in quality, the specific wrongness of something that photosynthesized and respired and did all the things living things did while being fundamentally not what it appeared. The trees were the worst. Full canopy, full leaf cover, the structural appearance of health — and underneath it something that had been replaced so gradually that the replacement was complete before the outside changed. He had learned to read this. The specific stillness of a tree that had no wind moving through it on a day when everything else moved. The way the bark had taken on a faint luminescence that wasn't quite luminescence, just the absence of the specific way bark absorbed light replaced by the specific way corrupted material reflected it.

Even the air tasted different here.

Not bad exactly. Just — present. Air wasn't supposed to be present. Air was supposed to be nothing, the stuff you moved through, the medium between you and everything else. Here it had weight. A faint mineral quality underneath the taste of ordinary air, the specific mineral quality of rock that had been changed from the inside and was slowly releasing what it was becoming into the atmosphere around it.

He had been breathing this air his entire life.

He breathed it now without thinking about it.

In the distance the fog began.

It started as a thickening — the horizon losing its definition the way horizons lost definition in weather, except weather moved and this didn't. It sat. Grey and purple and the specific dirty quality of something that wasn't mist but was using mist's appearance, the fog of the corruption's deep regions where the transformation was complete and had been complete long enough to produce its own atmosphere. He couldn't see into it. Nobody could see into it from this distance. But you didn't need to see into it to know what was in it — the specific quality of the fog communicated what it contained the way smoke communicated fire. Things that had been other things once. Things that operated on the corruption's logic rather than the world's. Things that were not going to stay in the fog indefinitely.

He noted the fog's position relative to the edge he was walking.

He noted the direction it wasn't moving.

He adjusted his path by four degrees without breaking stride.

*"Are you listening?"*

---

Mara was looking at him with the specific expression of someone who had been talking for a while and had arrived at the specific awareness of not being listened to and found this mildly unacceptable. Not angry — she had calibrated his attention across two hours of walking and had learned that his attention was a specific thing, directed and complete when it was present and entirely elsewhere when it wasn't, and that attempting to force it back through volume or accusation was less effective than the direct question.

*"Are you listening?"* she said again, in case the first time hadn't landed.

*"Yes,"* he said.

She looked at him.

*"What did I just say."*

A pause.

*"Something about a market,"* he said. *"And someone falling."*

She considered this. It was technically accurate in the way that summaries were technically accurate — containing the correct elements in the wrong proportion, the specific summary of someone who had received the sound of words without the content of them.

*"Garan fell into the fruit stall,"* she said, with the specific emphasis of someone correcting a summary that had missed the point entirely. *"All of it. Every piece of fruit. And then he tried to catch them and knocked over the next stall which was the candle stall and then there was fruit everywhere and wax everywhere and everyone was covered in both and Garan was just standing in the middle of it covered in melon and candle wax looking like he couldn't decide whether to laugh or run."*

She paused.

*"It was very funny,"* she said.

He nodded.

*"Were you there,"* he said.

*"Obviously,"* she said, with the specific certainty of someone for whom obviously was the correct answer and the answer had always been the correct answer and the question was slightly insulting in its skepticism.

She looked ahead.

She was there. She had been there. She could see it — the market, the fruit, Garan's face, the specific chaos of two stalls worth of inventory distributed across the marketplace floor. She could see all of it. The light on the stalls, the sound of it, the way everyone had stopped what they were doing to look and then started laughing simultaneously, the specific shared laughter of a crowd that had witnessed something that had hurt nobody and was therefore completely available for entertainment.

She could see all of it perfectly.

She had constructed it perfectly.

She had been constructing things like it for long enough that the construction was automatic, that the memories felt like memories rather than architecture, that the specific warmth of them was indistinguishable from the warmth of things that had actually happened.

She looked at the corruption's edge.

She looked at the dead grass and the wrong rocks and the distant fog that sat on the horizon like a held breath.

She kept talking.

---

The walk had the specific quality of a thing that existed in two registers simultaneously.

In one register it was the corruption's edge on a grey afternoon — the infected landscape doing what infected landscapes did, the wrongness of it present and consistent and readable to anyone who had the literacy for it. The purple veining in the rock deepening as they walked, the discoloration in the soil more pronounced, the trees more thoroughly replaced. The fog in the distance not moving but not staying exactly the same either — shifting internally, the density of it changing in the specific way that things changed when what was inside them was also moving.

He read it continuously.

The four-degree adjustment had been sufficient. The path he was walking kept the worst of it at a manageable distance — close enough to maintain the navigation landmark, far enough that what lived in the fog's margins stayed in the fog's margins. He had been doing this his whole life. The specific arithmetic of corruption proximity was as automatic as breathing.

In the other register there was Mara.

She talked the way certain things moved — not in bursts, not in waves, just continuously, with the specific uninterrupted quality of a stream that had found its channel and was following it without requiring any particular effort or decision. The story about Garan and the fruit stall had become a story about the candle vendor's reaction which had become a story about the candle vendor's daughter who apparently had a specific and well-documented history of strong reactions to minor inconveniences which had become a story about a different incident entirely involving the same daughter and a dog and a rain barrel that Mara described with the specific relish of someone who had been saving this particular detail for the right audience.

He listened in the way he listened to the forest.

Not to the content — to the pattern. The rhythm of it, the specific cadence of her voice, the way it moved between registers — high when something was funny, lower when she was setting up something, the specific intake of breath before a detail she found particularly good. He had spent twelve years reading the patterns of things. This was a pattern. Different from the forest's patterns. Not unpleasant.

The dog had apparently ended up on a roof.

He didn't ask how.

She told him anyway.

---

Two hours out from the battle site the landscape had changed.

Not dramatically — the corruption's edge was still to their left, still doing what it did, still the wrong kind of alive in the wrong kind of way. But ahead of it and to the right the terrain had shifted — the ground firmer, the soil darker, the specific quality of land that had not been touched by what touched everything to the left of them. Ordinary ground. The specific ordinariness of it was almost startling after two hours of the other kind.

He was reading it — the shift in soil composition, the specific change in the quality of the air, the way the vegetation on the right side of the path was green in the way that green was supposed to be rather than the way the corruption made green — when Mara stopped mid-sentence.

She pointed.

To the right. Her arm coming up, her finger extending, the specific gesture of someone indicating something obvious.

*"Look,"* she said. *"Walls. There's a kingdom."*

He looked.

The horizon to the right. The treeline. The sky above it, grey and flat and ordinary. He looked for the specific angular profile of constructed stone against the organic geometry of everything else.

He saw nothing.

*"Where,"* he said.

She looked at him with the expression of someone who had pointed at something obvious and was processing the fact that the obvious thing had not been received as obvious.

*"There,"* she said. *"Right there. In the horizon. Are you blind?"*

He looked again.

The treeline. The sky. The specific distance between where they were standing and where she was pointing. He applied the full attention he had been applying to the corruption's edge for two hours to the horizon she was indicating.

He saw nothing.

*"I don't see it,"* he said.

She stared at him.

Then she grabbed his arm — not gently, the specific grip of someone making a directional correction to something that wasn't going the right direction — and physically oriented him two degrees further right than he had been looking.

*"There,"* she said.

He looked.

Nothing.

He considered the situation. She had seen something. She was nine years old and she had seen something on a horizon he could not resolve into anything other than treeline and sky. Either she was seeing something that wasn't there — which was possible, the corruption edge produced atmospheric distortions occasionally — or she was seeing something that was there and his eyes weren't finding it.

He looked at her face.

She was not seeing something that wasn't there.

He turned right.

*"Okay,"* he said.

She looked at him for a moment — the specific look of someone who had expected either confirmation or continued argument and had received neither, who had expected him to see it eventually or admit he couldn't but not to simply accept her word and redirect without requiring either.

She filed it.

She fell into step beside him.

*"Your eyesight,"* she said after a moment, with the specific tone of someone being generous, *"is terrible."*

*"Yes,"* he said.

She looked at him sideways.

He was already looking ahead — at the treeline, at the horizon she had pointed at, at the walls he still couldn't see but was now walking toward on her word alone.

She made a note.

The terrain changed as they moved away from the corruption's edge.

Gradually at first — the specific gradual quality of transitions that happened over distance rather than at a line, the wrongness of the infected ground bleeding into ordinary ground the way the corruption bled into everything, through contact and time rather than through a clean border. The veined rocks becoming less veined. The wrong-alive grass becoming simply grass — green in the way green was supposed to be, the specific honest green of something that photosynthesized because it was alive rather than because it was performing being alive. The air losing its mineral weight. The fog on the horizon staying where it was, which was behind them now and to the left, the distance between them and it growing with each step.

He noted all of this without comment.

Mara had resumed talking.

*"Do you really not have any idea where you're going?"*

She had asked this at the battle site. She was asking it again now — not the same question, the same words carrying something different the second time, something that had nothing to do with professional assessment and everything to do with the specific genuine bafflement of someone who had been walking beside a person with no destination for several hours and was starting to find the absence of a destination personally concerning.

*"I have a destination,"* he said.

She looked at him.

*"Where,"* she said.

He was quiet for a moment.

*"I don't know how to get there yet,"* he said.

She processed this.

*"So you don't have a destination,"* she said.

*"I have a destination,"* he said. *"I don't have a route."*

She considered the distinction. She had navigated Ordenmere's streets and the surrounding territory since she was old enough to move independently through both. She understood routes — the specific knowledge of how to get from one place to another through a world that was not always cooperative about being navigated. She understood destinations. She did not fully understand the gap between having one and having the other as a permanent operating condition.

*"What are you going to do when we get to the kingdom,"* she said.

He didn't answer.

Not because he was avoiding the question. Because he didn't have an answer and he had learned from Caen that the correct response to not having an answer was silence rather than approximation.

She looked at the horizon.

The walls were not visible yet.

She kept walking.

---

They appeared without announcement.

One moment the horizon was treeline and sky and the specific grey of the afternoon. Then — between one step and the next, at the specific distance where the eye resolved ambiguity into certainty — the walls were there. Stone. The angular geometry of constructed things against the organic geometry of everything else. Real. Exactly where she had said they would be.

He looked at them.

He looked at her.

She was not looking at him. She was looking at the walls with the expression of someone seeing something they had expected to see and finding it where they expected it. No triumph in her face. No performance of having been right. Just the specific absence of surprise that came from never having doubted.

He looked at the walls again.

They were exactly where she had said.

He thought about the two hours of walking on her word. The horizon he had looked at four times and found nothing in. The right turn he had taken on her word alone because she had said it was there and he had no reason not to believe her.

He filed it.

---

The gates were large.

Stone and iron, the specific construction of something that had been built to keep things out and had been doing so for long enough that the keeping-out had become architectural habit. Two guards at the entrance — the specific posture of people who had been standing in the same place performing the same function for long enough that the function had become structural, less a job than a condition of existing in this particular spot.

They stopped him.

One of them — broader than the other, the kind of broad that came from years of wearing armor rather than years of training, his face carrying the specific expression of someone for whom this gate and this question were the entirety of the relevant universe — looked at Varen.

Then at the wolf hide.

Then at the knife, the sword.

Then at Varen again.

*"What's your business,"* he said.

Varen looked at him.

*"What,"* he said.

The guard's expression shifted by a fraction. Not anger — the specific recalibration of someone who had asked a routine question and received a response that didn't fit the routine.

*"Your business,"* he said again. *"Why are you here. What do you want."*

Varen considered this.

He was here because Mara had pointed at the horizon and said walls and he had turned right. He was here because Caen had mentioned a kingdom north of the cabin and north had eventually produced this. He was here because the corruption's edge had been his navigation and the corruption's edge had brought him here and he had not had a more specific destination than here at any point in the last two weeks.

He understood that this was not what the guard was asking for.

He did not know what the guard was asking for.

*"I'm here,"* he said carefully, *"because I was walking and this was where I arrived."*

The guard stared at him.

*"Identify Yourself."* he said. The specific clipped delivery of someone simplifying a process that had become more complicated than it was supposed to be.

*"Varen,"* he said.

*"Varen what."*

He considered this.

*"Just Varen,"* he said.

The guard's jaw was doing something. Not moving — the specific tension of a jaw that was being held still by conscious effort against the pressure of things that wanted to be said through it.

*"What is your purpose in Ordenmere,"* he said. The words arriving with the careful spacing of someone speaking to someone they had decided needed things said slowly.

Varen opened his mouth.

*"He's a traveler,"* Mara said.

She had materialized beside him with the specific quality of someone who had been standing slightly behind and to the left and had decided that now was the correct moment to stop being slightly behind and to the left. Her voice had changed — not dramatically, just the specific register shift of someone who had turned a dial from one setting to another, from the girl who had been telling him about Garan and the fruit stall to someone older and more practiced and completely at home in this specific kind of exchange.

*"Lost his companions two days out,"* she said. *"He's been following the road since. Just needs a place to sleep and resupply."*

The guard looked at her.

Something changed in his face.

Not surprise — recognition. The specific expression of someone who has seen a particular face before in a particular context and is now recalibrating the current situation based on that history. His eyes moved to the second guard — just briefly, just the fraction-of-a-second communication of two people who shared a context and had just received information relevant to that context.

*"I know you,"* the first guard said. Not to Varen. To Mara.

*"I have an honest face,"* Mara said. *"People say that."*

*"People say a lot of things,"* the guard said. He was looking at her with the specific look of someone who had a job to do and was being prevented from doing it by a situation he couldn't fully address in the current context. *"You want to tell me what you're doing outside the walls with—"* he looked at Varen again, at the wolf hide, at the knife nad sword, at the white hair and the dark eyes and the specific quality of someone who had been built in a forest and showed it *"—him."*

*"Like I said,"* Mara said. *"Traveler. Lost companions. Needs a bed."*

*"And you just happened to—"*

*"Gaveth,"* said the second guard.

The first guard — Gaveth — stopped.

He looked at his colleague. His colleague was looking at him with the specific expression of a message being sent through the medium of eye contact. The message had content that Varen could not read but that Mara received immediately and completely — he saw it in the specific quality of the stillness that came over her, the breath she didn't quite take, the fraction of a second where the performance held absolutely still because moving it could break it.

Gaveth looked at his colleague for a long moment.

Then he looked at Mara.

Then at Varen.

*"Move along,"* he said. Flat. The specific flatness of someone making a decision they weren't entirely comfortable with and were committing to anyway.

They moved along.

---

The gate closed behind them.

Ordenmere opened in front of them.

The town square — the specific organized chaos of a market in its final hour before closing, the stalls beginning their wrap-up with the practiced efficiency of people who had done this every day for years and had reduced the process to its minimum necessary motion. Vendors folding cloth, merchants counting the day's take, the specific sounds of a place transitioning from active to finished — wood on wood, coin on coin, the calls between people who were communicating in the shorthand of familiarity.

People.

He had not been in a space with this many people since he was seven years old and the space had been his village and the village had been burning by the time he was eight. He had forgotten — or not forgotten, never fully processed, the memory of it filed under things that had existed before the two years in the forest and the cabin and Caen — the specific quality of a crowd. Not the crowd itself but the texture of it. The way human bodies moving in proximity to each other produced a specific warmth that had nothing to do with temperature. The sound of ordinary life being conducted without urgency. Children running between the stalls with the specific recklessness of people who had not yet learned to calculate the cost of recklessness.

He stopped walking.

Just for a moment.

He saw a boy chase a girl between two stalls — maybe seven, maybe eight, the girl running ahead with the specific lead of someone who had started the race early and knew it, looking back over her shoulder, laughing — and something arrived in him without warning.

Warm.

Specific.

The specific warmth of something that had existed before everything else existed — before the corruption's edge and the wolf and the cabin and the vow — the specific warmth of a world in which the most important thing happening was a child running through a market ahead of her brother.

Gone.

Between one breath and the next. Filed before he could hold it. The specific mercy of a mind that had learned to process grief quickly and move on.

He kept walking.

Mara was beside him.

She was looking at him sideways with the expression of someone who had noticed something and was deciding whether to ask about it. She decided not to.

She kept walking.

---

*"You should rent a room before nightfall,"* she said.

They were moving through the market's closing edges — the stalls half-packed, the vendors paying them no particular attention, the specific anonymous quality of two people who looked like they belonged in the general category of people moving through a market at the end of a market day.

*"What's rent,"* he said.

She looked at him.

Not the look of someone receiving an unexpected answer — the look of someone receiving confirmation of something they had already begun to suspect. She had been constructing a model of Varen across the hours since the battle site and the model had been producing results that didn't fit any category of person she had encountered before. This result fit the model perfectly.

*"You pay money,"* she said, with the specific careful clarity of someone explaining something to someone who needed it explained clearly, *"to sleep somewhere that isn't the ground."*

*"I know what money is,"* he said.

*"Right,"* she said. *"Do you have any."*

A pause.

*"No,"* he said.

She stopped walking.

He continued for two steps before noting her absence and stopping and turning.

She was standing in the middle of the closing market looking at him with an expression he hadn't seen on her face before. Not the professional assessment face. Not the performing face. Something underneath both of those — something that arrived before the performance could get in front of it and was gone almost immediately, covered by the next expression before it could be examined.

She had felt bad for him.

She had felt it genuinely and immediately and she was already constructing the justification before the feeling had finished arriving — if she helped him he would be in her debt, debt was currency, she was already invested in this particular mark and a mark with no resources was a liability and a liability could become an asset with the right management and this was therefore a strategic decision rather than anything else.

She believed this justification completely.

She reached into her coat.

She produced coins — a specific number, counted quickly with the specific finger-dexterity of someone who had been handling coin since before her hands were big enough to palm it properly. The coins that had been on the seven dead people in the field outside the walls. She looked at the coins. She looked at him.

*"I'll pay for your room,"* she said. *"You can pay me back."*

*"With what,"* he said.

*"Figure it out,"* she said.

She started walking toward the nearest inn with the specific purposefulness of someone who had made a decision and was executing it before they could examine it too closely.

He followed.

The inn was called something he didn't catch. The innkeeper was a woman who asked how many nights with the specific efficiency of someone for whom this question had been asked ten thousand times and would be asked ten thousand more. Mara said one and paid and received a key and handed it to Varen with the specific motion of someone completing a transaction.

He looked at the key.

*"Where are you sleeping,"* he said.

*"I've got a room,"* she said.

She said it with the specific certainty of someone stating a fact.

He filed it.

*"Good night,"* she said.

She left.

#### **Part Two — First Night**

---

The room was small.

He had known smaller spaces — the cabin's single room, the specific tight warmth of it, the ceiling close enough that standing in the center you could touch it with your palm if you reached. This was not smaller than that. But it was different in the specific way that all spaces were different when they had been built for transaction rather than living — functional, sufficient, the specific impersonality of a place that had held many people and remembered none of them.

A bed. A table. A window that looked onto the alley between this building and the next. A candle on the table that the innkeeper had lit when she showed him the room with the specific efficiency of someone who had performed this action so many times that performing it had become indistinguishable from not performing it.

He stood in the center of it.

He looked at the bed.

He had slept on the ground for two weeks. Before that he had slept in the cabin's bedroll for ten years. Before that he had slept on the ground for two years in the forest. He understood beds in the abstract — Caen had explained them once in the specific way Caen explained things, as information rather than instruction, something worth knowing without particular emphasis on why. He understood that the purpose of them was the same as the purpose of the bedroll. He understood that the mechanics of using one were not complicated.

He sat on it.

The specific give of it — the way it received his weight and adjusted rather than simply bearing it — was different from anything he had slept on before. Not better or worse. Just different. He noted the difference the way he noted terrain.

He lay back.

The ceiling of the room looked back at him.

He lay with it.

---

The questions arrived the way things arrived when the body was still and the mind was no longer occupied with navigation and threat assessment and the specific ongoing arithmetic of survival — without invitation, in the order they chose rather than the order he would have chosen.

*What's your business.*

He hadn't known how to answer it. Not because he was hiding anything — he had nothing to hide, the guard was a stranger and strangers didn't have access to the vow, nobody had access to the vow except him — but because the question assumed a shape of purpose he didn't have. Business implied a transaction. A thing being sought or offered. A specific reason for being in a specific place that could be stated in practical terms to a practical person.

He didn't have a practical reason.

He had a vow.

*How long are you staying.*

The innkeeper. Routine question. The specific logistics of room allocation requiring the information. He hadn't had an answer for that either. He had said one night because Mara had said one night and one night was the answer she had given and he didn't have a different answer available.

How long was he staying.

He didn't know.

How long would any of this take. The road north had taken two weeks and produced Ordenmere. The road to the vow's conclusion — to the name at the end of the line, to the burned boy's promise fulfilled — how long was that road. He had no way to measure it. He had no map, no intelligence, no understanding of the distance between where he was and where he needed to be. He had a name and a direction and a capability that had been built to the ceiling of what a human body could be built to and he had — nothing else.

*Do you really not have any idea where you're going.*

Mara. Twice. The second time with something in it that wasn't professional.

He had a destination.

He didn't have a route.

He lay with this.

The candle on the table burned. The alley outside the window was quiet — the specific quiet of a space between buildings that didn't get direct light and therefore didn't get direct attention. Somewhere in the building below him the inn continued its evening business — the specific muffled sounds of a place still operating, voices through floorboards, the creak of movement.

He had never fallen asleep to the sounds of other people existing nearby.

He noticed this.

He closed his eyes.

He fell asleep before he found an answer.

---

The room Mara had a room in was not a room.

It was a space beneath a market stall in the lower district — not the stall itself, the crawl space beneath the platform the stall was built on, accessible through a gap between two boards that had been deliberately loosened years ago by hands smaller than hers were now. She had been sleeping here since she was six. She had improved it incrementally across three years — a piece of canvas for the ground, a blanket taken from a washing line two winters ago, the specific domestic modifications of someone who understood that the space they had was the space they had and improvements were better than complaints.

She moved through the market's empty night-stalls without a light.

She didn't need one.

She knew this market the way Varen knew the forest — not by sight but by body, the specific knowledge of a place that had been navigated so many times that the navigation had become automatic, the obstacles and the paths and the specific gaps between things stored in the muscle rather than the mind.

She was almost at the stall when she heard him.

---

He was sitting at the entrance to the alley that ran behind the lower market.

Not waiting — positioned, the specific distinction between someone who happened to be somewhere and someone who had placed themselves somewhere with the awareness that the person they were waiting for would eventually pass through it. A man of middle age, the kind of middle age that had been arrived at through specific choices rather than simply through time, the specific wear of a life that had been lived in ways that showed. He was well-dressed in the way that certain kinds of people were well-dressed — not from wealth exactly, from the understanding that appearance communicated authority and authority was worth the investment of appearance.

His name was Alister.

She had known he was there before she saw him. She had known the way she knew all dangerous things in her environment — through the specific atmospheric awareness of someone for whom the ability to sense danger before it presented itself had been necessary for long enough to become instinct.

She stopped.

She composed her face.

She walked toward him.

*"You're very late,"* he said.

His voice was pleasant. This was the thing about Alister that she had understood since she was six years old — the pleasantness was not warmth. It was the specific pleasantness of someone who had learned that pleasantness was more effective than threat for the kind of work he did, that a pleasant voice produced compliance more reliably than a loud one, that the most efficient control was the kind that didn't look like control.

*"I know,"* she said. *"I lost track of time. I went further out than I meant to."*

*"Mm,"* he said. *"I heard you came through the gates with someone."*

She said nothing.

*"I heard he looked like a barbarian,"* Alister said.

*"He was someone I was working,"* she said. *"A traveler. Came from outside."*

*"Working,"* he said.

The emphasis. Specific. The way he put weight on certain words when he wanted her to feel the weight of them — not threatening exactly, just present, the specific gravity of a man who had spent years making sure the people around him understood what his words meant underneath what his words said.

*"How much did you make today,"* he said. *"Working."*

She reached into her coat.

She produced what she had — the coins from the battle site minus what she had paid for Varen's room, the specific remainder of a day that had gone considerably differently than she had planned when she left the walls that morning.

She held it out.

He looked at it.

His expression didn't change in any way that could be described as changing. It just — became something slightly different from what it had been. The pleasantness remaining on the surface and something else moving underneath it the way things moved under ice.

*"My other workers,"* he said, *"made this in an hour."*

She said nothing.

*"You were gone all day,"* he said.

She said nothing.

He looked at her for a long moment with the specific quality of attention that she had learned to be very still under — the assessment of someone calculating something, running numbers, arriving at a conclusion about what the appropriate response to the current situation was.

Then he stood.

---

The dream arrived the way the worst dreams arrived — not as a descent into somewhere else but as a continuation of somewhere familiar, the specific cruelty of a dream that began in warmth.

He was eight years old.

He knew this the way you knew things in dreams — not from evidence, just from the absolute certainty that the dream provided as its own logic. Eight years old and in the village and the village was whole and the specific quality of the light was the quality of late afternoon light in a place that had trees at its edges and open ground at its center and people moving through it with the specific unhurried quality of people who were somewhere safe.

His sister was ahead of him.

He couldn't see her face. She was running — already running, she had started before him, she always started before him because she understood that the only way to win a race against someone with longer legs was to begin it before they knew it had started. She was seven years old and she ran the way seven year olds ran when they were happy — with her whole body, arms out slightly, the specific joyful recklessness of someone who had not yet learned to calculate the cost of recklessness.

He ran after her.

Their mother's voice behind them — *come inside, dinner* — the specific voice of a person he had not heard in twelve years arriving in the dream with complete and total accuracy, every quality of it preserved, the warmth of it and the mild exasperation of it and the specific way she said *come inside* that meant she had said it already and was prepared to say it again.

His father going through the door ahead of them both.

His sister reaching the door frame.

She disappeared through it — the specific disappearance of someone moving from outside to inside, from the light of the afternoon into the warmer light of a room where dinner was waiting, one moment present and the next moment inside.

He reached the door frame.

He stepped through it.

And the warmth was gone.

The specific cold of it arrived not as temperature but as absence — the warmth simply not there, replaced by the specific quality of air that had been changed by something that had no business changing it. The light was wrong. The orange was not the orange of hearth-fire but the orange of something larger and less contained, the orange of something that had gotten out of what was supposed to hold it.

He was standing in the door frame of his house.

The corner of the room.

He looked at it directly.

He had never looked at it directly.

He looked at it now and the dream held it in front of him with the specific mercilessness of dreams that had been waiting to show you something you had been filing away for a long time and had finally found the circumstances to show it.

He looked at it.

He did not look away.

---

He woke up.

The ceiling of the inn room. The candle burned down to a stub, the specific low light of something in its final hour. The sounds of the building around him — quieter now, the late-night sounds rather than the evening sounds, the building settling into its overnight state.

His chest was moving too fast.

He noted this. He noted the specific elevated quality of his heart rate — the physiological response to something the mind had experienced while the body was still, the body responding to what the mind had been through with the specific loyalty of something that didn't distinguish between real danger and dreamed danger.

He breathed.

Then it arrived.

Not from the dream — from somewhere the dream had opened up, the specific door that the dream had unlocked by taking him to the corner of the room, by making him look at it directly for the first time.

*Their flesh shall bear witness to what their faith could not.*

The verse and the corner simultaneously. The floating figure above the fire and the corner of the room — the before and after of the same moment, inseparable, arriving together as they always would from this point forward. He lay with them. He didn't file them. He held them both in front of him in the low light of the almost-dead candle and let them be what they were.

His breathing slowed.

His heart rate dropped.

He looked at the ceiling.

The questions from the evening were still there — *what's your business, how long are you staying, do you really not have any idea* — but they were different questions now. Not the questions of a person without an answer. The questions of a person whose answer had just been made completely and totally clear by a dream and a verse arriving simultaneously in a small room in a kingdom he just arrived at.

He knew his goal.

He had always known his goal.

What the night had given him — the dream, the corner looked at directly for the first time, the verse arriving in its wake, the specific weight of all of it settling into him rather than being filed away — was not the goal. It was the certainty that the path to the goal existed. That it was findable. That whatever it required — the time, the kingdoms, the road, the people who would cross his path and the things he would have to become — he would find it.

He would find the way.

He lay in the small room in Ordenmere with the stub of a candle burning itself out and the sounds of an inn settling into night and the wolf hide on the chair beside the bed and the broken sword leaning against the wall and the knife on the table within reach.

He closed his eyes.

Sleep came without resistance this time — the deep kind, the kind that came after something significant had passed through a person and left them emptied out in the specific way that made rest possible rather than just necessary.

The candle on the table burned lower.

The room settled into dark.

---

In the corner furthest from the window something shifted.

Not dramatically. Not with the specific announcement of something making itself known. Just a presence that had been part of the room's darkness becoming fractionally less dark — the way a shape emerged from shadow when you looked at it long enough, except she had not been there long enough for looking. She had simply arrived, the way she arrived everywhere, between one moment and the next, without doors.

She stood very still.

She looked at him.

She had been in this room for three hours. She had watched him lie down, watched the questions move through him in the way she read thought — not as words, as disturbance, the specific agitation of a mind working through something unresolved. She had watched him fall asleep. She had watched the dream — not its content, she couldn't read content, but its effect on the life force, the way it moved through him in waves, the specific turbulence of something being confronted rather than avoided.

Then the dream had broken open.

She had never — in all her time cultivating mortals, in all the exceptional individuals she had found and read and assessed and developed toward the harvest — she had never seen anything like what happened in the thirty seconds after he woke.

It had started as warmth.

The life force responding to something the mind had resolved — a specific consolidation, the kind that happened when scattered energy found a direction, when purpose and capability aligned in a person who had been carrying both separately and finally understood they belonged together. She had seen this before. It was the most productive moment in any cultivation — the moment a mortal understood what they were for.

But it hadn't stopped there.

It had kept going.

The consolidation had produced heat and the heat had produced light — not visible light, nothing the room's air carried, just the specific luminescence of life force at a density that exceeded anything she had a calibration for. Blue. The specific deep blue of something burning at a temperature beyond ordinary flame, beyond the orange and yellow of common fire, into the range where combustion became something else entirely.

It had enveloped him completely.

For thirty seconds the mortal sleeping in the small inn room in Ordenmere had been — she didn't have the word. Not bright. Not powerful. Those were insufficient. He had been the most alive thing she had ever been in proximity to. The ceiling she had been unable to find from the forest outside the cabin — she had felt it briefly, just the suggestion of it, just the lower edge of it, in those thirty seconds.

And it was very far above her.

Then it had settled.

Back into him. Back into the specific density she had been reading since she arrived — extraordinary, unparalleled in her experience, but contained again, held inside the body of a sleeping young man in a room that smelled of tallow and old wood.

She stood in the corner.

She was smiling.

Not with warmth — with the specific expression of someone who had come looking for information and had found considerably more than they came for. Who had recalibrated seven times in a forest outside Ordenmere and had just been given a reason to recalibrate again. Upward.

She looked at him for a moment longer.

Then she left.

The candle guttered once in her absence.

Then it went out.

The room was dark and quiet and Varen slept in it without dreaming and outside the window Ordenmere continued its night and in the darkness something platinum moved through the spaces between worlds with the specific excitement of a thing that had just received very interesting news.

# 10 \- The Commission Board

### **Chapter Ten — The Commission Board**

---

The jerked meat was the same as it had been every morning for two weeks.

He ate it the way he ate everything — seated on the edge of the bed, methodical, without particular attention to the eating itself because eating was fuel and fuel was logistics and logistics didn't require presence, just execution. The room was grey with morning light coming through the alley window. The candle was dead. The building around him was making the specific sounds of a place transitioning from night to day — movement in the floors above and below, muffled voices, the creak of the structure adjusting to the morning's temperature the way structures adjusted when they had been standing long enough to have their own relationship with weather.

He had slept without dreaming.

He noted this the way he noted everything useful — as information, filed, potentially relevant. The night before had produced something. The dream and the verse and the specific clarity that arrived in their wake. He had gone to sleep afterward with the specific settledness of a question that had found its answer and woken up with it still there, intact, the clarity not having dissolved the way clarity sometimes dissolved between sleeping and waking.

He knew his goal.

He would find the path.

He finished the jerked meat. He checked his things — the wolf hide, the sword, the knife, the bandages and herbs in the pack's inner pocket, the small reserve of dried food that would last another four days if managed correctly. Everything in its place. Everything with a function.

He left the room.

---

She was in the corridor outside his door.

*"Good morning,"* she said.

*"It is,"* he said. *"Did you eat,"* 

Something moved in her face. Not dramatically — just a fraction, the specific micromovement of someone receiving something they weren't expecting and adjusting for it before it showed. She covered it immediately.

*"Already had something,"* she said.

*"What."*

*"Food,"* she said. *"The edible kind. Are you ready or not."*

*He was ready.*

*They went downstairs.*

She looked at him for a moment — the specific look of someone who had received something they weren't expecting and was deciding what to do with it. Then she turned and started walking toward the stairs.

*"I don't know what kind of jungle you crawled out of,"* she said, *"but you can't survive here without money."*

*"I know,"* he said.

*"Good,"* she said. *"Come on. I have an idea."*

---

The town square in the morning was a different place from the town square at closing.

He understood this the way he understood seasonal changes in the forest — the same location, different conditions, different behavior from everything in it. The market was opening rather than closing, the specific energy of it running in the opposite direction from yesterday evening. Stalls being unfolded rather than packed. Goods being laid out rather than counted and stored. Voices calling to each other across the square in the shorthand of people who had been doing this beside each other long enough to have developed a private language of it.

People moving with purpose.

He watched them.

Not with the threat-assessment attention he had been giving everything since he arrived — the specific recalibration of the previous night had shifted something in how he occupied space. He watched them the way he had watched the town square yesterday evening, before the flash of warmth that had arrived and left without asking permission. With the specific attention of someone learning a new terrain.

A man arranging fruit with the particular care of someone who understood that presentation was part of the product. Two women negotiating over cloth, the negotiation following a rhythm that suggested it happened every morning and both of them knew how it would end and were enjoying the process anyway.

He looked away.

She was walking beside him, her eyes already moving through the market the way his eyes moved through the forest — not at things but through them, the ongoing catalogue of a person who was always assessing and had learned to make the assessment invisible. She had been talking since they left the inn. Something about the market — which vendors were worth knowing, which areas produced the best opportunities, which guards ran which patrol routes at which times.

He had listened to the pattern of it more than the content. The specific fluency of someone who knew this place intimately and was producing the knowledge in real time without appearing to reference it.

*"I'll find you a way to earn today,"* she said.

*"How,"* he said.

*"I have an idea,"* she said. *"Come on."*

---

They were moving through the market's busier section when he asked.

Not because he had been building toward it — it simply arrived, the question that the information had been producing since the night before, the specific logical conclusion of a file that had been accumulating entries since the battle site.

*"How do you know so much about this kingdom,"* he said.

She was mid-sentence about something. She finished the sentence — a detail about a vendor near the eastern stalls who was worth avoiding for reasons she had begun to enumerate — and then she paused.

A fraction of a second.

*"All kingdoms look the same anyway,"* she said. Already moving to the next sentence. *"The market's always in the center, the guards always patrol the same way, the commission board's always near the—"*

*"Commission board,"* he said.

*"Where you find work,"* she said. *"That's where we're going. Keep up."*

He kept up.

He filed the deflection under the same category as the other deflections — alongside the lie about being lost, alongside the too-complete knowledge of the guard rotation, alongside the way she had navigated the gate exchange with the specific familiarity of someone who had done it before. The file was getting very thick.

He said nothing about the file.

---

He noticed she was moving differently.

Not on the first block or the second — somewhere in the third, when the market's morning press had thinned slightly and she was moving more freely and the specific quality of how she moved was more legible. He had been reading living things in motion since he was eight years old. The wolf's weight distribution before it lunged. The elk's tell before it bolted. The specific tension a human body carried when it was protecting something.

She was protecting something.

The left side. The way she held her arm slightly closer to her body than she had held it yesterday. The specific compensation in her torso when she turned — the half-rotation instead of the full one, the body making the calculation that the full rotation cost too much and adjusting without being asked. The clothes covering more than yesterday's clothes had covered, the specific layering of someone who had dressed with concealment in mind rather than temperature.

He watched her move.

He said nothing yet.

---

The sound arrived without warning.

Brief. Contained within the walls of the military compound visible through the gap between two buildings on the square's eastern edge. Not loud — the walls absorbed most of it, reduced it to something that arrived at his ears already diminished, already processed through stone and distance. But what remained was enough.

His body stopped before his mind had finished identifying what it had heard.

Every instinct he had — the twelve years of calibration, the specific alarm system that Caen had built into him through a hundred sessions of *what do you do when something approaches that you don't have a category for* — fired simultaneously and arrived at the same conclusion.

Significant.

Not the explosion itself. Something about the quality of the sound — the specific report of it, the contained precision of it, the way it didn't dissipate the way explosions dissipated but ended, cleanly, like a word spoken rather than a thing detonated. He had heard the sound of the forest when something large moved through it. He had heard the wolf. He had heard the wind in the clearing above the cabin on the coldest nights. 

He had never heard anything like this.

The market continued.

Heads turned briefly toward the compound walls — *something in the training yard, soldiers testing some magic, nothing came over the wall* — and returned to their business with the practiced efficiency of a population that had learned to distinguish between things that required attention and things that didn't.

He did not return to his business.

He stood with his full attention on the compound wall and read it the way he read everything — methodically, completely, looking for what the evidence was telling him. The wall told him nothing. The wall had absorbed the sound and sealed it inside and was giving nothing back.

Something in there had made that sound.

He didn't know what.

He would know eventually.

Mara's hand on his sleeve — not grabbing, just present, the specific touch of someone redirecting attention.

*"Forget about it,"* she said. *"Soldiers. Come on."*

He let himself be moved.

He did not forget about it.

---

The commission board was at the edge of the market square — a wide post with a board nailed across it, papers pinned to the board in varying states of age and urgency. Some crisp and recent. Some worn at the edges, the ink faded to the specific grey of something that had been rained on and dried out more than once.

He read.

He could read — Caen had ensured this with the same flat practicality Caen had ensured everything, because illiteracy in a world that communicated through writing was a liability and Caen did not build liabilities into things he was making. He read the board with the specific focused attention he brought to unfamiliar terrain.

He understood the words.

He did not always understand what the words meant in combination with each other. The language of the board assumed a context — a specific shared understanding of how problems were categorized and valued and assigned to people willing to address them — that he was missing pieces of. He read a posting about something described as *corrupted presence, eastern road, three failed clearings* and understood each word individually and could not assemble them into a complete picture of what was being asked.

Mara read differently.

She scanned the board with her eyes moving in the specific pattern of someone who had learned to extract maximum information at minimum time — not reading left to right, top to bottom, but moving immediately to the numbers. The reward figures. Assessed in a fraction of a second. Then the task. Then the location. Then the difficulty, estimated from the desperation in the handwriting and the size of the number and the specific vocabulary used by someone who had been trying to solve a problem for long enough to be very specific about what the problem was.

Her eyes stopped.

She pointed.

He looked at the posting she had selected.

He looked at her.

*"What's wrong,"* he said.

She was still looking at the board.

*"Nothing,"* she said. *"This one. The reward is—"*

*"You're in pain,"* 

She stopped talking.

A beat.

*"I'm fine,"* she said. She started to turn back toward the board.

He reached out.

He took her arm — the left one, the one she had been holding slightly closer to her body since the second block of the market, the one whose movement had been producing the compensation in her torso all morning. He took it with the specific careful certainty of someone who had spent twelve years treating injuries in conditions that didn't offer gentleness as an option and had learned that careful and certain were not opposites.

She made a sound.

Small. Involuntary. The specific sound of a body that has been managing something successfully and has had the management interrupted. She went very still.

He held the arm with the same grip. Not tighter. Just present. He looked at her face.

She looked back at him.

The expression on her face was the specific expression of someone who has been seen and finds the experience unacceptable — not frightened, not sad, furious in the way that people were furious when something they had been working very hard to keep invisible had become visible without their permission.

*"What happened,"* he said.

*"I fell,"* she said.

He looked at her for a moment.

Then he released her arm. He reached into his pack. He produced the bandages — the clean strips of cloth he had carried since the cabin, maintained and replaced wherever cloth was available because the wilderness did not negotiate around injuries. He produced the small pouch of herbs. He set both on the ledge of the commission board beside him.

He looked at her.

*"Sit,"* he said. *"I'll tend it."*

She stared at him.

*"It's nothing — this is the middle of the market — there are people—"*

*"I can see that,"* he said.

He could. It was irrelevant.

*"I'M FINE,"* she said

Heads turned.

The specific brief attention of a market that had noticed something — two people at the commission board, one of them a child, the volume suggesting something worth looking at. The assessment lasted approximately two seconds. The determination — nothing dangerous, nothing requiring involvement, a disagreement between travelers — arrived and the heads returned to their owners' business with the practiced efficiency of a population that had learned to make these determinations quickly.

Mara clocked it immediately.

The anger closed down. The volume closed down. The expression closed down and the normal one came up in its place — the easy, present, unbothered expression that was Mara's surface as reliably as the wolf hide was his. She turned back to the board. She pointed at the posting again. She told him the reward amount in the tone of someone who had not just been shouting in a market.

*"Three Gold,"* she said. *"For a corrupted presence on the eastern road. Three previous attempts. The creature's been observed to operate close to the edge of the corruption and must be dealt with."*

He put the bandages back in the pack.

He put the herbs back.

He looked at the posting she was pointing at.

The corrupted presence. South west of the kingdom. Three previous attempts. Two gold — not desperate money, official money, the specific weight of a kingdom that monitored its corruption border and had watched three attempts fail and had decided the number needed to reflect the seriousness of what was out there. He read the location and he knew it. He had stood in it. He had walked through the grass with the purple at its edges and read seven bodies and reconstructed exactly what had killed them.

He knew this prey better than anyone who had attempted it.

*"I'm ready,"* he said. *"Let's go."*

Mara was looking at him.

*"You read the whole thing, right?"* she said. *"Not just the number. The actual job."*

*"I read it."*

*"Three groups already tried. Three. The last one didn't come back at all."* She tapped the posting with one finger. *"There are easier jobs. You don't have to take the one that's been eating people."*

*"It pays the most."*

*"It pays the most because it kills the most,"* she said. *"That's how it works. The reward goes up every time someone dies. That's not a good job, that's a warning with a number on it."*

*"I can handle it."*

He didn't say it loudly. He didn't say it the way men said things when they needed other people to believe them. He said it the way he said everything — flat, certain, a fact he was reporting rather than a position he was defending. He had read the tracks at the battle site. He knew what the coordination meant. He knew where it came from and he knew how to take it apart.

She looked at him for a moment.

She had spent a day learning to read him and she had learned at least this much — there was a specific quality his voice took when a decision had already been made, and arguing past that quality was a waste of breath. She had heard it now.

She stopped arguing.

*"Fine,"* she said. *"Your funeral."*

He turned and started walking toward the eastern gate.

---

She fell into step beside him.

He stopped.

She took another half-step before she registered that he had stopped, then stopped too, and looked up at him with the expression of someone waiting to find out why they were no longer moving.

*"Where are you going,"* he said.

*"With you. Obviously."*

*"No."*

She blinked.

*"What do you mean, no."*

*"You'll be no help on the job,"* he said.

He said it without weight. Not to wound her — the thought of wounding her didn't occur to him, because what he was saying was simply true and true things didn't require softening any more than the weather did. She would be no help. She was a child, she was injured, the thing on the eastern road had killed seven people who were none of those things. The arithmetic was clean.

*"You're hurt,"* he said. *"There's no reason for you to come."*

Something moved across her face.

He watched it move and didn't understand it. It wasn't anger — he knew her anger now, he had seen it an hour ago at this same board. This was underneath the anger. Something that arrived before she could get a performance in front of it, the way the thing at the inn had arrived before she could cover it.

She covered it now. Faster than last time. But he had seen it.

*"I can carry things,"* she said.

The words came quickly.

*"I can carry the gear so you're not weighed down. I can cook, I can start a fire, I know how to keep a camp quiet. You won't even know I'm there. I'll stay back, I'll stay out of the way, I won't slow you down, I—"*

*"I can do all of that myself,"* he said.

She stopped.

She stood in front of him at the edge of the market with the commission board behind her and the gate ahead and she had run out of the practical things, the useful things, the arguments that a person made when they were negotiating from a position of value. She had nothing left that was about carrying gear or starting fires.

What was left was the thing underneath.

*"I want to go with you,"* she said.

---

He was eight years old.

The morning light came through the trees at the edge of the village in long gold lines, the specific light of an early hour before the day had fully committed to itself. There was an axe in his hands that was slightly too big for him and a task in his head that his father had given him, and the task was wood, and the wood was in the forest, and he was going to do it because it was his to do.

She was there.

He couldn't see her face. He was looking at her and there was no face — just the shape of her, small, his sister, standing in the gold light with her hands at her sides and an expression he couldn't see but could feel, the specific expression of someone who already knew what the answer was going to be and was going to ask anyway.

*"I want to go with you,"* she said.

Her voice. He could hear her voice. After twelve years he could still hear exactly her voice, the specific pitch of it, the way it lifted slightly at the end of the sentence as if the wanting might be enough to change the outcome.

He looked at her.

*"Father asked me to get wood,"* he said. *"This isn't a girl's job."*

He said it the way children said things — without cruelty, without weight, with the casual certainty of someone who did not know that some doors, once you walked through them, did not open again. It seemed sufficient at the time. The reasoning seemed sound. It was wood, and he was the one who had been asked, and there was no reason for her to come.

He went into the forest.

She stayed.

That was the last—

---

*"Fine,"* he said.

The word was out of his mouth before he understood that it was coming. He heard himself say it the way you heard yourself say things in the moment after a decision had already been made somewhere below the level where decisions were supposed to happen.

Mara stared at him.

*"...Fine?"* she said.

*"Fine,"* he said again. *"Let's move."*

He turned and walked toward the gate.

She fell into step beside him before he had finished turning — fast, immediate, with the specific speed of someone who had spent her whole life understanding that the difference between getting something and losing it was sometimes a single second, and you did not waste the second by being surprised that the thing had been offered.

He didn't look at her.

He didn't understand why he had said it.

He turned the question over once, looking for the reasoning the way he looked for the logic in tracks, and found nothing — no calculation, no advantage, no sound argument that ended in *yes.* She would still be no help. She was still injured. The thing on the eastern road had still killed seven people. None of that had changed in the four seconds between *I can do all of that myself* and *fine.*
