Something had answered for him.

He didn't know what it was.

He filed it with the other things he didn't understand yet — the gap at the battle site, the people who stayed when staying meant dying, the thunder behind the compound wall. The file that kept growing. The file where things waited until they were ready to mean something.

He walked toward the gate.

She walked beside him.

---

The western gate was the same gate, the same guards, the same stone. They passed through it without being stopped this time — a man and a child leaving a kingdom in the early afternoon was not a thing that required questions, and the guards had questions only for the things that came in, not the things that left.

They stepped through.

Coming toward them through the same gate was a caravan.

Nuns first — walking, or something that had once been walking and was now a version of it, the specific gait of people whose bodies were still moving because stopping hadn't been authorized yet. Their habits were wrong — torn in places, darkened in others, the white of them carrying the specific grey-purple staining of corruption-touched ground alongside something darker that wasn't corruption at all. Some of them supported each other. Some walked alone with the specific sealed quality of people who had run out of the resource required to accept help.

Behind them a carriage.

Varen looked at the carriage.

The carriage was loaded. Not with supplies — with the covered shapes of things that had been people recently and were now being brought back inside the walls because the walls were where people were brought when they were finished being people outside them. The covers didn't disguise what they covered. He had read enough kill sites to know weight and shape and number.

He counted.

He filed it.

The procession passed through the gate in silence — the guards stepping back to let them through, the specific deference of men who understood that these women had just come from the place the guards were paid to protect people from, and that saying anything to them right now was something nobody wanted to be the person who did.

Mara had gone quiet.

Not the quiet of someone with nothing to say — she always had something to say. The quiet of someone who recognized what they were looking at and had decided that what they were looking at wasn't something you talked over. She watched the nuns pass with the specific expression of someone who had grown up inside these walls and understood what it meant when the border nuns came back like this.

The last of the caravan moved through the gate behind them.

Mara watched it go.

She walked beside him for a hundred steps without saying anything, which was long enough that the silence itself communicated something. Then —

*"You still want to do this commission."*

Not quite a question. The specific phrasing of someone who already knew the answer and was offering one more moment for the answer to be different.

He looked at the road ahead.

*"Yes,"* he said.

She looked at the covered shapes in the carriage as it passed through the gate behind them. She looked at the nuns walking with the specific gait of people whose bodies were still moving because stopping hadn't been authorized yet.

She looked at him.

*"Okay,"* she said.

She started talking about something else entirely. The story was already underway before he'd finished processing that she'd stopped pressing — something about a market vendor and a cat and a sequence of events that grew less plausible the longer it continued.

He listened for the pattern.

The road stretched south.

He kept walking.

# 11 \- The Thunder Inside the Walls

### **Chapter Eleven — The Thunder Inside the Walls**

---

The northern gate of the west district was the civilian face of the most militarized part of Ordenmere.

Merchants came through here. Supply deliveries. The ordinary daily business of a district that happened to sit alongside the kingdom's most serious defensive installation. The western gate was the other one — the one that faced the corruption border directly, the one that military traffic used, the one that didn't process merchants because merchants had no business being that close to the wall.

Ryn came through the northern gate.

Not because he couldn't have found another way in. Because a trade commission weapons consultant arriving for a routine meeting came through the civilian entrance. That was what routine meetings looked like. He was a man with a letter and a bag and a schedule, and men with letters and bags and schedules used the northern gate, and the northern gate guard looked at the letter and looked at him and waved him through without a second thought.

He walked into the west district.

He had been here before — surveyed it on his first pass through Ordenmere before he left for the forest, read its layout and its market and its rhythms with the specific thoroughness of someone who processed environments automatically and stored everything worth storing. He hadn't acted on it then. He hadn't been ready. He had a list of things to acquire and a sequence to acquire them in and the west district was somewhere in the middle of the sequence, not the beginning.

He was ready now.

He moved through the market.

The alchemy shop was where he had noted it on his first pass through the district — third stall from the northern end of the market's eastern row, the morning light catching the glass containers in the window in the specific way that told him the trader understood that presentation was part of the product.

He stepped inside.

The trader was a woman of middle age with the hands of someone who had been handling materials that required careful handling for long enough that carefulness had become structural rather than conscious. She looked at him the way traders looked at people who entered without browsing — directly, assessing, the specific attention of someone who had learned that people who knew what they wanted were either the best customers or the most difficult ones and the difference was determined in the first thirty seconds.

He looked at the shelf behind her.

Acid wood bark. Anechoic coating. Both priced with the specific confidence of someone who believed their customers didn't know what these things were actually worth at the source.

*"The bark and the coating,"* he said.

She named a price.

He reached into the bag.

He produced one vertebra.

She looked at it.

*"One,"* she said.

*"One,"* he said.

*"For both."* Not a question. The specific tone of someone establishing that they had heard correctly before they decided what to do with what they had heard.

*"For both,"* he said.

She made a sound that communicated several things simultaneously — that she knew what a vertebra was worth, that she had a price in mind that one vertebra did not meet, and that she was prepared to explain this at length if necessary.

*"You know what that is,"* she said.

*"I do,"* he said. *"Do you know what it costs to get one?"*

She looked at him.

*"Not the market price,"* he said. *"What it actually costs. Crimson territory, eastern continent, far enough in that the border patrols don't reach. You go in with equipment rated for Crimson exposure — which costs. You find something large enough to have vertebrae worth extracting — which takes time. You extract them from something that is still alive and has opinions about that — which costs differently. You preserve them correctly for transport — specific temperature, specific containment, not what most traders stock. You move them through three kingdoms with border controls that confiscate biological materials from active infection zones if they know what they're looking at."*

He paused.

*"That's what one vertebra costs,"* he said. *"Not the market price. The actual cost."*

The trader looked at the vertebra on her counter.

She looked at him.

*"Throw in the vile mushrooms,"* he said.

A beat.

*"The ones behind the blue jar,"* he said. *"Second shelf. You haven't displayed them."*

She turned and looked at the second shelf. She looked back at him with the specific expression of someone who had just updated their assessment of who they were dealing with and found the update uncomfortable.

*"The mushrooms,"* he said again. *"And we're done."*

She reached behind the blue jar.

She put the mushrooms on the counter beside the bark and the coating.

He put everything in the bag. He put the vertebra on the counter.

She picked it up without further comment.

He walked out.

---

The first blacksmith was on the corner where the market met the district's residential streets — a working forge, loud even at this hour, the specific productive noise of someone who started before the market opened and would still be working when it closed. Ryn produced a section of blueprint and laid it on the counter.

The blacksmith looked at it.

He looked at Ryn.

He looked at the blueprint again — the tolerances marked with a precision that communicated exactly what kind of customer this was going to be, the materials specified by name and grade, the dimensions exact to a fraction that most smiths would have found irritating and this one found interesting.

*"When,"* the blacksmith said.

*"Morning,"* Ryn said.

The blacksmith looked at the blueprint one more time.

*"Morning,"* he said.

The second blacksmith was two streets north. Different section. Same conversation, shorter — this one read blueprints faster and asked fewer questions, which Ryn filed as a sign of either competence or incuriosity and would determine which in the morning when he collected the work.

The third blacksmith's forge was near the western wall.

He had noted this on his first pass — the specific location of it, pressed against the wall's mass the way certain businesses pressed against walls when they had reasons to want their noise absorbed rather than distributed. The wall did that here. Whatever came out of this forge in terms of sound stayed in this corner of the district rather than traveling through it.

He had filed this without examining it.

He examined it now as he approached.

The forge itself was visible through the open front of the workshop — not large, not small, the specific size of something that had been built for a particular kind of work rather than for general use. The tools arranged around it with the specific organization of someone who knew exactly where everything was and had placed everything where it was for a reason that wasn't arbitrary. The workbench clean in the way that workbenches were clean when the person who used them processed cleanliness as part of the work rather than as maintenance separate from it.

The dwarf behind the counter was looking at him before he reached the door.

Not the look of a shopkeeper assessing a customer — the look of someone who had heard him coming and had formed an initial opinion before the visual confirmed or contradicted it. Short, broad through the shoulders and chest in the specific way of someone built for work that required sustained force, hands that were the most immediately striking thing about him — large, calloused to a texture that wasn't quite skin anymore, the specific hands of someone who had been doing this long enough that the work had changed the instrument. His face was the kind of face that didn't give things away unless it decided to.

He was looking at the blueprint section Ryn had already produced and laid on the counter.

He had not touched it yet.

*"I can make this,"* he said.

Not *what is it* or *what's it for* — just the direct assessment of someone who had looked at a specification and determined whether it was within his capability. It was. He had determined this in the time it took Ryn to walk from the doorway to the counter.

*"Morning,"* Ryn said.

The dwarf looked at him.

*"Morning,"* he said.

Ryn walked away before questions could form.

---

The inn was in the middle of the district — not the cheapest room and not the most expensive, chosen for the specific reason that the largest room on the second floor had a table wide enough to work on and a window that faced away from the street, which meant the light in the morning would come from the east and the noise from the market would be muffled by the building's mass.

He had assessed this through the window before booking it.

He paid without negotiating.

Some things were worth the full price.

He went upstairs. He closed the door. He looked at the table.

He cleared it — not carelessly, each item moved to a specific location, the surface prepared with the same methodical attention he brought to everything that mattered. Then he opened the bag.

---

The pouches came out first.

He arranged them in a specific order that wasn't arbitrary — each material placed in a position relative to the others that reflected how they would interact, the spatial logic of a man who thought in reactions and consequences rather than in objects and distances. The acid wood bark. The anechoic coating. A small sealed container of infernal suevite — volcanic glass from the Pyre's deepest reaches, formed where brimstone and ordinary rock had been fused under conditions that only the underworld generated, dense and hard in a way that absorbed energy rather than reflecting it. He had acquired this three kingdoms ago and had been waiting for the right application.

This was the right application.

Last — a vial of a viscous substance.

He held it up to the candle for a moment. The light came through it strangely — not quite transparent, not quite opaque, the specific optical property of something that existed between states. Viscous. The color of it in candlelight something between amber and nothing. He had been carrying this for longer than the suevite. He had known what he would eventually use it for since the moment he acquired it. He set it carefully in its position.

He looked at the arrangement on the table.

He picked up the first tool.

He began.

---

What followed was not dramatic.

It was work — the specific focused work of someone who was genuinely exceptional at something and was doing it, the kind of work that looked simple from the outside because the person doing it had internalized the complexity to the point where the complexity was no longer visible. The bark processed first — not ground, something more precise than grinding, a reduction that produced a consistency that looked like ordinary powder and behaved like something else entirely under the conditions he was going to put it through. The suevite next — shaped, which required tools most people wouldn't have thought to bring and a patience most people wouldn't have sustained. The anechoic coating applied in layers, each one allowed to set before the next, the candle burning lower with each pass.

The gel substance went in last.

He did not rush this step.

The candle burned to nothing.

He lit another.

The materials combined in an order that had been decided before he touched any of them — the sequence existing complete in his mind since the walk back from the forest, each step preparing for the next, the logic of it airtight in the way that the logic of things was airtight when the person constructing it understood every variable. Alchemy as equivalent exchange — what went in determining what came out, the practitioner's knowledge being the difference between transformation and destruction.

He made something.

He set it down.

He looked at it for a moment with the expression of someone verifying that the thing in front of them matched the thing in their head — checking, not admiring, the specific assessment of someone for whom the finished product was already the beginning of the next problem.

It matched.

He went to sleep.

---

The dream arrived the way the good ones arrived — without the fragmented quality of the flashes, without the specific incompleteness of color and warmth that usually constituted his visions. This one had duration. Enough duration to contain a place.

A tree.

Spring light through new leaves — the specific green of leaves that had just arrived and hadn't yet deepened into summer, the light coming through them broken into patterns that moved when the wind moved. He was sitting under it. He knew this from the grass under his hands, from the angle of the light, from the specific physical quality of being somewhere that had nothing urgent about it.

He was thinking about something.

He didn't know what. Something that required the face he apparently made when he was thinking too hard — he didn't know he made a face. He hadn't known until this moment, which meant someone had told him once, which meant—

She was there.

Gold hair. The specific gold of something that caught sunlight and gave it back warmer than it arrived. A face that the eye returned to not because it was performing beauty but because something in it was — complete. The face of someone who had arrived at themselves and was at ease with what they found.

She was looking at him.

Smiling.

Not at something funny — at him, at the face he was making, at the specific expression she had seen on this particular face enough times to have formed an opinion about it.

*"You're making that face again,"* she said. *"You're thinking too much."*

*Her voice was the kind that arrived in the ear like something that had always been there — soft without being quiet, warm without trying, the specific quality of a sound that the mind filed not as heard but as felt. He didn't know how long he had been listening to it before he understood that listening to it was the best thing he had done all day.* 

---

He opened his eyes.

The room. The table with its organized materials and the thing he had made sitting at the center of them. The window showing the specific grey of very early morning — before the sky had committed to dawn, before the market below had begun its noise.

He lay still.

Not confused. Not reaching for what was already retreating. He had learned that reaching made them go faster and he had learned to let them leave at their own pace and keep what could be kept in the keeping.

Gold hair.

*You're thinking too much.*

It was the longest one yet.

He didn't know why.

He didn't know that three feet of wall and a sleeping young man with white hair separated him from the answer.

He got up.

He had work to do.

---

The west district was quiet at this hour.

The military installation already active — patrols changing, the compound's internal rhythm running regardless of the civilian market's schedule. The market itself empty, the stalls covered, the specific pre-dawn stillness of a space that would be loud in two hours and wasn't yet.

He moved through it toward the first blacksmith.

The work was ready.

He examined each piece with the specific thoroughness of someone who had given exact specifications and was verifying that the exact specifications had been met. The first piece — good. The second — good. 

The third…

The first two smiths were straightforward — the work examined, assessed as correct, paid for, collected. He put the pieces in the bag and moved on.

The third forge was still warm when he arrived. The dwarf was behind the counter with the piece on the surface between them, his hands at his sides, watching Ryn approach with the specific quality of someone who had been waiting and was interested in what was about to happen.

Ryn stopped at the counter.

He picked up the piece.

He turned it once.

He set it back down.

He looked at the dwarf.

The dwarf looked back at him.

The tolerance was wrong. Not significantly — not the error of someone who had misread the specification or lacked the skill to meet it. The error of someone who had met the specification perfectly in every other regard and had introduced this particular deviation with the specific deliberateness of someone making a choice rather than making a mistake. The piece was otherwise flawless. The deviation was in exactly the location that would matter most under the conditions the piece was designed for.

He would know.

They were both in each other's minds at this point.

Ryn said nothing. He looked at the forge.

He had not looked at it properly on his first visit — had noted its location, noted its size, filed it and moved on to the blueprint conversation. He looked at it properly now.

The fire was burning brighter than any forge fire he had seen. Not hotter in the conventional sense — brighter, the specific luminescence of combustion that was receiving more oxygen than a forge fire normally received, the color of it shifted toward the white end of the spectrum where forge fires were usually orange and red. He looked for the bellows. There were no bellows. He looked for the tuyere — the pipe that directed forced air into the fire. There was no tuyere in the conventional arrangement.

He looked at the wall behind the forge.

A pipe. Emerging from the stone, running to a point below the forge's firebox, the junction concealed but not completely — the specific concealment of something that hadn't been designed to be hidden, just not designed to be obvious. And at the wall's base, at intervals, exhaust vents — small, the steam coming through them in the specific intermittent rhythm of a mechanism cycling rather than the continuous flow of passive ventilation.

A mechanism.

Constant forced air supply. No human labor required to maintain it. The forge running at a consistent temperature regardless of whether anyone was working the bellows because there were no bellows to work.

He assessed the entire system in the time it took to look at it.

He looked back at the dwarf.

The dwarf was still watching him.

*"The part you wanted made,"* the dwarf said. *"It's designed to withstand a blast."*

He said it the way you said things that were simply true — without emphasis, without the performance of revelation, just the flat delivery of someone reporting an observation.

*"I would know,"* he said.

Ryn said nothing.

The dwarf picked up the piece from the counter. He turned to the forge — to the bright consistent fire fed by the mechanism in the wall — and he worked. Not long. The correction was minor and his hands knew what they were doing and what they were doing required no ceremony. He worked with the specific efficiency of someone for whom this was simply finishing something that had been left unfinished.

He set the corrected piece back on the counter.

*"I understand you want to keep your invention to yourself,"* he said. He wasn't looking at Ryn now — looking at the piece, examining his own correction with the critical eye of someone who held their work to a standard that didn't negotiate. *"I would know."*

A pause.

*"It was a pleasure,"* he said. *"Working on a component like this. Intricate. Most people don't bring me intricate."* He looked up. *"Most people don't know what intricate is."*

Ryn looked at the forge one more time. The pipe in the wall. The exhaust vents. The fire burning brighter than fire had any business burning without someone actively working to keep it that way.

He smiled.

Not the performance smile — the real one, the one that appeared when something genuinely surprised him and he didn't bother concealing the surprise because concealing it would have been a waste.

His calculations had not accounted for this particular morning.

*"Aldric,"* the dwarf said. *"The blacksmith."*

Ryn looked at him.

He picked up the piece and put it in the bag with the others.

*"Ryn,"* he said. *"The trader."*

The dwarf's expression did something small — not quite a smile, the specific movement of someone who had received exactly what they expected and found the confirmation satisfying.

Ryn left.

The forge burned behind him, bright and constant, fed by something in the wall that nobody had asked him to explain and that he had built anyway because problems had solutions and solutions were worth building regardless of whether anyone was watching.

He walked toward the western brigade compound.

The bag was heavier than it had been yesterday.

He had a reason.

He walked toward the western brigade compound.

He had timed his arrival precisely.

The western brigade compound sat against the wall like it had grown there — not built against it but continuous with it, the stone of the compound and the stone of the wall the same stone, the same age, the specific architecture of something that had been conceived as a single defensive system rather than a structure added to an existing one.

The gate was the working kind.

Two guards. Equipment maintained past the standard the rest of the district bothered with — the specific standard of people who had internalized their readiness as identity. They looked at him the way the compound's entire west side looked at everything that approached it from the civilian direction — not hostile, just assessing, the automatic professional evaluation of things that came through the northern approach rather than the military one.

He produced the letter.

The guard read it.

Looked at him.

Read it again.

Ryn waited with the patience of someone for whom this was simply the interval between the previous thing and the next thing. A trade commission weapons consultant arriving for a routine morning meeting was not a thing that required suspicion. It was a thing that required processing. He waited for the processing to complete.

The guard handed the letter to the second guard.

The second guard read it.

They looked at each other with the brief communicative efficiency of two people who shared a context and were checking whether the other person's reading of the situation matched their own.

It matched.

*"Wait here,"* the first guard said.

He waited.

A junior officer appeared. Read the letter. Looked at Ryn. Made the specific face of someone who had decided that escorting this particular visitor to the captain's office was not going to be the most interesting part of his morning and was going to do it anyway because that was what the letter required.

*"This way,"* he said.

Ryn followed him inside.

---

The compound opened around him.

He read it the way he read everything — continuously, automatically, the picture assembling itself from accumulated specific details rather than from any single obvious thing. The training ground to the left, the marks in the dirt telling him about the drills they ran and what those drills were preparing for. The equipment store straight ahead, inventory visible through the open door, the balance of offensive and defensive material communicating a tactical philosophy more accurately than any stated doctrine.

The soldiers he passed looked at him.

He was used to this. He didn't look like what people expected to find in military compounds. He had learned early that this gap between expectation and reality was an asset — approximately thirty seconds of underestimation in every new room, and thirty seconds was usually sufficient.

The junior officer stopped at a door.

Knocked.

From inside — low, direct, the specific register of someone who communicated in the minimum necessary words.

*"Enter."*

The junior officer opened the door.

Ryn walked in.

---

Aldous Vorne was standing.

Not performing standing — just not sitting, the natural state of someone whose morning had already given him something to do before the first visitor arrived. Large in the way that was simply structural — the body built through decades of serious use, nothing decorative about any of it. The greatsword on the rack behind the desk was not decorative either. The desk itself was clean, organized, every item on it with a purpose and in its place.

He looked at Ryn.

The assessment was fast and complete — the practiced evaluation of someone who had spent a career reading threats and was running Ryn through the same process he ran everything through. Not hostile. Thorough.

He read the letter the junior officer handed him.

He looked at Ryn again.

*"You have a proposition for us,"* he said.

*"I'm here to revolutionize your military power,"* Ryn said.

Vorne looked at him for a moment. The specific look of a serious man receiving a large claim and deciding whether the claim warranted the time required to evaluate it. He looked at the bag on Ryn's shoulder. He looked at Ryn's face.

*"What does that mean specifically,"* he said.

*"It means I have ideas,"* Ryn said. *"But I'd rather show you than tell you."* He glanced toward the window — the training court visible through it, open, sufficient. *"Somewhere with more space."*

Vorne looked at him for one more moment.

Then he lifted the greatsword from the rack — not threateningly, just automatically, the specific reflex of a man who didn't go anywhere without it — and walked toward the door.

*"Show me,"* he said.

Ryn picked up the bag.

He followed the captain out.

The training court was the kind of space that told you what the people who built it thought training was for.

Not display — the walls were plain stone, no banners, no insignia beyond what function required. Not ceremony — the targets at the far end were maintained to the standard of things that got used rather than things that got kept. Open air, contained within the compound's walls, the morning light coming in from above at the angle that meant it was still early and the day hadn't fully committed to its business yet.

A few soldiers were present. Not an audience — just people whose morning routines happened here, who looked up when the captain walked in with a civilian and then looked back at what they were doing because the captain's movements were the captain's movements and commenting on them was not something soldiers in this compound did.

Vorne stopped in the middle of the court.

He turned.

He crossed his arms.

He waited with the specific patience of someone who had agreed to see something and was prepared to be unimpressed by it.

Ryn set the bag on the ground.

He opened it.

He produced the crossbow.

---

Vorne looked at it.

*"I've seen a crossbow,"* he said.

*"Not this one,"* Ryn said.

He held it up.

The first thing that registered was the material — no wood anywhere in the primary structure, the stock and the prod and the tiller all metal, the finish treated against weather and wear rather than polished for appearance. Not heavy — lighter than a wooden crossbow of comparable size, the weight distributed differently, centered toward the trigger assembly rather than the front end, which changed how it sat in the hands and how it moved when you raised it.

The second thing was the magazine.

Not a single bolt channel — a housing on the upper side of the tiller that held ten bolts in a staggered arrangement, each one seated in a slot that held it at the precise angle required for the loading mechanism to find it correctly. The bolts themselves shorter than standard, the heads shaped rather than fletched, the specific design of something that didn't need to stabilize the same way a conventional bolt stabilized because it wasn't traveling the same way.

The third thing was the mechanism itself.

He turned it so Vorne could see the side.

Two springs — not one, two, mounted on alternating tracks that ran the length of the tiller. The first spring drove the loading arm that pulled a bolt from the magazine and seated it in the channel. The second spring drove the prod, the stored tension releasing through the bolt on firing. The relationship between them was the key — while the second spring was releasing the first was already resetting, the loading arm already moving to collect the next bolt from the magazine, the two systems operating in sequence so that by the time the prod had fully discharged and begun its own reset the next bolt was already seated and waiting.

Consecutive shots.

Not rapid fire in the way of something that required the shooter to do nothing — the trigger still needed pulling, each shot a conscious action. But the interval between shots was the interval between trigger pulls and nothing else. No cranking. No manual reloading. The mechanism handling everything the mechanism could handle so the human handled only what the human needed to handle.

He raised it.

He fired.

The bolt crossed the court and hit the target at the far end with a force that conventional crossbows at this range didn't produce — the metal prod storing more tension than wood could hold, releasing it through a shorter bolt that lost less energy to drag. Before the sound of the first impact had fully reached the near end of the court he had pulled the trigger again.

Second bolt. Same target. Three inches from the first.

Again.

Third bolt. The target was beginning to show the specific damage of something being hit repeatedly in the same area by something that meant it.

Again. Again.

Five bolts in the time it would have taken a standard crossbow to fire one and begin reloading. The mechanism cycling between each shot with the smooth inevitability of something engineered to cycle — no hitching, no catching, the alternating springs doing their work in the sequence they had been designed to do it.

He lowered it.

The court was quiet.

The soldiers who had been doing their morning routines were no longer doing their morning routines. They were looking at the target. At the crossbow. At the five bolts grouped in a pattern that communicated something about both the weapon's consistency and the man holding it.

Vorne walked to the target.

He looked at the grouping. He looked at the depth of penetration — the bolts seated deeper than standard crossbow bolts at this range, the metal prod's additional tension evident in the specific way they had entered the target material. He looked at the spacing between impacts — each one arriving before the previous one's energy had fully dissipated through the material.

He came back.

*"The price,"* he said. *"And supply."*

*"I'm not selling the crossbow,"* Ryn said.

Vorne looked at him.

*"I'm selling knowledge,"* Ryn said. *"How to build it. How to produce it. After that it's yours. You don't need me."*

Vorne was quiet. He was looking at Ryn with the specific expression of a man who had been in enough transactions to know that offers this clean had things underneath them and was locating the thing.

*"What's the catch,"* he said.

*"No catch,"* Ryn said.

Vorne filed this — the specific way he filed things that were true and unusual simultaneously. A man who hid nothing either had nothing to hide or had something so well hidden it didn't need concealing. He would determine which over time.

---

She came through the door with five students behind her and the court changed.

Not dramatically. Not because she announced herself or demanded attention or did anything that could be described as an entrance in the performed sense. She simply arrived and the the space adjusted to her presence the way spaces adjusted to things that belonged in them completely.

Seris Dahl.

Dark hair. The kind of face that had been beautiful long enough to have stopped thinking about it — mature, composed, the specific ease of someone who had arrived at themselves years ago and had been living there comfortably since. Her attire was the attire of someone who had decided that what she was deserved to be communicated clearly — deep fabric, structured, the specific cut of something that was expensive without apologizing for it and practical without advertising the practicality. She looked like what she was. She didn't look like anything else.

Her students filed in behind her — five of them, each one carrying themselves with the particular confidence of people who had been exceptional long enough to have internalized it. Strong. Genuinely strong, each one capable of things that would end most confrontations before they became confrontations. They moved with the awareness of people who understood what they were and had made their peace with it.

Their teacher could handle fifty of their equivalent before breakfast.

She noticed the soldiers first. Then Vorne's posture — not his usual posture, the specific adjustment of someone whose genuine interest had been engaged rather than their professional attention. She crossed the court toward him.

Vorne told her what was happening. She looked at the crossbow. She looked at the target — the five bolts grouped in the pattern Ryn had put them in, the depth of penetration visible even from where she stood. She looked at Ryn with the specific expression of someone who had taken the measure of a situation completely and was not going to share the measurement.

She had seen impressive things.

She had watched mages collapse fortifications. She had stood in the aftermath of battles where divine energy had been spent like currency by people who had too much of it. She had seen what genuine power looked like when it was applied without restraint.

A better crossbow was a better crossbow.

She turned and walked toward the far end of the court where her students trained.

Her students followed.

---

One of the soldiers had the crossbow now.

He was testing it — the mechanism cycling under his hands, the bolts feeding from the magazine with the smooth consistency that the design produced when executed correctly. He fired five consecutive bolts at a fresh target, the specific surprise of a mechanism that delivered what it promised visible in the way he held it after the fifth shot, the weapon still raised, the trigger pulled and nothing happening because the magazine was empty and his mind hadn't caught up with that yet.

He lowered it.

He looked at it with the expression of someone who didn't have a category for what they were holding.

*"Is this a magic item?"* he said.

One of Seris's students stopped walking.

He turned.

He raised one hand — not dramatically, just the specific gesture of someone for whom this was the appropriate response to the appropriate provocation, requiring no more effort than pointing at something you wanted to indicate. A fireball left his palm and crossed the court and arrived at the target with the complete commitment of something that didn't do partial measures. The target ceased to exist. The area around the target ceased to exist in its previous configuration. The stone wall behind it was scorched in a radius that said everything necessary about the difference between what the crossbow had done and what he had just done.

He looked at the soldier.

*"Do not disrespect magic like that again,"* he said.

A pause that had weight in it.

*"Worm."*

He turned to walk.

The court was completely silent. Vorne said nothing. Seris said nothing. The soldier with the crossbow said nothing because the soldier with the crossbow was looking at what used to be the target and at the scorched radius around what used to be the target and was no longer confident in the question he had asked.

*"Say, worm—"*

Ryn said it lightly. Conversationally. The specific register of someone who was about to make a point and was enjoying the architecture of the setup — not cruel, not performative, just the natural pleasure of someone who had been building toward this moment since the fireball and was arriving at it at exactly the right pace.

He was looking at the soldier with the crossbow.

Everyone in the court understood immediately that he wasn't.

Seris had stopped walking. She hadn't turned around. But her students had — three of them at least, the reflexive attention of people attuned to shifts in their environment.

*"What if I told you,"* Ryn said, *"that you could be as powerful as a mage?"*

The student who had fired the fireball turned around slowly.

The look he gave Ryn was complete and total — the specific condescension of someone who had heard something beneath their consideration and was choosing to engage with it anyway, which was its own kind of contempt, the contempt of someone so certain of the outcome that participation cost them nothing.

The soldier looked at the scorched wall. At the radius of the scorch. At the specific absence where the target had been.

*"How,"* the soldier said. *"How could I compete with that."*

The student's eyes had not moved from Ryn.

*"Exactly,"* he said. *"How could you."*

---

Ryn reached into the bag.

He produced pieces and set them on a nearby table — metal, components, materials that didn't announce themselves as anything in particular, just parts, just things, the specific collection of objects that a man with a bag might carry for reasons not immediately apparent. He looked at the table for one second — the specific second of someone confirming that everything was where it needed to be — and began.

He was fast.

Disconcertingly fast. Not rushing — there was no rushing in it, no urgency, no suggestion that speed was the goal. The speed was simply what happened when someone had done something so many times that the motion required no conscious input, when the hands knew the sequence so completely that the mind was free to be elsewhere while the hands worked. The pieces went together with the specific inevitability of something that had always been going to be this shape — each component finding its position without hesitation, without adjustment, without the small corrections that accompanied unfamiliar assembly.

He turned around.

The court looked at what he was holding.

Nobody spoke.

It had a trigger — recognizable, similar in principle to the crossbow's mechanism, the part that initiated what followed. Beyond that it resisted every category available to the people looking at it. Longer than the crossbow. The barrel extending past what crossbows extended to, the exterior surface showing the precise flat planes of something worked carefully by someone who understood that imprecision here had consequences. The stock shaped for a specific kind of contact with the body — the curve of it not decorative, the geometry calculated, the whole thing carrying the quality of something that had been conceived fully before a single piece of it existed anywhere except in its maker's mind.

The soldiers were looking at it.

The students were looking at it.

Even the student who had fired the fireball was looking at it — with the expression of someone maintaining a position they were no longer entirely confident in.

Vorne looked at it.

He looked at it the way he had looked at the crossbow grouping — methodically, the military mind running it through every relevant scenario, finding the scenarios and finding them different from anything he had run before.

Ryn opened the chamber.

He produced a single round.

Small. Brass cased. The kind of thing you could hold between two fingers without it demanding attention. He held it for a moment — not for effect, just the specific brief pause of someone confirming a final detail before proceeding — and slid it into the chamber.

He closed it.

He walked to the soldier.

He placed the rifle in the soldier's hands. Positioned it — stock tight against the shoulder at the specific contact point that mattered, the grip correct, the barrel oriented toward a fresh target someone had placed at the far end of the court while the assembly was happening. He stepped back. He checked the angle. He adjusted it by a fraction.

He stepped back again.

*"Hold yourself,"* he said. *"This will not be easy."*

A pause.

*"Pull the trigger when you're ready."*

---

The soldier pulled the trigger.

The sound arrived in the training court the way it had arrived in the forest outside Ordenmere — the specific wrong report of something that didn't fit any category of sound the audience had for dangerous things. Not magic, which had a signature these people knew and could place. Not a conventional explosion, which dispersed, which spread, which announced itself in all directions simultaneously. Something else. Something that came from a single point and went in a single direction with the complete commitment of something that had been built to do exactly one thing.

The recoil hit the soldier like a physical argument that didn't wait for a response. He didn't fall — he almost fell, the specific almost of a body absorbing something it hadn't been prepared for and managing it at the final possible moment, one foot going back, the shoulder taking the full force of it, the barrel climbing before his hands remembered to bring it down.

Everyone looked at the target.

The target was standing.

For a fraction of a second this produced confusion — the sound had been enormous, the recoil had nearly put a trained soldier on the ground, and the target was still there, apparently intact, apparently untroubled by what had just happened. Then every eye in the court moved past the target to what was behind it.

The stone wall.

Where it had been smooth there was now a crater.

Not a hole — a crater, the specific geometry of an impact that had arrived with more force than the stone had been built to receive. The material around the impact point had not cracked the way stone cracked under conventional force — it had been displaced, pushed outward from a central point, the mass of it moved rather than broken, the result of something that had passed through the target without being meaningfully slowed and had introduced itself to the wall with everything it had left.

Seris was looking at it.

She had turned around at some point — nobody had seen when, nobody had been watching her when it happened, but she was facing the court now and she was looking at the crater with an expression that was different from every expression she had worn since she walked through the door. Not impressed — assessing, the specific focused attention of someone who had just received information that didn't fit their current model and was updating the model in real time.

The student who had fired the fireball was looking at the crater with an expression he was working very hard to keep arranged the way he wanted it. The effort was visible. It kept trying to become something else.

Vorne looked at the crater for a long time.

He looked at the rifle.

He looked at Ryn.

*"You're not selling this,"* he said. Not a question — the flat certainty of a man who had just watched something happen and understood immediately that the man who made it happen was not going to hand over the method.

*"I'll sell you the knowledge to build this,"* Ryn said. *"Same terms as the crossbow."*

Vorne looked at him.

*"What's the catch,"* he said.

Ryn smiled.

Not the performance smile. The real one.

*"The ammunition,"* he said. *"The weapon you can build. What goes inside it — that stays with me."*

Vorne was quiet. He looked at the crater again. He looked at the round that had produced it — small, unremarkable, the kind of thing you could hold between two fingers. He looked at Ryn.

He had found the catch.

He understood it completely.

He understood that the catch was elegant — not hidden, not deceptive, just the natural architecture of a dependency that didn't need to disguise itself because it was already too late to avoid it. The weapon without the ammunition was an impressive piece of metalwork. The ammunition without Ryn was an impossibility. The combination of both was what had just put a crater in his wall.

*"Name your price,"* he said.

---

Seris crossed the court.

She stopped in front of Ryn. She looked at the rifle in the soldier's hands with the specific attention of someone who had decided they wanted to understand something and was going to understand it.

*"May I,"* she said.

Ryn took the rifle from the soldier and held it out.

She took it. She turned it over — not carelessly, with the careful attention of someone handling something unfamiliar and intelligent enough to know that unfamiliar things warranted care. She examined the exterior. She ran her fingers along it in a specific way — not feeling for craftsmanship, feeling for something else, the specific sensitivity of a mage checking for runic work, for the embedded enchantments that would explain what she had just seen.

She found nothing.

She looked at the rifle again. At the mechanism. At the parts that could move and the parts that couldn't and the relationship between them — she read this correctly, the intelligence of it visible in how quickly her hands found the chamber, how quickly they found the thing that opened it.

The casing dropped.

It hit the stone floor of the training court and rang once — the specific small sound of brass on stone, clean and brief — and lay there.

She picked it up.

She turned it in her fingers. Looked at the end of it — the primer, the specific deformation of the base where the mechanism had struck it. She looked at the inside of the open end — the residue there, the specific evidence of a combustion that had occurred in a space this small and produced what she had watched it produce.

Then she put it to her nose.

The court went very still.

Not because of the gesture itself — because of what the gesture meant on the face of someone like her. Vorne's expression shifted by a fraction. The students looked at each other with the specific look of people who had just seen their teacher do something that didn't fit any category they had for their teacher's behavior.

She lowered the casing.

She looked at Ryn with eyes that had just updated something.

*"Suevite,"* she said. *"I can smell it."* A pause. *"It's not combustible. It's not even flammable."* She turned the casing once more. *"How does it fit in your recipe."*

Ryn made a sound that was almost a laugh — brief, genuine, the specific response of someone who had just been seen more clearly than they expected by someone they hadn't expected to see them clearly.

*"Trade secret,"* he said.

He held out his hand.

She looked at him for a moment — the expression of someone who had asked a question and received an answer that was technically an answer and contained nothing she could use and knew it and was deciding whether to push.

She placed the casing in his palm.

*"Interesting,"* she said.

She walked away.

Her students followed.

---

The negotiation was not long.

Vorne negotiated the way he did everything — directly, without theater, each position stated once and either accepted or countered and moved on from. Twenty gold for the crossbow schematics. One platinum for the rifle. One hundred rounds to start — ten allocated to each of his ten best soldiers, distributed with the specific military intelligence of someone who understood that a new capability in untrained hands was a liability rather than an asset. Thirty silver per round after that.

Ryn accepted without countering.

Vorne looked at him when he did.

*"You're not negotiating,"* he said.

*"The price is fair,"* Ryn said.

Vorne filed this. A man who didn't negotiate when the price was fair was either foolish or had already won. He had determined which.

They shook hands.

---

He walked out of the compound.

The west district's afternoon around him. The bag lighter in some ways and heavier in others — the schematics transferred, the demonstration complete, the rifle disassembled and back in its place. One platinum and twenty gold sitting in the transaction's wake like a fact that had just become permanent.

One hundred rounds.

He had work to do.

He kept walking.

# 12 \- A Day in the Life of a Nun

### **Chapter Twelve — A Day in the Life of a Nun**

---

The sun had not committed to rising yet.

This was the hour the work began — the grey hour, before the light, when the border was still cold and the corruption's edge was just a darker shape against a dark sky. The team had been in position since the body woke them, which was earlier than the schedule required, because the schedule had been the body for long enough now that the two were no longer separable.

Sixteen sisters in a loose line. Eight clerics at their points around the perimeter. The supervising nun walking the line one last time before the work began, confirming with her eyes what she already knew with her experience — that everyone was where they should be, that the morning was as ordinary as mornings out here ever were.

Sera was in her position near the center of the line.

She put her hands toward the ground and let the magic go into it.

The purification did what it always did. The corruption beneath the surface registered it and began to withdraw — the grey-purple veining in the soil retreating, the wrongness receding, the border moving back the way it moved back every morning. Centimeters. The work of an hour producing centimeters.

She had done the math years ago. She did not do it anymore. The border moved back centimeters here while it moved forward meters somewhere underground where their magic couldn't reach. The circle of it. The sisters scratching at the surface of something that moved freely beneath them.

*Is this what you want,* she thought. Not bitter. Just the question she carried, the one she had carried so long it had worn a smooth place in her like a stone carried in a pocket. *Is this your will.*

She kept working.

The morning was quiet.

---

The sister beside her was named Yel.

Sera knew this against the rule. You were not supposed to know the names. The rule existed for reasons the rule did not explain and did not need to — you learned the reasons the first time someone you knew the name of didn't come back. But Yel had said it once, quietly, during a night watch months ago, and the knowing had lodged where knowing lodges and could not be removed.

Yel was beside her and working and then there was a sound.

Not a scream. Nothing so complete as a scream. A sound between impact and tearing, brief, wet, and then the specific heavy sound of weight meeting the ground.

Sera turned.

Half of Yel was on the ground.

The other half was not anywhere. The ground where she had been standing was already closing — soil folding back over itself, the surface resealing as though it had never opened, as though Yel had simply been edited out of the morning between one moment and the next. There was no creature. There was nothing to see. There was only the consequence of something and the something was already gone.

For a moment nobody moved.

*"Form up\!"* The supervising nun's voice, cutting across the silence before the silence could become anything worse. *"Assembly point — now — move\!"*

The protocol took them.

---

The sisters pulled back from the line toward the center. The clerics closed the ring inward, weapons up, attention out — all of it facing the corruption's edge, because the edge was where things came from, the edge was always where things came from.

Sera moved with the others into the cluster.

She could see Yel from here. She made herself stop seeing Yel.

*"What was it?"* one of the sisters whispered. Young. Newer than most. Her voice doing the thing voices did when they were trying to stay quiet and trying not to break and failing at the second thing. *"Did anyone see — did anyone see what—"*

*"Quiet,"* the supervising nun said. *"Hold the formation."*

*"But what was it—"*

*"Hold. The. Formation."*

They held it. The sisters in the center. The clerics in the ring. The formation completing itself exactly the way it had been drilled, exactly the way it was supposed to, everyone facing the threat that was supposed to come from outside.

Sera looked at the ground beneath her feet.

She did not yet understand that the ground beneath her feet was the worst place to be standing.

---

It came from below the center.

No warning — no tremor, no vibration, nothing the clerics' training had taught them to feel for, because the thing slid through earth the way a knife slides through water and a knife in water makes no warning either. The mouth erupted upward through the middle of the cluster, rows of teeth that were not for eating spinning around a darkness that led nowhere, the whole diameter of it filling the space between bodies before any body could move.

Two sisters were simply gone.

A third looked down at where her arm had been. The creature's flank had passed through it, and the acid that slicked its skin had done the rest, and now there was a stump and an expression that had not yet become a scream. She sat down. She sat down very carefully, like someone lowering themselves into cold water.

The acid spray caught two more. One across the body — she folded around it, both hands coming up. One across the face. That one made no sound at all. She stood completely still with her hands halfway raised, not quite touching her own face, as if touching it would confirm something she was not ready to confirm.

The third cleric thrust both hands toward the diving creature and the earth answered him — the soil around the thing's sinking body clenching, trying to close on it, trying to hold it in a fist of packed ground.

It slid through the fist like the fist wasn't there.

The acid on its skin was not only a weapon. It was a lubricant, and the earth that was supposed to crush it instead slicked and parted around it, and the creature was gone through the closing soil without slowing, back underground through a different hole, a body-length from where it had surfaced.

It had not turned around.

Sera stared at the two holes — the one it came out of, the one it went into, a body-length apart — and the understanding arrived in the cluster like cold water finding a crack. It did not reverse. It did not poke up and pull back like the burrowing things they knew. It came forward, always forward, surfacing where it wanted and diving somewhere new.

*"It doesn't turn,"* one of the clerics said. His voice low and fast. *"It came up and it kept going — it doesn't turn around—"*

The fourth cleric used lightning.

It was the right magic. It was the wrong moment. The cluster was too tight and the creature was already sliding back into the earth and the bolt caught only a glancing edge of its flank — a flash, a crack, the body barely registering it — before the lightning found the rest of the space the formation occupied.

The sister standing beside Sera dropped.

There was no transition. She was upright and then she was on the ground and there was nothing left in her to heal, the lightning having passed through her on its way to a creature that was no longer there to receive it.

Sera looked at her.

She looked at the cleric who had fired.

He was looking at the fallen sister with the face of a man standing in the gap between what he meant and what he did, a gap that could not be closed, a gap he was going to be standing in for the rest of his life. His mouth moved. Nothing came out of it.

*"I didn't—"* he managed. *"She was — I didn't see her, she was behind the—"*

*"Spread out\!"* a different cleric shouted — the fifth, at the back of the formation, his voice rising over the rest. *"It's hunting the cluster — spread, get distance, SPREAD—"*

He moved first.

He stepped out of the formation to show them, to make the order real with his body, one stride into open ground —

— and the earth opened under that stride and took him, mouth-first, forward, gone, the order still unfinished in the air above the hole where he had been.

Nobody moved.

The man who had told them to move was gone for moving and the rest of them stood frozen in the exact cluster he had died trying to break, and the silence that followed had a specific texture, the texture of people who have just learned that the instruction and the death were the same instruction.

The sixth cleric threw fire at the creature's tail as it sank.

Not a plan. A reflex. The flame caught the last exposed segment and the acid-slicked skin reacted to the heat in a way it had not reacted to anything else, and the thing's pace beneath the surface stuttered — just slightly, just enough — and bought them the three seconds the dead man's order had been trying to buy.

*"Go,"* the supervising nun said. *"Spread. Now. He was right. GO."*

They spread.

---

The fourth cleric did not spread.

He ran.

There was no announcement and no shame in his face, which was the worst part — just the closed, private calculation of a man who had decided the field was lost and that he was not going to be lost with it. He turned from his position and ran for the green, low and fast, away from the sisters and the wounded and the thing in the ground.

The seventh cleric went up.

He was a wind mage; he could fly; and he flew. He rose off the field, fast, climbing.

*"Help us,"* the burned-body sister called up to him, her voice cracking around the pain. *"Please — come back — we need—"*

He did not come back.

He did not slow, did not circle, did not look down long enough for any of them to find his eyes. He climbed and he turned toward the walls and he went, smaller and smaller against the brightening sky, until he was nothing the field had to account for anymore.

*"He's leaving,"* a sister said, and the disbelief in it was almost worse than fear. *"He's — he's just leaving—"*

*"Forget him,"* the supervising nun said. *"Hold still. All of you. Hold still."*

The fourth cleric, running along the ground, was the one the earth chose.

It came up through him without slowing.

The field was smaller now. Fewer clerics. Fewer sisters. The arm-cut one sitting in the dirt with her remaining hand clamped over the stump. The burned-face one standing very still. Everyone who was left had finally, completely, stopped clustering.

---

The first and third clerics had their hands on the ground.

Earth mages, both of them — but they were not attacking now, not squeezing the soil the way the third had tried and failed to do early on. They were listening. Palms flat, magic pushed down into the earth not to change it but to feel it, to read the subtle shifts that the creature's passage made in the soil even when nothing showed on the surface.

*"It's moving,"* the first one said quietly. *"East side. Slow. It's — wait—"*

The burned-body sister flinched. The acid had reached something, and her body moved before her mind could hold it still, a small involuntary shift of weight from one foot to the other.

*"Move—"* the third cleric started. *"Get away—"*

The earth opened beneath her.

Between the cleric sensing it and the cleric saying it and her hearing it and her body trying to obey — in that gap, that handful of moments, the thing had already come and gone and she was not there anymore.

The supervising nun's voice came flat and terrible into the quiet that followed.

*"It only finds us when we move,"* she said. *"Do you understand? It feels us move. Hold still. Everyone — hold still. Do not move."*

The field went rigid.

The sisters froze where they stood. The clerics froze at their points. The whole shattered remnant of the team became a tableau of people not moving, each of them holding their position the way you held your breath, and the burned-face sister held still too, even as the acid kept working at her, even as it cost her something to stay where she was, because the alternative cost more.

Sera held still.

She was looking at the arm-cut sister on the ground.

---

The arm-cut sister was trying to heal herself.

Her good hand was pressed to the stump and the magic was going into it — the basic field-healing every sister learned, the kind Sera had performed a thousand times — but the bleeding was faster than the magic and the magic was not enough and her face had gone the color of the grey soil beneath her. She was not moving otherwise. She understood the rule too. She was sitting as still as a person could sit and pouring everything she had into a wound that was taking it faster than she could give.

It was not going to be enough.

Sera could see it was not going to be enough. She knew the look of a wound winning. She had her own mana, more than the dying sister had, hands that knew the work better — she could close it, or close enough of it, she could buy the time the replacement crew needed, she could—

She started to move.

She stopped.

*It only finds us when we move.*

If she crossed that ground the creature would feel two of them where there had been one. The dying sister's chances would not improve. Sera's would collapse. The arithmetic was clean and it was monstrous and it was correct, and Sera stood inside it, frozen, with her hands that could help held against her own body, looking at a person dying within twenty steps of her and not taking a single one of them.

The sister's good hand slipped off the stump.

She listed sideways. She did not catch herself. She came to rest on the red-grey ground and her chest moved and moved again and the movement was the small flag of a body still running on what was left in it.

Everyone knew the thing was coming for her.

Everyone knew there was nothing to be done.

And Sera, holding still, holding her own useless hands against herself, looked at the dying woman and the frozen survivors, and the question came up out of her that she had never let all the way up before.

Not *is this your will.* She had asked that for months and the asking had a floor under it, the floor of an institution that could be wrong while the goddess stayed whole.

This question had no floor.

*Where are you,* she thought. *They are dying in your name and they are dying for nothing and the border is in the same place it was a year ago and these women are coming apart in the dirt and where — where are you. Are you watching this. Are you anywhere. Where is she.*

---

*"When,"* the first cleric said.

His hands were flat on the ground. The third's were too. They had stopped listening for where the creature was and started listening for where it was going, and where it was going was the fallen sister, and they had stopped trying to prevent it because it could not be prevented, and they had started counting.

The sixth cleric had fire ready. The eighth had ice. The second had his hands open and waiting.

*"When,"* the first cleric said again. *"On me. It's coming up under her — it's — get ready —"*

*"WHEN,"* the third cleric shouted.

The earth erupted.

The fallen sister was gone in the first instant, taken on the upward drive — and then the head was out and rising, the forward length of the body following it up out of the ground.

The ice came first.

The eighth cleric drove sickles of it deep into the exposed sections, hard, the structural shock punching wounds into a thing that had spent the morning untouchable. The creature convulsed — the drilling head jerking, recoiling from the pain, stopping short of the new hole it had started to bore. It hung there, half its length out of the ground, caught between diving into ground that would drive the ice deeper and holding on the surface.

The sixth cleric opened a stream of fire.

Not a burst — a torrent, sustained, concentrated, pouring over the thing's exposed length and finding the wound channels the ice had opened and going into them. The acid-slicked skin had no answer for it. The creature spasmed, and the spasm drove the rest of it up out of the earth — the whole body convulsing forward and clear, tail and all, fully on the surface now because the fire had cooked the will to dig out of it, because a thing that only moves forward had nowhere left to go.

A high thin sound came out of the spinning teeth. Almost nothing. A kettle-whistle of agony from a mouth that had never been built to scream. It writhed on the open ground, burning, every length of it exposed, and it could not go forward and it could not go back.

The second cleric raised both hands. Spears of light emerged from his palms — a dozen of them, bright and concentrated, and he drove them all at once into the pinned and burning length of the World Feeder. 

It came apart.

And then it was just a thing on the ground, in pieces, smoking, and the field was quiet, and the quiet went on and on.

---

Sera was still standing where she had stopped herself.

Her hands were still against her body. She had not moved them. She had not moved at all. Around her the survivors were beginning to come back to themselves — a sister down on her knees, both hands over her mouth, the specific sounds of someone crying through their fingers; another standing rigid and shaking; the cleric who had fired the lightning sitting in the dirt staring at nothing.

*"It's down,"* someone said. *"It's down. It's — is it down? Is it—"*

*"It's down."*

The kneeling sister had both hands pressed together now, not over her mouth but in front of it, her whole body rocking, the words pouring out of her fast and low and broken.

*"Profaned Goddess, keep them — keep them in your light, keep them, take them up into the fire and keep them—"* Her voice climbed and cracked. *"Yel — where's Yel — Goddess, keep Yel, keep her, please, please keep her—"*

She could not finish. The prayer came apart in her throat and what was left of it folded her down to the ground.

Sera looked at her.

She looked at the hands pressed together, at the face turned up toward a sky that held nothing but a coward shrinking into the distance and the first real light of the morning. She looked at a woman praying with her whole shattered heart to the Goddess whose name was on all their banners.

*Where is she,* Sera thought.

And she had no answer, and the praying sister had no answer, and the sky gave them nothing, and the corruption was already creeping back across the ground they had bled to clear.

Sera looked at the field.

She looked at what the field held now. The pieces of the smoking creature. The pieces of the sisters whose names she had not been permitted to learn, scattered across ground that did not care whose they had been. 

She started walking.

Not toward the wounded. Not toward the sisters who needed her hands. She walked toward the place where the arm-cut sister had fallen, the place the creature had come up through last, and she crouched down at the edge of it.

The ground there was the rotten grey-purple she had been purifying her whole life.

Today it had a red in it.

She put her hands toward the soil and let the magic go, the same way she had let it go a thousand mornings, the same outward push that made the corruption recede. And the corruption receded — the grey-purple drew back, dissipated, surrendered to the purification the way it always did, retreating off the ground in a slow clean tide.

The red stayed.

She kept her hands down. She kept the magic flowing. The grey-purple kept withdrawing and the red kept not withdrawing, sitting exactly where it had soaked into the earth, untouched by everything her magic could do, and she looked at it with a mind that had gone past thinking and arrived somewhere blank and white and quiet.

She purified the rot.

She could not purify what they had spent to hold it back one more morning.

She kept going anyway. There was nothing else her hands knew how to do.

A hand came down on her shoulder.

She did not look up. The supervising nun's hand — she knew it from the weight of it, from the steadiness, from the fact that it did not shake when so much else was shaking. The hand of someone who had stood in a field like this before and knew that the field was not where you were allowed to come apart.

*"It's time to return,"* the supervising nun said.

Not gently. Not unkindly. Just true.

Sera took her hands off the ground.

She stood. She did not look at the red. She turned her back on it and on the smoking pieces and on the names she had not been allowed to keep, and she followed the supervising nun back toward the walls, where the kingdom was waking, where the people were already saying to one another how brave the sisters were, how the city slept safe because of what they did out there in the rot.

Behind her the corruption was already returning to the ground she had cleared.

She did not look back to watch it come.

The gate opened and the people were already there.

Not a crowd — Ordenmere didn't crowd for this anymore, it had seen the border caravans come back too many times to crowd. Just the ones who had been near the western gate when the signal came through, drawn the way people were drawn to the return of something they'd decided was sacred. Market workers with their hands stilled mid-task. An old man with his head bowed. A scatter of soldiers from the compound who had no business at this end of the district and had come anyway, standing with the specific stiffness of men who fought their own battles and didn't know what to do with people who fought this one.

And the children.

They came the way children came to things — fast, from everywhere, threading between adult legs to reach the front. They fell into step alongside the sisters as the caravan passed through the gate, matching the broken pace, looking up.

Sera walked through the middle of it.

A girl of seven or eight walked beside her for a stretch, looking up with her whole face open, and reached out and touched the hem of Sera's habit — not pulling, just touching, the way you touched a thing you weren't sure you were allowed to touch. Then she dropped back, satisfied, and ran to tell another child what she'd done.

*Be like them,* the children's faces said. The little girls looking at the sisters, the boys looking at the clerics. *I want to be like that.*

Sera had touched a sister's habit once. She had been six. There had been a procession through the capital and a woman in white had passed close enough to touch and Sera had reached out and made contact with what she wanted to become, and a year later the church had taken her in, and she had spent eighteen years becoming it.

She looked at the girl running back into the crowd.

She felt like she was wearing a dead woman's clothes.

The thought was precise and it didn't leave. In three days they'd be sent out again. The bodies in the carriage behind her would go into the ground without a name said over them, and these people — the ones bowing their heads, the children touching her hem — would have forgotten by the next market day, because forgetting was how the city survived what the city asked of the border. Nobody here would mourn the women under the covers. Nobody here knew their names.

*Neither do I,* she thought. *That's the rule. That's the whole rule.*

*To what end.*

She kept walking.

---

The monastery took them in the way it always did.

Eight years she'd been in this building. She knew it under her feet — the worn place on the third corridor stone, the door that stuck in damp weather, the particular grey of the afternoon light coming through the high windows of the dormitory. The sisters scattered without being told to. They had done this before. Everyone came back from the border and went to ground in their own corner, and you learned not to reach toward anyone, because the rule about names was really a rule about this: about not having too much to lose the next time the ground opened.

One sister sat on the edge of her bed and did not move. She'd sat down when they came in and she would still be there when someone came to check on her. She wasn't grieving yet. She was waiting to find out if the part of her that could grieve had survived the morning.

Another made her bed with perfect, mechanical care, smoothing a blanket that was already smooth, her hands completely steady and her eyes a thousand miles past the wall.

The one with the ruined face lay with her back to the room. The healers had taken her pain in the field. They had not been able to take anything else.

Maret stood at the front of the dormitory. She was the team's supervising nun — the one who had given the order to spread in the field, the one who had grabbed Sera's shoulder at the red ground — and she looked older than she had this morning, which was strange, because this morning had only been a few hours. 

*"Rest,"* she said. *"Chores can wait till the afternoon."*

She said it the way she'd said everything in the field — flat, level, an order given because an order was the only thing she had left to give. Then she turned and went to do the things the person in charge had to do when the person who'd been in charge was in the carriage.

---

The new one spoke into the quiet.

She was sixteen, maybe. New enough that she still adjusted her habit when she thought no one was looking, still wore it like a costume she was afraid to dishonor. She'd been counting the empty beds. Sera had watched her do it — the same count Sera used to do, before she'd taught herself to stop.

*"What happens to them?"* the girl said. *"The sisters who — will there be a funeral?"*

The room went still.

The sister making her bed stopped. The one on the edge of her bed did not move. No one looked at the girl. No one looked at anyone. It was the particular silence of a room full of people who all knew the answer and had each privately decided it was not theirs to be the one to say.

Maret stopped at the door.

She looked at the new girl for a moment — not unkindly. There was no cruelty in her anywhere, that was the thing about Maret, she had simply been worn down to the smooth hard surface that this work left when it didn't kill you. She was deciding, Sera could see it, how much of the truth a sixteen-year-old could be handed today.

*"Get some rest,"* Maret said.

And went out.

The girl looked around the room. At the faces turned away. At the empty beds. At the silence that had answered her more completely than any words could have. She sat down on the edge of her own bed, slowly, and she didn't ask again.

She had her answer. She just hadn't translated it yet.

---

Sera lay on her back and looked at the ceiling.

The water stain in the corner she'd meant to report for three years. The crack from the window frame. The light going long and grey across all of it. From the next bed came the sound of the sister there crying — small, swallowed, turned toward the wall, the careful crying of someone who'd accepted that privacy wasn't available and was trying to take up as little of the shared air with it as she could.

Sera counted the empty beds without deciding to.

She already had the number. She'd had it since the field. It hadn't changed.

She sat up. She looked at the grid of beds, the women folded into their separate griefs, the ruined face turned to the wall. The dormitory held it all and gave none of it anywhere to go.

She stood up and walked out.

---

She didn't have a destination. She walked the way she'd purified the ground that morning — not toward anything, just because her body needed to be doing something and walking was what was available.

The western district went on around her, indifferent and ordinary. Market noise from the north end. Two men arguing pleasantly about a price. A dog asleep in a doorway. The afternoon doing what afternoons did, the whole district absorbing the morning without a ripple, the way cities always absorbed what happened in them. She had never made her peace with that. The completeness of it. The way you could not tell, from the surface of a city, what it had swallowed.

*"Wait up."*

She stopped.

The new girl was a dozen steps behind her, hurrying to close the gap, one hand holding her habit against her side. Sera hadn't heard her. Or had heard her and filed the footsteps under the noise of the street and not turned.

The girl reached her and fell into step like it was the most natural thing in the world.

*"I'm Lise,"* she said.

Just like that. Her name, handed over plainly, the way you handed your name to someone you wanted to know.

*"You're not supposed to tell me that,"* Sera said.

*"I know."* The girl walked a few steps. *"When's the last time you said yours? Out loud?"*
