Sera opened her mouth to answer and found nothing there. She reached for it — the last time, the occasion, a face, a voice that had said it back — and her hand closed on empty space. There had been roll calls, years ago, in the capital. There had been a Mother Superior who'd used it once, sharply, when Sera was nineteen. After that the title had eaten the name. Sister. Sister. Sister. You stopped being a name and became a function, and the function was easier to send to the border than a name would have been.

*"Do you even remember?"* Lise said.

Sera walked a few more steps.

*"Sera,"* she said.

It came out strange. Not wrong — strange, the way a word you'd learned before you'd learned language came out strange, surfacing intact from somewhere below memory when something finally reached down for it. She heard herself say it and it sounded like a name belonging to someone she used to know.

Lise smiled, just a little.

Then her face folded back toward the thing that was actually sitting on it.

*"The sisters who died,"* she said. *"You didn't say. What really happens."*

Sera looked at the street ahead.

*"They'll be buried,"* she said. *"No ceremony."*

*"None?"*

*"None."*

*"But their families—"*

*"There are no families."* She said it the way Maret said things. Flat. Without anywhere for it to land softly. *"We're orphans. All of us. Children the church took in when there was no one else. There's no one to send word to. No one waiting anywhere."* She watched the dog asleep in the doorway. *"That's part of why they choose us. No one ever asks where we went."*

Lise was quiet for a while, she didn't know they were the same.

The market sounds went on up the street. Two women laughed about something. The world stayed exactly as full of itself as it had been before the carriage came through the gate.

*"It must be beautiful,"* Lise said. *"To die doing Providence's will."*

She said it quietly. She meant it. Every single word of it, the whole way down — the specific clean sincerity of someone who'd been told a thing her entire life by people who believed it, and who hadn't yet stood in a field and watched the thing get tested.

Sera looked at her.

At sixteen and the costume she was still afraid to dishonor. At the open conviction in her face. She had been this exact girl. They'd given her the habit in the capital and told her she would change the world, and she had believed it with her whole body, the way you could only believe something when you were young and someone who loved you had told it to you and there was no evidence yet against it. Eight years of evidence. Eight years of watching her own work wiped clean overnight, of the border sitting in the same place it had sat when she arrived, of corrupted things growing a new joint or a longer tooth between one season and the next while the church sent women with mops to push back an ocean. The worm this morning would not be the last thing. It would not even be the worst. The corruption was learning faster than they were dying, and they were dying quite fast.

She had so much she could say.

She could feel all of it, pressed up against the inside of her chest, looking for the door.

And she said none of it, because saying it meant reaching into this girl and taking out the thing that was keeping her upright, and the border was going to take it anyway, in three days or three months or three years, and Sera could not work out, standing here in the afternoon light, whether doing it now would be mercy or just the first cruelty of many.

*"I want to go back,"* she said.

She turned around.

Lise followed.

---

They came in through the courtyard gate.

Maret was there. Four clerics. They were doing something near the colonnade, and their movements had the specific unhurried economy of people who had done this exact thing before and knew every step of it — which was, Sera understood a half-second later, the worst part. That it had its own procedure. That the institution had worn a groove for this too.

She looked up.

She looked for about one second, and then she made herself stop looking.

Maret saw them. Saw Lise.

*"Inside,"* she said. Not loud. Not unkind. The flat command of a woman removing a child from a room the child should not be standing in. *"There's nothing to see here. Go on. Inside."*

Lise didn't move.

She was looking up.

Sera knew, watching her, the exact moment it landed — because Lise had known the name. She said it the way you said a name you actually knew rather than a face you were identifying. *Wenna.* Just that. Which meant they had spoken before the deployment, before the border, in the specific window when Lise was still new enough to ask people their names without thinking twice about the rule. A name offered and a name given back, and now Lise stood in the courtyard looking at the space between that morning and this afternoon, at what the healers had not been able to give back, at a face that had been a young woman's face yesterday and could not be looked at in a mirror today — and her own words from the street were still in the air around her, *it must be beautiful, it must be beautiful,* and the distance between the words and the thing above the colonnade was not a distance a sixteen-year-old could cross standing up.

*"Wenna,"* she said. Very quietly. Her mouth moving before the rest of her could stop it.

Then nothing.

She went inside.

She went the way people went when something had just rearranged the furniture of everything they believed and they hadn't yet found the new shape of the room — slowly, carefully, holding very still inside herself, the way you held still when the ground had taught you that moving was how it found you.

Sera watched her go.

Then she turned and walked back out through the gate.

---

She went around the side of the monastery, where the building's wall ran close to the next and made a narrow alley the afternoon light didn't quite reach. The city's noise arrived there muffled, secondhand, like something happening to other people. It was empty. She was, for the first time since before dawn, completely alone.

She stopped.

And the thing she had been holding at arm's length all day — through the field, through the gate, through the children's faces and the empty beds and the girl saying *it must be beautiful* — the arm simply gave out.

It didn't come the way crying came to people who cried. It came wrong. Halting, graceless, the rusted motion of a mechanism that had been still so long it had forgotten how to run. Her face did something she hadn't asked it to do and couldn't remember asking it to do in years. She didn't know where to put her hands. She pressed the back of one against her mouth and it didn't help and she pressed it harder and that didn't help either. There were no sounds at first, just the body trying to remember the shape of this and getting it wrong, and then the sounds came, small and broken and unpracticed, and she stood in the grey of the alley with her shoulders shaking and wept like someone using a language she'd forgotten she knew.

She was on her knees before she knew she'd gone down.

The ground of the alley was cold and she didn't feel it. Her hands came together the way they had come together every morning since she was six years old in the orphanage chapel, the sisters moving between the rows of children telling them to press their hands and close their eyes and reach, and Sera had reached, and she had kept reaching for eighteen years, and the reaching had always felt like it was going somewhere.

She reached now.

*"Providence."*

Out loud. In the alley. In the voice she had left at the bottom of herself after everything above it had been used up.

*"Providence, I'm here. I'm here, I'm — I've always been here. I was six years old and they put your name in my mouth and I kept it there, I kept it — I have kept it for eighteen years and I have never — I have never put it down, I have never—"*

Her voice broke.

She pressed her hands harder together. The knuckles whitened. She was shaking and she hadn't known she was shaking until now, the tremor running through her arms, through her hands, through the clasped fingers.

*"I watched them die today. I watched them die saying your name. The girl this morning, she said — she said it must be beautiful, she said it must be beautiful to die in your name, she believed it, she believed it completely, she was sixteen and she believed it the way I believed it and I need—"*

She stopped.

She pulled air in.

*"Please,"* she said. *"I'm not asking for much. I'm not asking you to come here, I'm not asking for a sign, I'm just — I just need to know that you're there. That you're somewhere. That you heard them. That the women in that carriage weren't just — that they weren't just numbers, that they mattered, that someone received them, that someone—"*

The alley was quiet.

Around the corner the western district went on being the western district. A cart went over a stone. Two voices rose and fell in laughter. The afternoon continued its slow passage across the sky above the narrow strip of alley she could see.

She waited.

She had waited her whole life. She knew how to wait.

She waited.

Providence did not come.

Not absence. Not the feeling of a door that had been closed against her. Just the alley. Just the cold ground through her habit and her own breath and the sounds of the city and the strip of ordinary grey sky.

She had been reaching her whole life and the reaching had never — not once — been completed from the other direction. She understood now that this was true. She had always suspected it. She had filed the suspicion under *insufficient faith, pray more, trust the institution.* And she had prayed more and she had trusted the institution and eight years at the border had produced the carriage and the empty beds and Lise's face in the courtyard and the red ground that her magic couldn't touch.

The answer wasn't in here.

The answer had never been in here.

If Providence's true will existed — if it was a real thing and not the institution's invention and not the hierarchy's tool — it was somewhere the institution had never shown her. Something older than the doctrine. Something that predated the church's politics and the hierarchy's comfort and the scheduled deployment that would send Lise to the border in three days.

She didn't know where that was.

She got up.

Her knees ached. She pressed her back against the monastery wall and looked at the sky until she was finished looking at it. Then she walked to the end of the alley and stood at its mouth and looked at the western district spread out in front of her — ordinary, indifferent, alive — and she did not go back through the monastery gate.

She walked into the street.

She was barely a street from the monastery gate when she heard footsteps behind her.

Not running. Just walking at the pace of someone who had decided to close a distance without making a production of it. Sera didn't stop. She kept moving and the footsteps kept moving and eventually Maret came alongside her and walked there and said nothing for a stretch.

The western district went on around them. The market noise from the north. A child shouting something to another child across a rooftop. The ordinary afternoon doing what it did.

Maret looked at her.

Sera felt the look and didn't return it.

*"You don't have to come after me,"* she said.

*"I know,"* Maret said.

They walked.

*"I've seen sisters leave before,"* Maret said after a while. Not accusatory. Not framing it as a category Sera now belonged to. Just a statement. *"I can usually tell from the face."*

*"And?"*

*"Your face isn't that."*

Sera looked at the street ahead.

*"What is it then,"* she said.

Maret was quiet for a moment.

*"Mine,"* she said. *"thirty years ago."*

---

They turned without deciding to, following the street as it curved westward along the district's edge, away from the market noise, toward the quieter end where the buildings sat lower and the afternoon had more room. Neither of them suggested it. They just went the way the street went.

*"I want answers,"* Sera said.

She said it the way she'd said her name in the alley — plainly, without performance, the word arriving in the air before she'd fully decided to put it there.

*"Not reassurance. Not the doctrine again. Not someone telling me that faith is supposed to be enough when the faith is — when it's the faith that's asking the question."* She stopped, started again. *"I have been in the church my whole life. Since I was six years old. I have given it everything it asked for and I have done everything it pointed me toward and I am standing here having done all of that and I don't know — I genuinely do not know — what any of it was for. What she actually wants. What the border is actually building toward. Whether the women in that carriage this morning died for something real or whether they died for the institution's version of something real, which is not the same thing."*

She stopped walking.

*"I cannot find the answer in there,"* she said. She meant the monastery. She meant the church. She meant eighteen years of reaching in a direction that had never completed itself. *"I have looked. I have looked in every place they showed me how to look and the answer isn't there. Maybe it was never there. Maybe the people who were supposed to keep it there lost it generations ago and nobody noticed because the institution kept running without it."*

Maret didn't say anything immediately.

She looked at the street. At the low buildings. At the strip of sky above them going orange at the far edge where the sun was beginning to think about descending.

*"You're not wrong,"* she said.

Sera looked at her.

*"About any of it,"* Maret said. *"The institution runs. That's what institutions do. They run on their own momentum long after whatever started them has — changed, or been forgotten, or become something else entirely. The women who know what's inside the doctrine and the women who run the doctrine stopped being the same women a long time ago."* She paused. *"I'm not telling you the answer is in there. I don't think it is."*

*"Then where is it,"* Sera said.

---

Maret walked a few more steps.

*"I thought about looking once,"* she said. *"Not in the church. Not in the doctrine or the chapel or the hierarchy."* She looked at her own hands. *"I thought about looking in the thing we work against. The corruption."*

Sera said nothing.

*"I thought — if I understood it. Actually understood it, not the doctrine's version of it, not this is the enemy, this is what we oppose — but what it actually was. What it wanted. What logic produced it."* She turned her palms over, looked at the backs of her hands. *"I thought that if I understood the opposition clearly enough I would understand what we were opposing it for. That the thing working against us would illuminate the thing we were working toward. The way — the way you understand a lock better by studying the key."*

*"Did you,"* Sera said. *"Look."*

*"No,"* Maret said.

*"Why."*

A long pause. Long enough that a cart went past them on the street and the sound of it came and went before Maret answered.

*"I told myself it was practical reasons,"* she said. *"The border was dangerous enough without going looking for more of it. I had sisters depending on me. The timing was never right."* She was quiet. *"None of that was true."*

*"Then what was."*

Maret stopped walking.

Sera stopped too.

They stood on the street in the cooling afternoon and Maret looked at some point in the middle distance the way people looked at things they'd been carrying for a long time and had never quite set down.

*"I was afraid,"* she said. *"Not of what was out there. I've been at the border long enough to have run out of that particular fear."* She paused. *"I was afraid of the answer. That I would look and I would find it and I would not — like it. That it would require something from me that I didn't have left to give. Or that it would show me something about what we'd been doing — about all of it — that I couldn't put back once I'd seen it."*

She looked at Sera.

*"My faith fills that emptiness,"* she said. *"It's not a good answer. But it's what I have. I chose it and I've kept choosing it and I'll probably keep choosing it until the border takes me or I'm too old to go out anymore."* A pause. *"Yours doesn't. Fill it. That's not because your faith is weaker than mine. It's because of how your faith works. It doesn't let you leave questions unanswered. It never has. It keeps pulling at the thread."*

She said it without judgment. As a plain observation. The way you described the weather — not approving or disapproving of it, just noting what it was doing.

*"You were always going to end up here,"* Maret said. *"The only question was when."*

---

Sera looked at her.

At the face that had been Maret's face for whatever years the border had given it — the specific worn surface of someone who had made her choices and lived inside them and had stopped pretending the choices didn't have a cost.

*"I don't know where to look,"* Sera said.

Maret was quiet for a moment.

*"When I first came to this posting, you couldn't see the corruption's edge from the walls on a clear day. Not even a hint of it on the horizon, the border was more than three weeks' hard travel from the western gate."* 

Sera looked at her.

*"three weeks,"* Maret said. *"You could travel for three weeks due west from where we stood this morning and still be in uncorrupted land. Fields. Villages. People who had never seen the edge of it."* She looked at the street. *"That was when I arrived. I've been here forty years."*

The number sat between them.

*"It will reach the walls,"* Maret said. *"in my lifetime probably. Definitely in yours. it will reach them. And when it does I will most likely still be going out every morning to push it back a little, because that's what there is to do and I've run out of the kind of thinking that asks whether the doing is enough."*

She said it without bitterness. Without self-pity. The specific flat delivery of someone who had looked at an impossible thing for long enough that impossible had stopped being a useful category.

*"You're asking the wrong person,"* she said. *"I never looked. I can't tell you where to look when I spent thirty years choosing not to."*

She paused.

*"But I will say this."* She looked westward, toward the military end of the district. *"There are people in this city who have spent their lives studying what we work against. Not to purify it. Not to push it back. To understand it. The way a surgeon understood disease — not to become it, to know it well enough to do something about it."* She let that sit. *"Different questions than ours. Different methods. I never thought much of the difference. Now I think the difference might be the point."*

She didn't say a name. She didn't point. She just let the direction exist in the air between them and let Sera decide what to do with it.

Then —

*"Where are you going to sleep tonight?"*

The question arrived simply. Practically. The specific practicality of someone who had managed people in crisis long enough to know that the next immediate thing mattered as much as the large impossible thing.

Sera looked at her.

*"I don't know,"* she said.

*"You can't go back in tonight." It wasn't rhetorical but it was a question she knew the answer to.*

*"No."*

Maret reached into the fold of her habit. She produced a small purse — not large, not heavy, the specific weight of someone giving what they could spare rather than what they had. She held it out.

Sera looked at it.

*"It's not charity,"* Maret said. *"You've earned three times this at the border and the church keeps the accounting. Consider it an outstanding debt."*

*Sera took it.*

She hesitated first.

Not long — just the specific beat of someone whose hands had been trained out of receiving things. Twenty-two years of the church's logic: you gave, you served, you went out and came back and went out again, and the transaction only ran one direction. A purse held out toward her was a category her hands didn't immediately know how to respond to.

Then she took it.

It sat in her palm — small, heavier than it looked, the specific weight of someone giving what they could spare and not making a performance of the sparing.

*"The habit is yours,"* Maret said. *"Whatever else happens — the habit is yours. You earned it."*

She looked at Sera one last time. The same face. Her own face from thirty years ago standing at the same edge and choosing differently.

She turned and walked back toward the monastery.

Sera watched her until she turned the corner and was gone.

---

Got it — back to Chapter 12, that closing passage.

Sera standing alone on the street processing what Maret said. Two specific things running through her mind:

**The corruption holding answers** — Maret said she thought about looking for Providence's truth in the thing that opposed Providence's work. That if she understood the opposition clearly enough she would understand what they were opposing it for. Sera turns this over. It's a different way of seeing the corruption entirely — not as the enemy to be pushed back but as a text to be read. Something that has logic, that has direction, that has been doing what it does for longer than the church has been opposing it. If the church's answers are hollow maybe the corruption's existence points toward something real. Not by joining it. By understanding it.

**Who Maret meant when she looked westward** — Sera retraces the moment. Maret didn't name anyone. She just looked in a direction and said *there are people in this city who spend their lives studying what we work against.* The western compound. The military installation. People who approach the corruption not with purification magic but with offensive capability — who have spent years learning what it produced and how it moved and what it responded to. A mage perhaps. Someone whose entire career was built on understanding the enemy rather than simply opposing it.

Sera doesn't know Seris's name yet. She just knows the direction.

---

Here's the revised closing passage:

---

She stood on the street alone.

The city went on around her. The market noise, the voices, the cart sounds, the dog she'd passed earlier still asleep in its doorway. The sky going orange at the edges where the afternoon was beginning to mean it. The western district doing what it did when nobody asked it to do anything else.

She looked down at her habit.

White still. Grey-purple stained at the hem from the border's ground — the specific grey-purple of soil that had been touched by something that didn't stop, that was touching more soil right now while she stood here, that would be touching different soil tomorrow. The fold Maret had adjusted sitting correctly now, the way it was supposed to sit.

She thought about what Maret had said.

Not the part about faith filling the emptiness — she had understood that, she had felt the shape of it in the way Maret carried herself, the specific settled quality of someone who had made a choice and kept making it and had stopped asking whether it was the right one. She understood it and she knew it wasn't available to her. Her faith didn't fill the emptiness. Her faith was the thing that kept measuring it.

She thought about the other part.

*I thought about looking in the thing we work against.*

*She had been turning that over since Maret said it. Not as philosophy — as direction. The corruption had been advancing for longer than Maret had been alive, and the purification work had been slowing it and nothing more. The method was failing. It had always been failing. Seventeen meters in one morning while they fought for their lives — that was the math, and the math didn't change no matter how many sisters went out.*

*But the corruption itself — the thing that moved and adapted and learned and produced the worm this morning and would produce something worse next month — it knew something the church didn't. Not because it was wise. Because it was working. Because whatever logic drove it forward was succeeding where the logic driving the purification was not.*

*If she understood that logic — really understood it, not the doctrine's version of it, not this is the enemy, oppose it — maybe she would understand what true purification actually required. What it would actually take to clean something rather than just slow its spread. The church had been treating symptoms for generations. The answer to what the disease actually was might live inside the disease itself.*

*That was what Maret had almost reached for.*

*That was what Sera was going to look for.*

She looked westward.

She retraced the moment — Maret's eyes going in that direction, the specific deliberateness of it, a woman who chose her gestures carefully making a choice about where to look while she talked about people who asked different questions. The military compound at the western end of the district. The high walls of it visible from here, the specific serious architecture of a place that had been built to do what the church couldn't do alone.

People who studied the corruption. Not to purify it — to understand it. Who had spent their careers learning what it produced and how it moved and what it responded to and what it was becoming. Who approached it not with the doctrine's framework but with something older and more honest — the framework of someone who needed to know their enemy completely because their enemy was going to kill them if they didn't.

A mage perhaps. Someone whose entire existence was oriented toward that understanding.

Maret hadn't named her.

She didn't need to.

Sera looked at the compound walls.

She looked down at her habit one more time. The grey-purple at the hem. The fold sitting correctly.

She didn't know what she was walking toward.

She started walking anyway.

# 13 \- The Trader's Afternoon

### **Chapter Thirteen — The Trader's Afternoon**

---

He walked out of the compound with the sealed writ in his coat.

Not the bag — his coat, the inner pocket that sat against his chest, the specific placement of something whose value was different in kind from tools and materials. The writ was paper. Paper that meant something because the western brigade's seal was on it and the western brigade had the resources to make the seal mean something and Ryn had correctly assessed all of this before walking through the compound gate that morning.

The training court was behind him. The crater in the wall. Seris's expression when she put the casing to her nose.

He had work to do.

---

The market was still in its morning mode when he moved through it — stalls fully open, the day's commerce at its peak, the specific productive noise of a place doing what it was built to do. He moved through it the way he moved through all markets — not browsing, executing. He knew what he needed and where it was. He had noted the relevant stalls yesterday on his first pass through the district and the noting had been sufficient.

He moved through it the way he moved through all markets — not browsing, executing. He knew what he needed and where it was. He had noted the relevant stalls yesterday on his first pass through the district and the noting had been sufficient.

He had enough materials for sixty rounds. He bought what he needed for the remaining forty — the specific additional quantities, acquired from the correct stalls at the correct prices without negotiating because the prices were correct and negotiating correct prices was a waste of everyone's time. He put everything in the bag in the spatial arrangement that kept reactive materials separated and stable.

He was done in an hour.

He found the garden on the district's quieter edge — a small green space that existed because someone had decided long ago that cities needed somewhere to breathe and nobody had gotten around to removing it. A tree at the center of it, old enough to have opinions about the space it occupied, the shade beneath it specific and complete.

He sat down under it.

He reached into his coat.

---

The field journal was old.

Not antique — just old in the way that objects became old when they were used constantly rather than stored carefully. Bound in dark leather that had taken the shape of his coat's inner pocket over however long he'd been carrying it. The pages inside a record of five years of thinking — equations in notation systems he'd invented because existing notation systems didn't have symbols for what he worked with, sketches of mechanisms and components and the spatial relationships between things that only existed in his mind until he put them on the page, notes in the compressed shorthand of someone who wrote for himself rather than for a reader.

He opened it to a clean page.

The casing sketch came first — brass, the specific dimensions, the primer placement, the tolerances marked. He worked quickly. This part was finished in his mind already, had been finished since he designed the round, and the sketch was transcription rather than creation. Clean lines. The specific precision of someone who had drawn technical schematics long enough that the hand moved without consultation.

He tore the page out.

Folded it. Put it in his coat.

He opened to the next clean page.

---

The problem was the soldier.

He had watched him almost fall backward and he had noted it the way he noted everything — as information, filed, to be addressed. The recoil was the weapon doing exactly what the weapon was designed to do — directing the round's force forward and absorbing the remainder through the shooter's body. The round's output exceeded what the weapon's current stock geometry managed efficiently. The shooter bore the difference.

He could change the formula — reduce the propellant's output, sacrifice some of the round's force for manageability. He drew the equation. Looked at it. Crossed it out.

He could change the stock — adjust the angle, redistribute the recoil across a larger contact surface, engineer the absorption rather than leaving it to the shooter's body to figure out. He sketched the stock from three angles. Looked at them. Tore the page out and looked at it differently and put it back down.

He could change both.

He started a new page. Chemical notation — the symbols he'd assigned to the acid wood bark, the suevite, the anechoic coating, the gel substance. He worked through the formula not as a reduction but as a question. The recoil was a pressure problem. The propellant was producing the correct output but distributing it across too many axes simultaneously — forward was what mattered, and everything that went sideways or backward was waste that the shooter's body absorbed.

He thought about different materials entirely.

Something that burned with a different pressure curve. Something that peaked later in the sequence, when the round had already committed to its direction, rather than immediately on ignition. He didn't have the answer. He had the question, which for him was usually the harder part — the answer was just the work that followed the question, and the work he knew how to do.

Pages accumulated. Some torn out and refolded. Some discarded and retrieved and looked at again. The shadow of the tree moved.

He got up.

Pages accumulated beside him.

Some torn out and refolded. Some discarded on the ground and retrieved and looked at again. One crumpled completely and then carefully uncrumpled because the idea in the corner of it was worth keeping even if the rest wasn't.

He looked at the tree's shadow.

It had moved considerably from where it was when he sat down. He calculated the angle against the sun's position and arrived at a time and stood up.

He had somewhere to be.

---

Aldric was at the forge when Ryn came through the door.

He didn't look up immediately. He was working on something — Ryn didn't examine what, it wasn't his business — with the specific focused attention of someone for whom work was not a state they entered and exited but simply the condition of being awake. The forge behind him burned with the specific bright consistent fire that no bellows produced, the pipe in the wall doing its work, the steam exhaust at the base doing its work, the whole mechanism running with the quiet competence of something that had been designed correctly.

Ryn put the folded page on the counter.

Aldric set down what he was holding. He picked up the page. He unfolded it and looked at it with the same attention he'd given the first blueprint section — not scanning, reading, tracing the logic of the design the way someone traced a route on a map, following it to its destination before assessing whether the destination was where they wanted to go.

He looked at the dimensions. The tolerances. The specific taper of the case mouth and what that taper implied about what was going inside it and what was going to happen to it when it got there.

He set the page down.

*"A hundred,"* he said.

*"Morning,"* Ryn said.

He walked out.

---

The afternoon had settled into its slower register by the time he turned back toward the inn — the market past its peak, the district finding its quieter second half, the light going long and warm across the western wall. He had materials. He had the casing commission placed. He had a hundred rounds to make and the evening ahead of him and the specific productive satisfaction of a day that had gone the way days went when the calculations came out correctly.

He was thinking about the recoil problem when he saw her.

A nun. Alone. Moving through the street with the specific quality of someone whose body had somewhere to be while the mind was somewhere else entirely. White habit, grey-purple at the hem in the specific way that habits came back from the corruption border. He registered this without deciding to — the border staining, the specific color of it, the fact that she was alone and that nuns from the border teams didn't usually walk the district streets alone in the afternoon.

He got a glimpse of her face.

The tree arrived before he could account for it.

Not the full vision — just the fragment that always came when it came, the specific two-second intrusion of something that didn't belong to the present moment. The tree. Spring light through new leaves, the specific green of leaves that had just arrived. The warmth of sitting somewhere that had nothing urgent about it.

Gone.

He was still looking at her face.

Their eyes met.

He read her the way he read everything — fast, complete, automatic. She had been crying. Recently. The specific residue of it still present. And underneath that something larger — the quality of someone who had just stepped off something significant and was still in the air above where they'd been standing.

He opened his mouth.

*"Good afternoon, sister."*

He didn't know why he said it. He didn't talk to strangers on streets — not out of coldness, just out of the specific economy of someone who understood that most interactions cost more than they returned and had calibrated accordingly. He had no business with this woman. He had nothing to sell her and nothing to learn from her and no reason to be standing still on a street in the afternoon saying good afternoon to a nun he had never seen before.

He said it anyway.

Before the part of him that made decisions had weighed in.

She looked at him.

She smiled — pushed through something, genuine underneath the pushing, the specific warmth of a person whose warmth had survived everything the day had done to it. She responded. A few words, gentle, her voice arriving in the ear the way certain things arrived — low, unhurried, the kind that didn't need volume to reach you.

She continued walking.

He stood where he was for a moment longer than the situation called for.

Then he turned toward the inn.

---

He couldn't stop thinking about her.

This was the thing that was strange. He processed people — that was simply true, it was the mechanism through which he moved through the world, people as variables, their behaviors as predictable outputs from understandable inputs once you'd identified the correct inputs. He didn't experience this as coldness. It was just how his mind worked. It had always worked this way, as far as he could remember, which was five years, which was the extent of the back there was.

The dwarf had been interesting. Genuinely, specifically interesting — the forge mechanism, the deliberate mistake, the two *I would know*s delivered with the flat certainty of someone who genuinely would. He had walked away from that forge thinking about it. But the thinking had been the thinking of a man who had encountered an elegant solution to an engineering problem he hadn't known was solvable and wanted to understand the solution.

The mage had been different — harder to hold at a consistent angle, the kind of variable that changed the shape of the equation rather than solving for it, someone whose capabilities exceeded the register he'd expected to find in a military compound and who had asked the one question that actually mattered. That had stayed with him too. But it had stayed with him the way problems stayed — as something to be returned to, examined, eventually understood.

The nun was neither of these things.

He couldn't find the mechanism of his interest. He looked for it the way he looked for everything — methodically, following the logic backward from the result to the cause — and kept arriving at her face on the street and the smile that had come through everything the day had done to her and the voice that arrived in the ear like something unhurried, and none of these things resolved into a category he could work with.

She had looked at him.

That was part of it. Most people on a street didn't. They processed him the way he processed them — as environmental data, a variable in the navigational calculation of moving through a crowded space, noted and filed and moved past. She had looked at him the way you looked at a person. Registered him. Responded to him as a specific individual rather than as a body in a corridor.

He had been in this district barely a day. One night, one morning, barely an afternoon. In five years of moving through the world he had grown accustomed to the rate at which interesting things appeared — occasional, irregular, the specific pleasant surprise of a city that produced something worth his attention.

This district had produced three before the sun went down.

The dwarf with his forge and his deliberate mistake. The mage with her spent casing and her single correct question. And now a nun walking alone through the western district with the biggest decision of her life still written on her face and something genuine left in her anyway, something that came through when a stranger said good afternoon, something that survived.

He couldn't stop thinking about her the entire walk back.

He filed this under things he didn't have a category for yet.

The inn appeared ahead of him.

He had a hundred rounds to make.

He went inside.

---

She didn't know what she was walking toward.

She knew the direction — westward, the way Maret's eyes had gone when she talked about people who asked different questions. The military compound at the western end of the district, the high walls of it visible above the rooftops. She had walked past it a hundred times in eight years without looking at it directly. She looked at it now.

The gate was the working kind. Two guards, equipment maintained past the standard the rest of the district bothered with. They saw her coming from a distance — the white habit, the grey-purple at the hem, a nun alone in the late afternoon heading toward the military compound without a companion or a purpose visible on her face.

One of them stepped forward as she reached the gate.

*"Sister. Can we help you?"*

She stopped.

She looked at him.

She had no answer ready. She had walked the whole way here without preparing an answer because she hadn't known what the question would be and she still didn't, standing in front of it, know what she was asking for.

*"Are you alright?"* the second guard said.

*"Yes,"* she said.

*"Are you lost?"*

*"No."*

They looked at each other. A nun who wasn't lost and wasn't hurt and wasn't alright and had arrived at their gate without a request.

*"Can we get you anything? Water?"*

*"I don't—"* She stopped. Started again. *"I don't know what I need."*

They looked at each other again — the brief communicative efficiency of two people who shared a context and were checking whether the other person's reading of the situation matched their own. It matched. Neither of them knew what to do with this.

*"Come inside,"* the first one said. Not unkindly. Just the practical response of someone who had decided that whatever this was, it shouldn't happen at the gate. *"Come sit down."*

They brought her into the gatehouse. A chair. A cup of water that she held without drinking. The room was small and functional — the specific interior of a space built for brief occupation rather than habitation, a table, two chairs, a rack of equipment along one wall. She sat in it and looked at the cup and didn't know what she was doing here.

One of the guards excused himself. He said the captain would be informed. He said it carefully, the way people said things when they were managing a situation they hadn't been trained for.

The other guard stayed. He stood near the door and didn't speak and she was grateful he didn't speak because she had nothing left to answer questions with. She sat with the cup in her hands and looked at the table and felt the specific guilt of someone who had walked into a place where people had real work to do and taken up a chair and a cup of water and a guard's afternoon for no reason she could articulate.

She thought about leaving.

The guard came back after a few minutes and told her the captain had been informed and would be down when he could. He said it without apology — the captain was a busy man and a sitting nun was not an emergency. She nodded. She understood completely. She wished she had not come.

She sat.

The gatehouse was quiet in the specific way that functional rooms were quiet when they weren't being used for their function — the equipment on the wall, the table, the two chairs, all of it waiting for something more purposeful than her. She turned the cup in her hands. She thought about leaving before he came down. She thought about it seriously — standing up, setting the cup on the table, walking out the gate, saving everyone the remainder of the interruption.

She didn't move.

Time passed. Enough of it that the guilt had settled into something more specific — not just the guilt of wasting a guard's afternoon but the guilt of someone who had followed a direction she wasn't sure she'd read correctly and had arrived somewhere she had no business being and couldn't explain why she'd come and couldn't leave and couldn't stay.

Then the footsteps in the corridor.

She heard him before she saw him — the specific quality of footsteps that belonged to someone who moved through spaces with absolute certainty of their right to be in them. He came through the door and looked at her and she could see immediately that he was a man who processed the world through direct questions and was about to process her the same way.

He was large. The greatsword on his back not decorative. The face of someone who had held a difficult position for a long time and had stopped finding it remarkable.

He pulled the second chair out and sat down across from her. Not looming — just present, the specific unhurried directness of someone for whom getting to the point was a form of respect.

*"Can you speak?"*

*"Yes,"* she said.

*"Are you lost?"*

*"No."* Not in the way he meant.

*"Are you hurt?"*

*"No."*

*"Do you need something here?"*

She looked at the cup in her hands.

She didn't answer.

Vorne looked at her. He was running the results of his questions through whatever framework he used for results and the results were not producing a conclusion he could act on. She could see this — the specific quality of a competent man encountering a problem that his competence didn't address.

He sat with it. He didn't fill the silence with more questions.

---

The footsteps in the corridor were different from his.

Lighter. The specific sound of shoes that were not built for silence and didn't try to be — the kind of footwear that announced its owner because its owner had decided long ago that announcement was preferable to surprise. Two sets of lighter footsteps behind them, stopping when the first set stopped.

Sera looked up.

The woman in the doorway was looking at her habit before she was looking at her. At the grey-purple staining at the hem. Reading it with the specific focused attention of someone for whom that particular staining was a text rather than a stain.

Dark hair. The attire of someone who had decided that what she was deserved to be communicated clearly — structured, expensive without apologizing for it. Two young women stopped behind her in the corridor, waiting.

She turned slightly toward the two young women behind her.

*"Go on,"* she said. Quietly. Not dismissive — the specific tone of someone who treated the people around her well enough that they moved when she asked without needing to be told twice. The footsteps in the corridor resumed and faded.

*"Lady Seris,"* Vorne said.

The woman's eyes moved from the hem of the habit to the face above it.

*"You've found yourself another interesting one, Vorne,"* she said. Vorne gave her a brief account of what little he knew. She listened without interrupting.

*"Can I have the room?"*

Vorne looked at her for a moment. In however many years they had worked alongside each other she had not often involved herself in things that weren't her concern. He noted this without comment. He stood and went out.

The door closed.

---

Seris sat down where Vorne had been sitting. She looked at Sera directly — not the habit now, the person wearing it — with the specific complete attention of someone who was reading rather than assessing, who wanted to understand rather than categorize.

*"Sit straight,"* she said. *"Chin up. Fix your collar."*

Sera obeyed before she decided to. Her spine straightened and her chin came up and her hands went to the collar of her habit and adjusted it without her mind having issued the instruction. Eighteen years of an institution's ambient corrections living in her body below the level of conscious response.

*"Are you from the west district branch?"*

*"Yes."*

*"How long?"*

*"Eight years."*

*"Does Maret know you're gone?"*

She answered her own question before Sera could open her mouth.

*"Of course she does."*

Sera's eyes opened slightly. Seris moved past the reaction without acknowledging it.

*"Why did you leave?"*

Sera kept her posture. She had been asked this question in various forms all afternoon and she had been finding different ways around it and she was tired of finding ways around things.

*"I don't want to follow the church anymore,"* she said.

Seris looked at her.

*"No one is keeping you,"* she said. *"They wouldn't want a non-believer anyway."*

*"I believe."*

*"What do you believe in?"*

The question arrived simply and sat there. Sera reached for the answer and found the space where the answer should have been occupied by something she couldn't name — not doubt, not absence, just the specific gap between what she believed and what the church had told her she believed, a gap that had been growing for years and had become uncrossable this morning.

*"That's right,"* Seris said. *"You don't know."*

Not cruelly. Not with contempt. Just the flat delivery of someone stating an observation they had made and were not going to pretend they hadn't made.

*"Your faith is weak. What did you come here for? You thought you could run from the church and find help here?"*

*"No."*

*"Then what. What do you want?"*

And the thing Sera had been carrying all day — through the field and the gate and the children's faces and the empty beds and Lise's words and the courtyard and the alley — came up out of her not dramatically but completely, the way things came up when the container had been full for too long.

*"I want to know if it mattered,"* she said. *"I want to know if my life mattered. I want to know if their lives mattered — the women in that carriage this morning, the ones who went out every day for years and came back with less of themselves each time and went out again. I want to know if this was her will."*

She stopped.

Something resolved in the stopping. The question she had been circling all day arriving at its own center.

*"I want to know what her will actually is,"* she said.

As if answering the question before it. If this — the border, the casualties, the corruption advancing seventeen meters while they fought for their lives — if this was Providence's will and the answer was no, then what was. What had any of it been pointing toward.

Seris's eyes had not moved from her face through any of it.

The room was quiet.

*"Why did you come here?"*

Calmly. Not the same question — a different question wearing the same words. She knew Maret had something to do with it. She waited for Sera to find her way to that or not.

Sera looked at the cup still in her hands.

*"I don't know,"* she said. And then, because the afternoon had used up whatever remained of her capacity for sitting in rooms she didn't belong in: *"I'm so sorry. I've bothered all of you for nothing. I should go."*

She stood up.

She walked to the door and through it.

---

Vorne was in the corridor, back against the wall, arms crossed, the specific posture of someone who had been waiting without minding the waiting. She looked at him.

*"I'm sorry for the disturbance,"* she said. *"Truly."*

He said nothing.

She kept walking toward the gate.

*"Do you have somewhere to stay?"*

Seris. Behind her, still in the doorway.

Sera stopped.

*"No."*

*"Do you have coin?"*

*"Yes."*

*"There's an inn half an hour's walk from here. You know it?"*

*"Yes."*

*"Stay there tonight. Be at this gate early morning."*

Sera processed this. The instruction arriving with the specific quality of something that didn't leave room for negotiation and wasn't asking for it.

*"Yes,"* she said.

*"You can go."*

*"Yes,"* she said.

She went.

---

The gate closed behind her.

In the corridor Vorne unfolded his arms and looked at Seris with the specific look of a man who had known someone for long enough to find them surprising and was finding them surprising now.

*"Not like you,"* he said. *"Taking in a lost stray."*

Seris looked at the gate where Sera had been.

*"This stray could be a lot of things,"* she said. *"Lost isn't one of them."*

She turned and continued down the corridor in the direction she had been going before the gatehouse stopped her — toward the quieter end of the compound, toward her quarters, the long day finally being permitted to end. 

He was back in the room before the afternoon had fully decided to become evening.

He set the bag on the table and opened it and began. The materials were organized the way they'd been organized since the market — each component in its position, the reactive ones separated, everything laid out in the sequence the work required. His hands moved through the setup the way they moved through everything practiced — without consulting the mind, the mind free to be elsewhere while the hands executed.

He worked for a couple of hours.

When he was done he had what he needed for the full hundred rounds minus the casings — those came from Aldric in the morning. He'd assemble them then and deliver to the compound before noon. He was ahead of schedule. He put everything away in the specific careful arrangement that kept it stable overnight and stood up and registered that he was hungry.

He went downstairs.

---

The lobby was quieter than it had been the previous evening.

Not empty — occupied, the tables filled with the usual end-of-day presence of people who had finished their day and were not yet ready to go to their rooms. But the noise was wrong. Suppressed. The conversations running at a lower register than the space called for, the way conversations ran when everyone's attention was pulled toward a single point and nobody wanted to be seen pulling toward it.

He came around the corner of the stairs.

He looked toward the front desk.

He understood immediately.

---

A nun at an inn's front desk.

The lobby full of people who were very focused on their meals and their conversations and who were watching the front desk with the completeness of people who had forgotten they were supposed to be pretending not to. The murmurs moving between tables — not quite loud enough to be heard clearly, loud enough that everyone could hear something was being said about the thing they were all pretending not to look at.

*Why would a nun need a room when the monastery is twenty minutes away.*

The question generating itself at every table without anyone needing to ask it out loud. The theories following immediately after, the way theories did when facts were scarce and imaginations were available — she'd been removed, she'd done something, she'd said something, blasphemy perhaps, or discipline, or something no one had quite worked out yet but that would become clear in the telling and retelling before the week was out.

Ryn came to the bottom of the stairs and stopped.

He looked at her.

He recognized her from the street. The white habit, the grey-purple at the hem from wherever she'd come from this morning. He read her the way he read everything — automatically, completely, the professional assessment running underneath whatever else was happening.

The decision he had seen on her face on the street was still there — more settled now, the rawness of it beginning to consolidate into something that would eventually be portable. She was exhausted. Not the tiredness of a long day in the conventional sense — the specific deep exhaustion of someone who had been spending since before dawn and had spent past the point where the spending had a comfortable floor. She was running on the specific remainder of a person who had used most of what they had and was still standing mostly out of habit.

Whatever this day had been for her — and he didn't know what it had been, he had the staining on her habit and the decision on her face and the exhaustion in how she held herself and nothing more specific than that — it had been the longest kind. The kind that made the morning feel like it belonged to a different week.

He thought about speaking to her.

In five years of moving through cities he had never once failed to find the angle — the specific entry point, the thing you said to a stranger that made the stranger stop being a stranger without either party having formally decided to do that. He found angles the way he found everything else — by reading what was there and understanding what it wanted. It had never failed him.

He looked for the angle now and found it immediately and then did nothing with it.

Not because the conversation wouldn't be welcome exactly. Because she was the kind of person who wouldn't shut it down. Anyone else standing at that desk in her condition — that tired, that privately undone, that much in need of the room upstairs and nothing between her and it — would give a stranger nothing. Would make the conversation impossible before it started. A closed face, a turned shoulder, the specific efficient dismissal of someone who had nothing left and knew it and acted accordingly.

She wouldn't do that.

That was the thing. He could see it in the same face he'd read on the street — the warmth in it that had survived everything the day had done to it, the specific quality of someone who would receive a conversation even when receiving it cost them something, who wouldn't make a stranger feel unwelcome even at the end of the longest day of their life.

He knew this about her from thirty seconds on a street and a glimpse of her face at a front desk.

He said nothing.

---

The innkeeper handed her the key.

*"Thank you,"* she said.

Her voice the same as it had been on the street. Low. Unhurried. The warmth in it intact, present even now, given to an innkeeper handing her a key at the end of a day that had used everything else up.

She turned from the desk.

She walked toward the stairs.

She passed him.

She didn't look up. She was looking at the middle distance the way people looked at it when they were navigating by feel rather than sight, when the body knew where it was going and the mind had been given the night off. Her shoulder passed within arm's reach of him.

He didn't say anything.

She went upstairs.

The lobby exhaled behind her — the murmurs resuming, the theories continuing their development, the spectacle processed and filed and now available for discussion at normal volume.

Ryn stood at the bottom of the stairs for a moment.

He looked at the place where she'd been standing.

Then he went to find something to eat.

### 

---

She closed the door.

The room was small and functional and indifferent to her in the specific way that rooms were indifferent when they had held many people and remembered none of them. A bed. A table. A window onto the alley between this building and the next. A candle someone had lit when she arrived, burning low already.

She took off her habit.

She held it for a moment — the white of it, the specific grey-purple at the hem where the border's ground had pressed itself into the fabric over the course of a morning that had started before the sun committed to rising. She looked at it the way she had looked at the ground beside the arm-cut sister — at the evidence of what the day had produced, at the specific material record of where she had been and what had happened there.

She was exhausted in a way that didn't have a bottom to it.

She used her purification magic on the staining anyway.

Not because it mattered practically. Not because the habit needed to be clean tonight rather than tomorrow. Something else — the specific importance of a thing that couldn't be explained efficiently, the way certain actions were important not for what they produced but for what they meant to do them. The magic went into the fabric the way it went into the border soil — the grey-purple retreating from the cloth, dissipating, the specific reversal of the spread's advance performed now on a habit in a room in an inn instead of on the ground outside the walls.

The habit came clean.

The red wasn't there to stay this time.

She folded it carefully. Set it on the chair.

She sat on the edge of the bed in the silence of the room and didn't know what to do with her hands.

---

The knock was soft.

She opened the door.

A platter on the floor of the corridor — a full meal, more food than she would have thought to order for herself, arranged with the specific care of someone who had decided what she needed rather than asking. Bread. Something warm in a bowl. A small dish of something she couldn't identify in the corridor's dim light but that smelled like it had been made with attention.

She looked both ways down the corridor.

Nobody.

She looked back at the platter.

And hunger arrived — all at once, like a memory she suddenly remembered having, the body catching up with what it had been owed since before dawn, since the border, since the last time she'd eaten which was yesterday evening and felt like a different person's life. Her stomach registered the smell of the food and produced a response so immediate and so physical that she almost laughed. Almost.

She brought the platter inside.

She ate.

---

She laid down.

The wool of the bed received her with the specific give of something that had absorbed many people's exhaustion and had room for one more. She felt her weight sink into it — the specific physical relief of a body that had been standing and walking and holding itself upright for longer than it was built to do without rest being permitted, finally, to stop. Her feet ached. Her shoulders ached. Things she hadn't registered while they were happening announced themselves now that the day had no more use for her attention.

She let them announce themselves.

She didn't think about the morning.

The morning was too large for tonight. It would be there tomorrow — it would always be there, somewhere, it would always be this morning in some part of her that she hadn't finished going through yet — but tonight she put it down. Not because she had resolved it. Because the body had simply run out of the resource required to hold it up any longer.

She thought about Lise.

Not the words — she'd been carrying the words all day and she left them at the edge of the bed where the day's other things were piling up. Just Lise as a person. Sixteen years old, sincere in the specific complete way that people were sincere before the thing they were sincere about had been tested. She walked toward the border with her whole heart open. She had known Wenna's name. She had stood in the courtyard and understood something without being able to say what she'd understood, and she had gone inside the way Maret told her to, and tomorrow or the day after or the day after that she would go to the border for the first time and the border would begin its education.

Sera hoped she came back from it.

She thought about Maret.

The thirty years of it. The border that had been weeks' walk away when she started and was few hours from the gate now and would be at the gate eventually and Maret would still be going out in the mornings when it arrived. Not with bitterness — She thought about Maret without judgment — which was easier than she'd expected, standing now on the other side of the conversation. Just empathy. The specific empathy of someone who understood what the choice had cost and what it had provided and why a person might keep making it.  Maret had chosen her filling. She had kept choosing it. There was a kind of faithfulness in that which Sera respected even though she couldn't share it.

She thought about Seris.

Different from Maret's contentedness — something more directed in it, more active. Seris wasn't filled. She was pointed. The specific assurance of someone who had oriented themselves toward something real and had been moving toward it long enough that the movement had become the condition of being alive rather than a thing they did within that condition. She had looked at Sera with the complete attention of someone for whom the world was information and had found Sera's information worth processing. She hadn't offered comfort. She hadn't offered the doctrine. She had asked the questions that needed asking and had listened to the answers without flinching and had said *be at this gate early tomorrow* as if early tomorrow was simply the next thing and the next thing was available.

It was available.

That was the thing Sera kept returning to as her eyes grew heavy. Not the enormity of what she'd walked away from or the uncertainty of what came next. Just the specific small fact that tomorrow morning existed and she would be in it and Seris had given her somewhere to be when she got there.

The candle on the table burned itself out.

The room went dark.

She was already asleep.

# 14 \- The Road, The Site, The Camp

### **Chapter Fourteen — The Road, The Site, The Camp**

---

*"—and that's how the baker ended up on the roof," Mara said, "with one shoe and someone else's goat."*

*She delivered it with the satisfaction of someone who had been building toward it for a while and found the building worth the time. The road went on. The corruption's edge ran alongside them to the left.*

*Varen said nothing for a moment.*

*Then —*

*"What were those. When we left."*

She knew what he meant. The procession through the western gate — the sisters walking with the specific gait of people still moving because stopping hadn't been authorized, the carriage behind them with its covered shapes.

Her face changed.

Not sadness. Not pity. Something harder than either — the specific contempt of someone who had grown up outside every institution the city offered and had watched those institutions from the outside long enough to have formed conclusions that were accurate in some ways and incomplete in others and fully committed to in all of them.

*"Nuns,"* she said. *"They work at the corruption border. Purification — they use magic to push the spread back."*

Varen thought about this.

The corruption was the thing he'd been navigating beside his entire life. Avoiding it when avoidance was available. Opposing it when it wasn't. The sisters going out every day to push it back made sense to him in exactly that framework — not noble, not foolish, just the practical response of people doing what the situation required.

He thought about it.

If you couldn't move away from the thing you moved the boundary between you and it. That was just sense. He filed the sisters' work under sense and moved on.

*"That seems logical,"* he said.

Mara looked at him.

*"They die for it,"* she said. *"Constantly. They throw their lives away because their god told them to."* She said it with the finality of someone who had reached a verdict and filed it and wasn't reopening it. *"Fools."*

The word god caught him before anything else she'd said.

*"Their god speaks to them," he said. "A god tells them to do this?"*

*"That's what they believe," Mara said.*

*"There are still gods."*

*He said it before he meant to say it — the word still surfacing from everything Caen had put in him. The crusade. The gods that fell. The world that remained after them. Caen had described a world that had been emptied of gods. The idea that something had survived, that something had evaded the man from the magma and his dragon, hadn't been part of what Caen gave him.*

*Mara looked at him.*

*"Yes," she said. "The nuns serve a goddess. Providence — the Profaned Goddess they call her." Then — "What did you mean still?"*

He didn't register the question.

*"Where is she,"* he said.

*"Where is — who, Providence?"* She almost laughed. *"Nobody knows where she is. Half the city thinks the whole thing is a story someone made up a long time ago and nobody got around to stopping."*  She waved a hand. *"Why do you ask. And how do you know what a god is. And what did you mean still — what does still mean—"*

*"Caen told me,"* he said.

*"Who is Caen."*

He opened his mouth.

He closed it.

He had never had to answer this question before. Caen was simply the fixed point of his entire existence — the thing everything else had been organized around, the presence that the cabin had made sense because of. Fixed points didn't require labels. You didn't name the ground beneath your feet. You just stood on it.

*"Caen is... Caen,"* he said.

Mara stared at him.

*"Is he your friend?"*

He thought about it. The word friend described something — a category of relationship, a specific kind of closeness, something people had with other people who were separate from them in the way that Caen had never been separate from him and had also never been present in the way friends were present. He didn't have the right word. He wasn't sure the right word existed.

*"Caen is Caen,"* he said again.

She looked at him for a moment with the expression of someone who had decided to let it go for now.

*"What did he tell you,"* she said.

He told her.

Everything Caen had told him across ten years of campfire stories — Yharim, the boy from the magma, the dragon, the vow. The crusade against the gods. The kingdoms that fell. The Corruption and the Crimson produced from the remains of gods improperly handled. The world that emerged from the war — broken and continuing and organized around the wreckage of what had been before.

He delivered it the way he delivered everything — flat, direct, without editorializing. Just the story as he had received it, in the order it had been given.

Mara listened.

She was nine years old and she had spent her entire life inside the walls of Ordenmere and she had heard things in markets and overheard things between merchants and learned things from the specific education of someone who survived by paying attention. She knew more about the world than most adults gave her credit for.

She had never heard any of this.

The dissonance of it settled on her face — the specific expression of someone who had just received information from a source that shouldn't have it, from someone she'd found picking through a battlefield outside the city walls, from a person who had never spoken to another human being in twelve years before he met her. Knowledge that even the scholars she'd heard murmuring in market corners didn't possess.

She thought he was lying.

Then she remembered that he didn't have the capacity to lie. She had established this comprehensively across the past day and a half and it was one of the most reliable things she knew about him.

She thought Caen was lying.

*"Maybe this Caen was joking with you," she said. "Made the whole thing up."* 

Varen was quiet for a moment. He considered it the way he considered things — genuinely, methodically, following the logic to wherever it led.

*"Why would he lie,"* he said.

He didn't think he lied. He filed the question without resolving it.

*"This Yharim,"* Mara said. *"Where is he."*

*"I don't know,"* Varen said. *"But I'm going to find him."*

She stopped walking.

She looked at him.

*"You're going to find him,"* she said.

*"Yes."*

*"Did you listen to your own story."* She said it slowly, with the specific emphasis of someone making sure each word landed before the next one arrived. *"Even if none of it was complete nonsense — what would make you want to find someone like that. What are you going to do, give him a piece of mind ?" she said laughing.*

He said nothing.

*"What are you going to say next — you'll find Providence too?"* Sarcastic. The specific sarcasm of someone who had made a joke and was pleased with it.

She looked at his face.

The joke had landed on something real.

*"Youre actually thinking about it,"* she said.

He said nothing.

She looked at the road ahead. At the corruption's edge visible to the left, the grey-purple of it running alongside them the way it had been running alongside them for two hours.

*"Do you think the church would know where she is,"* he said.

She had walked with pickpockets, merchants, drunk soldiers and stray dogs. None of them had told her they were going to find the most dangerous person in the history of the world.

She kept walking.

---

The site appeared after another hour.

Or where the site had been. The clearing at the edge of the corruption where the seven adventurers had died — where Varen had read their bodies and found the gap he couldn't explain and where Mara had tried to pick his pocket and failed — was gone. Not the physical location. The clearing was still there. But the corruption had moved through it completely in the days since, absorbing everything the clearing had contained. The bodies. The equipment. The specific evidence of seven people who had stayed together and died together, consumed now into the rot, the grey-purple ground covering all of it as though the site had never existed.

Varen stood at the edge of it.

He looked at where the tracks had been.

Gone. The corruption had taken them along with everything else. But he had read them when they were there — the direction they were going, the specific southeast bearing of something that had come from deeper in the infected territory and had returned to it. He held the remembered bearing against the current landscape and calculated.

*"We should go deeper,"* he said.

He had assessed the risk the way he assessed all risks — against what he had been built to do. Hunting. Tracking. Moving through territory that wanted to kill him and coming back out. The corruption was worse than the forest but the principle was the same. He could manage it.

Mara said nothing for a moment.

She looked at the corruption. The grey-purple of it. The specific wrong quality of the air above it, the fog visible in the distance hiding what the fog always hid. She had been outside the walls many times. She had never gone into the corruption.

She had insisted on coming.

*"The commission said there was recorded activity on the border,"* she said. *"They've been picking people off this stretch for weeks,"* she said. *"Three groups went looking and none of them came back talking about it. They're not hiding. They'll come."* 

He looked at her.

His way was faster. Hers was slower. His carried more risk. Hers carried less. Both were within what he could manage. She had made the practical argument correctly and he could find no flaw in the logic of it. 

He looked at where they were standing — the open ground of the corrupted clearing, exposed on three sides, the specific tactical disadvantage of somewhere that offered nothing to put your back against and nowhere to control an approach from.

*"Not here,"* he said.

He turned and read the terrain around them the way he read all terrain — for what it offered, for what it concealed, for where the advantage lived. The hill to the west — steep sided, the slope providing natural cover on one side, the elevated ground giving a sightline over the clearing without being in it. The corruption hadn't reached the hill's base yet. The ground there was still ordinary.

He walked toward it.

Mara followed.

---

The camp was small.

No fire. Fire announced position and position was what they were trying to control. Varen moved through the setup with the economy of someone who had made camp in worse places under worse conditions more times than he could count — everything placed where it needed to be, nothing wasted, the specific efficiency of someone for whom this was simply what you did when you stopped moving.

Mara helped without being asked.

She set her things beside his without ceremony. She had watched him set up and had replicated the logic of it — the sightline toward the clearing, the hill at their backs, the specific arrangement of a camp designed for quick movement rather than comfort.

She sat down.

She looked at the corruption's edge visible from here — the grey-purple of it, the fog beyond it, the specific quality of something that was alive in the way that wrong things were alive.

She didn't say anything about being scared.

He didn't ask.

They waited.

Varen gathered wood while there was light to gather it by.

Not for a fire — fire announced position and position was the thing they were controlling. For later. For the long wait that might come, for the specific contingency of needing something dry and ready if the cold set in or the wait stretched past what either of them had planned for. He moved through the scrub at the hill's base picking up what the ground offered, and Mara stayed close.

Closer than she needed to. He noticed it the way he noticed everything — the specific distance she maintained, near enough that he was always between her and the open ground toward the corruption. She didn't say anything about it. She was telling herself that she'd run if things went wrong, that staying close was strategy rather than fear.

They set the wood at camp.

They sat down.

---

*"How long did you live in the west district?"*

*"All my life, dummy."* A beat. *"I mean — I just got here yesterday. Remember."*

The correction came a half-second too late.

He looked at her.

He'd asked because he'd had suspicions. The story had never quite held — the specific way her details shifted depending on what the moment required, the gap between how well she knew the district and how recently she claimed to have arrived. He hadn't pushed before. He pushed now, gently, the way you pushed something you already knew was going to give.

*"What were you doing here,"* he said. *"Before. You weren't lost. You weren't separated from anyone."*

She was quiet.

Then she told him — the way a child told the truth after being caught in the lie, reluctantly, in pieces, each piece extracted by the silence that followed the last one.

*"I came here with the seven,"* she said. *"The dead ones."*

He waited.

*"They had coins. I could see it — the way they carried their bags, the way they moved. I climbed onto their wagon while they were stopped. I was going to take something and go. But they came back before I could get down, so I hid. I stayed quiet under the canvas and I waited for them to make camp so I could slip out in the dark."* She looked at her hands. *"Then something attacked them. I didn't see what. I ran. I didn't look back. I just ran and I kept running until I couldn't hear it anymore."*

*"Did you try to steal from them,"* he said.

*"Yes."*

There was something in how she said it. A shame she didn't usually carry — she lied without shame, she stole without shame, those were tools and tools didn't produce shame. But this was being seen, and being seen was different.

*"Did you try to steal from me,"* he said.

*"Yes."*

She waited.

He watched her wait — the specific stillness of someone braced for judgment, for anger, for whatever a person did when they learned they'd been targeted. She'd been waiting for it since the moment they met, he understood now. The whole day and a half of her stories and her closeness and her stubbornness sitting on top of this, the expectation that the truth would eventually surface and the surfacing would cost her.

*"Why,"* he said.

*"I thought you'd kill me."*

---

He remembered how afraid she'd been when he caught her wrist that first day. The way she couldn't speak. The way her whole small body had gone rigid in the grip of something that expected to die.

He didn't pass judgment.

Not for the lying. A rabbit would lie to a wolf if lying meant it kept its life — would freeze, would feign, would do whatever the shape of its fear required, and the wolf didn't hold the lie against the rabbit because the lie was just the rabbit being a rabbit. She had lied to him the way a small thing lied to a large one. There was nothing in that to judge.

Not for the stealing either. He had taken food from the mouths of animals before — pulled a kill from a fox that had gotten there first, taken what he needed because he needed it and the needing was the only law that applied that far from anything. He saw what she'd done the same way. Survival did what survival did. It wasn't a flaw in her. It was the proof she'd lived.

She was still waiting.

*"Are you hungry,"* he said.

It wasn't what she'd braced for. He watched the question land wrong — watched her recalibrate, the expected judgment not arriving, something ordinary arriving in its place.

*"Yes,"* she said.

*"Let's find something to eat."*

A pause.

*"Yes,"* she said.

---

He walked. She walked right beside him.

They moved away from the corruption's edge, toward the higher ground to the west where the land was still ordinary and animals still moved through it the way animals moved through land that hadn't been touched yet. The light was going long and gold. The corruption behind them, the clean world ahead, the specific line between the two visible if you knew how to look for it.

He saw the rabbit at a distance that didn't seem like it should contain a rabbit.
