Its fur had gone the exact color of the scrub around it — the specific dun-grey that made it not a rabbit but a texture in the landscape, a thing the eye passed over because the eye had nothing to catch on. Mara, beside him, didn't see it. He could tell she didn't see it from the way she kept scanning past it, looking for something more obvious, the rabbit invisible to her in the specific way that perfect camouflage was invisible to anyone whose eyes hadn't spent twelve years learning to find exactly this.

He picked up a rock.

He threw it.

The throw had the specific economy of everything he did — no wasted motion, the arm doing only what the arm needed to do, the rock leaving his hand with a precision and a force that didn't match the casualness of the gesture. It crossed the distance in a flat line and arrived at the rabbit's head and the rabbit's head was simply no longer there. No suffering. No second required. The thing was alive and then it was meat and the transition between the two had taken less time than the sound of the impact took to reach them.

Mara stared at the spot.

She hadn't seen the rabbit until it stopped being a rabbit. Most skilled hunters wouldn't have seen it from half that distance — wouldn't have picked the shape out of the scrub, wouldn't have trusted the throw if they had, wouldn't have committed that much force to a target that small that far away on the first attempt.

He walked over and collected it.

They went back to camp.

---

They saw it as they approached.

A creature, at the edge of their camp, its head low, moving through their things with the specific investigative quality of something scouting a position.

It was three times the size of a direwolf.

No fur — just hide, grey and tight over muscle, the surface of it wrong in the specific way that corruption-made things were wrong. Where its eyes should have been there was only smooth skin, unbroken, the skull built around senses that didn't require light. Its claws were longer than his knife and clearly sharper, and there were more of them than a thing needed, rows of them, the feet built less for moving than for ending. It was pure muscle from the shoulders back. Nothing about it was decorative. Nothing about it was for anything except destruction.

He had read this thing's footprints at the site.

He had assessed the size from the depth of the prints, the weight from the spacing, the build from the gait — and his assessments had been correct, every one of them, the creature in front of him matching the creature he'd reconstructed from the marks in the ground.

What he hadn't reconstructed was this. The specific quality of something that looked designed — not evolved, not grown, but made, built to a purpose with the purpose visible in every line of it. Built to catch the things the corruption couldn't catch on its own. Built to destroy what resisted.

He was ready to engage.

His weight shifted. His left hand found the knife and his right the sword. The specific stillness of a body organizing itself around a thing it intended to kill settled over him the way it always settled —

The creature lifted its head.

The skin where its eyes should have been began to pulse — rapidly, a fast rhythmic movement under the surface, something happening beneath the hide that had no equivalent he could name. The creature went still. Then it turned from the camp entirely and ran — toward the center of the corruption, away from them, the way a thing ran when something had called it and the call was not a thing it could refuse.

Its speed was extraordinary.

It was out of sight in a moment. Not the time it took to register the running — the time it took to register that the running had already finished, the creature gone into the grey distance before the eye had caught up with the fact of its movement.

The camp was still.

---

Mara could not believe what she'd seen.

The fear she'd been managing all day — the fear she'd been telling herself was strategy, was caution, was anything other than what it was — came up through her and stayed up. She couldn't put it back down. She'd seen the thing now. She'd seen the size of it and the speed of it and the specific designed wrongness of it and there was no version of telling herself she'd run if things went wrong that survived contact with what she'd just watched.

*"I don't think we should do this,"* she said. *"There's no way. Not on our own. Did you see the size of it? The speed of it?"*

Varen wasn't listening.

His mind was somewhere else entirely — ten years old, in a different clearing, a knife in a hand that had been smaller then, a direwolf in front of him and the specific certainty that the next few seconds would decide whether he continued to exist. He had stood in front of that wolf. He had not dropped the knife. Everything he was had started in that clearing, in that decision, in the specific moment where a feral child decided he would not be prey.

This was that. Again. Larger and worse and built by something that wanted the world dead, but underneath the difference it was the same thing — another shape of the wolf, another step on a staircase he had been climbing his whole life without ever seeing the top of it. He hadn't asked for the staircase. He just understood, with the specific clarity that had organized his entire existence, that the steps were there to be climbed and that he was the one who had to climb them.

It had stopped being a commission for coin somewhere in the last few seconds.

*"I must continue,"* he said.

*"Have you lost your mind?"* Mara said.

He looked at her.

*"Do you want to leave?"* he said. *"You can go back."*

No hostility in it. No challenge. Just the flat presentation of an option that was genuinely available — she could go, the road was there, nothing held her here. He meant it as a kindness, or as close to a kindness as the plain statement of a fact could be.

*"I want to see this through,"* he said. *"I'll pay back what I owe you."*

She looked at him in something past disbelief.

She was trying to work out what he was — whether he was delusional, whether the thing in his head had come loose from the thing in front of him, or whether he was simply so certain of himself that he genuinely intended to stand alone against a creature that had thrown a horse to the ground hard enough to make the horse a stain. She'd seen the site. She knew what these things did. And she couldn't tell, looking at his face, which of the two explanations was true.

She decided it might be both.

*"Fine,"* she said. *"But if things get rough, I'm leaving."*

The words made complete sense to him.

He didn't understand why she'd felt the need to say them out loud — of course she'd leave if things got rough, leaving when things got rough was the correct response to things getting rough, it was what the rabbit did and the rabbit was right to do it. That she'd announced it as a condition, as though it were something he might object to, was the part he couldn't follow.

He filed it.

They went back to camp and both of them knew the creature would return.

Probably not alone.

Varen didn't say this. He didn't need to. He set the rabbit down and stood at the camp's edge looking at the treeline for a moment — reading it, the way he read everything, for what it offered and what it concealed and where the advantage lived — and then he began to move.

---

He set a perimeter first.

Not a wall — a boundary, marked in the specific language of someone who had spent twelve years learning how territory worked and what it communicated. Stones placed at intervals. Branches arranged at angles that would tell him in the dark if something had moved through them. Small things. Invisible to anything that didn't know what to look for. He moved through the treeline at the hill's base laying them out with the efficiency of someone executing a plan that had already been complete in his head since he chose this spot.

Mara followed him.

Not helping — just following. She had stopped pretending she had reasons for staying close. She stayed close because the alternative was standing in the camp alone with the treeline around her and the corruption's edge visible beyond it and no version of that was available to her right now.

He didn't say anything about it.

---

The wood came next.

Not the small pile he'd gathered before — he went back into the scrub and came back with more, and went back again, and came back again, until the stack at camp was large enough to feed a fire for days if the days required it. He worked quickly and without rest, the specific efficiency of someone for whom physical work was simply the execution of a decision rather than an effort. Mara watched him carry the third load in and looked at the stack and understood that he was not planning for tonight. He was planning for however long it took.

She sat down and stayed out of the way.

---

He set the torches last.

He'd made them from what the hill offered — branches stripped and wrapped with strips of cloth from the pack, the specific construction of someone who had made fire in worse conditions with worse materials. He moved through the treeline placing them at intervals — not randomly, not decoratively, but at specific points that he had chosen the way a hunter chose positions.

He was choosing where to fight.

The treeline ahead of the camp opened slightly at the border's edge and then narrowed — the trees coming closer together as they went deeper, the gaps between them shrinking from the width of something large moving freely to the width of something large moving with difficulty to the width of something large not moving at all. He walked the path twice, reading it, confirming what he'd seen the first time. The narrowing was gradual enough that the creatures would be committed to it before they understood what the narrowing meant.

The torches went at the points where the narrowing began.

The points where a creature the size of what they'd seen would start to slow.

He placed the last torch and came back to camp and looked at what he'd made.

Not a trap — he didn't have the materials for a trap. Just the specific geometry of terrain used correctly. The fire would light what needed to be lit. The path would give him what the open clearing wouldn't — the narrowing, the forced single-file, the removal of the size advantage that had made three other groups into evidence at a battle site.

He came back to camp.

He sat down.

---

The sun went.

It went the way it always went — gradually and then completely, the light going orange and then grey and then the specific darkness of a night in open country with no city behind you and no shelter ahead. The corruption's edge was less visible in the dark but more present, the fog of it catching what little light the stars offered and giving it back wrong.

Mara sat beside him.

Not close enough to touch — just within arm's reach, the specific distance of someone who had negotiated with themselves about how much proximity they were willing to admit to and had settled here.

She looked at the torches standing unlit in the treeline.

She looked at the wood stacked at camp.

She looked at him.

He was still. The specific stillness of someone who was not waiting so much as simply existing in the interval between the last thing and the next thing — the way he occupied silences, the way he occupied everything, without friction, without the restlessness that other people brought to waiting.

The fire burned low between them.

The night settled in around the camp like something patient.

He was ready.

# 15 \- What Comes Next

### **Chapter Fifteen — What Comes Next** 

---

He came down for breakfast when the inn was in its morning mode — the lobby quieter than the evening, the specific functional atmosphere of people beginning their day without particular ceremony. He found a table. He ordered what was available. He ate.

He looked toward the stairs without deciding to.

She was already gone. The key was at the desk. The room upstairs held nothing of her except the fact of having held her. He thought about the food he'd left outside her door the previous evening — whether it was still warm when she found it, whether she'd eaten before she slept or after, whether the wool bed had been sufficient for someone who had just walked away from the only life she'd known.

He stopped.

He had work.

He finished breakfast and put his coat on and went out into the morning.

---

Aldric's forge was already running when he arrived.

Of course it was. The mechanism in the wall fed the fire regardless of what hour it was or whether anyone was working the bellows — which was the point, which was why the fire was burning at exactly the same consistent brightness it had been burning at yesterday morning when Ryn first walked in and the morning before that and every morning before that going back to whenever Aldric had installed the mechanism and stopped thinking about bellows entirely.

He walked in.

He didn't announce himself.

Aldric had his back to the door — working at the table rather than the forge, hunched over something, his broad shoulders blocking whatever was in front of him. The forge burned behind him. The tools on the wall caught the light.

Ryn heard it.

A sound — continuous, rhythmic, coming from whatever was in front of Aldric. Tic. Tic. Tic. Tic. Each one distinct and brief and immediately followed by the next. He stood at the entrance and listened and registered not the sound but the interval between sounds — the specific consistent space between each tic and the next, identical, the same duration each time, a regularity that didn't belong to anything that breathed or burned or moved under its own impulsion.

Nothing produced that regularity by accident.

*"Dammit to hell."*

Aldric's voice — low, directed at whatever was in front of him rather than at Ryn. The ticking stopped. He set something down. He turned around.

Ryn was standing there.

*"Didn't hear you come in,"* Aldric said. Not accusatory. Just the observation of someone who preferred to know when his space had a new person in it. *"Make a noise next time."*

*"My apologies,"* Ryn said.

---

*"Your order's ready,"* Aldric said. *"Right here."*

He moved toward the end of the counter where the commission sat wrapped in cloth. He stopped.

He turned and looked at Ryn.

Not the look of a man with something to say — the look of a man who had noticed something and was deciding whether to address it. Ryn was not looking at the table. He was specifically, deliberately, visibly not looking at the table, which communicated the same thing that looking at it would have communicated, possibly more so.

Aldric looked at him long enough that the looking required a response.

*"Are you alright,"* Ryn said.

A pause.

*"Say, trader."* Aldric crossed his arms. *"I have something I want to ask you. If you have the time."*

Ryn looked at him.

*"I can spare a few moments,"* he said. *"What is it?"*

Aldric's expression did something small — not quite a smile, the specific movement of someone who had just received a straight line and was choosing not to take it.

*"Well,"* he said. *"Time is our subject, as it happens."*

He lifted the counter.

---

The table was covered.

Not cluttered — every component placed with intention, the specific organized spread of someone who knew exactly what they had and where they'd put it and why. But there were so many of them. Small parts, smaller than anything Ryn had built, smaller than anything he'd designed, the specific scale of work that required not just precision but a different relationship to precision than he'd ever needed to develop.

He sat down.

He looked.

His mind moved through what was in front of him the way it moved through everything — reading, not cataloguing, following the logic of each component to what the logic suggested about its purpose, about what it would do when it was part of something larger, about what the something larger was trying to be.

A long flat ribbon of steel coiled tightly inside a brass barrel — housed, contained, the tension of the winding visible in the set of it even at rest. The stored energy of something wound under pressure, waiting for the moment of release. He could see from the gauge of the steel and the diameter of the coil how much force it would produce as it unwound — a consistent declining force, the tension greatest at full wind and least at full release, the challenge of that decline visible immediately to anyone who understood what the decline would do to whatever it was powering.

A wheel — small, the diameter of a coin, the teeth around its edge not the teeth of a gear in any conventional sense. Club-shaped. Each tooth curved forward at its tip like a finger beckoning, the geometry of it specific, the curve not decorative but functional in a way he needed another component to understand.

He looked for the other component.

He found it — a small forked piece, two prongs extending from a central pivot, each prong ending in a face angled to catch and release the club-shaped teeth of the wheel in sequence. He held it up. He understood immediately. The wheel turned, a tooth pushed against one prong of the fork, the fork rocked on its pivot, the other prong caught the next tooth, the wheel advanced by exactly one tooth, the fork rocked back, and the cycle repeated — the coiled ribbon's stored energy released not all at once but in the smallest possible increments, one tooth at a time, the release regulated by the rocking of the fork into something that happened at a consistent interval.

Consistent.

The same interval each time.

He set the forked piece down.

He looked at Aldric.

Aldric was watching him with his arms crossed and an expression that was not quite neutral.

Ryn looked to his right. Fine-tipped tools lay in a row — metal, the tips worked to a fineness that his own instruments didn't approach, the specific implements of someone who operated at a scale that required a different kind of hand than he'd trained.

His hands moved.

He didn't decide to let them move. They moved the way they'd moved in the training court when he assembled the rifle — the specific automatic competence of a mind that had understood something and was executing the understanding without waiting for instruction. He picked up the coiled ribbon and seated it in its brass housing. He positioned the wheel. He positioned the forked piece at the angle that the geometry of the teeth required. He added the components that connected them — the pivots, the bridges that held the pivots in place, each one placed with a speed that made Aldric unfold his arms and lean forward slightly.

He wound the coiled ribbon.

The mechanism began to move.

---

The sound arrived and Ryn went still.

Not from surprise — from the specific focused attention of someone receiving information they wanted to receive completely. The forked piece rocked. It caught a tooth. Released it. The wheel advanced. The fork rocked back. It caught the next tooth.

Tic.

Tic.

Tic.

He understood what Aldric had said. *Time is our subject.* He understood it now not as a statement about the conversation they were having but as a statement about what was on the table. This mechanism — if it worked with sufficient consistency — could keep time. Not approximately. Not by reading the shadow of a stick in the ground or waiting for the church bells or looking at the sky and estimating. Precisely. Mechanically. The time carried inside the device independent of everything outside it — the clouds, the season, the time of day, the location, the person holding it. Time that didn't need to be read from the world because it was being produced by the mechanism itself.

He listened to the ticking.

He listened to it the way he listened to things that mattered.

Then he heard it.

A change — barely perceptible, a fraction of a fraction, the interval between ticks slightly longer than it had been a moment ago. Not consistent anymore. Drifting. The mechanism slowing in increments too small to see but audible to someone who had been listening for them.

He looked at the contact points.

Where the prongs of the forked piece caught and released the teeth of the escape wheel — there. Metal meeting metal at the highest frequency in the entire mechanism. Every tick was a collision at that point. Every collision produced friction. The friction was accumulating in the steel, producing wear at the contact points, the wear introducing inconsistency into the interval.

The mechanism needed something at those points that reduced the friction to a level where the wear was negligible.

He looked at Aldric.

Aldric was looking at him.

*"The contact points,"* Ryn said.

*"Yes,"* Aldric said.

---

They worked.

Not because either of them decided to work together — because the problem was there and they were both the kind of person who couldn't leave a problem that was there. They moved through the solution space the way two people moved through it when they processed at the same speed and didn't need to explain things to each other — each step following from the last without commentary, the collaboration happening in the work rather than in the discussion of the work.

Ryn disassembled.

He changed the angle of the prong faces — shallower, reducing the impact force at each catch. He reassembled. He wound the ribbon. The mechanism started and ran and drifted faster than before. The shallower angle had reduced one variable and introduced a worse one — the prongs weren't catching cleanly, the release inconsistent, the interval between ticks varying more not less.

He looked at why.

He disassembled again.

He changed something else — the weight distribution of the forked piece, shifting the balance point of the pivot to change how the rocking motion felt at the contact points. He reassembled. Better. The ticking more consistent, the drift slower.

Then it failed.

Not drift this time — the mechanism stopped entirely, the forked piece catching a tooth and not releasing, the stored energy of the coiled ribbon pressing against the contact point until something gave.

He disassembled.

He held the mainspring — the coiled ribbon — and looked at it. Felt the tension of it between his fingers. The force it produced declining as it unwound was not linear — it dropped sharply in the last third of its travel, producing a sudden change in how hard it pushed against the escapement, which changed how the fork met the teeth, which changed the friction at the contact points.

*"The ribbon,"* he said.

*"The tension curve,"* Aldric said.

They looked at each other.

They changed the material. Not steel — something softer, a different alloy, one that maintained more consistent tension across its full range of travel, the decline gentler, the force it delivered to the escapement more uniform from full wind to near empty.

Aldric made it. Ryn watched him make it at the forge with the specific attention of someone studying a process rather than waiting for its output.

They installed it.

They wound it.

The ticking arrived — and it was better. Significantly better. The consistency of it audible immediately, the interval between ticks holding for longer, the drift appearing later and more slowly than before.

Then it drifted.

The same problem. The contact points. The friction accumulating at the same place it always accumulated, the material change buying time rather than solving the problem, the fundamental issue sitting at the escapement untouched.

Ryn picked up the forked piece and looked at the contact faces under the light.

The steel was already showing it — not visible wear yet but the beginning of what wear looked like before it became visible. Every tick was doing this. The accumulation was inevitable in steel. The problem wasn't the mainspring tension or the angle of the prong faces or the weight distribution of the pivot. Those were symptoms. The problem was here, at the contact points, where the mechanism touched itself most frequently and most forcefully, and no adjustment to anything else would address it.

He set the forked piece down.

He thought about friction. About hardness. About the specific properties of materials formed under conditions that produced things ordinary materials weren't. He let the thinking go where it wanted to go without directing it — the specific productive passivity of someone who had learned that the best thinking happened when you stopped trying to think and let the connections form without interference.

Something pulled at the edge of it.

He didn't reach for it yet.

He looked at the window.

The light coming through it was wrong.

He processed this — the angle of it, the specific quality of afternoon light that was different from morning light in ways that were immediately readable to someone who had been reading light for five years as a primary means of knowing where in the day he was. He calculated the interval between the light he was seeing now and the light that had been coming through the window when he walked in.

He had lost track of time.

He sat with this for a moment. Not with the time itself — with the losing of it. In five years of moving through the world he had always known where the time was. Not approximately. Precisely. The position of the sun, the temperature of the air, the quality of the light — these things told him what he needed to know and he read them the way he read everything else, automatically, continuously, the reading so embedded in how he moved through the world that its absence registered like a missing sense.

He had been sitting at this table and the time had simply gone. Taken by the mechanism on the table, by the ticking of it, by the specific total absorption of a problem that had reached into him and taken every available resource without asking and without his noticing until now.

He looked at the mechanism spread across the table. At the disassembled parts. At the forked piece with its contact faces that were the problem and would remain the problem until someone found the right material to address them and he had a thought about that — the beginning of a thought, something pulling at the edge — but the compound was waiting, the rounds were in his room, the delivery was owed before the end of the day.

He put the thought away.

*"Let's continue this another time,"* he said.

Aldric looked at him. Then at the table. Then at him again — the specific look of someone who had also lost track of time and was now recalibrating.

He went and collected Ryn's commission from the end of the counter and brought it back and set it down without comment.

Ryn picked it up.

He looked at the table one more time.

He left.

Her body woke her before the light did.

Not gradually — completely, the specific full-wakefulness of someone whose body had decided that today required all of it from the first moment. She lay in the wool bed for exactly as long as it took to confirm she was awake and then she sat up.

The room was grey and quiet. The candle had been out since she fell asleep. Through the window the sky was the specific pre-dawn color of something that hadn't committed to morning yet but was working toward it.

She got up.

She put on her habit — clean, the purification she'd done last night having taken the border's grey-purple out of the hem completely, the white of it restored to something that looked like it belonged to someone who hadn't spent the previous morning at the corruption's edge watching people die. She smoothed it. She adjusted the collar the way Maret had adjusted it on the street, the fold sitting correctly.

She picked up the platter from the table where she'd left it.

---

The innkeeper was behind the desk when she came downstairs, doing the specific morning work of an inn before the inn's morning had properly begun — ledgers, keys, the quiet administrative business of a place that never fully stopped.

She looked up.

*"Good morning, sister."*

*"Good morning."* Sera set the platter on the desk. *"Thank you for the food last night. I wanted to return this and — I'd like to pay for it, if you'll tell me what I owe."*

The innkeeper looked at the platter.

She looked at her.

*"I didn't bring you any food,"* she said.

Sera looked at her.

*"Someone left a platter outside my door last night,"* she said. *"A full meal."*

*"Wasn't us,"* she said. Not defensively — just the flat statement of someone reporting an accurate fact. *"We don't do evening service. Haven't since the previous owner."*

They looked at each other for a moment — the specific mutual confusion of two people who had each assumed the other had the answer and had discovered simultaneously that neither of them did.

*"Well,"* Sera said.

*"Well,"* the innkeeper said.

She set the platter aside and ordered breakfast and ate at a table by the window while the district outside began its morning. She felt — not well, not restored to anything resembling the person she'd been two days ago — but better than yesterday. The specific incremental better of someone who had slept and eaten and was beginning to understand that the body continued regardless of what the mind was working through.

The church bell rang somewhere in the district.

She put her coin on the table and went out.

---

She arrived at the compound gate early.

The guards recognized her — or recognized the habit, which amounted to the same thing — and nodded her through to the gatehouse without requiring explanation. She sat on the bench inside and waited.

The morning came through the gatehouse window in pieces — the sound of the compound beginning its day, boots on stone, the specific productive noise of a military installation whose rhythm didn't wait for the sun to finish rising. She sat with her hands in her lap and didn't think about what she was going to say because she didn't know what she was going to say and thinking about it hadn't produced anything useful on the walk over.

After a while she heard them.

Two sets of footsteps — lighter than the soldiers', purposeful, arriving at the gate with the specific punctuality of people who were never late and didn't regard punctuality as a virtue because for them it was simply the condition of being who they were. She looked out through the gatehouse door.

Two young women. The female students — she hadn't seen them yesterday, she'd only heard them leave when Seris dismissed them. They stood at the gate with the specific bearing of people who had been trained by someone who considered bearing important, their posture the kind that looked natural because it had been practiced past the point where it required effort.

Sera stepped out of the gatehouse.

*"Good morning,"* she said.

They looked at her.

They said nothing.

Not rudely — just the specific silence of people who hadn't been given a protocol for this situation and were defaulting to the absence of protocol rather than improvising one. They looked at her the way you looked at something that had appeared where you hadn't expected anything to appear and were waiting for it to clarify what it was.

Sera looked at the gate.

She looked at the students.

She looked at the gate again.

The church bell rang.

---

Seris came around the corner.

She walked the way she'd walked through the training court yesterday — not quickly, not slowly, at the pace of someone for whom the city arranged itself rather than the other way around. The morning light caught her dark hair. Her shoes announced her on the stone the way her shoes always announced her, the specific sound of someone who had decided long ago that announcement was preferable to silence and had dressed accordingly.

The two students moved.

Not dramatically — just the specific adjustment of people whose teacher had appeared and whose bodies had registered it before their minds had finished processing it. They came to attention in a way that wasn't military and wasn't ceremonial but was something in between — the formal greeting of students to someone whose authority over them was total and was total because it had been earned rather than assigned.

*"Magister."* Both of them, simultaneously, a small precise inclination of the head.

Sera's body moved before she decided to let it move.

She copied them — the same inclination, the same timing, the word arriving in her mouth from somewhere she hadn't known it was stored.

*"Magister."*

The students looked at her.

Seris looked at her students.

*"Go ahead inside,"* she said.

They went. Their footsteps crossed the compound and faded.

Seris looked at Sera.

Sera looked at Seris.

*"Did you not hear me?"*

Sera opened her mouth. Something came out of it that wasn't quite a word.

Seris waited.

*"Go ahead inside,"* she said again. The same tone — not impatient, not unkind, just the flat repetition of someone who had said a thing once and was now saying it a second time and didn't expect to say it a third.

*"Yes, Magister,"* Sera said.

She went inside.

The corridor opened into a wider space — a waiting area off the main compound, functional, a bench along one wall, a window facing the interior courtyard. The two female students were already there. And three others — young men, the remaining students, standing with the specific easy confidence of people who had been in a place long enough to own it without thinking about it.

All five of them looked at her.

Not hostilely. Just the specific assessment of people who had not been told to expect her and were now deciding what category she belonged to. She was wearing a habit. She was standing in a military compound. She had arrived through the gate rather than through any of the channels they had come through. The calculation was visible on their faces — who is this, why is she here, what does this mean for us.

Sera looked back at them.

She didn't know why she was here. She didn't know why she'd said *yes Magister* at the gate. She didn't know what she was doing standing in a military compound with five mages who were all clearly exceptional and clearly wondering the same thing about her that she was wondering about herself.

She said nothing.

They said nothing.

They waited.

Seris arrived the way she always arrived — the shoes announcing her before the turn of the corridor revealed her, the specific sound of someone who moved through spaces without adjusting herself to them. The students moved. The formal greeting — *Magister* — delivered by all five simultaneously, the two women and the three men, the small precise inclination of the head that Sera had copied at the gate without knowing she was going to.

*"Today you'll learn to move mana through the body,"* Seris said. *"Not concentrated in the hands. Through the body — from the source of it to the point of use, the full channel. We'll work on it in the court."*

*"Yes, Magister."*

Five voices. Then five sets of footsteps moving past Sera toward the training ground, the students filing out without looking at her again — or looking at her in the specific way that managed to communicate a great deal while technically not looking.

Their footsteps faded through the compound's interior and left the corridor quiet.

Sera stayed where she was.

Seris looked at her. She didn't repeat the instruction she'd given the students. She waited with the specific patience of someone who had learned that silence was more productive than prompting and was letting it be productive now.

*"Why am I here, Magister."*

Seris turned fully toward her.

*"I told you to be here early and you came,"* she said. *"That answers my question. What's the answer to yours."*

Sera looked at her.

*"I thought — I thought you might help me find what I was looking for."*

*"And what are you looking for."*

*"I want to know about Providence."*

*"Everyone wants to know about Providence,"* Seris said. *"The church has been selling answers about Providence for longer than either of us has been alive. You had eighteen years of those answers. What do you want from me that you couldn't get from them."*

*"The truth,"* Sera said.

*"The truth."* Seris said it without inflection, neither approving nor dismissing. *"Say you find it. Say I point you at something and you look at it and it's the truth, the real thing, not the church's version. Then what. Peace? Is that what you're after — you find the truth and you finally have peace."*

*"I don't know,"* Sera said.

*"Good,"* Seris said. *"At least that's honest."* She moved to the window and looked out at the training ground where her students had begun their morning work — five figures moving through the compound's open space with the specific focused energy of people who knew exactly what they wanted and were pursuing it without complication. *"What if you don't like it. What if the truth is something you'd rather not know. What then — where does the peace go. What are you left with."*

Sera said nothing.

*"Maret chose her filling,"* Seris said. Still looking out the window. *"She told you that herself, I imagine. She's at peace. Your sisters — the ones who go out every morning and come back with less of themselves each time and go out again — most of them are at peace too, in their way. They have the work and the faith and that's enough."* She turned. *"Why couldn't you do that. Is it that you're smarter than all of them."*

*"No,"* Sera said.

*"Are you better than them."*

*"No."* The word came out with more force than she intended. *"I am not."*

*"Then what is it."*

The corridor was quiet. Outside the students moved through their forms. The compound's morning continued around them, indifferent.

*"I want to know,"* Sera said, *"if the reason Providence would allow so many of her followers to die for her is as important as their lives."* She said it carefully, the way you said things you'd been carrying for a long time and were finally setting down. *"I need to know if her will carries that weight. If those women meant less to her than whatever it is she's building toward."*

Seris watched her.

*"Once I find the answer,"* Sera said, *"then I'll worry about whether I like it."*

Something moved across Seris's face. Not approval. Not admiration. Something older and more private than either — the specific expression of someone who had said exactly those words once and was now on the other side of them and knew what the other side looked like.

She let it pass.

*"How do you intend to find it,"* she said.

*"I want to find Providence."*

Seris looked at her.

She didn't show what the statement produced in her. She let a moment pass and then said — *"And how exactly are you planning to do that."*

*"I don't know yet,"* Sera said. *"But I know where I've been looking and I know it's not there."* She looked at the floor and then back up. *"Eighteen years. ten in the capital learning what they wanted me to learn, eight years at the border doing what they wanted me to do. Every day we purified the ground and every day the rot came back. Every day we were told this was her will. The people saw us as champions and we believed it and our faith made us believe it more."* Her voice stayed level. *"And the rot is closer to the walls now than when I started. And it keeps learning. It keeps crawling. And one day it will be at the gates and the believers will be standing there asking Providence where she is, the same question I asked in an alley yesterday, and I don't want to be the person who knew and said nothing."*

*"Their faith is not your responsibility,"* Seris said.

*"No,"* Sera said. *"But the question is mine. I've been carrying it for years and the church had nothing for it. I came here because Maret looked this direction when she talked about people who ask different questions."* A pause. *"I'm starting to understand that the rot is not here to test our faith. It's not a trial Providence designed. Our methods have failed — not recently, for years, maybe longer — and something has to change."*

*"And you want to change it."*

*"Someone has to."*

*"A century of your predecessors tried,"* Seris said. *"Hundreds of them. Better resourced than you. More powerful than you. All of them at the same border pushing the same ground back the same centimeters."*

*"And you're the one who's going to change it."*

Sera put her head down.

A moment passed.

*"And why not,"* she said. Barely audible. The specific quiet of someone who had run out of louder arguments and found this one at the bottom, small and certain and not going anywhere.

Seris looked at her for a long moment.

*"I know the truth of the rot,"* she said.

Sera's head came up.

*"How."*

*"I spent years studying it,"* Seris said. *"Not opposing it. Not pushing it back. Studying it — what it is, where it comes from, what logic produces it."* She held Sera's gaze. *"I'm willing to share what I know. In exchange you'll work for me — organizing research, maintaining records, practical tasks. You'll earn your place here the way everyone earns their place here."* She said it plainly. As a transaction. As only a transaction. *"That's the arrangement. Those are the terms."*

Sera processed this.

*"Yes, Magister,"* she said.

Seris nodded once.

*"Well then."* She moved toward the door that led to the training ground. She stopped without turning. *"Are you coming to the court or are you leaving."*

Sera looked at the door.

She thought about the alley. About the red ground that her magic couldn't touch. About the question that had no floor that she'd asked in the dark with nobody listening.

*"I'm coming,"* she said.

Seris walked out.

Sera followed.

### **The Training Ground**

---

They had been attempting it for a while before she arrived.

The exercise was clear enough — Seris had told them before she left to go in and try. Move the mana through the body rather than concentrating it in the hands. They knew how to do the second thing. The first thing was what they were working out.

Bael had something visible happening. A shimmer around his arms, red-tinted, the heat of it faint but present. He held it for a few seconds at a time before it collapsed and he started again, each attempt slightly longer than the last, the specific stubborn repetition of someone who learned by forcing rather than understanding.

Iren was doing something smaller — barely visible, a green quality to the air immediately around her, stable but so contained it barely counted. She adjusted it constantly, the adjustments small and precise, working at the margins of something rather than committing to it.

The others were producing varying degrees of nothing with varying degrees of frustration about it.

*"Why is she here,"* Davan said. Not quietly.

*"No idea,"* Myre said.

*"She didn't go through trials,"* Solen said. *"We went through months of them."*

*"Maybe Magister had reasons,"* Iren said.

*"Magister always has reasons,"* Bael said. *"Doesn't mean I understand them."* He let the cowl collapse and looked at his hands. *"She's a nun. She purifies ground. That's not what we do here."*

Nobody argued with this. They went back to the exercise. The shimmer around Bael's arms rebuilt itself and held for four seconds this time before collapsing. Myre produced a sharp bright crackle that lasted less than two and left her shaking her hand like she'd touched something hot.

Then the shoes.

The specific sound of them on the stone of the corridor leading to the training ground — the announcement of someone who had decided long ago that announcement suited her better than surprise. They straightened without deciding to. The formation assembled itself the way it always assembled when she came — bodies knowing the routine before the minds had finished registering it.

Seris came through the door.

Sera behind her.

*"Magister."*

Five voices. Five precise inclinations of the head.

She had watched them from the window before coming down — had seen what each of them was doing and what each of them wasn't doing and had arrived with the full picture already assembled. She looked at the training ground the way she looked at everything — completely, briefly, the assessment done before anyone noticed it happening. 

*"A new student will be joining you today,"* she said.

She turned to Sera.

*"Introduce yourself."*

Sera looked at the five of them. At the specific quality of their attention — not hostile, just the complete assessing focus of people who had learned to read everything in their environment as relevant until proven otherwise.

*"I'm Sera,"* she said. *"It's a pleasure to join you."*

The name landed.

Just Sera. No second name after it, no family attached to it, the specific social incompleteness of someone who either didn't have one or hadn't offered it. The students looked at each other — the brief communicative efficiency of people who shared a context and were confirming that the others had caught what they had caught.

Seris had no family name either. The name Dahl was a name she manifested, She had learned to ignore this form of comment years ago.

*"She'll also be operating as my practitioner,"* Seris said. *"Introduce yourselves to your new classmate."*

Bael went first.

*"Bael Vorenthal."* He said it the way he said everything — with the flat assurance of someone for whom stating a name was simply a formality because the name was going to mean something regardless.

*"Iren Thessaly."* Quietly, precisely, the name fitting the person saying it.

*"Davan Astorel."* A nod with it — the specific economy of someone who communicated in movement as readily as in words.

*"Solen Arenthios."* Easy, unhurried, the name offered the way water found its level.

*"Myre Telvaris."* Direct, no ceremony, her eyes staying on Sera a fraction longer than the others' had.

Sera looked at each of them in turn.

*"What type of magic do you use,"* Bael said.

*"Purification magic,"* Sera said. *"And minor healing."*

*"So you're an actual nun."* Not a question. *"Not just dressed like one."*

*"Yes,"* Sera said. *"Eighteen years. I joined the church at six. I worked the border for eight."*

The whispers moved between the students — not hidden, not intended to be hidden, the specific low register of people communicating something they didn't mind being heard.

*"So you left the border,"* Bael said, *"to come work for Magister Seris."* A pause, measured, the pause of someone arriving at the thing they wanted to say. *"I thought you nuns loved dying out there."*

It arrived on Sera's face before she could manage it.

Her mind went to the morning — to the field, to the arm-cut sister's good hand slipping off the stump, to Wenna in the courtyard, to Lise's voice saying *it must be beautiful to die doing Providence's will* — and it was all of it, all at once, visible for a moment in the specific way things were visible when they were too large to contain on short notice.

*"That's enough."*

Seris. Flat, level, the specific two-word register of someone who had made a decision about where a thing ended and was communicating the decision. Not protection. Not pity. Just the clean authority of someone who decided the conversation was finished.

It was finished.

---

*"Bael,"* Seris said. *"Show me what you were doing before I came in."*

He moved to the center of the training ground. He settled his weight. He focused.

The cowl built around him — a shimmer of red heat that spread from his core outward, his mana moving through his body in the visible way that significant output made visible, the nature of it flame, aggressive, the specific character of someone whose magic matched the person producing it. It was powerful. The output was significant. Even from where Sera stood she could feel the heat of it — not just warmth but a directed heat, the kind that had intention in it.

But his hands burned brighter than everything else. The concentration there was double what it was anywhere else on his body — the years of learning to cast through his hands leaving a groove in him that the exercise was supposed to undo, the groove resisting. His cowl was uneven. The inconsistency was costing him — more mana than the same output should have required, the inefficiency visible in how quickly his jaw set.

*"Hold it,"* Seris said.

He held it. His face tightened.

*"Why is the mana heavier in your hands."*

He looked at his hands. He tried to move the concentration away from them — redistribute, even out, do what she was asking. The hands thinned. The rest of the body didn't compensate in time. The cowl became uneven in the other direction — too little in the hands now, not enough elsewhere, the whole thing requiring more force to maintain than he had available.

He pushed harder.

The cowl broke.

Seris said nothing. She moved to Iren.

Iren's cowl was green and calm — barely visible at the edges, the nature of it earthy, patient, the specific quality of something that grew rather than burned. Stable. Even across her body, no concentration point pulling harder than the others. But too small. Too conservative. The cowl so thin it offered nothing — stability without substance, the form correct and the content insufficient.

No comment. She moved to Davan.

Davan's was wind-natured — light, fast, moving through him in visible pulses rather than a steady flow, the mana cycling through his body in irregular bursts that briefly illuminated his outline and then dimmed between pulses. Interesting. Not what the exercise required but interesting.

Solen's was fluid — water-natured, the most even distribution she'd seen from any of them, the mana moving through his body without favoring any point. But it bled at the edges. The cowl dispersed outward rather than holding, the boundary of it permeable, the mana leaving him faster than he replenished it.

Myre's came up sharp and bright — lightning-natured, precise, the output clean and significant for approximately three seconds before it collapsed entirely. No degradation, no gradual failure. Just present and then absent, the switch between the two states instantaneous.

Seris reached Sera.

All of them watched. Bael watching the hardest — the specific focused attention of someone who had formed an opinion and was waiting for the evidence to confirm it.

*"They taught you to sense the divine energy," Seris said. "Providence's blessing — the energy that occupies the space around you. They showed you how to absorb it and push it out through your palms to purify. In this space you'll call that energy mana. That's what it is. That's what we'll call it.*

*"They taught you to feel it through your skin. To absorb it and direct it outward through your hands to purify the ground. Today I want you to feel it and let it stay. Let it engulf your body. Do not push it out — let your body accept it instead."*

Sera looked at her hands.

She had been pushing the energy out through her hands for eighteen years. The motion of absorbing and releasing was so embedded in her that her hands already knew what to do before her mind had finished forming the instruction. The undoing of that — the keeping of it, the staying — was not something she knew how to do yet.

She tried to understand the instruction before she tried to execute it.

She focused. She felt the mana — felt it the way she had always felt it, the specific familiar presence of something her body recognized without effort, the thing she'd been reaching toward since she was six years old in the capital's chapel. She felt it and instead of gathering it toward her hands she let it spread. Let it come in through her skin and stay — not directing it anywhere, just receiving it, the body opening to something it had always been taught to immediately redirect.

Her hands pulled toward it anyway.

She stopped them.

The mana spread through her body unevenly — more here, less there, the distribution rough, the specific imprecision of a first attempt at reversing an eighteen-year pattern. She absorbed more than she meant to. Significantly more. The cowl that formed around her was larger than she intended, the output exceeding what she had planned by a margin that surprised her.

And it was bright.

Not red like Bael's. Not green like Iren's. Bright — a warm quality to it, the nature of it something that the five students looked at and reached for the closest category available to them and found it insufficient. It burned without heat. It illuminated without being light exactly. It held for less time than Bael's had held and consumed more mana doing it and when it collapsed it collapsed completely.

The training ground was quiet.

Seris looked at Sera.

She said nothing.

She turned back to the group.

*"Again,"* she said. *"All of you. From the beginning."*

---

*He was back in the room before the morning had committed to itself.*

*The materials were where he'd left them the night before — organized, separated, everything in its position. He cleared the table and began. The casings had come from Aldric that morning, precise to the tolerances he'd specified, the corrections made, each one examined and passed before he put it in the bag. Now he seated each round — the propellant compound first, packed to the specific density the formula required, then the projectile, then the primer, each step executed with the focused efficiency of someone for whom this was simply the execution of a plan that had been complete in his head since the night before.*

*An hour.*

*He put the completed order in the bag and went out.*

*The gatehouse was quiet.*

*Ryn sat on the bench with the completed order beside him and waited for the guards to take him to Vorne's office. He had been waiting for approximately four minutes. He knew this without checking anything — the quality of the light through the window, the sounds of the compound settling into its mid-morning rhythm, the specific elapsed texture of four minutes of sitting in a functional room with nothing to do.*

*He looked out the window.*

*The training ground was visible from here. He recognized her immediately — Seris, moving between her students with the specific economy of someone for whom teaching was a physical practice rather than a verbal one, her attention going from one student to the next with the complete sequential focus of someone who processed the world in full rather than in approximations. Her students were doing something with mana that he didn't have a framework for but read correctly as significant — a visible quality to the air immediately around each of them, different for each one, the nature of it varying in color and texture and stability in ways that communicated something about the person producing it.*

*He watched.*

*Then he saw the white habit.*

*He looked closer.*

*Gold hair tied back. The habit clean — no border staining, no evidence of yesterday on it at all. She was standing at the edge of the group with the specific quality of someone who was present in a space without yet belonging to it. She looked better than yesterday. Not well — better. The specific difference between someone at the absolute bottom of the worst day of their life and someone the morning after it, the body having done what bodies did overnight and produced something that was not recovery but was at least its beginning.*

*He decided to go down.*

---

*He walked out to the training ground.*

*It was her turn.*

*He was still approaching when she focused — he saw the moment of it, the specific internal gathering of someone about to attempt something, and then the cowl formed around her. Bright. Warm. The nature of it something his eye went to and couldn't quite place, the brightness of it not quite fire and not quite light and not quite anything he had a name for. It held for a moment and then collapsed and she stood with her hands slightly raised and the specific expression of someone assessing their own attempt.*

*He was close now.*

*The tree arrived before he could account for it — the spring light, the new leaves, the warmth of sitting somewhere that had nothing urgent about it. Two seconds. Gone. The warmth and the emptiness arriving together the way they always arrived together, departing the same way, leaving him standing in a military training ground in the morning with the specific residue of something he couldn't hold onto no matter how still he tried to be when it came.*

*He kept walking.*

*"Good morning," he said. "I apologize for interrupting."*

*The students looked at him.*

*The students looked at him.*

*Bael looked at him the way you looked at someone who had embarrassed you in front of the person whose opinion mattered most to you and had done it without apparent effort and had walked away smiling. Not curiosity. Not assessment. Just the specific flat quality of someone who had filed a name under a category and the category was not favorable.*

*The others watched — not for Bael's cue, just the specific attention of people who remembered the crater in the wall and the soldier almost falling backward and were present for whatever came next.*

*Sera looked at him with no recognition at all.*

*"Good morning, Magister," Ryn said.* 

*Seris turned around.*

*"Good morning," she said.*

*“My name is Ryn Casvel. Trader, inventor, entrepreneur. I didn't get the chance to introduce myself properly yesterday — I wanted to remedy that. It's a pleasure to make your acquaintance."*

*Seris looked at him.*

*"And an alchemist," Seris said.*

*Ryn smiled — not the performance smile, the real one, brief, the specific response of someone who had just been seen more clearly than they expected and found the accuracy amusing rather than threatening.*

*"Far from it," he said. "Just a humble pyrotechnician."*

*Seris looked at him knowing that even his humility was lying.*

*She filed it.*

*"Seris Dahl," she said. "Magister, western brigade."*

---

*He walked toward Sera.*

*The students watched.* 

*"Good morning, sister," Ryn said. "A pleasure to see you again."*

*Something moved across Sera's face.*

*Small. Almost nothing. The word sister arriving and producing a response she managed before it fully surfaced — a fraction of a second where something was visible and then wasn't. He caught it the way he caught everything — automatically, completely, filed before he had consciously decided to file it.*

*He had already read the rest. The clean habit, the military compound, the morning light showing her standing here rather than at any monastery. He had a conclusion. He kept it to himself.*

*She looked at him.*

*"I'm sorry," she said. "I don't — have we met?"*

*"Don't be sorry," he said. "I'm just glad you're doing better."*

*She looked at him — the specific look of someone trying to work out how a stranger could know she hadn't been doing well. She didn't find the answer. She thanked him anyway, the warmth of it genuine, given freely to someone who had no particular claim to it.*

*"I'm Sera," she said. "Thank you for your concern— I'm not sure how you knew , but thank you."*

*"You're doing better," he said. "That much is clear."*

*The warmth of her response was genuine — not performed, not reflexive, just the specific quality of someone whose warmth kept being given even to people who had no particular claim to it, who had survived everything and kept being warm anyway. She thanked him again. He received it the way he received things that didn't fit his usual categories — without knowing what to do with it, which was itself unusual, which he noted and did not examine.*

*"Well," he said. "My apologies again for interrupting. I'll leave you to your work."*

*He turned to go.*

*His eyes met Bael's on the way.*

*He gave him the smirk — small, unhurried, the specific expression of someone who knew exactly what effect they'd had and found it quietly amusing and wasn't going to pretend otherwise. He held it for exactly long enough and then walked inside.*

---

*Vorne's office was the same as yesterday. The desk, the greatsword on the rack, the specific organized economy of a man who thought in terms of function and maintained his space accordingly. The remaining payment sat on the desk in a sealed document — the second writ, the balance of what was owed after the initial deposit.*

*Ryn picked it up.*

*"The rounds," Vorne said. "My men will test them this afternoon."*

*"They'll hold," Ryn said.*

*Vorne looked at him with the specific expression of someone who had learned to distinguish between confidence and certainty and was assessing which one he was looking at. He decided.*

*"I expect they will," he said.*

*They shook hands.*

---

*He walked out of the compound into the western district's morning.*

*The sealed writ went into his coat alongside the field journal and the notes he'd torn from the pages at the garden yesterday. He walked with the specific unhurried pace of someone who had nowhere urgent to be and was using the walk to think.*

*He thought about the clock mechanism on Aldric's table — the coiled ribbon, the club-toothed wheel, the contact faces that needed something he couldn't yet figure out. He thought about the recoil problem, still unsolved, sitting in his field journal as a question without an answer.*

*He thought about Sera.*

*Not analytically. That was still the thing — still, even now, still not analytically. Just the word sister on her face and what it produced, and the warmth that came through regardless, and the specific fact that she was standing in a military training ground the morning after the worst day of her life and had said thank you to a stranger who had said good afternoon to her on a street and then appeared in a training court and interrupted her exercise.*

*He noted, without examining it too closely, that he already had reasons to come back.*

*The compound gate was behind him.*

*The western district was ahead.*

*He kept walking.*

*Seris called the end of the session the way she called everything — without ceremony, just the flat word that meant the thing was finished.*

*"That's enough for today."*

*The students came out of their attempts with varying degrees of relief and varying degrees of frustration — Bael the latter, his jaw set in the specific way of someone who had been given a problem he couldn't solve through force and found the experience personally offensive. The others filed into the corridor in the easy loose movement of people transitioning from one part of the day to the next.*

*Seris spoke briefly to the group. Tomorrow. What to work on before then. The specific practical instructions of someone who treated the interval between sessions as productive time rather than rest. The three young men nodded and peeled off toward the male quarters.*

*The two women stopped at the gate.*

*Sera stood at the gate behind them.*

*She looked at the compound around her — the training ground, the corridors, the specific institutional architecture of a place that had been built for a purpose and communicated that purpose in every line of it. She looked at the gate.*

*She opened the coin pouch.*

*Maret's purse — she hadn't counted it properly before. She tipped the coins into her palm now and did the count. Her fingers moved through them. She did it again to be sure.*

*One more night at the inn. Maybe two if she ate carefully. After that the arithmetic produced an answer she didn't want to look at directly.*

*She looked at it anyway.*

*Right, she thought. Right.*

*She closed the pouch. She looked at the gate. She thought about Seris saying be at this gate early tomorrow and about what tomorrow looked like from where she was standing and about the specific distance between what she had and what the next week required.*

*"Come on."*

*She looked up.*

*Myre Telvaris was standing three steps away, already turned back toward her, with the specific expression of someone who had somewhere to be and had been asked to do something on the way and was doing it with the minimum available patience.*

*"We don't have all day," Myre said.*

*Sera looked at her.*

*"I'm sorry," she said. "I don't — where are we going."*

*Myre looked at her with the expression of someone deciding whether to answer this or simply start walking and let the destination explain itself.*

*She started walking.*

*Sera followed.*

*Iren Thessaly fell into step beside her — not beside Myre, beside Sera, the specific placement of someone who had assessed a situation and decided that the situation required a different approach than the one currently being deployed.*

*"Magister Seris arranged a room for you," Iren said. "In the dormitory. With us." A pause. "She told us before the session. While you were inside with her."*

*Sera looked at her.*

*"She did," she said.*

*Not a question. Just the specific sound of someone receiving information that reconfigured several things simultaneously — the coin pouch in her hand, the arithmetic she'd just done, the specific relief of an answer arriving before the question had fully formed into something she'd have to ask out loud.*

*"She did," Iren confirmed.*

*They walked.*

*Sera looked at the back of Myre's head moving ahead of them — the specific brisk pace of someone who considered the task assigned and was completing it without editorial. She looked at Iren beside her, who had offered the information with the calm matter-of-factness of someone for whom being useful was simply the correct response to a situation that required it.*

*She thought about the dormitory at the monastery. The grid of beds. The empty ones. The sound of the sister crying in the dark.*

*Different, she thought. This will be different.*

*She didn't know yet if different meant better. She knew it meant she had somewhere to sleep tonight that didn't cost her the last of what Maret had given her. She knew it meant tomorrow morning existed and she knew where she needed to be when it arrived.*

*For now that was sufficient.*

*"Thank you," she said to Iren.*

*Iren nodded once.*

*Ahead of them Myre pushed open a door without looking back to see if they were following — confident they were, or indifferent to whether they were, or some specific combination of both that Sera hadn't yet learned to read.*

*She followed anyway.*

*The dormitory wing was quieter than the rest of the compound — fewer footsteps, fewer voices, the specific hush of a space built for rest rather than work. Myre pushed the door open without ceremony and walked in first, leaving Sera and Iren to follow.*

*It was nothing like the monastery's dormitory.*

*No grid of identical beds stretching the length of a long hall. This was smaller — six beds total, three to a side, each one with its own narrow shelf and a chest at its foot. Two of the beds were clearly Iren's and Myre's, marked by small differences — a folded cloak here, a row of carefully arranged vials there. The other four sat empty, stripped down to bare frames and thin mattresses.*

*"This one's free," Myre said, pointing to the bed nearest the window without much interest. "Take it or one of the others. Doesn't matter to me."*

*"Thank you," Sera said.*

*Iren moved past her toward the far wall, gesturing as she went. "Washroom's through there, shared between this wing and the one across the hall. Water runs cold most mornings unless you're up before the soldiers — they use it first and don't leave much warm behind them."*

*"There's a chest for your things," Myre added, already sitting on her own bed and pulling off her boots. "Nobody touches anyone else's. That's the one rule that actually gets enforced around here."*

*Sera looked at the empty bed by the window. She had nothing to put in the chest beside it — no spare clothes, no possessions beyond the small purse Maret had given her and the habit she was wearing.*

*"Is there somewhere I could—" she started, then stopped, unsure how to finish the question.*

*"Get supplies?" Iren said, reading the hesitation correctly. "There's a quartermaster near the eastern barracks. Basic things — blankets, a second set of clothes — Magister usually arranges it for new arrivals. She'll have already sent word, probably."*

*"Magister already arranged your supplies," Myre said. "She sent word before training even started this morning. You'll find it laid out somewhere near here, probably."*

*She glanced around the room and spotted it — a folded set of clothes sitting on the chest at the foot of  one of the empty beds, plain and grey-toned, the standard cut worn by everyone attached to the compound who wasn't soldier or officer.*

*"There it is," Myre said, noticing it at the same time. "Quick work, even for her."* 

*"You'll figure out the rest as you go," Iren said. "Everyone does."* 

*They went to the washrooms together — Myre first, brisk and efficient about it, in and out before Sera had finished untying her hair. Iren took longer, methodical in the way she did everything, and Sera went last, the habit folded over one arm, a thin towel borrowed from the shelf by the door.* 

*The room was communal — a long stone trough fed by a pipe in the wall, no partitions, no privacy beyond whatever courtesy the other women in the compound extended each other by habit. She'd grown up in rooms like this. Eighteen years in dormitories and shared quarters had worn the strangeness out of her long before she ever needed it to.*

*She undressed, set the habit aside on a dry stretch of stone, and washed quickly in water as cold as promised.*

*When she finished she dried herself, dressed again in the habit — there was nothing else to put on yet — and carried the towel back folded over her arm.*

*The room was quiet when she returned. Myre already settling into her bed, the single lamp between the beds casting most of the space in low gold light. Iren glanced up as she came in but said nothing.*

*Sera knelt at her own chest.*

*She unfastened the habit there, in front of them, without particular self-consciousness — the same unremarkable practicality of changing in a room full of other women that she'd known her whole life. The white of it was pale in the lamplight, the fabric worn soft from eighteen years of wear and the purification she'd worked into it the night before. She folded it the way she always folded it, corners matched, the motion automatic even now.*

*The habit is yours, Maret had said. Whatever else happens — the habit is yours. You earned it.*

*She laid it carefully into the chest. Not discarded — kept. Hers, the way Maret had told her it would always be hers, regardless of where she went or what she became from here.*

*She picked up the grey uniform.*

*It was simple. Unremarkable. Nothing like the habit's specific weight or history — just plain cloth, cut for function, the kind of thing a hundred other people in this compound wore without a second thought. She put it on slowly, feeling the strangeness of it against her skin, the particular unfamiliarity of wearing something that didn't carry eighteen years inside it.*

*She closed the chest.*

*Across the room, Myre had already gone quiet, her breathing settling into sleep. Iren was still awake, watching the lamp flicker, her expression unreadable in the low light.*

*"Goodnight," Sera said.*

*"Goodnight," Iren said.*

*She lay down. The bed was unfamiliar, the ceiling above her a different shape than the one she'd memorized over eight years at the border branch. She closed her eyes and let the day finally finish with her.*

# 16 \-The Cabin Between Worlds 2

### **Chapter Fourteen —  The Cabin Between Worlds 2** 

---

The rabbit was good — better than he'd expected for something killed at that distance with a rock. They'd cleaned it together at the camp's edge, Mara's hands surprisingly steady once the work began, and now it cooked over the fire he'd allowed himself once they were far enough from the corruption's edge that a small flame wouldn't carry.

She ate quickly. He ate the way he ate everything — without ceremony, fuel rather than pleasure.

*"Where did you learn to hunt like that,"* she said.

*"Caen taught me."*

*"Ah. Of course. Caen taught you."* She said the name with the specific exaggeration of someone testing how a word sounded when you said it enough times. *"And where is this Caen now."*

*"He left a while ago."* Varen looked at the fire. *"He'll come back. He always does."*

*"Did he teach you to fight too?"*

*"Yes."*

*"Why."*

*"Because I need to be strong."*

*"No dummy — I mean."* She set down what was left of her share. *"What does teaching you do for him. What does he get out of it."*

Varen looked at her.

*"I don't know,"* he said.

She stared at him.

*"How long have you known him."*

*"Twelve years."*

*"Twelve years."* She said it like the number itself was the problem. *"That's older than I am. You're telling me you've been training with this man for twelve years and you never once asked why."*

*"No."*

*"Why not."*

*"We didn't talk much."*

*"I can see that,"* she said.

---

The sun was most of the way down. The fire had settled into the steady low burn that meant it would last the night without much tending. Mara had gone quiet, the specific quiet of someone processing twelve years of a relationship she couldn't make sense of, and Varen had gone still in the way he went still when there was nothing immediate left to assess.

Neither of them noticed her.

She had been there since he first spoke the name — hours earlier, on the road, the word arriving from his mouth and landing in her with the specific weight of something she had been told, explicitly, generations of envoys before her had been told, was never to be spoken. She had stayed close since then, unseen, watching to see what would come of a name like that being loose in the world from someone with no business carrying it.

Nothing had come of it.

He'd said it once, plainly, without understanding what he'd said, and then he and the girl had moved on to other things — the corruption, the commission, the dead at the battle site — and the name had dissolved into the rest of the conversation as if it weighed no more than anything else either of them had said.

She had followed them all the way to the camp and stayed at its edge through the evening, through the rabbit, through the fire neither of them noticed her sitting just beyond.

She was still watching when the force took her.

---

It arrived without warning and without a sound any version of her senses could process — not pulled so much as removed, the camp and the fire and the two figures beside it gone in the same instant, replaced by wood walls and a familiar low ceiling and the specific dimensions of a cabin that wasn't a cabin.

Varen's head turned, very slightly, toward the treeline.

A flicker. Something that had been there and now wasn't — gone too fast to identify, gone before the feeling of it had fully registered. He looked at the space where it had been for a moment.

Then he went back to the fire.

He filed it, the way he filed things he didn't understand. To be resolved later, if it resolved at all.

---

Caen's hand was already at her throat when the cabin finished assembling around her.

*"What do you think you're doing,"* he said.

*"I can ask you the same th—."*

His grip closed before the sentence finished — not a warning, a correction, the specific pressure of someone communicating that the question itself had been a mistake.

*"You are in no position to ask me anything."*

She couldn't speak. Her hands came up instinctively and found nothing to do about the grip and stopped.

He loosened it. Slightly. Enough.

*"Why are you watching him."*

*"I wanted to know,"* she managed, *"why you haven't cultivated him."*

He said nothing. He let her continue, which was its own kind of permission.

*"I saw his life force. In the inn yesterday. It's impressive — more than impressive. He would be the finest meal the Devourer has had in so long. I thought —"* She swallowed against his hand. *"I thought maybe you were letting him grow. Saving him for something larger."*

*"And what else did you learn."*

*"I heard him say the name."*

Silence.

*"A few hours ago,"* she said. *"To the girl. The name we are not permitted to speak."*

*"You told him that name."*

*"why."*

*"Why would you te—."*

The grip tightened — not a correction this time. Something heavier than that, the specific weight of a hand deciding whether a loose end was worth the trouble of becoming a problem later, when the cleaner solution was available now.

---

The knock came from nowhere — there was no door, there had never been a door, and the sound of knuckles on wood arrived anyway, three measured taps against a surface that didn't exist.

The cabin ended.

Not faded — ended, the wood walls and the low ceiling gone in the same instant they had arrived, the void reasserting itself around all three of them with nothing left to mark where the construct had been.

The voice came from everywhere and nowhere, serpentine, unhurried.

*"Now, now. Old friend. Let's not turn on each other so quickly."*

Caen did not release her.

*"This isn't your concern, Weaver."*

*"My servant says otherwise."*

*"Your servant."* Caen's voice carried something sharp underneath its flatness. *"The envoys are under my command. Not yours."*

*"Mm."* The Weaver's shape moved somewhere in the dark beyond them — not approaching directly, circling, the specific motion of something that preferred to arrive at a thing sideways. *"And yet this one finds herself in need of new employment. I'm sure you wouldn't object."*

The pressure in the void shifted — two auras testing each other's edges, neither yielding, the specific tension of two powers who had measured each other many times before and knew exactly how far the other could be pushed without consequence.

Caen let her go.

Entirely. His hand simply opened and she dropped, catching herself on nothing, the void offering no floor to land on and no need for one.

*"Leave us,"* the Weaver said.

Lyris left.

---

*"Stay out of my way, Weaver."*

The serpentine shape moved closer, spiraling slowly around where Caen stood — the specific posture of something that intimidated through proximity and patience rather than direct confrontation, a predator that preferred to be felt before it was seen.

*"And if I don't, Signus."*

*"I was there,"* Caen said, *"when the Devourer decided you were worth something. He let you force your way up through the ranks during the war. He watched you take territory that wasn't yours to take and decided, for his own reasons, to allow it."* A pause. *"The war ended. You have given him nothing since. He sees that."*

*"Shut up."*

*"You know he sees that."*

*"Shut up."* The Weaver's voice lost some of its languor.

*"How stable do you think your position is,"* Caen said. *"How long do you think it will be before he decides you are worth more to him as sustenance than as a general."*

*"Shut your mouth."*

The words had found something. Caen could feel it in the way the Weaver's aura contracted — not retreat, but the specific tightening of something that had just been struck somewhere it didn't have armor.

*"This is the last time I tell you, Weaver,"* Caen said. *"Stay out of my way."*

A long pause.

*"Don't be so sure,"* the Weaver said.

He withdrew — the spiral around Caen unwinding, his presence receding into the void's deeper dark until there was nothing left of him to feel.

---

The void took its time settling.

It had no settling to do, properly — no dust, no echo, nothing physical that needed to find rest after a disturbance. But Caen stood in the space where the cabin had been anyway, motionless, the way he stood when there was work to do that wasn't visible from outside him.

He ran the encounter back.
