Not the threat itself — the threat had been the easy part, the part that resolved itself the moment he understood what Weaver actually wanted. Weaver hadn't come because he cared what happened to one envoy. He'd come because he was already watching, already positioned close enough to intervene the instant it became useful to him. That was the detail that mattered. Not the confrontation. The timing of it.

He should have expected it. He hadn't, quite, and the gap between expecting it and being surprised by it was small but real, and he didn't like that it was there at all.

---

He turned to the other matter.

He hadn't killed her. He let that sit in him plainly, without dressing it up as anything other than what it was — not mercy, not hesitation, just arithmetic. A dead envoy solved nothing. The name was already spoken, already heard, already sitting somewhere inside her whether she lived or not. Killing her now would not unspeak it. It would only hand Weaver a body and a reason to ask questions louder than he was already asking them.

Better she lived, accounted for, watched.

Better the problem stayed small and contained in one place than scattered into something he could no longer locate.

---

What he knew was simple. She had heard the name. She'd said as much herself, and he believed her on that point because there had been no reason for her to volunteer it otherwise — she could have denied everything and he might never have confirmed it.

What he didn't know was the rest of it.

He turned the conversation over again — what Varen had said, what the girl beside him had said, the specific order of it. He hadn't been close enough to hear all of it directly; he'd felt it the way he felt most things involving Varen now, secondhand, through the particular disturbance a name like that made in the world when it was spoken aloud by someone with no business carrying it. He suspected — he could not confirm — that there had been more to it. That somewhere in that conversation Varen had said something beyond the name itself. A reason. An intention.

If she'd heard that too, the problem was no longer a name floating loose in the world.

It was a name attached to a purpose.

And purpose was the one thing Weaver would not be able to resist chewing on.

---

There was one thing working in his favor, and he turned it over carefully because he didn't fully trust it to hold.

Varen had never said why.

Caen didn't know this with certainty — he hadn't heard every word — but he knew Varen, knew the particular shape of his silences, knew that twelve years of training a boy who didn't ask questions had produced someone who also didn't often answer the ones that mattered with more than the truth required and nothing further. If Varen had said *I'm going to find him* and stopped there, the sentence was a fact without a motive attached, and a fact without a motive was harder for someone like Weaver to weaponize.

It was thin. It wouldn't hold forever. Eventually Varen would have a reason he could put into words, and eventually he'd say it to someone, and Caen had no way of controlling when that happened or who was listening when it did.

---

The actual problem remained.

He had told Weaver, plainly, that the envoys answered to him. That was true on paper and had been true in practice for longer than Weaver had held any rank worth noting. But Lyris had gone looking on her own initiative, had reported to Weaver before she'd reported to him, had let herself be claimed at the threshold of a confrontation without resisting it. The chain of command existed. The loyalty behind it did not — not entirely, not anymore, not where it mattered.

He couldn't kill the channel. He'd just decided that.

He couldn't seal it through threat alone — he'd made the threat, twice now, and Weaver had answered both times with *don't be so sure,* which was not the response of someone who intended to comply.

He needed something else. A different lever. Something that made staying loyal to him worth more to her than whatever Weaver was offering, or something that made the information itself worth less by the time it reached him.

He didn't have it yet.

He stood alone in the void for a long time, turning the problem over without finding its edges, and somewhere beyond him in the dark, a boy he'd raised was asleep beside a fire he hadn't told anyone to build, with a name in his mouth that was already further from his control than he wanted to admit.

The fire had burned low and steady, the way he'd built it to.

Mara was asleep on the other side of it, curled in on herself, her breathing even. Varen lay with his back against the slope of the hill and didn't sleep yet. Her questions were still moving through him, slow, without urgency, the way unresolved things moved through him when there was nothing else demanding his attention.

*Why did Caen do all of it.*

He turned it over. The wolf. The year of recovery, the broth spooned into him when he couldn't lift his own arm, the years after that — the knife drills, the silences, the leaving and the returning. Twelve years and he had never once asked what any of it was for. He tried to ask now, lying in the dark, and found he didn't have the right question. Caen was Caen. The fact of him had never required a reason before. It didn't produce one now just because Mara had asked.

He let it go.

He closed his eyes and arranged himself the way he always arranged himself to sleep — on his side, knees drawn slightly, one hand never far from the knife, his body settling into stillness without ever fully leaving its post. Ears tuned to the wind, to the specific absence of sound that meant nothing was moving nearby. Twelve years of training had made even his rest a kind of readiness. He had woken from a dead sleep before, knife already in hand, before his mind had caught up to why.

It was a good system.

It had exactly one gap, and the gap was shaped like the man who'd built it.

---

Caen sat down across the fire without announcing himself.

He had come straight from the void, the confrontation with Weaver still settling in him the way confrontations like that always settled — slowly, incompletely. He looked at Varen first. The position was correct. Knees drawn, hand near the blade, breathing slow and even — every detail exactly as he'd taught it, the posture so thoroughly absorbed that the boy had stopped needing to think about it years ago.

He looked at the girl.

She had curled into herself completely, knees to her chest, one hand twitching slightly against her own collarbone. He watched her for a moment before he understood — she was talking, very quietly, the words too soft and slurred to make out individually, but the rhythm of them unmistakable. Counting. Numbers murmured into the dark, gold, then silver, then gold again, the small ledger of her sleeping mind running its tally without her permission. Somewhere in the middle of it she giggled — quiet, private, delighted by some sum only she could see. 

He watched them both for a while.

He didn't reach for the fire. He didn't need to, and there was no reason to leave evidence of himself behind — and yet his hand found a length of the gathered wood anyway, and he fed two pieces into the flame before he could decide not to, the fire taking them slowly, the light strengthening by a degree that would last the rest of the night without further tending.

He stayed a while longer.

Then he left.

---

Varen woke sometime before dawn, the way he always woke — completely, all at once, no transition between sleep and alert.

The fire was higher than he remembered leaving it. He looked at the wood — more of it gone into the flame than the night should have required, the burn steady and strong instead of the low husband he'd built it to be.

He looked at Mara.

She hadn't moved. If anything she'd gone deeper — mouth open now, a thin trail of drool catching the firelight, dead to the world in the specific way of someone who hadn't fed wood to anything in her sleep.

He looked at the fire again.

Something had been here.

He didn't pursue it. He filed it, the way he filed the flicker he'd caught at the treeline hours ago — a fact without an explanation, set aside to resolve itself later or never. He got up. He walked the edge of the camp once, checking the dark beyond the firelight, finding nothing that confirmed or denied anything.

He sat back down.

He went back to sleep.

# 17- A Trader A Wolf And A Thief

### **Chapter Seventeen — A Trader A Wolf And A Thief**

---

He was back under the same tree before the morning had fully decided what kind of day it wanted to be.

The garden hadn't changed since yesterday. Same shade, same green-broken light, same indifferent calm of a public space. He sat where he'd sat before. He opened the field journal to the page he'd left half-finished — the sketches of the stock, the chemical notation, the crossed-out attempts at a formula that shaped the recoil differently rather than simply reducing it.

He looked at it for a long time without writing anything.

*The recoil is not a flaw in the design,* he thought. *It's a consequence of the design.*

He turned the idea over the way he turned everything over — slowly, from every angle, looking for where it broke.

A bullet at rest had no motion. After firing, it had a great deal of motion, moving in one direction at considerable speed. Nothing had created that motion from nothing — it had been *exchanged.* The explosion pushed the bullet forward; by the same exact measure, something had to be pushed backward. The weapon. The hand holding the weapon. The shoulder behind the hand.

He hadn't built a flaw into the rifle.

He'd built a law into it. One that applied everywhere, to everything, that he simply hadn't had a clean way to name before this morning. *For every push forward, an equal push back.* He didn't know if anyone else had put words to this. He suspected, somewhere, someone probably had — the world was old, and full of people who thought carefully about things — but he hadn't read it, hadn't been taught it, had simply arrived at it himself sitting under a tree with a torn-up field journal in his lap.

It didn't matter who'd thought of it first.

What mattered was that it couldn't be avoided. Only managed.

He closed his eyes for a moment.

*If the backward push can't be removed,* he thought, *then it has to be absorbed. Spread out. Slowed down enough that the body can survive receiving it.*

Steel didn't do that. Steel transmitted force almost perfectly — efficient, but in entirely the wrong direction for a soldier's shoulder. He needed something that behaved differently depending on how fast the force arrived. Something that would sit calm and soft against a man's body all day, and then, in the single instant the round fired, change completely — go rigid just long enough to catch the shock and spread it wide, then soften again before the next breath.

He didn't have that material.

He knew, with the same certainty he applied to everything, exactly one person in this city who might.

He closed the journal and stood up.

---

Aldric's forge was as it always was — too bright for a fire with no bellows, the wall pipe doing its quiet work, the air smelling of hot metal and something faintly mineral underneath it.

*"Trader,"* Aldric said, not looking up from the bench. *"Did you find something for our problem?"*

*"No,"* Ryn said. *"Unfortunately my mind's been on another one. I was hoping you could help me with it."*

Aldric set down his tool.

*"What is it."*

Ryn placed the combustion chamber on the counter between them — the small brass cylinder, scorched faintly at one end, the same one that had put a crater in Vorne's training-court wall.

*"Steel isn't absorbing the impact the way I need it to,"* he said. *"I need something that can take the force of the combustion and not simply pass it straight through to whoever's holding the weapon."*

Aldric picked it up. Turned it. Looked at the scoring on the inside with the specific attention of someone who'd spent a lifetime reading what fire did to metal.

*"Of course it isn't,"* he said. *"Knowing you, you've put more force into this little thing than anyone alive has put into something this size."*

Ryn laughed — short, caught out, the laugh of someone who knew exactly how accurate the accusation was.

He explained it the way he'd worked it out under the tree — not with the name of any law, because he had none to give it, just the shape of the idea. Push something forward hard enough, and something equal pushes back. There was no way to fire a round with enough force to crater stone without that same force trying to put the shooter on the ground behind it.

Aldric listened without interrupting.

*"So you need something soft,"* he said, when Ryn finished. *"And hard. At the same time."* He set the chamber down. *"That can't be done. Not to my knowledge. Soft things give — that's what makes them soft, and it's also what makes them useless against something moving that fast. Hard things hold their shape — which is exactly why they don't absorb anything, they just hand the blow straight on through."*

*"I know,"* Ryn said.

*"Then you already know there's no answer."*

*"There's an answer,"* Ryn said. *"It's just not a material that decides what it is in advance."*

Aldric looked at him.

*"It needs to be one thing while it's resting,"* Ryn said, *"and a different thing the instant force hits it. Soft enough to sit comfortably against a man's shoulder all day. Then, for the fraction of a second the round fires, hard — hard enough to spread that shock wide instead of letting it punch straight through. And then soft again, immediately, before the next breath."*

Aldric was quiet for a moment.

*"You're describing something that isn't one material,"* he said slowly. *"You're describing something that changes its mind depending on how it's touched."*

*"Yes."*

*"I don't have that."*

*"I might,"* Ryn said.

He reached into his coat and set the small flask on the counter between them.

Aldric looked at it.

*"What's this."*

*"Ooze. Extracted from Murelings."* Ryn turned the flask so the light caught what was inside — dense, faintly luminous, somewhere between liquid and something that had forgotten it used to be liquid. *"I've been trying to find a use for it for weeks. On its own, raw, it's nearly worthless — flammable, and not in any useful way, just messy and dangerous to store. But I found a way to crystallize it."*

*"And?"*

*"It does something strange when it's crystallized. Press it slowly — gently, with steady pressure — and it flows. Morphs around whatever's pushing on it, the way wax does under a warm thumb. But hit it. Shock it, fast, all at once—"* He made a short motion with his hand. *"It goes brittle. Hard as glass for an instant. And then it cracks."*

Aldric leaned over the flask, studying it the way he studied everything that might be useful — completely, without rushing.

*"So it already knows how to be two things,"* he said.

*"It knows how to be two things in the wrong order,"* Ryn said. *"I need the hardness without the breaking. If I could find a version of this that hardens under shock and then simply — releases. Goes soft again instead of shattering. That's the material. That's the whole answer."*

Aldric set the flask down carefully.

*"That's not a recipe I have,"* he said. *"Murel's not my trade. Metal, stone, fire — those I know down to the bone. This—"* He nudged the flask. *"This is something else entirely. Living material. Not my craft."*

*"I know,"* Ryn said. *"I'm not asking you to fix it. I'm asking if you've ever heard of anything that might."*

Aldric was quiet for a long moment.

*"There's a village,"* he said. *"South-west of here. Used to farm Murelings — kept a whole operation going, sold the gel to half the trade routes through this district before my time. The rot took it. Years back now."*

Ryn went still.

*"I heard — and I want to be honest with you, trader, this is only what I heard, secondhand, from someone who heard it from someone else — that the Murelings out there changed. That whatever's left of them isn't quite Mureling anymore. The rot got into them, fused with the tissue somehow, made them into something different."* He shook his head slightly. *"I don't know if it's true. I never went and I never met anyone who went and came back able to tell me what they actually found. It might be worth nothing. It might be a story that grew taller every time it got repeated."*

Ryn looked at the flask on the counter.

*Fused with the corruption,* he thought. *Not destroyed by it. Changed by it.*

If the rot did to Murel what it did to everything else — adapted it, pushed it past its original limits into something the original creature was never capable of — then crystallized corrupted Murel might not share its uncorrupted cousin's brittleness at all. The corruption rewrote rules wherever it touched. It might, have made a gel that hardened and held without breaking.

It was a guess. An expensive, possibly fatal guess.

It was also the only lead he had.

*"Where is it,"* he said.

*"South-west,"* Aldric said. *"Half a day's walk if you don't get lost, longer if the road's grown over since the last time anyone bothered with it."* He looked at Ryn directly. *"And good luck finding mercenaries willing to take you there. Nobody hires out for rot-villages. "*

*"That won't be necessary,"* Ryn said. *"I'll go myself."*

Aldric looked at him.

He looked at him properly this time — not the quick assessment of a customer walking through the door, but a longer, slower study, taking in the coat, the boots, the specific well-kept look of a man who dressed like commerce rather than survival.

*"What part of village taken by the rot are you not understanding,"* Aldric said. *"Was the price of all that cleverness your common sense?"*

Ryn laughed — genuinely, this time, not the caught-out laugh from before.

*"I appreciate the concern,"* he said. *"But I have a problem, and I intend to fix it."*

*They'd waited the whole day for the second time.*

*The waiting had its own weight now. It wasn't the same as yesterday's stillness — that had been alert, sharp, the two of them watching the corruption's edge for movement that never came. Today's had worn down to something duller. Hours of sitting with the wood gathered and the perimeter set and nothing arriving to test any of it. The sun crawled west. Mara had stopped pretending she wasn't bored sometime around midday and had started actually being bored, which Varen noted as a different kind of fear than the one she'd carried yesterday — fear that had learned to wait inside itself rather than show on the surface.*

*By the time the light started going gold, he was reconsidering the plan.*

*"We've given this two days," he said. "If nothing comes by morning—"*

*"One more night," Mara said. She didn't let him finish. "Then tomorrow we go deeper, like you wanted from the start. You said yourself we could manage either way. Manage the waiting too."*

*He looked at her.*

*He looked at the corruption's edge, grey-purple deepening as the light went orange and then began its slow fade toward nothing.*

*"Fine," he said. "It's already too late tonight to change anything regardless."*

*She didn't argue further. She sat back down by the unlit wood and watched the sky finish the job the sun had started.*

---

*It was full dark, the fire still unlit, when the wildlife went quiet.*

*Not gradually. All at once — the specific totality of it, every small sound that had been filling the night a moment ago simply gone, the way the world had gone quiet before the wolf all those years ago, before anything that had ever mattered. Most people wouldn't have noticed the difference. The forest didn't usually announce itself by stopping.*

*He knew exactly what it meant.*

*"Mara."*

*She was already looking at him. Something in his voice had reached her before the words did.*

*He pointed at a tree behind the camp — thick-trunked, the lowest branches within easy reach, the kind of tree built for someone small and frightened to disappear into quickly.*

*"Up. Now. Whatever you see, don't make a sound."*

*She didn't ask why.*

*She climbed.*

*He moved through the perimeter lighting each torch in sequence — fast, methodical, no wasted motion, the flame catching one after another until the treeline burned with staggered orange light around the camp's edge. He came back to the dead fire and crouched beside it just long enough to strike it alive, the small flame catching the gathered wood.*

*He stood. Knife in his left hand. Caen's sword in his right.*

*He waited.*

*She waited.*

---

*The clicking began somewhere past the firelight — not loud, not urgent-sounding, just steady, patient, the sound of something that had all the time it needed.*

*Varen didn't move.*

*It came into the light slowly. Something that size should have shaken the ground, should have announced itself in a hundred small sounds — the give of dead leaves, the snap of brush, the displaced air of something with that much mass moving through it. It made none of that. It crossed the clearing in total silence, the specific wrongness of a predator that had given up every sound a body that large should make.*

*It stopped inches from his face.*

*He didn't breathe louder. He didn't move. The smooth skin where its eyes should have been turned slightly, reading him the only way it could — sound, scent, the faint static of something alive standing very still in front of it — and for one held second it didn't know what it had found.*

*It hunts by hearing, he thought. Not sight. Confirmed.*

*He drove the knife into its neck and pulled it down in one motion.*

*It reared.*

*The size of it upright was obscene — twice his height, easily, the muscle of it visible even in poor light, every part of it built for exactly this. It slashed. He blocked with the sword and the force of the impact threw him back a full stride, more force than his own weight should have absorbed, his boots skidding through dirt before he caught himself.*

*"Don't make a sound," he said to the dark where Mara was hiding. "Not one."*

*The creature lifted its head.*

*The call it made wasn't loud. It didn't need to be. It moved through the ground instead of the air, a vibration that passed through stone and root and the soles of his boots, the specific frequency of something built to travel rather than to be heard. He understood immediately what it meant. More are coming. The knife wound at its throat hadn't slowed it at all — the cut sat open and dark and the creature didn't register it as injury.*

*He couldn't take another hit like the last one.*

*He moved.*

*Low, fast, dodging the next slash by inches, and cut the hamstring of its right hind leg in the same motion. It staggered. He cut the left.*

*It tried to stand and kept falling — its hind legs no longer answering it, the muscle severed clean, and through all of it the creature made no sound that resembled pain. No flinch. No retreat. Just the mechanical failure of a limb that no longer worked, met with the same flat indifference it had met everything else with.*

*It doesn't feel any of this, he thought.*

*With its legs gone he climbed onto its back and drove the sword down through the base of its skull, through the place where a spine met a brain on every living thing he had ever killed.*

*It didn't fall.*

*He stayed on its back a moment longer than he wanted to, processing the failure, the sword still buried at the join of neck and skull and the creature still trying to move beneath him despite everything he'd taken from it.*

*No brain there. Not where it should be.*

*He dropped down. He circled, watching it the way he watched everything — for the next available thing to exploit. And he saw it: the creature's head was no longer tracking him the way it had a moment ago. The skin over its sensory organs had stopped pulsing the way it pulsed when it was reading sound. Whatever the strike at the base of its skull had done, it hadn't killed the creature.*

*It had made it deaf.*

*He moved in and cut its front leg at the joint where it met the body. Then, in the same breath, he drove the sword up under its jaw and through its neck, the blade emerging clean on the other side, and he put his full weight down the length of it.*

*The creature stopped.*

*All of it. At once.*

---

*"Is it over," Mara whispered from the tree.*

*"Don't move," he said. "Not a muscle."*

*The clicking started again before he'd finished the sentence.*

*Five sources this time. North, up the hill. Northwest. West. Two from the southwest, close together, moving in tandem. His perimeter, the cover he'd built, the path back toward the deeper woods — all of it lay south. He needed every one of them in a single place if he was going to survive what was coming, and he had perhaps a minute to make that happen.*

*The creature he'd just killed twitched against the ground — nerve and muscle still firing without anything left to direct them, the body convinced it was still alive in whatever way bodies like this convinced themselves of anything.*

*The five arrived at once.*

*And instead of circling toward him, they went for the corpse.*

*All five of them, tearing into the body he'd just dropped — not investigating the kill, not searching for what had done it, just attacking it the way they might attack any wounded thing that had stopped moving the way the pack expected it to move. The connection between them had been cut somewhere in that strike at the base of the skull, though Varen didn't understand this yet, only that whatever bound the pack together as one coordinated will had stopped including the one he'd silenced.*

*He used the chaos.*

*He ran south, into the woods, fast and low.*

*They heard him the instant he moved — the clicking shifting direction in unison, abandoning the corpse — but he'd bought himself ground, and he kept it, vaulting into the lower branches of the first tree thick enough to hold his weight and moving through the canopy rather than the floor below it.*

---

*The trees thickened as he went deeper, and the creatures slowed.*

*Their size worked against them here in a way it hadn't in the open clearing — too much mass to move quickly through trunks set close together, too much bulk to climb the way he climbed. He watched from above as they bunched and separated, the pack's formation breaking apart against terrain it wasn't built for.*

*He found his opening. The one with the most room around it, the least boxed in by trunk and root — he dropped onto its back and repeated the strike, base of the skull, the same motion, and retreated up into the branches before it could turn on him.*

*It went deaf the same way the first one had.*

*He watched.*

*The remaining four converged on it within seconds — one tearing into its shoulder, deep, the wound opening dark and wide. A second circled through the lower branches and bit into its hind leg, ripping a long piece of muscle away whole. The crippled, senseless creature didn't understand any of it. It thrashed. It attacked whatever was nearest with no ability to tell friend from threat from empty air, and in its thrashing it began moving — north. Back toward the camp.*

*A third creature slashed the same wound on its leg, deepening it.*

*The crippled one staggered on, dragging the ruined leg, attacking nothing and everything by turns, and Varen watched it from above and understood exactly where it was heading before it got there.*

*Mara's tree.*

*He dropped — not onto the crippled one, but onto the nearer of the two tearing into it, the one that had taken the meat from its leg. He cut its left axilla in one motion, then its right, immobilizing it fast, buying himself room to deal with what mattered.*

*It wasn't enough.*

*The second of the two — the one that had opened the shoulder wound — lunged at him mouth-first. He tried to leap above its head, aiming the same strike at the base of its skull that had worked twice already, but it lifted its head a fraction too fast, and his blade caught only the smooth skin where its eyes should have been instead. It staggered, half-deafened now on one side, its sense of direction broken but not its mobility, and it turned on him anyway, slashing.*

*He blocked.*

*The force of it threw him back into a tree trunk hard enough that something in his sword arm gave — a flare of white pain up through the shoulder, the arm answering wrong when he asked it to move.*

*And in that same instant, the crippled creature finally reached Mara's tree.*

*It hit the trunk full force.*

---

*Mara felt the whole tree shudder under her before she understood what had caused it.*

*Her hands lost the branch.*

*For one endless half-second she was simply falling — the camp and the torchlight and the screaming and the smell of blood all spinning past her at once, no time to think, no time to do anything but feel the absence of the branch where her hands had been — and then her fingers caught the lower limb on instinct alone, her body slamming against the trunk, her grip the only thing standing between her and the ground.*

*She hung there.*

*Below her, the last two creatures reached the crippled, senseless one and tore it apart in seconds — and the instant it stopped moving, both of them turned.*

*Toward her.*

*She could see their heads lift. The smooth skin pulsing where eyes should have been, reading the vibration of her own held breath, her own racing heart, the small tremor in her arms as her grip began to fail.*

*"Varen—"*

*She didn't get the rest of his name out before her hands gave entirely.*

---

*He heard her voice break and everything in him narrowed to a single point.*

*He finished the half-deafened creature in front of him with a strike he didn't fully feel land — his arm screaming, his hand barely closing around the hilt — and he was already running before the body hit the ground, sprinting through trees and roots and his own ragged breathing, and he was still three trees away when he saw her fall.*

*She hit the ground.*

*She didn't get up fast enough.*

*The last two creatures were already moving, already closing the distance, and he was not going to make it — he understood this with total clarity even as his legs kept driving him forward, even as every part of him refused to accept the math his eyes were doing automatically. He threw the knife. It buried itself in the ear-skin of the nearer creature and it staggered, disoriented, shaking its head against a wound it had no framework for.*

*It bought nothing.*

*The other one was still coming and there was still too much ground between him and her and he was not going to reach her in time.*

*He looked at her face.*

*She was looking back at him — not screaming, not even reaching for him, just looking, the way she'd looked at him that first day on the road when she didn't yet understand that he wouldn't hurt her, except now it was worse, now there was something in her eyes that had already started to understand what was about to happen and had nowhere to put that understanding except toward him, like he could still do something about it from three strides away.*

*The corner of a room arrived in him without permission.*

*Eight years old. A doorframe. A face he had spent twelve years refusing to let himself remember the shape of, and even now it didn't come — just the absence where a face should be, and a voice instead, small and certain. I want to go with you. And his own voice underneath it, the old useless cruelty of it, this isn't a girl's job, the words he'd carried without knowing he was carrying them, the ones that had been waiting in him for the exact moment he needed to fail someone again.*

*He hadn't been fast enough then either.*

*Not again.*

*It wasn't a thought so much as something that tore through him faster than thought — his legs already burning, his lungs already past what they had left to give, and none of it enough, none of it ever going to be enough, the ground between them the same ground it had always been, too much of it, always too much.*

*He was three strides away.*

*He was not going to make it.*

*And then he was.*

*The flashback hadn't slowed him — it had done the opposite, some old animal part of him answering the panic with everything it had left, a surge of strength that came from somewhere past conscious reach, the same place that had once kept a feral ten-year-old alive in the woods on nothing but refusal. He closed the last three strides in a single lunge.*

*He swung the sword with everything that surge gave him.*

*The blade went through the nearer creature's neck clean — bone and all, no resistance, no slowing, the strike carrying through the kill with so much force that the creature's headless body kept moving on its own momentum, the legs still driving forward, the bulk of it crashing past Mara and the tree in a final lurching stagger before it finally folded and went still.*

*The second creature was already turning.*

*There was no time to disable it, no angle left to dodge without leaving Mara exposed to whatever came next. He didn't try. He planted himself between her and it and braced to take the hit on his own body if that's what it cost — his sword arm screaming, his balance unsteady, every part of him simply refusing to be anywhere else.*

*Thunder came first.*

*The creature's nape simply stopped existing — the vertebrae gone with it, the massive head left hanging by nothing but skin and muscle, swinging from a column that no longer had anything inside it to hold it up.*

*A second crack.*

*The head was gone entirely.*

*The body folded sideways and didn't move again.*

---

*Varen turned.*

*Mara was on the ground, covered — covered completely, in rot and tissue and things that had been parts of creatures only seconds ago — and for one terrible suspended moment he couldn't tell how much of it was hers.*

*"Mara."*

*She blinked up at him. Alive. Breathing. Shaking badly, but alive, her eyes finding his face and holding there with the specific desperate fixedness of someone who needed one solid thing to look at and had chosen him.*

*He went to her immediately, his knees hitting the ground hard enough that it should have hurt and didn't register at all. His hands moved over her arms, her shoulders, searching for the wrongness, the give of broken bone, the wet heat of a wound that belonged to her rather than to something already dead.*

*He found nothing.*

*All of it — every drop, every fragment — had come from somewhere else.*

*She was whole.*

*He didn't move his hands away immediately. He stayed there, kneeling in front of her with his palms still resting against her shoulders, his own arm hanging useless and screaming at his side, his breath tearing in and out of him in a way it hadn't since he was a child running toward smoke that used to be a home.* 

*"You're alright," he said. It came out almost like a question, which it had never once been before. "You're alright."*

*He stayed there with her a moment longer than the situation required.*

*Then, slowly, both of them turned toward the camp*

---

*Someone was walking toward them.*

*The fire behind him had burned low but not out, and it lit him from behind so that for several long strides he was only a shape — a silhouette with no face, moving without hurry across the clearing toward where they knelt among the dead.*

*He stepped past the line of torches.*

*The light found him properly then — a man, well dressed, far too well dressed for where he was standing, his coat dark and clean and entirely wrong for a place that had just been a slaughterhouse. In his hand he held something metal, small, smoke curling faintly from one end of it, the shape of it utterly unfamiliar to either of them.*

*He looked at the two of them. At the bodies. At the blood.*

*He said nothing yet.*

*Ryn lowered the metal thing and put it away — not into the bag slung over his shoulder, but into the inner pocket of his coat, the way a man put away something that belonged only to him.*

*He looked at the two of them. At the bodies scattered through the trees, the blood, the rot already creeping faintly at the edges of the kills.*

*"Quite a dangerous place for a child," he said. "You seem capable enough to realize that yourself."*

*Varen stayed quiet. He knew the man was right, and there was nothing useful in arguing with something true.*

*Ryn looked between them again, reassessing.*

*"I assumed at first you were part of the missing group," he said. "The ones people have been talking about. But that's wrong — you're someone else entirely." His eyes went to Varen's clothes, the wolf hide, the worn leather, none of it cut or dyed the way Ordenmere's tailors cut anything. "And judging by what you're wearing, you're not from Ordenmere at all."*

*"I heard that thunder sound yesterday," Varen said. "In Ordenmere."*

*"So you arrived recently." Ryn considered this. "Where's the rest of your group. You're here for the bounty, I take it."*

*"Yes, we are," Mara said, snapping upright with a speed that surprised even her. "And don't think for one second you're taking our reward. We did all the heavy lifting."*

*Ryn laughed — short, genuine.*

*"I'm impressed you can still think about the reward after what just happened to you," he said. "Don't worry. I'm not here for your bounty."*

*He looked at Varen's arm, the way it hung wrong at his side.*

*"You took quite a hit. That could be broken. Let me see it."*

*Varen stepped back before he could get closer.*

*"Why are you here."*

*"That's none of your business, technically," Ryn said, without heat. "But I'm heading west of here. There's an abandoned village."*

*"You mean the Murel village," Mara said. "It's half a day's walk into the rot. You expect us to believe that?" She looked him over — the coat, the boots, the specific cleanliness of a man who didn't look like he belonged anywhere near a corruption border. "Fancy pants."*

*Ryn smiled. "You've heard of it. Good. Yes, I'm going there. I'm looking for something." He glanced at the arm again. "But that needs looking at first."*

*Varen stood. "I have bandages. At our camp."*

*"I'd be glad to join you there for the night, if you don't mind," Ryn said. "It's late, and I'm not particularly fond of starting fires from nothing."*

*Mara looked him over once more — the coat, the boots, the specific shine of a man who'd clearly never gone hungry — and arrived at her conclusion.*

*"Sure thing, fancy pants."*

*Varen wasn't fully certain. He allowed it anyway.*

---

*The camp still held the corpse of the first creature he'd taken down — the one whose neck he'd opened before the call went out, lying where it had fallen, already beginning to show the dull grey sheen of the rot reclaiming what had briefly been alive. None of them moved it. The fire had been scattered during the fight, embers and half-burned wood thrown wide, but Varen rebuilt it with one working arm, methodical despite the pain, until the flame caught and held.*

*They sat around it together — the three of them, the dead Corrupter just beyond the firelight where its size still seemed to take up more room than it had any right to.*

*Varen pulled the wolf hide off his shoulders and set it aside.*

*He checked his own arm first — fingers pressing along the bone from shoulder to wrist, methodical, reading the structure the way he read everything. No fractures. The shoulder had come out of its socket, though — the joint sitting visibly wrong, the muscle around it already swelling.*

*He braced his back against a fallen branch behind him, took the wrist of the injured arm in his other hand, and pulled — slow, then sudden, the specific controlled violence of someone who had done this to himself before and knew exactly how much force the joint needed before it would give. It went back into place with a wet, audible shift.*

*He didn't make a sound.*

*He flexed the arm once, testing the range, wincing only slightly at the deep bruising that remained. He reached into his pack and produced a small bundle of dried herbs, crushing them between his palms with practiced economy, adding a few drops of water from his canteen until they turned into a dark, fragrant paste.*

*Ryn watched the whole process without interrupting.*

*He recognized the precision of it — not the desperate improvisation of someone managing an injury for the first time, but the calm repetition of technique drilled into someone by a teacher who'd done this many times before and made sure the lesson stuck.*

*Varen worked the paste into the bruised shoulder and bound it with a strip of cloth, tight but not restrictive, the whole process finished in under a minute.*

*"Where did you learn to do that," Ryn asked.*

*"Caen taught me."*

*Ryn looked at Varen. Then at Mara, his expression asking the obvious question — who's Caen — without saying it aloud.*

*Mara looked back at him with an expression that said, just as clearly, don't even ask.*

*They understood each other completely without another word passing between them.*

*"My name's Ryn, by the way," he said. "I'm a trader."*

*"I'm Mara. This is Varen."*

*Varen looked at the inner pocket of Ryn's coat.*

*"What kind of magic was that," he said.*

*"It's not magic," Ryn said. "It's physics."*

*"Philips? Who on earth is Philips?" mara said.*

*Ryn laughed despite himself.*

*"Not Phillips. Physics." He settled back slightly. "It's the study of how the universe actually works — the rules underneath everything. Matter, energy, force. Why things push and pull the way they do, why they move the way they move. All of it has rules, whether anyone's bothered to write them down or not."*

*Mara stared at him.*

*"Okay, just — stop talking. I don't understand a word of that."*

*Ryn smiled, reached into his coat, and drew the weapon out again.*

*Varen went still, watching every inch of the motion.*

*It was metal — that much was obvious — but the shape of it belonged to nothing either of them had seen. A grip carved to fit a hand exactly, the curve of it worn smooth in places by use. A long barrel, longer than any blade was wide, dark and faintly scorched near the open end. A cylinder set just behind the barrel, six small chambers visible around its circumference, each one a perfect dark circle.*

*It was heavier than its size suggested — Ryn handled it the way you handled something that demanded both hands eventually, even if he held it easily in one for now.*

*There was no string. No mechanism that pulled back and released the way a crossbow's did. Just the cylinder, and a small lever beneath the barrel, and the specific quiet of something that hadn't been fired in this moment and was giving away nothing about what it had just done.*

*Varen's eyes moved over every part of it — reading it the only way he knew how to read anything, for function, for danger, for the shape of what it could do to a body. He found no answers. Nothing about its construction told him how thunder came out of something that small.*

*""This," Ryn said, "is going to take a little longer to explain than physics did."*

*He turned the weapon over once in his hand. "Here's the part that matters to you, though. Anyone can use this. Doesn't take training, doesn't take talent — you point it, you pull, it does what you just watched it do. And I can make you one. For a price."*

*"How much," Mara asked.*

*"Five gold."*

*Mara's mouth opened slightly. Even Varen, who measured value the way he measured everything else — without much interest — registered the number against the two gold they'd accepted for this entire commission.*

*"We could afford it," Mara said, recovering fast, "but we don't need it."*

*Ryn laughed.*

*"Fair enough," he said, and put it back into his coat without further argument.*

*He looked between them again.*

*"Just the two of you came out here?"*

*"Yes," Mara said.*

*"I'd call you both insane," Ryn said, looking at Varen now, at the bodies scattered through the trees beyond the firelight, "except judging by the number of corpses, you clearly had it under control. I don't think you needed my help at all, If—"*

*He stopped.*

*The sentence had been heading somewhere he didn't need to finish — he wouldn't have gotten hit if she hadn't been there to fall out of a tree — and he caught it before it cleared his teeth.*

*Mara had already heard the shape of it anyway. She knew exactly what he'd almost said, the same thing she'd been telling herself since she hit the ground. Ryn saw it land on her face and felt, immediately and uselessly, that he'd hurt something he hadn't meant to touch.*

*"I underestimated them," Varen said.*

*Both of them looked at him.*

*"I went in expecting four. There were six. I should have read the call more carefully before I engaged the first one — I didn't account for how many it would bring." He looked at the fire. "I'm glad I listened to her plan. If I'd pushed deeper into the corruption the way I wanted to, I'd have met all six at once with no perimeter and no torches."*

*It wasn't true.*

*He had not underestimated the creatures. He would not have struggled meeting six of them in open ground rather than scattered through the dark. He had simply said the version of events that put the weight somewhere other than on the small shaking girl across the fire from him — and he said it without hesitation, without the particular friction he expected lying to produce, the words arriving smooth and complete and entirely unlike the truth.*

*He had never lied before in his life, at least not since that day.*

*He didn't fully understand, even as he said it, that he was capable of this.*

*Ryn looked at him for a moment.*

*He knew, the way he knew most things, that it wasn't true. He said nothing about it.*

*Mara's face had gone faintly red.*

*"Well," Ryn said, "you must be quite the tactician, then. Glad she had you to convince."*

*"I didn't convince him of anything," Mara said, too fast, looking anywhere but at either of them. "He just — listens sometimes. When it's smart to."*

---

*"How much are you making from this," Ryn asked.*

*"Why," Mara said, narrowing her eyes. "You're not planning on stealing it, are you."*

*"Just curious."*

*"Two gold," she said, lifting her chin slightly, the way she said things she expected to land as impressive.*

*Ryn looked at her.*

*"Two gold. For what five of those."*

*"It's six," Mara confirmed, with the same pride.*

*"You nearly died," Ryn said, "for two gold." He considered something. "Did you register the job with the authorities before you left? Formally — tell them you were taking the commission?"*

*Mara's expression shifted.*

*"No," she said. "Why would—"*

*"Bounties like this increase the longer the threat goes unaddressed," Ryn said. "Every day it sits open, every failed group, the kingdom raises the price to attract someone willing to actually finish it. If you'd registered properly before leaving, you might be walking back to four gold, five. Maybe more, given how long this one's been open."*

*Mara said nothing.*

*She was furious at herself in the specific way of someone realizing they'd left money on a table they hadn't known existed.*

*Ryn let the silence sit for exactly as long as it needed to and then moved past it.*

*"I have a proposition," he said. "I'm short on time, and I need samples from a corrupted creature out at a village west of here — the Murel farm. I came alone because I didn't have time to find mercenaries willing to make the trip. You two have already proven you can survive what's out there." He paused. "Join me. "*

*"No," Mara said immediately.*

*"I'll pay six gold. Three times what you came for."*

*Mara looked at him.*

*"Deal," she said, before the sentence had fully landed in her own ears.*

*Varen said nothing in objection. Work was work, and the arithmetic suited him fine.*

---

*Mara fell asleep not long after, curled into the same fetal shape she always slept in, already murmuring something about coins before her eyes had fully closed.*

*Ryn watched her for a moment.*

*"Your daughter?" he asked.*

*"No."*

*"Too young to be her father, Unless I'm misjudging your age badly. Sister? "*

*"I met her," Varen said, "about fifty steps from where we're sitting now. Two days ago."*

*Ryn looked at him.*

*"You met her two days ago," he said slowly, "and tonight you stood in front of something that should have killed you to keep her from getting hit."*

*"Yes."*

*"Why."*

*Varen was quiet for a moment.*

*"I don't understand it myself," he said. "I had openings tonight where I could have come out of this without injury. My body didn't take them. It went toward her instead, every time, without asking me first."*

*Ryn looked at the fire.*

*"I don't know what to tell you about that," he said, "except this — she's full of life. More than most people manage to be, even ones who've never had a reason not to be." He glanced at her — drooling slightly, murmuring numbers into the dirt, smiling at something only she could see. "And people like that get into you. You don't decide it. It just happens, and then one day you find yourself doing something impossible just to keep that exact look on their face a little longer. You'd do almost anything for one more smile like that."*

*For half a second something else arrived behind his eyes — gold hair, spring light, a woman's face turned toward him with the particular warmth of someone who knew him completely. You're making that face again. The fragment came and went so fast it barely registered as having happened at all.*

*She had smiled at him. That was all. The picture was already gone.*

*Varen watched him say all of it.*

*He filed every piece of it the way he filed everything — without understanding most of it yet, certain only that it mattered, certain he would need it later.*

*He looked at Mara.*

*Then both of them went to sleep.*

# 18 \- What the Blood Left Behind

### **Chapter Eighteen —  What the Blood Left Behind** 

---

The clearing was small and unremarkable — far enough from any road that nobody would stumble onto it by accident, the grass scorched in patches from previous sessions, the trees at its edge bearing the scars of overshot attempts. Brask stood at its center, hands raised, sweat already beading at his temple despite the cool air.

*"Again,"* Lyris said.

She stood a measured distance away, arms folded, watching him with the patient stillness of someone who had done this many times before and would do it many times again.

Brask closed his eyes. He drew a slow breath. The air around his hands began to thicken — not visibly, but with the particular pressure that came before something significant, the mana gathering toward him from the surrounding space in a way that made the grass at his feet flatten slightly outward.

*"More,"* Lyris said. *"You're stopping too early. You're afraid of how much you can actually hold."*

*"I don't want to lose control of it."*

*"You won't. Not yet. Not at this volume."* Her voice stayed even. *"Take more than feels safe. That's where the work actually starts."*

He breathed again, deeper this time, and the air around him thickened further — the pressure building, his jaw tightening with the effort of holding something his body wasn't yet fully built to hold.

*"Now,"* she said. *"Release all of it at once. Not a stream. Not control. Everything, in a single instant."*

He thrust both hands forward.

The release came apart from him in a single violent burst — a shockwave of raw force that tore through the clearing, splitting bark from the nearest trees and throwing loose stone and dirt in every direction. It was not elegant. It was not aimed with any real precision. But it was large, and it was fast, and for a half-second the air itself seemed to bend around the force of it.

Brask stumbled back, breathing hard, his arms trembling.

Lyris watched the dust settle.

*"Better,"* she said. *"You held more than last time before you let go. The release was cleaner."*

*"It still goes everywhere,"* Brask said, frustrated. *"I can't point it. I can't choose what it hits."*

*"You're not meant to be able to, yet,"* she said. *"Precision is a different discipline entirely — one you'll never need if you can't first hold enough mana to be worth aiming. Right now you're learning capacity. Direction comes after capacity, not before it."*

He nodded, still catching his breath, and looked at the wreckage of bark and stone scattered across the clearing with something like pride.

---

He sat down on a fallen log to rest, and Lyris remained standing, watching him with the specific attentiveness of someone cataloguing more than his physical exhaustion.

*"Can I ask you something,"* he said.

*"You can ask."*

*"Where were you. The past few days. You just — weren't here. No warning, no explanation, and then you were back this morning like nothing happened."*

Lyris looked at him for a moment.

*"I had important matters to attend to,"* she said.

The answer arrived smooth, complete, offering nothing further and inviting no follow-up — the specific quality of a sentence built to close a door rather than open one.

Brask waited, as if more might come.

It didn't.

They went back to the exercise.

Brask squared his stance again, drew the mana in tighter this time, holding more of it than before — sweat already running down the side of his face from the effort.

*"Same as before,"* Lyris said. *"All of it, at once."*

He released.

The shockwave tore through the clearing again, splitting bark, scattering loose stone — and in that exact instant, Lyris felt cold.

Not the cold of weather. The cold of something arriving. The air around her seemed to lose its temperature all at once, a chill that had nothing to do with Brask's attack and everything to do with something else entirely, something that had just stepped into the space behind him.

She looked past Brask's shoulder.

Caen was standing there.

Directly across from him, close enough to touch, utterly indifferent to the dust and debris settling around him as though none of it could reach him at all. Brask didn't react. Didn't turn. Didn't see anything.

He was only letting her see him.

Brask lowered his hands, breathing hard, and turned to her with the eager, exhausted look of someone waiting for approval.

*"How did that one feel? Was it stronger?"*

*"That's enough for today,"* Lyris said.

He blinked, surprised by the abruptness, but nodded — used by now to not questioning the shape of her instructions.

*"Will you come tomorrow?"* he asked, already gathering his things, his village close enough that he didn't need to ask about the walk back.

*"Yes,"* she said.

He left.

She stayed where she was, watching the treeline long after he'd disappeared into it, saying nothing — because she had learned, recently and thoroughly, that speaking to Caen out of turn was a mistake she didn't intend to repeat.

---

*"Impressive specimen,"* Caen said.

*"Why am I alive,"* she said.

*"I'm still figuring that out myself."* He looked at the wreckage of the clearing, unbothered, as though appraising the boy's work rather than anything else. *"What did you hear. How much did he say about the unnamed one."*

*"He wants to find him."*

*"Did he say why."*

*"No."*

Caen was in front of her before she finished the word — no visible motion between where he'd been and where he now stood, simply there, his hand coming to rest on her shoulder with a gentleness that made the wrongness of it worse rather than better.

She looked into his eyes.

There was nothing in them. Not darkness — absence, a void where something should have been looking back at her, and she understood in that instant exactly how far beneath Caen's surface she was being permitted to see.

*"Are you lying to me,"* he said.

*"No. I'm not lying. He didn't say anything else — the girl interrupted him before he could."*

*"How much did you tell Weaver."*

*"I haven't reported yet."* Her voice was steady only through enormous effort. *"The only thing he knows is that your boy spoke the name. I haven't gone back into the void since. I was — I was too afraid to."*

Caen looked into her the way he'd looked into the void itself — searching, complete, the specific total scrutiny of someone for whom a lie would have been immediately, mechanically obvious.

She wasn't lying.

*"Do you want to remain existing,"* he said.

*"Yes."*

He touched her lips, lightly, with one finger.

*"This mouth of yours,"* he said, *"is what got you into this situation."* His hand slid down to her throat — gently, almost tenderly, the gentleness somehow worse than violence would have been. *"And every part of this situation is interfering with my plan."*

His grip tightened.

Only slightly. Just enough that she felt it in her spine, in the place where fear lived before it reached the rest of the body.

*"But,"* he said, *"I can make this work."*

She understood immediately what he meant.

*"I can't lie to Weaver,"* she said, the words coming fast, urgent. *"If he learns I've been holding anything back, he'll end me. You know he will."*

*"If Weaver doesn't kill you,"* Caen said, *"I will. And believe it or not, I'm generous enough to make it painless."*

His grip eased — not released, just eased, enough for her to breathe properly again.

*"You've made yourself indispensable to my plan whether I like it or not,"* he said. *"Your interference could cause it to fail. And if that happens, I will have nothing left to lose — and you will be the first thing I take, I promise you that. Don't imagine for one moment that Weaver would protect you from me if it came to that."*

He let her go entirely.

*"But if you continue to serve me,"* he said, *"I'll guarantee your survival when — not if — Weaver decides you've become obsolete to him. You'll report to him. You'll tell him only what I permit you to tell him."* He looked at her, waiting. *"Does this sound like a reasonable arrangement to you."*

*"Yes, Lord Signus."*

*He was gone before the second word finished leaving her mouth.*

*Her knees nearly went. She caught herself against nothing, pressed a hand flat to her own throat where his had been, and felt her pulse slam against her palm for a long time before it slowed.*

*She sat down on the log Brask had left an hour ago, legs no longer trusting themselves, and stayed there until her hands stopped shaking.* 

The morning came in grey and slow, the kind of light that hadn't decided yet whether the day would be warm. Sera woke before the others, the unfamiliar shape of the new bed still strange against her back. She lay still for a moment listening to the compound settle into its early sounds — boots somewhere on stone, the distant clatter of the kitchens starting their work.

Myre stirred not long after, sitting up at the same unremarkable hour as always — no different from any other morning, just the ordinary business of waking. She rubbed at her eyes, glanced over, and gave Sera a small nod by way of greeting.

Sera dressed in the grey uniform — still unfamiliar in the shoulders, the cut entirely unlike the habit's looser drape — and was ready before the other two had finished with their own routines.

They went down to the small kitchen attached to the women's wing together — a modest hearth, a row of shelves, the specific lived-in clutter of a space three or four people used and nobody officially owned. Iren put bread and something warm together with the practiced economy of someone who'd done this every morning for longer than Sera had been here, and they ate quickly, standing, the way people ate when the day was already pulling at them.

---

They walked out to the training court together and took up their usual place to wait, the morning still cool enough that Sera could see her own breath.

*"Why are there only five of you,"* she asked, into the quiet. *"Students, I mean. Someone as capable as Magister Seris — I'd have expected the line to be longer."*

Iren glanced at her.

*"You don't just ask to study under a master,"* she said. *"There are years of work before anyone even qualifies to be considered. Foundational training, examinations, sponsorship from someone established enough to vouch for you. It's not a door most people get near, let alone through."*

*"And even once you qualify,"* Myre added, *"Seris doesn't take everyone who does. Most masters take whoever clears the requirement — fill their roster, build their reputation through numbers. She doesn't work that way."*

*"How many applied,"* Sera asked.

*"More than you'd think,"* Myre said. *"She took five."*

Sera said nothing for a long moment.

She thought about the gate. About Maret's purse pressed into her hand. About *be at this gate early tomorrow* — none of it a qualification, none of it years of foundational work or sponsorship or examination, just a conversation in a small room and a decision Seris had made for reasons she still hadn't fully explained even to herself.

It must have shown on her face, because she felt both of them notice it at the same time — the small shift, the specific quiet of someone realizing exactly how thin their claim to a place actually was.

Iren opened her mouth. Nothing came out of it. She looked, for a moment, like she wanted to say something reassuring and couldn't find the shape of it fast enough.

*"She knows what she's doing,"* Myre said, filling the gap the only way she knew how — bluntly, without dressing it up. *"She wouldn't have taken you in if she didn't see something worth taking. Seris doesn't do things she doesn't mean. Ever. Not once, since I've known her."*

It wasn't gentle. It wasn't meant to be. But underneath the roughness of it was something Myre clearly believed completely, said plainly because plain was the only register she had for things that mattered to her.

*Iren already knows this about her,* Sera thought, watching the small loosening in Iren's shoulders now that Myre had said the thing she herself hadn't managed to.

The church bell rang somewhere across the compound.

Seris came around the corner exactly on time, the way she always did — no hurry in it, no lateness either, just the precise arrival of someone for whom punctuality wasn't a virtue so much as a fact about how she moved through the world.

They fell into formation.

*"Magister."*

---

Inside, the three young men were already waiting at the edge of the training ground. Bael's eyes moved over Sera once — the grey uniform now, the habit gone — and he said nothing about it at all, which Sera had already learned to read as its own particular kind of statement.

*"We'll continue from yesterday,"* Seris said, and led them out.

---

The improvement was visible even to Sera's untrained eye. Yesterday none of them had managed to hold a cowl for more than a handful of seconds before it collapsed. Today the shapes held longer, steadier — but Seris watched all of it with the specific dissatisfaction of someone measuring against a standard nobody had reached yet.

*"You're all still fighting it,"* she said, moving between them. *"Holding it together through effort. I don't want effort. I want it effortless. Effort fails the moment you're tired, or frightened, or distracted. Effortless doesn't fail at all."*

They were midway through another attempt when the gate at the far end of the court swung open.

Vorne walked out with three guards behind him, each one carrying the rifles built from Ryn's schematics — the same design the students had already watched demonstrated earlier, now finished and distributed, the blacksmiths having worked faster than expected once the tolerances proved as precise as promised. They were heading away from the walls, clearly intending to fire them somewhere that wouldn't leave a second crater in anything load-bearing. 

The students watched them pass.

*"Eyes forward,"* Seris said, and they returned to the exercise.

---

Solen had held his cowl longest yesterday, though it bled at the edges the whole time — mana leaking outward in thin, wasteful threads even while the core stayed intact. Today he'd tried correcting it by taking in less.

*"Wrong,"* Seris said, watching him. *"You're not meant to fight the mana for control. Take in everything your body will allow — all of it, completely. The bleeding isn't a sign you've taken too much. It's a sign the surface of the cowl isn't holding properly. That's what needs the work. Not the intake."*

Solen adjusted, frowning in concentration, and the cowl thickened around him again — unstable for a moment, then settling, the bleeding visibly less.

Bael's problem ran the opposite direction. He held his shape through sheer insistence, jaw set, every line of him fighting the mana into the form he wanted it to take.

*"You're forcing it,"* Seris told him. *"Stop trying to control it. Guide it. There's a difference, and until you find it you'll keep burning yourself out holding something that never wanted to be held that way in the first place."*

Iren's cowl was more present today than yesterday — visibly thicker, the green shimmer of it steadier around her — but still well short of what Seris clearly expected eventually.

*"You're not taking it in with your whole body,"* Seris said, circling her once. *"Part of you is still holding back. Find where. Stop."*

Sera listened to all of it.

She tried, in her own attempt, to do what she'd watched Solen attempt — accepting rather than resisting, letting the mana spread through her without forcing it into a shape the way Bael had. It came easier than she expected. The cowl around her brightened, held, steady for several seconds longer than her very first attempt yesterday.

Myre and Davan worked through their own corrections nearby, each showing the same incremental progress — Seris moving between all six of them now, naming exactly where each one was still resisting something they no longer needed to resist.

By the time the light had shifted well past midday, every one of them had made some measure of progress.

None of them had reached what Seris was actually asking for.

*"That's enough for today,"* she said.

The students began to disperse — the usual loose unwinding of a session ending — until Seris's voice caught Sera before she'd taken more than a few steps.

*"Sera. Come to my office this afternoon."*

*"Yes, Magister."*

Myre glanced over.

She said nothing. She just kept walking, a half-step faster than before — not envy of Sera exactly, just the old familiar question rising in her again, the one she'd been carrying long before Sera ever arrived at the gate, about whether she had actually earned her place here at all, or whether Seris simply hadn't gotten around yet to deciding she hadn't.

---

They went back to the washroom together that evening, the routine already settling into something familiar after only two nights. Sera moved through it with less hesitation than the night before — undressing without the small instinct to check who was watching, finding her place at the trough without needing to be shown.

Iren talked through the day's lesson as they washed, going over what each of them had managed and what they hadn't. *"Solen's close,"* she said. *"Closer than any of us, honestly. If he stops fighting the bleed he'll have it within the week."*

*"And Bael?"*

*"Bael will have it eventually,"* Iren said, with the specific diplomatic flatness of someone choosing her words around a person she didn't dislike but also didn't want to overpraise. *"He just needs to stop trying to win against it."*

When they'd dried off and dressed again, Sera asked the question that had been sitting in her since the session ended.

*"Where's Magister Seris's office?"*

*"I'll take you,"* Myre said. *"It's close to our quarters anyway."*

---

She walked Sera there in the gathering afternoon light — a short distance, down one corridor and along another, the compound's geography slowly becoming less foreign with each day. Myre stopped at a plain door, unremarkable except for the slight wear on its handle from frequent use.

*"Here,"* she said, and left without further comment, already turning back the way they'd come.

Sera knocked.

*"Enter,"* Seris said, from somewhere inside.

---

The office was larger than Sera had expected — far larger than anything at the border branch, the walls almost entirely given over to bookcases that rose higher than she could comfortably see the tops of. A large table sat between the door and Seris's desk, covered in loose papers, sketched circles, and lines of unfamiliar lettering that meant nothing to her at a glance. Behind the desk, a wide window let in the last of the day's light.

Seris was seated, an old book open in front of her, a pen moving steadily across a notebook beside it. She didn't look up.

*"Third bookcase from the window,"* she said. *"Fourth shelf down. There's a book bound in dark green, the spine cracked near the top — bring it to me."*

Sera looked around the room for a moment before she found her bearings — the bookcases arranged in a way that took a few seconds to read properly, the third one from the window further than she'd first assumed. She counted shelves carefully, found the fourth, and ran her eyes along the spines until she spotted the cracked green binding.

The title was strange. It had a word she never heard of, Runic, but a strip of paper had been pasted over the original title at some point, the lettering on it in a different hand and what looked like a different language entirely, parts of the original cover still visible beneath where the paper had begun to lift at one corner.

She brought it to the desk.

---

Seris took it without looking up, opened it directly to a page somewhere past the middle — not searching, not flipping, just opening to the exact place as though she'd memorized its position in advance. She read for a moment, glanced between it and the book already open in front of her, and wrote something brief in her notes.

She closed both books.

*"Put them back,"* she said.

Sera took the green one first and returned it easily enough, the gap on the shelf still holding its shape from where she'd removed it. The second book — the one Seris had already been reading before Sera arrived — she held for a moment, unsure.

She glanced at Seris.

Seris was already absorbed again in her notes, giving no indication she intended to clarify.

Sera looked back at the shelves instead, and after a moment she noticed it — the order wasn't random. The titles ran roughly alphabetical, shelf by shelf, the kind of system that revealed itself only once you started actually looking rather than assuming chaos.

She found the gap that matched. She slid the book into place.

She watched Seris work for a while, careful not to drift too close — there was something in the focused quiet of the room that felt like it shouldn't be disturbed by proximity. From a small distance she could see what had looked, at first glance, like clutter on the table: now, watching the way Seris's eyes moved between specific stacks, the way one set of pages clearly cross-referenced another, the apparent disorder revealed itself as a system she simply hadn't learned to read yet.

*"I've never seen this language before,"* Sera said eventually. *"Though I suppose I've only ever lived in cities landlocked on this continent. Wherever it's from, it's beyond what I'd recognize."*

*"It's not spoken,"* Seris said, still writing. *"Not by any people I know of. Not now, and as far as I can tell, not for a very long time."* She finally looked up. *"I don't know where it came from. I don't know who made it, or what made it. I'm not even certain language is the right word for what it is."*

*"Then what do you know about it?"*

*"That someone — or something — found a way to store magic power inside these letters."*

---

Sera looked at the table, at the small circular diagrams covered in unfamiliar script, the careful annotations beside them.

*"Do the letters you've drawn have magic in them?"*

*"I haven't worked out how to make that happen yet,"* Seris said. *"There's very little to base the research on. Fragments. A handful of sources, most of them damaged or incomplete."* She tapped the open book in front of her. *"But I have learned this much — these letters can store mana directly into an object."*

*"For what purpose,"* Sera asked. *"Why would anyone want to store magic inside something?"*

Something shifted in Seris's expression — a flicker of genuine animation, more than Sera had seen from her in two days of careful, measured instruction.

*"The possibilities are nearly endless,"* she said. *"A light that never goes out. A well that never runs dry. Anything you can imagine, given the right understanding — anything that needs power, given power that never needs renewing."*

Sera thought about this for a moment.

*"In the capital,"* she said slowly, *"they use pylons to travel between kingdoms. It's rare — reserved for important people, or those with church connections."* She looked up. *"The pylon crystal — is that the same thing? Does it store mana the way these letters do?"*

*"No,"* Seris said. *"The pylons require a constant supply of mana from the people who operate them. Without the workers feeding it continuously, the crystal is nothing — just stone, inert, useless. What this language does is different. It supplies itself. No one has to keep feeding it anything, ever again, once it's properly made."*

Sera turned this over.

*"Then whoever left this language behind,"* she said, *"must have left more than just writing. There should be objects somewhere. Things they actually made with it."*

Seris looked at her for a moment with something close to approval.

*"You arrived at that faster than I expected,"* she said.

---

She reached beneath her desk and pulled out a small chest, setting it on the surface in front of her. When she opened it, a soft light spilled out before the object itself was even visible.

She lifted out a lantern.

It was ancient — unmistakably so, the metal of its frame pitted and worn, whole sections of it crumbled away entirely, the thing held together by what seemed like sheer stubbornness more than structural integrity. It looked as though a firm breath might finish what centuries had started.

It had no oil reservoir. No wick. No fuel source of any kind that Sera could see.

It was still glowing, faintly, even now.

Seris fed a small thread of mana into it.

The light strengthened — and the letters appeared, spreading across the lantern's surface, tracing its full original shape even across the sections that had crumbled away entirely. Where metal was missing, the script still completed the form, faint lines of light filling in what should have been empty space, as though the lantern remembered a shape its body no longer fully possessed.

*"I commissioned a replica,"* Seris said, watching the light settle. *"Same size. Same shape, down to the measurements. I copied the letters exactly — every stroke, every angle, position for position."*

*"It didn't work."* Seris set the ancient lantern down carefully. *"I fed it mana after I finished writing. Nothing. I fed it mana while I was still writing, mid-stroke, trying every order I could think of. Nothing."* She looked at the old lantern's faint, steady glow. *"I've tried nearly everything I know to try. I haven't found whatever I'm missing."*

*"Maybe," Sera said, "if you found other artifacts with the same runes — different versions, different objects — you might see something here you can't see now. A comparison."*

*Seris closed the lantern's chest carefully, the latch settling with a small click.*

*"It's not that simple," she said. "Artifacts like this aren't easy to come by. When they are found, they're taken — protected, hoarded, locked away by people who have no idea what they're looking at and even less idea what to do with it. There are pieces sitting in the capital's castle right now that almost no one is permitted to even know exist. And the handful of people privileged enough to know — they're not allowed to touch them either. Not without a dozen layers of permission that take years to grant, if they're ever granted at all."*

*"Then why tell me," Sera asked. "If it's guarded that closely."*

*Seris looked at her for a moment.*

*"Because my assistant should understand what she's assisting with," she said. "These are called enchanted artifacts. Scholars have spent lifetimes on the writing alone — generations of careful, brilliant people — and not one of them has come close to understanding it. I'm not the first to fail. I won't be the last."*

*She set the chest back under her desk, the motion deliberate, final — the specific closing of a drawer she intended to open again another day, just not today.*

*"I promised you something else, though," she said. "Sit."*

*Sera sat.*

---

*"What do you know about the rot," Seris said. "Tell me what the church taught you. All of it. I want to hear the version you were given before I tell you anything else."*

*Sera recited it. "The rot — the Corruption — is the Unmaking. The church says it's a punishment, or a trial — divine retribution against those who turned away from Providence's light long ago. A consequence of impurity left to fester. Providence didn't cause it. She opposes it. She's tasked her followers with holding it back until she's strong enough to address it permanently, at the root."* 

*Seris listened to all of it without interrupting.*

*"That's roughly what I expected," she said, when Sera finished. "And it's mostly invention."*

*Sera felt something tighten in her chest.*

*"Not all of it is a lie, exactly," Seris continued. "It started as an explanation — something the church needed to give people for a thing nobody understood. A story that filled a gap and reinforced faith at the same time, which made it useful, which made it spread. But as the corruption grew — as it became harder to ignore, as it crept closer to more people's homes — its place in the doctrine grew with it. It went from a footnote to the centerpiece. Now it's not just an unfortunate consequence anymore. It's Providence's defining enemy. The thing her entire church exists to fight."*

*"That's not true?"*

*"It's not that simple a question," Seris said. "Let me ask you something else first. What do you know about the crawling flesh — the affliction plaguing the Scorched Expanse, far to the south."* 

*Sera shook her head slowly.*

*"I don't know what that is."*

*"It plagues the land the way the rot plagues ours," Seris said. "Different texture, different behavior, but the same fundamental thing."*

*"The church has never mentioned it. Not once. Not to me."*

*"Of course it hasn't," Seris said. "It doesn't need to. Not yet. It's not your problem, not your border, not anyone your church needs frightened into obedience right now."*

*Sera sat with that for a moment.*

*"What does that mean," she said. "Not yet."*

*Seris didn't answer immediately. She looked at Sera instead — a long, careful look, the kind that weighed something before deciding whether to hand it over.*

*"I want to ask you one more time," she said. "Before I go further. Do you actually want to know what the rot is. Not the comfortable version. The real one."*

*Sera's hands had gone still in her lap.*

*"Yes," she said.*

---

*"What do you know about the gods," Seris said.*

*Sera opened her mouth to answer.*
