*He had been moving backward and now he stopped — not because the situation had improved but because the two soldiers nearest to the compound had just been blasted by the man's wind and the fire had come after them immediately and there was nothing behind him worth retreating toward anymore. The compound entrance was forty feet away. He looked at it. He looked at the six soldiers he had left on the ground.*

*He looked up at the garrison.*

*More archers had arrived at different sections of the wall — the night watch responding to the sound of it, taking positions wherever the crenels were still intact. More guards were pressing toward the compound exit, the ones inside wanting to come out.*

*"Stay put," Haes said. Loud enough to reach them. "Nobody comes out."*

*He found the soldier furthest from the compound — a young one, ten feet from the building wall to his left, shield up, eyes on the fire.*

*"You," Haes said. "Head to the chapel. Tell them the Godless Hand is here."*

*The soldier looked at him.*

*"Go," Haes said.*

*As Haes pushed forward — driving toward Elysia's position to draw her attention, forcing her to track him rather than the garrison — the soldier slipped sideways between the buildings and was gone, swallowed by the dark narrow space between structures, his footsteps already fading south.*

*Haes didn't watch him go. He was already moving.*

*Elysia turned the fire toward him. He took it on the shield and kept moving — angling, making himself a moving target. The parts of him the shield didn't cover began to communicate the temperature. The pauldron on his right shoulder was turning color — the metal going from its ordinary grey to something with red underneath it, not glowing yet but promising to. The vambrace on his forearm where the shield's edge met his arm. The gorget at his throat. The heat arriving through the metal the way heat arrived through metal — slowly, then suddenly, the material storing it until it couldn't anymore.* 

*She stopped the continuous stream.*

*The fireball that replaced it was different — concentrated, faster, the specific output of someone who had assessed a target and decided to stop being patient about it. It hit his shield and the force of it threw him backward, the shield leaving his hand, Haes hitting the ground on his back.*

*The second one came before he finished landing.*

*He rolled. The fireball hit the ground where he'd been — the stone scorching to the point of cracking, the heat of it close enough to feel on his face. He found his shield three feet away, grabbed it, got his back against the stone fence at the edge of the street. One of his soldiers was already there. They pressed into the cover together.*

*The two remaining soldiers on open ground made it back into the compound.*

*Haes looked at the compound entrance. Harold was there — his right hand, inside, already reading the situation. Their eyes met across the distance.*

*Harold turned without being told and disappeared inside.*

*He came back with two men carrying a large wooden container between them — heavy, the specific weight of something packed carefully for storage. Harold opened it. Twenty crossbows inside, bolts bundled separately, the manufacturing that Ryn's schematics had made possible sitting in a wooden box in the northern compound's storage because Vorne had sent them here.*

*Harold picked two.*

*He pointed at five of them — sent them up to the garrison with five crossbows, the archers there receiving them through the gap in the compound's upper access. The remaining thirteen stayed with the compound soldiers.*

*Harold walked to the compound entrance and looked at the soldier behind the stone fence with haes.*

*He tossed the second crossbow.*

*The soldier caught it.*

---

*The garrison received their five crossbows and the difference was immediate.*

*The barrage that came down on the man was not the individual rhythm of five archers timing their own shots — it was a coordinated release, bolts arriving in a pattern that his wind deflection couldn't fully account for. He caught most of them. He didn't catch all of them.*

*The bolt that hit him went into his shoulder — deep, the impact staggering him.*

*Harold saw the window from the compound entrance and fired.*

*At the floor-level windows of the compound — narrow, built for defense — soldiers were already pressing crossbows through the gaps, firing at Elysia in the intervals between her sweeps.* 

*Elysia saw Harold fire and redirected — the continuous flame coming off her hand and pouring into the compound entrance, forcing Harold back inside, the metal door frame beginning to heat at the edges.*

*Haes moved.*

*He and the soldier with him came around through the gap between buildings — south, then east, circling behind the two Godless Hand members while Elysia was focused on the compound entrance and the man was dealing with the bolt in his shoulder. They came out behind them. The soldier raised the crossbow and fired at Elysia.*

*The man's hand came up.*

*A wind barrier — not a blast, a sustained field, the bolts deflecting off it at angles without reaching either of them. He turned to her.*

*"Elysia," he said. "This is not working."*

*He reached up to his shoulder. The bolt had gone in at an angle — deep into the joint, the head lodged against bone. He took hold of it and worked it loose. The sound it made coming out was not clean. His face made no response to it — not stoicism, just the genuine absence of the expected reaction, the specific quality of someone for whom pain had been renegotiated into a different category years ago.*

*He looked at the bolt for a moment and dropped it.*

*His cowl built around him — the wind-nature of it visible in the way the air moved near his body, his clothes pressing flat against his skin as the mana accelerated outward. He channeled it downward. His feet left the ground — slowly at first, then with more authority, the wind carrying him upward until he was above the garrison wall, above the crenels, looking down at everything from a position that gave him the entire compound laid out beneath him and no cover between him and any of it.*

*He planted himself there.*

*Elysia created her cowl. The fire-nature of it built fast around her — hot, immediate, the red-orange quality of it pushing heat outward into the already-warm air around her. It was larger than anything Bael had produced in the training court and it cost her nothing visible to hold it.* 

*She turned — away from the compound entrance, away from Harold, turning to find where Haes and the soldier had come from, the tattoos on her forehead catching the firelight in the specific way that dense small writing caught light when it covered skin, the letters illegible at any distance but present, covering everything from her hairline to her brow.*

*She found the position Haes had fired from.*

*She raised her hand.*

*The fire that came out of it was different from everything before it — not wider, not more of what she'd been doing. Narrower. Concentrated to a point that the air around it whistled, the specific sound of something moving faster than the surrounding air could accommodate. It hit the stone surface of the building Haes was using for cover and the stone didn't crack. It morphed. The surface of it softening, the edges of the impact point beginning to flow rather than shatter, the specific behavior of material that had been introduced to a temperature it wasn't built to resist.*

*The doors of the houses nearest to this section of street began to open.*

*Not in panic. In the cautious investigation of people who had heard something they couldn't identify from inside their walls and had decided to look. They opened their doors and saw the light — enormous, bright, the specific quality of fire at a scale that made ordinary fire look like a candle — and they stood in their doorways and they looked at it from the distance the street provided and they didn't yet understand what they were looking at.*

*The whistle of the concentrated flame continued.*

*The stone kept moving.*

---

*The southern gate was quiet when Vorne arrived.*

*Too quiet. The guards at the post had the specific posture of men who had been sitting in the same position for long enough that the position had become something else — heads dipped, shoulders settled, the involuntary surrender of bodies that had decided nothing was going to happen tonight and had begun to act accordingly.*

*They came up fast when they heard the horses.*

*Vorne was off his mount before it fully stopped. He held out his hand without looking at either guard.*

*"The log."*

*One of them produced it. He took it and read — quickly, the specific focused speed of someone who knew what they were looking for and was moving through everything else to find it. The royal carriage. A delivery notation. Nothing else. He looked at both guards.*

*"Is this all the traffic this gate has seen today."*

*"Yes, Captain," the first guard said.*

*Vorne looked at the second guard. The second guard was looking at the ground to the left of Vorne's boots — the specific quality of someone whose eyes had decided that direct contact was inadvisable.*

*Vorne reached out and took hold of the shoulder armor — the western district sigil stamped into the metal, the sigil that meant something, that was supposed to mean something — and lifted. The guard came up with it, feet leaving the ground by an inch, the armor doing the work his legs hadn't been asked to do.*

*"I will ask again," Vorne said, "and I want a different answer."*

*"Five children, sir," the guard said. "We let five children through. Back to the passage. It was before curfew, they were just—"*

*"Who else."*

*"No one, sir. I swear it. No one else."*

*Vorne looked at him for a moment. Then he set him down, and removed the shoulder armor with the sigil from his person in a single clean motion. He held it. He looked at it. He put it under his arm.*

*The guard stood without it, looking diminished in the specific way people looked diminished when something that represented their authority was no longer on their body.*

*Vorne turned away.*

*Some relief. The southern gate hadn't been used. Whatever was happening in the district, it hadn't come through here and it wasn't going out through here. But the sweep hadn't reported back yet and he didn't have the full picture and he held his position and waited for it.*

---

*The soldier Haes had sent south ran through the dark city with the specific driven movement of someone who had been given one job and intended to complete it regardless of what the dark and the empty streets and the curfew silence around him suggested about the wisdom of running through them alone.*

*The moonlight was the only light. The district had settled into its nighttime self — shutters closed, the market empty, the streets belonging to nobody. His boots on the stone were the loudest thing for blocks in every direction.*

*He heard the horse before he saw it.*

*One of Vorne's riders — sweeping the district, moving at a measured pace through the residential streets south of the northern compound. The soldier flagged him down. He told him what he knew: a man and a woman, a carriage, the garrison under attack, Lieutenant Haes holding the compound.*

*The rider's face changed. He pulled the soldier up onto the horse behind him and they rode — south first, to the chapel, the rider sending a separate man back toward the western compound with the report before they arrived.*

*The chapel sat in the western district with the specific settled permanence of something that had been there long enough that the district had built itself around it rather than the other way around. Its doors were closed. Two clerics stood at the entrance — young, the night watch, the kind of posting given to people who were trusted to stand still and look present rather than to do anything in particular.*

*They heard the words Godless Hand and moved immediately.*

*The doors opened inward. One of them went at a run through the nave, past the altar, through the door behind it. The other stayed.*

*Father Ignatius came out two minutes later.*

*He was seventy-three years old and looked like something that had survived longer than most things survived by being harder than most things were hard. Thin — the thinness of someone whose body had reduced itself over decades to the minimum required for continued operation. His hair was white and full, swept back from a face that was all angles, the cheekbones prominent, the jaw still defined, the skin pulled tight over a framework that age had clarified rather than softened. His hands, when they moved, moved with the specific deliberate authority of someone who had learned that deliberate was more frightening than fast.*

*And his eyes.*

*Blue — the specific pale blue of something that had very little warmth in it, the color of water in winter, of sky before a storm decided what it was going to do. They were remarkable eyes. They moved through the soldier's report with a quality of attention that processed everything and gave nothing back, the way a ledger received information without having opinions about it.*

*He was silent for a moment after the soldier finished.*

*Then he turned to the clerics behind him.*

*"Sound the bell," he said.*

*The bell of Providence's chapel in the western district of Ordenmere was not a modest instrument. It had been installed when the chapel was built — larger than anything a single person could ring without the mechanism that had been designed specifically for it, the sound of it calibrated to carry across the full extent of the district's thousands of acres regardless of wind or weather. It had been rung three times in living memory, each time for something that warranted the whole district knowing simultaneously.*

*It rang now.*

*The sound of it arrived everywhere at once — not loud in the way that nearby things were loud, but present in the way that large things were present, the vibration of it felt in walls and floors and chests before the ears fully processed it as sound. It moved through the district's evening quiet and the quiet simply ceased.*

*Father Ignatius looked at his clerics.*

*"Four of you. Northern gate." He looked at them. "Tobias. Julian. Gideon." A pause. "Leonard."*

*Three of them moved toward the stable. Leonard didn't, he flew.*

---

*The bell moved through the district and the district responded the way districts responded to things that announced themselves at that volume in the middle of the night — doors opening, one by one, the specific cautious progression of people who had heard something they couldn't identify and had decided that looking was preferable to not knowing. They came out in various states of undress, in various states of wakefulness, and stood in their doorways or at their gates and looked north where the bell had come from and saw nothing yet and looked at each other and said nothing useful and stayed where they were because going inside felt wrong and going toward it felt worse.* 

*The students heard it from the dormitory.*

*Myre was the first one out — the door open before the bell's second resonance had finished, the training ground visible from the dormitory entrance, the night sky above it empty and dark. Iren and sera came behind her.* 

*The male students emerged from their wing simultaneously — Bael first, then Davan close behind him, Solen a half-step after. They came out into the compound's open space and stood and looked at the sky in the direction the bell had come from.*

*Nothing yet. Just the bell, still fading.*

*"That's the chapel bell," Iren said.*

*Nobody answered her. They were all looking at the same piece of sky.*

*Seris was already outside.*

*She was still standing outside the dormitory— dressed, still, the specific quality of someone who had been awake and thinking and had heard the bell as a confirmation of something rather than a surprise. She looked at the sky. She looked at the compound gate. She looked at the six students who had come out and arranged themselves around her.*

*Davan looked at Seris.*

*"Magister," he said. "What's happening."*

*She was already turning toward them — opening her mouth to tell them to go back to their quarters, the flat authority of it already present in her posture — when something in the sky above the northern part of the district changed.*

*All of them stopped.*

---

*The bell was still fading when the northern compound's situation was this: the crenels were gone — the garrison wall's upper edge broken and crumbling in three sections, the archers who had been positioned there either dead or driven down to the compound floor. The metal door of the compound entrance had been under Elysia's sustained fire long enough that the edges of it were no longer the color metal was supposed to be, the heat working inward from the frame. Harold was behind it with the soldiers, the floor-level windows still producing bolts at intervals but fewer now, the supply of angles narrowing as the door's frame warped. Haes was outside — unable to do anything, one soldier beside him, the crossbow in his hands, the pauldron on his right shoulder dark with heat, the gorget at his throat the same, the parts of him the shield hadn't covered communicating everything the fire had spent the last several minutes saying.* 

*The bell changed something.*

*Elysia heard it. She stopped the fire. In the sudden absence of it the street was dark and quiet in a way it hadn't been for the last several minutes, the afterimage of the flame still present in everyone's vision.*

*She looked above the garrison where the man hovered.*

*"Severin."*

*He was already moving toward her.*

*He came down — descended, the wind carrying him back to ground level, his feet finding the street. She put her arm on his shoulder. He put his hand on her waist.*

*The wind built around them — not a blast, a sustained lift, channeled downward the way he'd channeled it to his own feet. They rose together. The street falling away beneath them, the compound wall dropping below eye level, the rooftops of the northern district spreading out around them as they cleared the highest structures and kept going.*

*When they were high enough she raised her free hand.*

*The fire that came from it was not directed at anything. It went upward — into the open air above the district, above the rooftops, above everything — and it went bright, brighter than anything she had produced in the fight below, the full output of her cowl concentrated into a single upward column that caught the night air and held it and turned the sky above the western district the specific orange-red of something burning at a scale that didn't happen by accident.*

*A beacon.*

*Visible for miles.*

---

*Seris saw it.*

*Her students saw it — all six of them, standing in the open space, heads tilted back, the light of it reaching their faces from a distance that made it look enormous. Bael's jaw set. Davan went completely still, which was not a thing Davan usually did. Solen looked at it with the specific expression of someone filing information faster than they could process what it meant.*

*Myre looked at Seris.*

*Seris was looking at the beacon with the flat focused attention she brought to things she needed to understand before she could speak about them.*

*She said nothing.*

---

*Vorne saw it from the southern gate.*

*He was still holding the sigil from the guard's shoulder armor. He looked at the beacon in the sky above the northern part of the district and something in his face did what faces did when a calculation resolved in the worst direction — not surprise, not fear, just the specific settling of someone who had suspected and is now confirmed and has to decide what to do with the confirmation.*

*He looked at his riders.*

*He looked at the southern gate behind him.*

*He got back on his horse.*

---

*On the roof near western gate, Highmore and Emmeline had been still since they entered the district.*

*They had not moved from the position they had taken when they first came over the gate's neighboring rooftop — prone, below the roofline, the district spread out below them in its curfew dark. They had watched Vorne's riders sweep the streets. They had watched the chapel bell. They had watched the compound mobilize and Vorne ride south.*

*They had waited.*

*The beacon changed that.*

*The woman stood first. The man was already moving.*

---

*The rider arrived at the western compound gate at a controlled pace — not panicked, the professional speed of someone delivering a report rather than fleeing something. He pulled up at the gate and looked at the two guards there.*

*"Where is Captain Vorne."*

*"Rode south, sir. The southern gate."*

*He absorbed this. "I need to report — the man and woman Vorne is looking for, they're at the northern compound. Lieutenant Haes is engaged, the compound is—"*

*"Are they now," a voice said.*

*Not from the gate. From the street.*

*The rider turned.*

*A man and a woman were walking toward the compound entrance from the direction of the district's interior — unhurried, the specific pace of people who had somewhere to be and weren't worried about getting there. The man was in his forties — clean-shaved, dark hair grown below his ears and pushed back from his face, the natural oil of it catching what little light the street offered. Black eyes, the kind that registered everything in a room without appearing to move. A face that was handsome in the specific way of someone who had never needed to do anything with it — not performing it, just carrying it. He wore dark robes, clean, the specific deliberate quality of someone who had changed specifically for this or removed what was covering it.*

*The woman beside him was around the same age — brown hair reaching her waist in a single neat braid, not a strand out of place, no grey in it despite her age, the braid the specific maintenance of someone for whom precision was a habit rather than an effort. Mature, composed, the dark robes on her the same as his. She walked with the unhurried certainty of someone who had been waiting a long time and had arrived at the end of the waiting without losing any of the patience it had taken to get there.*

*The guards at the compound entrance looked at the rider.*

*"Is this them," one of them said. "The ones the captain is—"*

*"No," the rider said. He was already reaching for his reins. "I need to ride to the southern gate, I need to warn—"*

*The rider reached for his reins. "I need to ride to the southern gate, I need to warn—"*

*The word didn't finish.*

*The lower half of the rider's body left the saddle. The horse's head left its neck. Both things happened at the same moment — the rider's torso going forward over the pommel on pure momentum, the horse's body continuing three full strides on legs that didn't know yet, the enormous weight of it finally registering and coming down onto the stone with a sound that shook the ground under the guards' boots. The rider's upper half was on the street. The rest of him was still in the saddle of a horse that was no longer a horse.*

*The blood reached the guards before either of them moved.*

*One of the guards made a sound.*

*The other one had stopped being able to move.*

*They looked at the man in the dark robes. He was lowering his hand.*

*"That won't be necessary," the man said. "We're not planning on staying long."*

# 23 \- What The Tyrant Left Behind \- Part 2

**Chapter Twenty-Three — What The Tyrant Left Behind \- Part 2**

---

Vorne was already turning the horse north when he heard it.

The crashing arrived before he had turned fully — the specific sound of something structural giving way at scale, stone separating from stone with the finality of something that had been holding and had simply stopped holding. He turned. The rubble was already on the ground, covering the gate area in a spread of broken stone and mortar dust, the debris field of a wall section that was no longer a wall section. He looked up. A portion of the southern wall was missing — the gap in it clean-edged against the night sky, twenty feet across at least, the break too precise to be decay.

The horses shied. 

The dust moved through the torchlight at the gate in slow billowing rolls, the specific unhurried expansion of something that had nowhere urgent to be. His riders had pulled their horses back. The guards at the gate were unseen.

The dust settled.

A man stood in it.

Not buried, not running — standing, in the specific way of someone who had known the wall was coming down and had calculated exactly where to be when it did. The debris had missed him by the margin of a choice rather than the margin of luck. He reached up and pushed his hood back from his face. The cloth underneath was grey-brown, the common shade of the road, and it was not a district soldier's armor.

Vorne was off the horse before he decided to dismount.

The man looked up. Not at Vorne — at the sky above where the wall had been. Following something upward with his eyes. Vorne followed his gaze.

The moonlight caught it — a figure in the air above the gate, above the roofline, above everything. And then something else: a light, emanating from the figure, different from the beacon from the north. That one had been orange-red, the specific color of fire at scale. This one was white. Brighter, calmer, the specific quality of something that wasn't burning but simply was — steady and cold and precise against the dark sky above the southern gate.

The greatsword was already in Vorne's hand.

He became aware of it the way you became aware of things you had done before your mind caught up — the weight of it familiar, the grip settled into his palms with the specific ease of something that had been there ten thousand times before. He looked at his men.

Tristan first. Sir Tristan Castellan, the specific settled authority of someone who had been tested in enough situations that testing had simply become the condition he operated in. Then Berrick. Sir Berrick Morvayn — the fastest sword hand Vorne had ever personally fought beside, the one whose body processed threat and response as a single operation without the gap most people had between them. Then Lucian. Sir Lucian Hallow — the youngest of the three, quieter than the other two, the one who said little and positioned himself correctly every time without being told, the specific competence of someone who understood a situation completely before they acted on it.

They had been carrying the rifles for two days. They held them like the weapons they were — with the respect of men who understood that a new tool required new understanding, not the casual familiarity they carried their swords with. Not yet.

They looked back at him. They understood.

The fifteen crossbow soldiers behind them were already moving — Tristan reading the ground, directing the formation with the quiet efficiency of a man who had done this in worse situations and had learned that noise was a liability.

Vorne held his position.

He looked at the man on the ground. Broad across the shoulders — the specific breadth of someone built for sustained physical work rather than the lean efficiency of most mages he had encountered. His attire was not armor. The grey-brown cloth of it communicated traveler rather than soldier, but something in the way he stood communicated neither. He stood the way people stood when they were completely certain of the ground under their feet.

*"Who are you,"* Vorne said. *"And what is your purpose."*

*"My name is Cedric,"* the man said. His voice had the specific quality of someone who enjoyed conversation and was aware that this was not the moment for it and intended to have it anyway. *"And that up there is—"*

*"I didn't ask your name. I asked who you are."*

Cedric looked at him. Something moved in his face — not offense, something closer to appreciation.

*"We are in open ground, Captain,"* Tristan said from behind him, low.

*"We don't know what they're capable of,"* Vorne said. *"It could be in their favor if we moved."*

*"Staying here won't be in your favor either,"* Cedric said. The reply arriving easily, directed at a conversation he hadn't been included in. *"To be honest with you — I didn't want to meet you today, Aldous. I hoped you would be with Emmeline and Highmore at this moment. But here we are."*

*"You know my name,"* Vorne said.

*"Of course I know the great Aldo—"*

A voice from above. Dry, flat, the specific register of someone for whom this entire exchange was an expenditure they hadn't budgeted for.

*"Perhaps we call for a round of ale."*

The figure descended.

He was thin — the thinness of someone whose body had been built for something other than impact, the lean specific construction of precision rather than force. Pale, young, the kind of young that sat uneasily with the quality of stillness in his face. He was standing on something. Not hovering, not floating — standing, his feet planted on an object that moved through the air with the specific controlled ease of something that had been doing this long enough that movement had become its default state. Nobody on the ground had a word for the object. Nobody on the ground had seen anything like it. It was a broom — the shape of it unmistakable — and it moved through the air as if the air was simply another surface.

*"Don't be so crude, Silas,"* Cedric said.

He looked at Vorne with something that was neither threat nor challenge but sat between them — the specific expression of someone who had assessed a situation completely and found it interesting.

*"It's not every day you get to kill someone like Aldous here."*

---

Vorne looked at Berrick.

Berrick lifted the rifle.

Cedric's hand came out — not fast, just present, the motion of someone responding to something their body had registered before their mind did. Earth came from his palm — not solid yet, wet, the specific consistency of disturbed soil, moving with the fluid quality of something between states. It went solid in the instant it needed to, a barrier forming in front of him in the specific time between Berrick's shoulder dropping and the trigger moving.

The shot hit the barrier — the sound of it enormous in the night street, the specific crack of the rifle arriving before the impact registered, the kind of sound that had no precedent in anyone's experience who hadn't been standing near one when it fired, the echo of it bouncing off the gate's remaining wall and the buildings on either side and coming back diminished but still present.

The barrier shattered.

The bullet passed next to Cedric's face — the velocity of it close enough that he felt it as heat, as pressure, as the specific sensation of something moving very fast through the air immediately adjacent to your skin. The barrier was already dissolving back into mana, the edges of it losing coherence, the stone returning to the ambient field it had come from.

Cedric whistled.

Not performed — genuine. The specific sound of someone who had just encountered something they hadn't fully accounted for and found the encounter interesting rather than frightening.

Tristan fired at Silas. Silas moved — the broom carrying him sideways without visible effort, the bolt passing through the space where he had been.

Lucian raised the rifle at Cedric.

Cedric's hand came out again. Stone this time — denser than the first barrier, the earth already having made its assessment of what the first barrier needed to be and calibrating upward. The bullet did not care, the barrier shattered and the bullet went throught.

Cedric was not behind it.

The dust from the shattering expanded outward in the specific brief cloud that stone produced when it was broken quickly — grey-white, the same color as the wall dust still settling at the gate, hanging in the torchlight for the two seconds before it dissolved back into the air. In those two seconds Cedric moved left, using the cover of it.

When the dust cleared he realized he was not running alone.

Vorne had already closed the distance.

Someone that size — the specific mass of a man who carried a greatsword as a primary weapon and had built his body around the requirements of that choice for the better part of two decades — had no business covering ground that quickly. But he had, and Cedric processed this in the specific way you processed things when the information arrived a fraction of a second after you needed it: too late to use it for the thing it was supposed to prevent, only fast enough to survive the consequence of having needed it sooner.

The greatsword came down.

Cedric pulled his own sword — shorter, lighter, a different category of weapon entirely — and caught the greatsword not at the blade but at the angle of it, redirecting Vorne's momentum rather than opposing it, the force of the swing carrying the greatsword past him and into the space where he hadn't been. Vorne felt the redirect the instant it happened and stopped the sword before it hit the ground — a feat of physical control that communicated everything necessary about what kind of fighter he was — and then his body was already moving, the greatsword coming up and around in a full rotation, the arc of it describing a circle that ended exactly where Cedric was.

Cedric's hands came up. Stone built around his forearms in the specific rapid formation of someone who had done this enough times that the magic had become a physical reflex — a vambrace on each arm, thick, the stone still settling into its final shape when the greatsword arrived. He caught it with both arms, the impact of it traveling through the stone and through his arms and into his shoulders and driving him backward — six feet of ground covered involuntarily, his boots scoring two parallel lines in the street stones before he stopped.

Lucian fired the moment Cedric was stationary.

The barrier Cedric produced was thicker than either of the previous ones — the calibration happening in real time, his magic reading what the situation required and producing it. The barrier exploded outward when the bullet hit it, the stone fragmenting in every direction, the dust coming again. When it cleared Cedric was gone.

Not from Vorne's eyes. Vorne had never lost him.

*"Silas,"* Cedric called. He was moving — dodging Vorne's attacks, the specific fluid evasion of someone who had been hit hard enough once to understand the importance of not being hit — his voice carrying the specific quality of someone conducting two operations simultaneously and finding this entirely manageable.

*"Yes,"* Silas said from above. Calm. The crossbow barrage that the fifteen soldiers had been directing at him was a problem he was solving without apparent urgency, the broom carrying him through the lines of flight with the specific efficiency of something that had already calculated all available angles.

*"Would you be so kind,"* Cedric said, redirecting a greatsword strike with his forearm — the stone vambrace absorbing the impact — *"and stop those three from interrupting our dance. Please."*

A pause.

*"How can I say no,"* Silas said, *"since you asked so nicely."*

---

He hovered.

Still — the broom holding its position against the wind with the absolute stability of something that didn't need to negotiate with gravity. Below him the fifteen soldiers were still directing their crossbows upward, the bolts rising and falling short or passing through the space he had already vacated. He ignored them.

His cowl built around him.

The light came first — his nature expressing itself the way natures did when the cowl was present, the specific quality of his element visible in the specific quality of what gathered around his body. Light. Not the warm orange of fire or the cool blue of water — light, the specific sourceless illumination of something that was producing radiance rather than reflecting it, the cowl around him brightening until the brightness became the point rather than the byproduct.

He released it.

The light that came off him was not a weapon — it was a condition. It arrived everywhere simultaneously, the specific quality of something that didn't travel so much as exist, and the effect of it on every pair of eyes below was immediate and total. The soldiers couldn't open their eyes. Vorne was far enough to turn away when he caught a glimpse of the light. Cedric — who had been expecting it — turned his face away at the moment of release and still felt the afterimage burning through his closed eyelids.

In the darkness behind their eyes Silas put his hands up and began to speak.

The language was not one anyone on the ground had heard before. Not the formal register of Ordenmere's court, not the trading pidgin of the western districts, not the liturgical language of Providence's church. Something else — older in its quality, the specific sound of syllables that had been shaped by a different set of constraints than the ones that produced the languages they knew. He spoke it with the specific flat authority of Silas saying anything — not devotional, not incantatory, just the recitation of something that needed to be said in order for something else to happen.

He released his mana while he spoke.

It came from his hands and took shape in the air in front of him — not the elemental form that mana usually took when a mage released it, not fire or water or wind or earth. Symbols. Letters from the same script the mana was taking shape as, moving in the air with the specific quality of things that were still finding their positions, the symbols drifting and then orienting, drifting and then orienting, until they fell into formation with the specific finality of something that had always been going to end up in exactly this arrangement.

A circle.

Floating above Silas's head — light runes, the script of them luminous, the circle complete and turning slowly in the air with the specific unhurried rotation of something that had been set in motion and would continue until it was told not to. The soldiers below whose eyes were beginning to adjust looked up and saw it — the circle, the symbols, the specific quality of something that didn't belong to any magical tradition anyone in Ordenmere had been taught to recognize.

*"Thus it is written in the ash of the old gods,"* Silas said.

The circle opened.

They came through it in a rush — not one by one but all at once, the way things came through openings when the opening was the only thing that had been holding them back. Ravens. The light caught only their silhouettes — the shape of a raven, the specific outline of wings and beak and the compact mass of a body built for speed, but the interior of each silhouette was not flesh, not feather, not anything that belonged to a living creature. Darkness. The specific absence of light that was not the same as shadow — something more intentional than shadow, the dark flame of it trailing from their bodies as they moved, the shadows of them leaving their bodies like smoke from something that burned without fuel. And the eyes — the only point of color in each silhouette, red, the specific red of something that was looking at you and had already decided what it was going to do.

They were slightly larger than they should have been. Not dramatically — just enough. The specific wrongness of a familiar thing at an unfamiliar scale.

There were more than a dozen.

They circled once above silas in the specific formation of things that were being directed rather than things that were choosing, and then Silas looked at Lucian.

---

The ravens went for him like a decision that had already been made.

They came in a line.

Not a flock — a line, the specific formation of things moving in coordinated single file, the silhouettes of them strung together in the air like a shadow that had learned to travel independently of the thing casting it. Moving fast. The line of them cutting through the torchlight and the darkness between the torches in a continuous stream of shadow and red.

Lucian raised the rifle and fired into the line.

The shot passed through multiple of them simultaneously — the silhouettes coming apart where the bullet passed, the darkness dispersing, the red eyes going out in sequence along the line. And then they reformed. Each one reconstituting in the instant after the bullet passed, the darkness pulling back together around the outline of a raven, the red eyes returning, the line closing the gaps the shot had opened before the sound of the shot had finished echoing off the walls.

The reformed ravens arrived with the others. Lucian had time to understand what this meant — that the rifle was a tool for a problem that couldn't be solved with a tool — and then they were on him.

The sound they made was not the sound of birds. It was the sound of edges — the specific rapid percussion of things that were cutting, the claws of them finding the gaps in his armor with the specific intelligence of things that had been told to find gaps, the beaks of them driving into the spaces between plates with a precision that communicated direction rather than animal instinct. He swung the rifle like a club and it connected and a raven came apart and reformed and the ones that were already on him kept cutting.

He dropped the rifle.

The sword came out — the specific motion of a trained hand finding a familiar grip in an unfamiliar situation, the body defaulting to what it knew when what it knew was all it had left. He swung. He connected. Ravens came apart and reformed. The ones that were circling hadn't landed yet — they were a wall around him, the tornado of it visible from outside as a column of darkness that moved when he moved, that contracted when he contracted, that had made itself into an enclosure around a man who was still fighting inside it.

His horse went first.

The ravens that had been circling descended on it from above in a single coordinated motion — the horse screaming once, the sound of it cutting through the fight the way animal sounds cut through things, and then the screaming stopping, and the horse throwing Lucian as it went down, the body of it hitting the street stones and Lucian hitting the street stones separately, the pouch he had been wearing no longer where it was supposed to be, the armor he had been wearing no longer where it was supposed to be, pieces of it scattered in the specific pattern of something that had been removed by force rather than by design.

He was on the ground.

He kept fighting. That was the thing — he kept fighting, the sword still in his hand, still connecting, ravens still coming apart and reforming, the ground around him going red in the specific way the ground went red when something large had been injured and the ground was receiving what the body could no longer contain. He kept fighting with the specific stubborn competence of someone whose body had not yet finished processing what his situation actually was.

Then he stopped.

The ravens stopped.

They pulled back — not fled, pulled back, the specific controlled withdrawal of things responding to a direction. They reformed above Silas in a loose formation, the darkness of them settling, the red eyes going dim to embers.

The street where Lucian had been was not a place anymore. It was a record — the specific terrible record that violence left when it had been thorough and had taken its time. The armor in pieces. The sword still in a hand that was no longer attached to anything that could use it. The red of it reaching the walls on either side, still moving in the slow specific way that things moved when gravity was the only remaining force acting on them.

Vorne stopped.

It happened between one attack and the next — the stillness arriving in the space where the next movement should have been.

Tristan and Berrick had stopped moving. The two knights standing with the specific quality of men who had seen death in many forms and were now encountering a form that expanded the category beyond what they had understood it contained. Neither of them spoke. Neither of them looked away.

Around them the soldiers and their horses had pulled back — the horses communicating what the soldiers were still processing, the animals having arrived at their assessment faster and more honestly, several of them pressing against the far wall of the gate with the specific bodily urgency of creatures that wanted to be somewhere else and were being prevented. The soldiers holding their reins were holding them with the mechanical attention of people whose minds were entirely elsewhere.

And Vorne.

He looked at what remained of Lucian for exactly as long as he allowed himself to look at it.

For one second he was still.

Sand hit his face.

The stream of it came from Cedric's hand — not attacking, interrupting, the specific targeted release of someone who had identified a window and was using it before it closed. It hit Vorne across the eyes and the nose and the mouth and then it went solid — the earth magic asserting itself, the sand compressing and hardening against his skin, the specific terrible sensation of something that had been a fluid becoming a fixed state while it was still in contact with his face, the weight of it pulling at his skin, the pressure of it against his eyes, the world going from what it had been to nothing in the time it took the sand to decide what it was going to be. 

He came down from above.

His sword was descending — and then it wasn't just his sword, because midway through the descent the sword was changing, stone building around the blade and the hilt, adding mass and length in the specific rapid accumulation of someone who had calculated exactly how much heavier a descending blade needed to be to produce a specific result, the stone making the sword longer and heavier and the gravity of the descent adding to what the stone had already added, the whole thing arriving at Vorne with the force of something that had been engineered specifically for this moment.

Vorne's left arm came up.

The vambrace took it — the specific sound of stone hitting metal, the force of it traveling up through the vambrace and into the arm and the shoulder and the specific grinding sensation of metal giving way at the edge of what it was built to absorb. The vambrace broke. The arm underneath was scraped — the stone edge of Cedric's augmented sword finding the skin where the broken vambrace no longer protected it. But the redirect happened — the sword going sideways rather than through, the force of it dissipating into the street stones beside Vorne rather than into Vorne.

Cedric made the stone disappear. The sword went light again in the instant after impact — the mass returning to mana, the weapon returning to what it had been before the descent, the specific rapid reversal of someone who understood that a heavy sword in close quarters after a failed strike was a liability.

Vorne stood up.

His eyes were clearing. The sand was turning back to mana. The world was reassembling itself in his vision — the gate, the rubble, the street, Cedric in front of him, the sky above with Silas still on the broom and the ravens in their loose formation.

And the street where Lucian had been.

He looked at it for exactly as long as he allowed himself to look at it.

*"You don't have time to worry about anyone,"* Cedric said. Something in his voice that wasn't quite satisfaction — the specific quality of someone who understood the weight of what had just happened and wasn't pretending otherwise. *"You will all be together soon."*

Vorne said nothing.

Cedric reached up and took hold of his robe. He pulled it off in a single motion and let it fall. Underneath it: broad shoulders, strong arms, the specific honed construction of someone who had built their body for exactly this kind of work. Light leather armor — not the heavy plate of a soldier, the specific pragmatic coverage of someone who had decided that mobility was worth more than protection. He looked like what he was: a mage who had decided that being a mage didn't mean being fragile, and had spent considerable time and effort proving the point.

*"A mage who isn't puny,"* Vorne said.

*"I always liked to get up close and personal,"* Cedric said, *"with the people I kill."*

He lunged.

The distance between them closed in the time it took to process that it was closing — the greatsword already in motion, the specific arc of it describing the line between where Vorne was and where Cedric was, and Cedric processing this and creating stone in front of him.

The greatsword broke the barrier.

It continued through the breaking of it and found Cedric on the other side — not at full force, the barrier having taken what the barrier could take, but not nothing either. Cedric's stone shoulder plate was already there when it arrived — built in the instant between the barrier breaking and the sword arriving, the stone taking what the barrier hadn't, the impact of it driving him backward and sideways, his boots leaving parallel marks in the street stones.

He stopped. He straightened.

Vorne was looking at his sword. Checking the edge where it had hit stone — twice now, the second time at significant force.

*"I know who you are, heretic,"* Vorne said.

*"A brute who isn't simple,"* Cedric said. *"I'm almost surprised."*

*"You attack small helpless villages,"* Vorne said. He moved — the greatsword moving with him, the attack arriving as a continuation of the sentence rather than a pause after it. *"You burn farmers. You burn women and children in their homes and you recite scripture over the fire."* Another attack, Cedric evading, the stone building where it needed to build and dissolving where it needed to dissolve. *"You thought you could move up to a bigger target. You got arrogant."*

Cedric said nothing to this.

He was smiling.

Not performed — genuine, the specific smile of someone who was engaged in exactly the thing they had come here to do and was finding it every bit as good as they had anticipated.

---

At the western compound the rider and his horse were already cooling on the stone. 

Highmore lowered his hand.

The guard's sword hit the ground before the rest of what had been holding it. Steel on stone, loud in the empty street, and then the other sounds arriving after it — the sounds that explained why the sword had no one holding it anymore. The second guard was already running. He had made his decision the moment the rider came apart and he was executing it with everything he had, his footsteps carrying down the dark curfew street, each one distinct in the quiet, the rhythm of them communicating everything about the quality of the running.

The footsteps stopped.

The footsteps stopped between one step and the next and what replaced them was the sound of a body losing its architecture — the wet heavy impact of mass hitting stone without the structure that usually kept mass upright, the specific sound of meat and bone arriving at the ground all at once, the echo of it bouncing off the buildings on either side before the street absorbed it and went quiet.

Highmore lowered his hand.

They walked forward.

The guard who had stayed was still there — sword out, the point of it between him and the two figures coming toward him. He had not run. This was the whole of what could be said in his favor. His eyes moved between them and to the street where the rider had been and back to them, trying to locate the edges of what he was dealing with and finding them further out than expected in every direction.

*"How brave,"* Emmeline said.

She reached out and took the blade. Not the grip — the flat of it, her fingers closing around the steel with the casual certainty of someone who understood what would happen. The cold from her palm was not gradual. It arrived and committed — finding the crystalline structure of the metal and dismantling it, the steel losing its coherence and coming away from itself in pieces too small to be called pieces. The sword became not-sword between her fingers without drama. She let the remnants fall.

She put her hand on his face.

The cold moved from her palm into his skin with intention — finding what warmth did in living tissue and undoing it. His face changed. Not slowly. The surface of it going from what it had been to something else without the usual intermediate stages, the last expression on it the expression of someone about to experience something, preserved in the cold before the experience completed.

She slammed his head against the gate.

The sound it made was wrong. Something that should have had give didn't. The gate held. He did not. What remained was on the gate and on the ground and said everything that needed to be said about the difference between those two outcomes.

Emmeline stepped back.

*"Pilgrims,"* she said. She turned to Highmore. *"What type of plan was this."*

*"It's not that bad."*

*"It's moronic."*

*"It wasn't moronic when you all agreed to it."*

Something moved in her expression — the look of someone who had an answer and was choosing not to use it.

*"How was I supposed to know he was that paranoid,"* Highmore said. He looked at the compound entrance — the western brigade compound, its gate intact, its walls torchlit, its interior quiet in the way of a place whose captain had taken every available soldier south. *"I didn't see any of you come up with a better plan."*

*"The plan went to shit regardless of who made it. Now there's nothing for us to do here. The compound is emptied."*

*"Do you think Silas and Cedric can handle themselves." He said.*

She was quiet a moment — running a calculation she didn't like the result of.

*"I want to believe that. But those idiots up north couldn't handle the situation quietly and now the church is alerted."* She looked at the compound. *"Maybe we should split up and join them. The western brigade is defenseless anyway."*

*"Agreed. We—"*

The footsteps came first.

Not running. Measured, unhurried, coming from the dark between the torches at the compound entrance. Each step placed with the certainty of someone who had decided where they were going and was going there.

*"The only one defenseless here,"* the voice said, *"is you."*

The footsteps didn't stop until the voice had a face.

She walked the way she always walked — her shoes announcing her the way they always did, the sound of someone who had decided long ago that announcement was preferable to surprise. Clean attire, deep structured fabric. She looked at the two of them with the flat attention she brought to problems she needed to understand before she could address them.

*"You must be the Magister that is assigned here,"* Highmore said.

*"And you must be the heretics,"* Seris said. *"You moved up in the world."*

*"You're not really thinking about stopping us,"* Emmeline said. Said as an observation rather than a question, the certainty of someone who had assessed the situation and arrived at a conclusion. *"We're all scholars of the arcane after all."*

Seris looked at her.

*"Don't bring me down to your level."*

*"I've heard enough,"* Highmore said.

He lifted his hand and released. The attack was invisible — no color, no sound before impact, no visual information to prepare you for what was coming. It arrived at its destination and the destination experienced the consequence. The kind of attack that ended conversations.

The water barrier arrived before it did.

Built from Seris's extended palm with the unhurried certainty of someone who had read the situation and prepared the response before the threat completed its delivery. The invisible attack hit the water. The surface rippled once — a single disturbance moving outward from the point of impact — and then was still.

Seris looked at the still water.

She looked at Highmore.

She took the barrier down.

The water stream that replaced it was pressurized beyond what water usually agreed to be — narrow, concentrated, the sound of it cutting through the air between them. It went for Highmore directly.

Emmeline's cold met it.

Not ice. No moisture in it, no crystalline structure in the conventional sense. Pure cold — the absence of heat rather than the presence of a substance, arriving at the water stream and doing what extreme cold did when it was more committed than the thing it was touching. The stream crystallized at the leading edge, the mana structure losing coherence, the water breaking down into the ambient field.

Seris moved it back.

Seris moved it back. The deflected stream redirected under her direction, its remaining momentum sent at Highmore from a different angle. It passed through everything in its path. The ground — a clean cut in the stone. The brick of the wall beside him — another cut, the same clean quality of something that went through rather than into. Everything it touched received the record of its passing.

His barrier stopped it.

For a moment. Then the force continued through the holding, the barrier taking what it could take and the rest arriving at Highmore regardless. His boots slid on the street stones, his back finding the gate behind him. He stood against it.

Emmeline and Highmore built their cowls simultaneously — the parallel motion of two people who had worked together long enough that certain responses had become synchronized. Emmeline's cold-nature cowl expressed itself as absence rather than presence, the air around her becoming colder, the moisture in the atmosphere crystallizing into a faint shimmer. Highmore's was invisible — only the way his hair moved and the air near his body behaved told you anything was there.

*"Don't let your guard down,"* Emmeline said.

*"You don't say,"* Highmore said.

*Seris looked at him.*

*"Highmore," she said. Not a question. The name arriving with the weight of someone who knew exactly what it carried. "Of Oakhaven."*

*Something moved in his face.*

*"You nearly started a war twenty years ago," she said.* 

He said nothing. The surprise was gone, replaced with the expression of someone who had processed an unexpected development and arrived at their response to it.

Both of them lifted their hands.

Highmore's air blast came first — stronger than the first release, communicating that what he had done before had been calibration rather than effort. Emmeline's cold stream came simultaneously — both hands now, the temperature drop around her visible as a distortion in the torchlight, the air between her hands and Seris going wrong.

Four water tentacles extended from behind her, from her back, each one moving with the independent deliberate motion of something that had its own direction while remaining connected to the same intention. She kept her hands free. The tentacles moved around her, through the air between her and the two figures, four separate paths converging on four separate targets simultaneously. 

Water, moving the way water moved when someone who understood it completely was directing it — not the way a wave moved or a stream moved but the way something moved when it had been given direction and permission and nothing else.

She used two to move.

The air blast arrived at where she had been — the gate behind her taking the impact, a fine crack appearing in the mortar at the point of maximum force. She wasn't there. The tentacles had carried her sideways and up, the water taking her weight with the ease of something that had been doing this long enough that doing it was no longer a question.

The other two went for Emmeline.

The cold stream intercepted one — the water crystallizing before it reached her. The second came from the other direction. Emmeline moved. Not fast enough. The tentacle caught her at the shoulder and redirected her with the force of something communicating that the encounter could be ended, that the margin between this and the version that ended it was a decision rather than a capability. She found the ground on one knee.

Seris came back at Highmore.

Narrower stream this time, more pressurized, the sound of it higher in pitch. It hit his barrier and the barrier held for less time than the first one had. Then the stream was through and Highmore was going backward, the gate was behind him and the gate received the stream and Highmore and the force of all of it at once. The gate went. Highmore going with it into the dark outside.

Seris moved through the opening.

On her way through she extended her right hand and the water whip came from it — fast, coiling around Emmeline before she could react. Seris threw her. Not with care, not with the minimum necessary — with the force of someone who had decided the conversation about minimum necessary was over, Emmeline leaving the ground and traveling through the air and arriving where Highmore had landed with the impact of something that had been thrown rather than placed. 

Seris stepped through the broken gate.

---

Outside.

The moon was the only light beyond the two torches on the gate's exterior wall, their flames moving in the open air beyond the district's walls. open ground on either side, the dark unconcerned with what was happening in the small lit radius of the torches.

Highmore was already standing.

Emmeline was already standing.

They had landed close to each other — the distance of people who had been thrown rather than people who had chosen their positions. They collected themselves with the efficiency of people for whom being thrown was not unprecedented. Highmore checked his hands. Emmeline checked hers. They looked at each other briefly — the brief exchange of two people who had worked together long enough to communicate without words — and then they looked at the gate.

At Seris walking through it.

The grey-brown robes dropped. Highmore's first, the fabric falling from his shoulders and pooling on the road. Emmeline's followed, her neat braid catching the moonlight as the robe left her. Underneath: clothing that communicated an entirely different category of life from the road-traveler presentation they had maintained since Gate 1 that morning. Clean. Cut for someone rather than for anyone. The fabric communicating investment. Expensive in the way of people who had grown up around expensive things and wore them without thinking about it.

They looked at Seris walking toward them.

*"I see why Vorne left the western area without looking back,"* Emmeline said.

Highmore watched Seris — her pace, the certainty of someone moving through a situation with complete confidence in where it was going.

*"It pains me,"* he said, *"to see someone of this level under the shadow of a doctrine."*

Seris laughed.

Not because something was funny. The laugh of someone who had just heard something that communicated such a complete absence of self-awareness that the only adequate response was the sound of it — brief, genuine, entirely without warmth.

She kept walking.

At the southern gate Vorne was still standing over what remained of Lucian. At the western compound the rider and his horse were already cooling on the stone.

*"Magister Seris—"*

Iren's voice carried from the broken gate — all six of them there. They stood in the gap where the gate had been, the compound behind them, the dark road and the two figures ahead of them and Seris between.

Seris didn't look back.

*"I told you to get back inside."*

Emmeline looked past her at the students. Something shifted in her face — not the assessment of targets, something closer to the assessment of information. She looked at Highmore.

*"Seris,"* she said. *"As in Seris Dahl."*

*"Why the fuck would she be here,"* Highmore said.

Seris didn't answer either of them.

*"Get back to safety,"* she said again.

The invisible attack came without announcement — Highmore's hand lifting and releasing in the same motion, the compressed air already traveling before anyone had registered the hand moving. It was aimed at the students. Seris's water barrier met it — the surface of it absorbing the impact, the ripple moving outward and dissipating.

Bael released a fireball.

It crossed the distance between him and Highmore in the time it took to leave his hand. Highmore deflected it with no visible effort — a casual redirect of compressed air, the fireball going sideways into the dark road and dying in the dirt. He didn't even look at it while it was happening. He was still looking at Seris.

*"The northern valley sorceress,"* Emmeline said. She said it slowly, the words arriving with the quality of someone fitting pieces together while speaking. *"A Magister. Here in Ordenmere."* She paused. *"This has to be a mistake."*

Emmeline released the cold at Seris — both streams, bigger than before, the ground between them beginning to change as the cold reached it, frost spreading outward from where her feet were planted and moving toward Seris in a widening front.

Highmore looked at the students. At Bael specifically — the one who had just thrown the fireball, the one whose posture still communicated the intention to throw another one. He lifted his hand.

Davan moved.

He was already moving before the release — something in the air around Highmore's hand changing in a way that only someone whose nature was wind would catch, the pressure differential of compressed air being gathered before it was sent. He crossed the distance between himself and Bael in two steps and put his body between Bael and the attack and pushed Bael sideways.

He yelled for them to get down and threw himself sideways, his shoulder hitting Bael and carrying them both out of the direct line. The others dropped — instinct, the specific animal response to a human body moving fast and a voice cutting through the air with urgency. The attack passed over them, the shockwave of it reaching them as they went down, the compressed air expanding outward from its path and communicating its force to every body in its radius. They hit the ground. All of them. None of them taking the full direct impact, all of them taking enough. 

Seris's water stream pushed the cold back.

Not deflected — pushed, the stream driving into the front of Emmeline's cold and compressing it backward, the temperature where the two met producing something between states that dissolved into mana from both sides simultaneously. The cold retreated. Emmeline retreated with it, one step, her footing adjusting.

*"There's no mistake about it,"* Highmore said. He was looking at Seris with the expression of someone who had arrived at a conclusion they hadn't expected to arrive at tonight and was sitting with the weight of it. *"This is her in the flesh."*

---

*"You need to turn back,"* Seris said. *"Immediately."*

She said it without looking at her students. Her attention was on Emmeline and Highmore — the flat focused attention of someone managing two problems while communicating about a third. The students were getting up from the ground — some faster than others, Bael already on his feet, Myre up immediately, Davan pulling himself up while checking on Solen beside him, Iren and Sera rising together, all of them moving with the specific speed of people whose bodies had absorbed a shock and were already past it. 

*"Magister—"* Bael started.

*"Inside,"* Seris said.

*"Let's get back,"* Myre said. She was already moving — not away from the situation but toward the compound interior, the decision made, her voice carrying the flat authority of someone who had assessed the situation correctly and was not interested in discussing the assessment. *"We'll only be in the way."*

The others followed. Not willingly — the reluctance of it visible in how slowly they moved, in how many of them looked back. Davan kept his eyes on Highmore until the angle of the compound wall took Highmore out of his sightline. 

Bael stood at the edge of the compound interior and looked at Seris — at her back, at the two figures beyond her, at the broken gate and the dark road and Highmore who had redirected his fireball without looking at it. Sera stood beside him.

They turned and went inside together.

---

Highmore pushed himself forward.

The compressed air came from behind him — not a blast directed outward but directed inward, at himself, the force of it hitting his back and translating into forward momentum the way a wind hits a sail. He accelerated. Not running — something past running, the speed of it wrong for a person moving under their own power, the distance between him and the gate closing faster than the distance should close, his body communicating the specific quality of something that had been launched rather than something that had chosen to move.

Seris turned from Emmeline.

The cold came bigger than it had come before. Both of Emmeline's hands now, the output of them combined into a single front that moved toward Seris faster than the individual streams had moved — and the ground came with it. The permafrost spreading outward from Emmeline's feet in a widening circle, the stone of the road outside the gate going from ordinary stone to something else, the moisture in it crystallizing, the surface locking, the specific creaking sound of water changing state under pressure moving outward in a ring around where Emmeline stood.

Seris's footing changed.

She adjusted — the water tentacles from her back finding the ground and the wall beside her and using both, her body moving without her feet needing to be entirely reliable. But the cold was larger than before and the permafrost was moving and Emmeline had bought Highmore the second he needed.

He released while he was still moving.

The attack hit the gate frame and the stone surrounding it — the compressed air arriving at the structure with the force of something that had been accelerating for the full distance between where he had been and where the gate was. The frame came apart. The stone surrounding it — a significant portion of it, the wall weakened at the point of impact, the structural integrity of that section simply ending — came away from the wall and went inward, the debris field of it carrying into the compound. Highmore went through the gap with it, carried by his own momentum, landing inside the compound on his feet with the controlled landing of someone who had accounted for the arrival.

He looked up.

The students were twenty feet from where the gate had been — they had turned at the sound of it coming apart, and now Highmore was in front of them, having come through the gate and landed in the space between them and safety. The compound interior was in front of them. The destroyed gate was behind them.  

*"Are you her students,"* he said.

*"Yes,"* Bael said. The word arriving flat and certain, the way Bael said everything he was certain about.

*"What an honor,"* Highmore said. He looked at each of them — the assessment of someone reading a room, the eye moving from face to face with the particular attention of someone who understood that people communicated their capability before they demonstrated it. *"You must be quite the significant bunch."*

*"We all know what an honor this is,"* Myre said.

He looked at her. Something moved in his face — amusement, quick and genuine, the kind that arrived before the person producing it decided whether to show it. 

*"Let me put that to the test,"* he said.

His hand came up.

Davan felt it before he saw it — the air near Highmore's hand changing, the pressure of it building in the way pressure built when compressed air was being gathered, the way he had felt it outside before Highmore released at the students the first time. He had felt it then and moved too late for it to matter. He felt it now and moved.

*"Down—"*

He released his own air blast at Highmore's — the wind coming from his palm fast and concentrated, the output of someone who had been working on this for months and had produced something real in the training court that morning. It hit Highmore's invisible attack.

It pushed it the way a child pushed a door that was already closing.

The invisible attack arrived at the students like a wall. If Highmore's previous attacks were a greatsword then this was the flat of a hand — less force, more spread, designed to test, to move rather than cut. It moved them. All of them at once, the force distributed across every body in its radius without prejudice, the ground receiving them one after another in the way grounds received people who had been knocked off their feet — without ceremony, without cushioning, the stone communicating exactly how hard it was.

They stayed down.

---

Outside the gate the cold and the water were still going.

The front between them had moved — the water pushing the cold back by increments, Seris maintaining the pressure of it, the stream from her hands driving into Emmeline's output and refusing to yield. But the cold was adapting. Emmeline was reading the pressure of the water and finding the angles where it was thinner — guarding when the stream came direct, moving when a tentacle came for her, the fight outside the gate settling into the rhythm of two people who had been going long enough to understand each other's patterns.

Then Seris looked through the hole where the gate had been.

Her students were on the ground.

Something changed in the quality of what she was producing. Not anger — something past the category of anger, something that had already processed anger and arrived at the other side of it where the decisions lived. Her cowl built around her. It appeared without announcement — no visible gathering, no shimmer of preparation, just present, the water-nature of it surrounding her body with the density of something that had been held back and was no longer being held back.

*"You have severely overstayed your welcome,"* she said.

The tentacles came back from her back — four of them, larger than before, faster than before, the water of them moving with the pressure of her cowl feeding them directly. The stream from her hands went thinner and the thinning made it faster and the speed of it made it cut rather than push — the water arriving at Emmeline's cold stream and going through it rather than pushing against it, the cold breaking apart where the stream passed and the pieces of it dissolving into mana before they could reconstitute.

Emmeline guarded. She moved. She guarded again.

The tentacle came from her left — not from where Seris was standing, from the angle the tentacle had taken to get behind her, the water having moved around the outside of the exchange while Emmeline was tracking the stream. It found her. Wrapped around her. And slammed her into the ground with the force of something that had decided the conversation about force was over — the impact of it communicating itself through the permafrost and into the road beneath and into the wall beside the gate and into everything in the immediate vicinity that was capable of receiving a vibration.

Emmeline hit the ground and stayed there for a moment.

Seris was already moving — back through the hole where the gate had been, into the compound, toward her students on the training ground floor.

---

The cold came from the branch differently from how Emmeline's cold came. Ice — but not the way ice formed when a mage produced it, not the gradual accumulation of frozen moisture building from a point outward. It erupted. All at once, from every edge of the gate hole simultaneously, as if the air inside the gap had received a single instruction and every particle of it had obeyed at the same instant. The glacier filled the gap completely — not a thin seal but a mass, deep and solid and white, the surface of it smoking faintly in the night air the way dry ice smoked, the vapor rising in thin wisps that caught the torchlight and disappeared. The hole in the wall was gone. In its place: a glacier where a gate had been, thick enough that the compound on the other side of it was not visible, not audible, simply absent. 

Emmeline was standing.

She had gotten up from the ground and she was standing at the edge of the gate hole and she had something in her hand. Small — too small to be a walking stick,A tree branch — deep rich brown, the wood of it old and dense,  the diameter of something found rather than made. Except it hadn't been found. The gem at the end of it caught what little torchlight remained and held it — blue, the color of ice, the color of something that was very cold at its core. The branch itself was covered in ice. Not coated — covered, the ice growing from the surface of it the way ice grew from things when the thing at the center was cold enough to pull moisture from the air and hold it.

Seris looked at what was in Emmeline's hand.

On the other side of the glacier her students were on the ground and Highmore was standing over them and she was on the wrong side of a wall of ice with an enchanted artifact between her and all of it.

She looked at it for one more second.

Then she looked at Emmeline.

---

The chapel was quiet when Maret arrived.

The soldier was still there — standing at the edge of the nave where the clerics had left him after taking his report, the specific posture of someone who had delivered something and was waiting to be told what to do next. The clerics who had heard the words Godless Hand and moved immediately were now at the back of the chapel with Father Ignatius, who had come out two minutes after being woken and had not yet said anything to anyone.

He stood with his hands clasped in front of him. Still. The stillness of someone who had learned that stillness communicated more than movement and had practiced it until it was no longer a choice.

Maret looked at him and then looked at the floor.

*"Was it really wise to send Leonard with them, Father,"* she said.

Ignatius didn't answer immediately. He looked at the soldier. He looked at the door through which Tobias, Julian, Gideon, and Leonard had left — three of them on horses, one of them already in the air, the wind carrying him north faster than any horse could follow.

*"He is a cleric in her Profaned Church,"* Ignatius said. *"He will fight in her name."*

*"You weren't there, Father."*

Brother Valerius. His voice coming from the left side of the nave where he stood with Hadrian and Mathias, Cyrus and Dorian. His voice had the quality of something that had been held for a long time and had found a gap and come through it. 

*"You didn't see how he didn't even look back,"* Valerius said. *"While we were dropping like flies. He went up and he turned and he didn't look back once."*

Ignatius turned.

The movement was slow — not the slowness of someone who was uncertain about what they were doing but the slowness of someone who wanted the person they were turning toward to experience every degree of the turn. His eyes found Valerius and Valerius tried to find somewhere else for his own eyes to go and found that there was nowhere. The blue of Ignatius's eyes was not the blue of anything warm — not sky, not water at its comfortable depth. The blue of something that had very little in it and wanted very little from you except your complete attention, and it was getting it, and Valerius stood inside the getting of it with the specific stillness of someone who had just understood that speaking had been a mistake and that the understanding had arrived too late to be useful.

The other clerics in the nave lowered their heads. Maret looked at the wall to her left. The soldier near the door became extremely interested in the floor.

Ignatius walked toward Valerius.

Slowly.
