The same deliberate pace as the turn, each step placed with the authority of someone who had decided long ago that deliberate was more frightening than fast and had been proving this point for seventy-three years. Valerius's eyes tried to find the floor and couldn't — the blue pulling them back up the way voids pulled things, not through force but through the absence of anything to resist.

*"Your failures,"* Ignatius said, *"to carry her will — are yours."* A pause — the pause of someone letting a sentence finish its work before adding to it. *"And yours only."*

Valerius said nothing. He was still in those eyes, still inside the blue of them, and the blue gave nothing back and asked for everything and he stood in the asking until Ignatius decided the asking was done and moved those eyes elsewhere.

They moved south. Through the chapel wall, through the district, toward the specific white light that was visible above the rooftops to the south — steady, cold. His chin lifted slightly. His hands, still clasped, tightened once and released.

*"There's more of them,"* Maret said quietly.

What happened to Father Ignatius's face in the next moment was not anger the way anger usually arrived — not a building, not a progression from one state to another. It was an arrival. Complete and immediate, the way weather arrived when weather had been decided somewhere else and had simply reached you now. His teeth came together. The muscles at the sides of his jaw communicated everything about the force behind the closure. His lips parted slightly and the drool that came with the specific clenching fury of a man biting down on something he could not bite through caught the candlelight at the corner of his mouth and he didn't notice it or didn't care.

Nobody in the chapel moved.

Nobody breathed at a volume that could be heard.

*"How dare they—"*

The words came out compressed, each one its own separate act of force, the voice of someone whose body was producing more than the voice could contain.

*"How dare those heretics sully her holy grounds."* 

He stopped. Not because he had finished. Because something happened to him — the same abruptness with which the rage had arrived, it departed, and what replaced it was not calm exactly but the specific quality of a face that had been returned to its owner by whoever had briefly been using it. The drool was still at the corner of his mouth. He didn't address it. His hands unclasped and reclasped. His chin came down from where it had gone.

The chapel held the silence of people who had been through this before and knew that the only safe response was to remain exactly as they were until the all-clear arrived on its own terms.

It arrived.

*"The nonbelievers,"* Ignatius said, *"will regret setting foot in our kingdom."*

His voice was level. Conversational, almost. The voice of someone discussing a matter that had been settled and required only the appropriate administrative response. He looked at Valerius. At Hadrian. At Mathias.

*"Valerius. Hadrian. Mathias," he said. "South."*

He turned and walked back toward the altar without waiting to see if they moved.

They moved.

---

The street was wrong before anything was visible.

The smell arrived first — not wood smoke, something underneath it, something the body understood before the mind finished catching up. The kind of smell that didn't have a clean name because the things that produced it weren't supposed to produce it. Then the glow — orange and low, bleeding around the corner of the buildings ahead, painting the underside of the smoke rising above the rooftops in the color of something that had been burning for a long time.

The civilians were in their doorways.

They had come out when the bell rang and stayed when the glow appeared in the northern sky and none of them had gone back inside. They stood at the edges of their thresholds — not in the street, not retreating, just present in the gap between their homes and whatever was happening ahead of them. Some had candles. Some had nothing. They looked north with the expressions of people who had decided that not knowing was worse than seeing and were now revising that decision one degree at a time as the glow grew stronger. Nobody spoke. A child was pressed against an older woman's side with both arms wrapped around her waist and his face turned away from the glow and she had one hand on the back of his head holding him there, not looking down, looking north.

They did not move from their doorways.

The northern compound was gone.

Not damaged — gone, the way things were gone when the distinction between the thing and its absence had been settled completely and permanently. The walls existed in pieces — sections of them still standing, sections of them horizontal, sections of them simply not present in any form that communicated what they had been. The fire covered everything underneath and between and around the pieces that remained. It did not move the way fire moved when it was climbing structure or finding fuel. It sat. It sat the way it sat when it had already consumed what it came for and had found other things to consume and had been doing this long enough that the consuming was simply what the place was now.

It was fed by the rubble.

And by what the rubble was covering.

The soldiers had not all made it inside when the gate came apart. The ones who hadn't were part of the ground now — part of what the fire was sitting on, part of what the fire was eating, the heat having done to them over the course of the evening what heat did when it had enough of it and nothing to interrupt it. The smell was the smell of that. The glow had a specific quality at its base, where the fire met the ground, where the ground was not only stone anymore. The civilians in their doorways could smell it from where they stood. Most of them had stopped breathing through their noses.

---

A woman was standing at the edge of it.

Her back to the street. Not moving — not watching, not waiting, simply present, arrived at where she intended to be. The fire lit her from the front — blonde hair, pale skin, the dense small letters covering every inch of her forehead from hairline to brow. In the center where the letters were largest, readable in the firelight:

*Tyrant, make of this land a place kept clean of false light. Keep me and what I love from kneeling to what was stolen and called divine.*

Her eyes were open. She didn't blink. The black of them held the orange fire without moving, without adjusting, the burning compound living in them as a reflection that didn't distort.

In front of her was a shape.

Kneeling.

The geometry of a man was still there — the breadth of the shoulders, the mass of the torso, the angle of the head — but nothing soft remained anywhere in it. Dense, dark, glowing faintly at the edges, the material of it having been introduced to something it was not built to survive and having arrived at whatever it was going to be on the other side of that introduction. The armor had not come off. It had melted into what it had been worn to protect, the metal and the man fused into a single object that was neither the one nor the other. The sigil of the western district on the shoulder — warped, barely, still there.

Beside the shape, half-buried in the ground where it had fallen — a sword. The blade blackened, the grip gone, the metal of it still holding its shape because metal held its shape longer than everything else. A shield on the other side, the leather burned away, the metal frame warped but intact, one edge of it sunk into the softened ground.

Haes had not gone down without both of them in his hands.

She was reciting something over him. Her voice low, unhurried, the cadence of something said from memory so many times it had become automatic.

*They made idols of the stolen. What they worshipped held no power over what comes after. The false light fails at the threshold. Punishment receives what devotion could not.*

Severin came up behind her.

He looked at the shape on the ground. He looked at the sky to the west where Highmore's signal should have come and hadn't.

*"Highmore didn't make the signal,"* he said. *"Do you think something has happened."*

Elysia didn't answer. Didn't stop reciting.

Severin looked at her for a moment and looked away. She always became this way after burning people. He had learned not to interrupt it.

He walked a few steps and found a crossbow on the ground. One of many — scattered across the rubble, warped by heat, some of them broken, some of them intact enough to be recognizable. He picked one up and turned it over. The mechanism — the loading system, the spring arrangement, the tolerances of the components — was not what he expected from a military crossbow. He had seen military crossbows. He had broken through the lines of soldiers carrying them. This was different. The engineering of it was deliberate in a way that communicated something more than a standard commission. He turned it over again. These things had given them more trouble than a crossbow had any right to give — the coordinated barrage from the garrison had been the moment in the fight that came closest to costing him something real, and he still had the bolt hole in his shoulder to prove it. He was holding the reason for that in his hands and still couldn't identify what made it different from the ones he knew. 

He threw it back on the ground.

*"We will hold the position for another half hour,"* he said. *"If the western signal doesn't arrive we move."*

Elysia stopped reciting.

*"We move,"* she said. *"Move to what exactly."*

*"We continue the mission. With or without them."*

She smiled like she heard exactly what she wanted to hear.

---

The figure appeared above them.

Church robes — white, unmistakable, the firelight finding them immediately and making them visible against the dark sky above the compound. He had come from the south, from the direction of the chapel, and he had arrived above the compound and stopped moving and was looking down at what was below him.

His face did the thing faces did when they received something too large for the face to organize quickly — not one expression but several arriving in sequence without any of them finishing, the eyes moving across the fire and the rubble and the shape kneeling in front of Elysia and the glow of everything that the compound had become, and underneath all of it the smell arriving even at his altitude, and his body making its own assessment of what was below him independent of whatever his mind was trying to do with it.

He didn't move.

Below him Elysia and Severin looked up.

The church robes did something to both of their faces. Not surprise — they had known something would come from the chapel eventually. Something older than surprise, something that didn't need a trigger because it was always there underneath everything else, waiting for something to point it at. Severin's jaw set. Elysia's eyes went wide and her blinking stopped and the fire in them changed quality — still the same orange, still the same reflection, but with something behind it now that the burning compound didn't put there.

She raised her hand.

The fire came without announcement.

Leonard moved before he understood why he was moving — something in the quality of the air below him changed and his body responded to the change before the information had finished traveling. The fire arrived where he had been. He felt the heat of it on his skin even through the miss, the proximity of it close enough to communicate exactly how close it had been. The evasion cost him his position — his body dropping before his wind caught him again, the drop carrying him into the edge of the fire on the ground. He hit it. He used his air to push the oxygen away from himself, the fire dying against the absence of what it needed, the wind killing it in the small radius around his body.

The stream came.

He made a barrier — compressed air held in front of him, the force of Elysia's sustained output pressing against it. He rose, pushing himself up and out of the reach of the ground fire, the barrier still holding.

Severin was already above him.

The blast came from above and hit Leonard's wind — not meeting it head on but finding the edge of it and redirecting it, the air that had been holding Leonard up suddenly doing something else, the loss of it immediate. He dropped. The ground received him hard, harder than a controlled landing, the body communicating the difference between arriving and falling in terms it couldn't be misunderstood.

Elysia walked toward him.

Severin watched from above.

*"This is as far as your faith will take you,"* Elysia said.

Leonard released an air slash at her — horizontal, fast, aimed at the space she occupied. Severin's blast came from above simultaneously, the two attacks meeting at her feet and canceling each other in the air between her and Leonard. The ground between them was still.

*"Where is she now,"* Elysia said. She looked at what had been the compound. *"Look at this. This will be the state of the entire city before dawn. Who will be your savior."*

Leonard was watching both of them — Elysia on the ground, Severin above, reading the angles.

*"So you're here to make an example,"* he said.

Her eyes went wide. She stopped blinking.

*"We got a clever one,"* Severin said.

*"Tonight Providence church will know they are not untouchable,"* Elysia said. *"You will all pay for worshipping the usurpers."*

*"It is by her profaned gift that we rise above you heretics,"* Leonard said.

Severin laughed.

Leonard released a stream of air at Elysia — sustained, the full output of his cowl behind it. She replied. Her fire came back harder than his air went out, the gap between them not in the elements but in the people behind them, and his stream came apart against hers and the remnants of it scattered before they reached her. He bolted sideways and up, breaking contact before she finished the job. 

Severin followed him in the air.

Easily. The ease communicating more than force would have.

*"Is this how her gift has risen you above us,"* Severin said. Still laughing.

Leonard pushed north — fast, the wind carrying him, the speed of it real. Severin's blast hit him from behind anyway. The ground received him harder than the first time. Harder than the second time. The body's accounting arriving more completely with each entry.

Severin came down.

Leonard was on his belly. Broken ribs. Dislocated shoulder. Each breath arriving as something that had to be worked for rather than something that simply happened. Severin knelt beside him and brought his face close to Leonard's ear.

*"The only reason you're not a pile of ash,"* he said, *"is because she wants something to fill the time while we wait. Can you please entertain her until we get the last signal. I don't think I can make her wait any longer."*

Leonard put his hand on the ground and pushed. The arm with the dislocated shoulder found the ground too and the socket communicated its state and his face met the ground. He pushed again with the good arm. He got his knees under him. His feet. He stood — the standing of someone whose body was producing it through something other than capacity.

He coughed.

Blood came with it.

*"What is her gift about to show us now,"* Severin said. The grin still on his face.

The sound of horses arrived behind them.

The three arrived at the edge of what the street had become.

They came down from their horses and sent them away — the horses needed no convincing, the animals having already made their assessment of the smell and the light and the specific quality of the air this close to the compound and having arrived at a strong preference for somewhere else. Julian, Gideon, and Tobias stood where the horses had been and looked at what was in front of them.

Tobias was the one who couldn't stop looking.

He moved his eyes across it — the fire, the rubble, the walls that were no longer walls, the ground that was no longer only ground. He had not been at the border. He had come from the chapel tonight with the words Godless Hand in his ears and a general understanding of what those words meant and no specific understanding of what those words produced. He was acquiring the specific understanding now. His eyes moved and moved and kept finding new things to land on and kept finding that the things they landed on required them to move again, and underneath all of the looking was the smell, which was the thing his eyes couldn't help him with, which was doing its own work independent of everything else.

He said a prayer.

Not loud. Quiet — the reflexive private recitation of someone reaching for the thing they always reached for when reaching was all they had.

Elysia heard it.

She turned from the shape on the ground. The fire stream left her hand before she had fully turned, aimed at the sound of it, the prayer itself functioning as a target. Tobias made his barrier just in time — just, the heat of the stream reaching him through the barrier's edge, the proximity of it communicating exactly how close it had been.

*"That is all that you can do,"* Elysia said. *"Pray. Let's see where your prayer takes you."*

*"Help me,"* Leonard said.

The words came out wrong — the broken ribs making every word cost something he didn't have, the blood in his throat giving the sound a wet quality that words weren't supposed to have. He was still on the ground, still on his belly, his eyes finding the three clerics in the firelight.

Severin turned his head slightly to look at the three of them. One eye on Leonard. He had not moved from where he was standing.

Elysia was looking at the robes.

Not at the people wearing them. At the robes — the white of them in the firelight, the specific white of Providence's church, the cloth that said everything it said without saying anything.

*"Those robes,"* Severin said, gesturing toward Leonard with a tilt of his head, *"would look much better in red."*

Elysia was already reciting something. Under her breath, inaudible, the lips moving in the firelight.

*"You are outnumbered,"* Tobias said. *"Surrender now or die in her name."*

*"It's you who will die in her name,"* Severin said. He put emphasis on her — the word arriving with the specific weight of someone who knew exactly what it meant to the people he was saying it to. He raised his hand toward Leonard. *"And we won't be outnumbered for long."*

Leonard was crying for help again. Between the coughing and the blood it was barely language — just the sound of someone who still had enough left to ask and not enough left to ask clearly.

Tobias released a water slash at Severin.

Elysia met it with her fire — the stream hitting the water slash and overwhelming it before it reached Severin, the water breaking apart and dissolving into what it was.  Severin's hand came around toward Leonard simultaneously. The compressed air hit the barrier Leonard had made — the last barrier, built from whatever he had left, the cowl around him thin and dim and everything he could still produce. The barrier broke. The attack continued through the breaking and hit him and he went onto his back.

All of it arrived at once.

The ribs. The shoulder. The chest. Every injury the evening had produced communicating simultaneously through the impact, the body's full accounting delivered in a single moment with nowhere left to defer it. He lay on his back and the sky above the compound was orange from the fire and the smoke moved across it and he could not get air in the way air was supposed to go in.

He was going to choke.

He knew he was going to choke. The blood that had been building in his chest since the third time he hit the ground was moving now, finding the path that gravity and the position of his body were offering it, and if he stayed on his back it would find his throat and he would drown in it and there would be nothing left to do about that.

He turned himself.

What the turning cost him was not describable in terms that fit cleanly into any single category. Every degree of rotation — from his back toward his side, the slow arc of it — produced a report from the ribs that was not pain the way pain usually worked, not the sharp arriving thing that peaked and receded, but something sustained and total, something that occupied every degree of the turning from the first to the last and was still present when the turning was done. The shoulder participated. The shoulder had been participating all evening and had not stopped. The blood in his chest moved as he moved and some of it came up and out — out of his mouth, running down his chin, dripping from his jaw onto the stone beside his face. He could feel the warmth of it against his cheek. His own blood, warm, while everything else was cold.

He was on his side.

He could breathe. Barely — the shallow mechanical breathing of someone whose lungs were doing the minimum they could do and not a fraction more. But he could breathe.

His eyes found Julian and Gideon.

They were looking at him.

*"You are more stubborn than you look,"* Severin said. He was walking toward Leonard, unhurried, the walk of someone who had somewhere to be and was not concerned about when he arrived. *"I'll give you that."*

Tobias built his cowl.

*"Profaned Lady, I am your instrument. Let your will move through my hands. Let what opposes you know your reach."*

He released a water slash at Severin.

*"This is getting old,"* Elysia said. She met the slash with fire. The water broke apart before it reached anyone.

Tobias looked at Julian. At Gideon.

*"I can keep her busy,"* he said. *"Help him."*

They didn't say anything.

They looked at Leonard on the ground. At the blood under his face and the arm that wasn't in its socket and the way his chest moved when he breathed. They looked at him and they said nothing and they didn't move and the silence they produced was not the silence of people who hadn't heard but the silence of people who had already decided and were now occupying the space where the decision lived.

Tobias didn't understand what he was looking at.

Severin and Elysia didn't understand it either. Their faces communicated this — the specific expression of two people who had come here to burn and had not expected to watch the church do something like this, had not budgeted for this in their understanding of the faithful, the confusion of encountering something that didn't fit the theology they had built their lives around.

Leonard wasn't confused.

He had known the moment their eyes found him on the ground. He had known before the silence, before the stillness, before Tobias told them to help him and the request landed in the silence they were already inside. He had known because he knew what he had done at the border and he knew that they had been in that field and he knew that they had watched him go and he knew that the calculation they were running now had a specific answer and the answer was not him.

*"Please,"* he said. The word came out wet, shaped wrong, the blood and the broken breathing making it something that barely qualified as language. *"I'm begging you. Please help me."*

Julian looked at the fire.

Gideon looked at the fire.

*"This is what is wrong with you worshippers,"* Severin said. He was standing over Leonard now. Looking down at him. *"You will beg and plead to anyone and anything. It is in your nature."* He looked at the face on the ground — the tears that had mixed with the blood and the snot and the mouth that was still working around words that couldn't fully form. *"Who will you beg for now."*

Leonard's begging shifted. It turned away from the clerics who weren't moving and turned toward the man standing over him — toward Severin, toward the hand still raised, the compressed air still gathered in it. He begged Severin. The words of it coming out in whatever order they could come out, please and spare and mercy arriving in no particular sequence around the blood and the struggling breath.

Severin looked at his face for a long moment.

He made a disgusted face. Not performed — genuine, the specific involuntary expression of someone who had seen something they found aesthetically offensive and couldn't hide the finding.

*"Did you forget her name,"* he said. *"Or is it because at this particular moment you think she is inferior to me."*

Leonard's mouth stopped forming the begging. Something shifted in what he was trying to say — the words changing, the address changing, the prayer forming behind his lips instead of the begging, the thing he had said every morning since he could speak assembling itself from what was left of him.

The compressed air hit Leonard's head before the prayer finished leaving his mouth.

The stone received what the stone received. The fire kept burning. Severin put his hand away and looked at what was on the ground with the expression of someone who had done what needed doing.

*"What are you doing,"* Tobias said. His voice had changed — the trained authority stripped out of it, something underneath it that training didn't produce. He was looking at Julian. At Gideon. *"Why are you just standing there."*

*"There wasn't anything we could do,"* Gideon said.

Tobias looked at him. He looked at the lie in the sentence and he looked at Gideon's face and he didn't understand why the lie was there.

Severin laughed.

Not the laugh from before — not the entertained laugh of someone finding Leonard amusing in the air. This laugh had a different quality. The laugh of someone who had just received information they found genuinely interesting.

*"You certainly could have saved his life,"* Severin said. *"You just watched your comrade die and did nothing."* He looked at Elysia. *"And I thought the Hand were brutal."*

Gideon and Julian finally moved.

The light spears came from Gideon's palms in a barrage — not one at a time, not the tentative output of someone who had been standing still and was now moving, but a sustained volley, fast and bright, aimed at Severin with the precision of someone who had been watching his position in the air for long enough to know exactly where to send them. Julian's ice sickles followed immediately — not after, immediately, the two of them having found the same moment without discussing it, the coordination of people who had trained together long enough that certain things didn't require discussion anymore.

Severin rose. The light spears' angle required him to go up — he read it and went up before the first one arrived, the air carrying him above the trajectory. The ice sickles came after him, curving upward, Julian adjusting the angle in real time as Severin moved. Elysia answered the sickles — her fire meeting them before they reached Severin, the ice dissolving into mana against the heat of it.

In the moment Elysia's attention went to the sickles Tobias released.

The water slash came from his left hand — not the dominant hand, the off hand, the slash smaller than what his right could produce but faster, arriving in the space Elysia's fire had briefly vacated. It got closer than anything had gotten so far. She turned back to it and her fire met it and broke it but she had moved to meet it and the moving had cost her something.

Tobias noted this and filed it and kept moving.

---

He was not trying to beat her.

This was the thing about fighting with water that fire users took time to understand — water did not try to beat fire, water tried to find where fire was not and fill that space. Tobias was not attacking Elysia. He was attacking the geometry around her — the angles that forced her to adjust, the spaces that pulled her attention in directions that thinned what she had pointed at Severin, the pressure points that made holding her position cost more than it should. Every slash he released was a question about where she was going to be next rather than a statement about where she was now.

Above them Severin was being moved.

Not dramatically — not the way Leonard had been moved, not the way Haes's soldiers had been moved. Subtly. Julian's ice sickles came from angles that closed when Severin went up, opened when he went down, closed again when he adjusted. Gideon's light spears came in patterns — not random, not the same pattern twice, the patterns changing as Gideon read Severin's adjustments and adjusted his own. The compressed air Severin was spending to stay mobile and stay above the trajectories was adding up. His blasts were coming faster than they had been coming at the start of the night.

He was managing it.

Managing it was costing him.

---

Three exchanges in Tobias found what he had been looking for.

He had been watching her load — the way the fire gathered before it came, the right hand dominant, the left hand supporting, the brief asymmetry of it in the moment before the stream released. In that moment the left side thinned. Not significantly. But enough — enough for something that knew exactly where to go and when to go there.

He sent a water slash wide.

Deliberately wide — aimed at nothing, at the space to Elysia's left where the slash would do nothing except arrive. She read it and moved to meet it, the left side coming forward, and in the moving the right side opened.

Gideon's light spears were already there.

They hit her, the right side of her torso, the spears arriving in the gap that the movement had made and finding it before she could close it. She was pushed back. Not far — one step, two, the impact carrying her backward across the ground of what had been the compound's outer edge. The fire stream broke. The sustained output that had not broken all evening — not when Tobias's slashes hit it, not when Severin needed her attention elsewhere, not once — broke, the fire losing its shape and dissipating into the air around her, the ground where it had been landing going dark.

Elysia took two steps back and stopped.

The fire around her rebuilt immediately — her cowl reasserting, the stream coming back. But in the time it took to rebuild Julian's ice sickles were already moving, coming at her right side while it was still recovering, and she had to turn to meet them and the turning cost her the angle she had on Tobias and Tobias's water slash arrived at the space she had vacated.

Severin felt the shift before he saw it.

The fraction of his attention that went to Elysia when she stepped back was the fraction Gideon had been waiting for. The light spears came at him from below while he was looking sideways and he moved late — not too late, but late enough that the deflection was not clean, the compressed air catching most of them and not all of them. What got through communicated itself and he moved to compensate and Julian's ice sickles were already accounting for the compensation.

He took a hit.

Small. Real.

Below him the three clerics were moving with the specific cohesion of people who had found their rhythm and were inside it now — Tobias reading the geometry, Gideon and Julian executing, the three of them operating as a single thing with three points of output rather than three separate people attacking the same targets.

Severin and Elysia looked at each other.

Nothing was said. Nothing needed to be. They had been working together long enough that certain decisions didn't require language — the look between them was the decision, the agreement reached in the space of a breath, and then they were moving differently than they had been moving before.

One at a time.

They started with Gideon.

Elysia turned the full weight of her fire on him — not the measured output she had been producing while managing three targets, the full sustained stream of it, the thing that had leveled the compound and melted Haes's armor into his body and eaten through stone walls, directed now at a single man. Gideon's efficiency evaporated. He had been attacking with the clean precision of someone who had trained for this his entire life and had found his rhythm — now he was defending, the shift arriving faster than he was ready for it, his barrier going up and the fire hitting it and the barrier holding but only just, the heat of it communicating itself through the barrier's edge in a way that told him everything about how long the barrier was going to hold.

He moved. He tried to make distance — sideways, away from the wall that arrived at his back, looking for space.

Severin was already moving.

The compressed air hit his own back and he crossed the ground between himself and Gideon in the time it took Gideon to take two steps. He released at close range — the air blast arriving at Gideon from the front while Elysia's stream came from the side and Julian and Tobias tried to close in from behind.

Elysia turned her stream on Julian and Tobias before they could reach Severin. The fire swept across the ground between them and forced them back — not hitting them, not yet, the threat of it enough to interrupt their approach.

Gideon released his light spears into Severin's air blast.

The attacks met between them — light and compressed air finding each other in the space between Gideon's hands and Severin's, the two forces canceling in a burst that illuminated the compound's ruins for a moment and then went dark.

*"Starting to feel the heat?"* Severin said.

Gideon didn't answer. He was looking for the wall — trying to get it to his side rather than his back, trying to find the angle that gave him room to move. He didn't find it fast enough. The wall found him — his back against it, the stone cold through his robes, Elysia in front of him and Severin to his left and the other two clerics thirty feet away with Elysia's fire between them and him.

His barrier went up.

Severin attacked. Elysia attacked. One then the other — the rhythm of it deliberate, not simultaneous, taking turns so that Gideon couldn't use the window between attacks to do anything except prepare for the next one. Attack, barrier, attack, barrier — the barrier rebuilding each time but rebuilding a little thinner, a little less than it had been before, the output of his cowl being spent faster than it could recover.

*"How long do you think that holds?"* Elysia said.

Gideon said nothing. He was spending everything he had on the barrier and had nothing left for words.

Tobias released a water slash at Severin — trying to interrupt the rhythm, trying to buy Gideon a breath. Severin deflected it without turning fully toward Tobias, the compressed air catching the slash and redirecting it into the rubble to his right. He didn't even look.

*"Your brother needs you again,"* Severin said to Tobias without turning. *"And there's nothing you can do about it."*

Julian was trying to find an angle — moving laterally, looking for the approach that got him past Elysia's stream without walking into it. He hadn't found it. Every time he moved she adjusted without breaking her rhythm on Gideon's barrier.

Gideon's barrier was thinning. He could feel it — the specific feeling of something that was supposed to be solid becoming less solid, the fire getting closer with each exchange, the cold of the wall at his back and the heat of Elysia's output in front of him and nowhere to go between them.

Elysia released a blast — not a stream, a concentrated blast, the full weight of her cowl behind a single output directed at the center of his barrier.

The barrier broke.

Severin released immediately after — the compressed air already loaded, already coming, arriving at Gideon in the instant his barrier came apart and left him with nothing between himself and the air blast.

Gideon jumped.

The wall behind him had a hole in it where he had been standing — the stone gone, the edges of the gap still hot, the specific clean devastation of something that had arrived with more force than the material was built to receive. Gideon hit the ground sideways — rolling, the training taking over, his body absorbing the landing and converting it into momentum rather than impact.

*"Quick,"* Severin said. He sounded almost impressed.

Tobias released at Elysia — a water slash, fast, aimed at her right side while her attention was still on where Gideon had been. Julian moved at the same moment — not releasing, moving, lunging forward with both hands extended toward the ground between Severin and Gideon.

The ice wall came up.

Fast — faster than ice usually came, the full output of Julian's cowl behind it, a wall of it emerging from his hand and onto the ground between Severin and Gideon. Severin was already loading — the compressed air gathered, ready, the blast already in motion when the wall arrived between him and his target.

The blast hit the ice.

The wall held — the ice absorbing the force of it, the surface cracking but not breaking, the cracks spreading outward from the point of impact and stopping before they reached the edges. Julian's hands were flat against the wall, pressed to the ice, his cowl feeding it continuously — he couldn't take his hands away or the wall would start coming apart, the mana that was holding it returning to the ambient field the moment the intention behind it stopped.

He stayed there. His hands on the ice. His stamina going into it.

The wall bought what the wall needed to buy.

Gideon got back to his feet.

Elysia turned from where Gideon had been and sent a fire blast at Julian — at his back, at the man with both hands on the ice and nothing left to defend himself with. It came fast, aimed at the gap between Julian's shoulder blades.

Tobias intercepted it.

He released again immediately, the second attack leaving his hand before the first had finished landing, the quick succession of it giving Elysia no window between the defense and the next attack arriving at her.

She barely got her fire up in time.

The defense was not clean — the water pushing through the edge of it, the force of what got past carrying her back a step, then another. The water came in a barrage, slash after another. She planted her feet. She stopped. But she was back — back from where she had been, back toward Severin, the ground she had occupied since the fight began no longer hers.

Severin felt her against his back.

The formation they had been working from — the specific geometry of two people who knew how to work together — broken, the ground around them belonging to the three clerics rather than to them.

The ice wall came down.

Julian pulled his hands away and the ice began dissipating immediately — the mana returning to the field, the wall losing coherence from the top down, the cold of it releasing into the air around the compound in a breath that was briefly visible and then gone. He was breathing hard. The wall had cost him and the cost was visible.

The three clerics were surrounding them.

Tobias to their left. Julian in front. Gideon to their right — watching Severin specifically, watching the air above him, his light spears ready for the moment Severin tried to rise.

*"It's over,"* Tobias said.

Severin looked at the spears ready in Gideon's hands. He looked at Julian's position. He looked at the water slash already forming in Tobias's palm.

He looked at Elysia.

The cloaks came off.

Not dramatically — just dropped, the grey-brown cloth falling from their shoulders and hitting the rubble around their feet. What was underneath was black. Not the grey-brown of road travelers, not the traveling clothes they had been wearing since that morning. Black, and empty in the specific way of robes that communicated devotion rather than function, the specific garment of people for whom what they wore was not separate from what they believed.

Elysia reached up and tied her hair back.

Severin reached into his bag.

What he produced did not look like anything any of the three clerics had a category for. A book — but the word book was barely adequate for what he was holding. The pages were thick. Not the thin pages of contemporary manuscripts, not the paper that scribes had been producing for the last two centuries. Thick, the thickness of something made before thin pages existed, before the technology of thinness had been developed, the pages communicating age in the way only materials communicated age — through what they were made of and how the making had been done. The cover had writing on it. The writing was not in any language any of them had seen — not Ordenmere's script, not the trade languages, not the liturgical languages of Providence's church. Something else. Something that looked old in the same way the pages looked old, the script of it belonging to a time that predated every institution currently operating in the world.

Severin handed it to Elysia.

She took it. She held it in both hands. She looked at it for a moment — not reading it, just holding it, the way you held something you had been carrying for a long time before you used it.

She pushed her mana into it.

The edges caught fire.

Not the fire she produced with her cowl — not the red-orange sustained output that had been burning all evening, that had consumed the compound and the soldiers in it and Haes's armor into his body. This fire was different. It seemed to belong to the book rather than to Elysia — as if the fire had always been there, inside the cover, inside the thick pages, and the mana she had pushed into it had not created the fire but had simply told it that it was allowed to be visible now. The writing on the cover lit up — the script of it traced in the fire, each letter finding its edge and holding it, the cover becoming legible in fire in a language that was still unreadable.

The book moved.

Still in her hands — she was still holding it, her hands still under it — but it opened on its own. Not the way books opened when someone opened them. The way books opened when something inside them had decided it was time. The cover went back. The pages turned — not one by one, all of them at once, finding the place they were going to without anyone directing them there.

Four pages.

The three clerics were looking at the four pages and the four pages had small circles on them — not drawn, inscribed, the circles precise in a way that communicated instrument rather than hand, the lines of them too consistent to have been made by someone drawing freehand. Around the circles and between them and inside them: writing. Thin, dense, too small to read from where the clerics were standing. Too small to read from anywhere. And in a script that matched the cover — the same language that nobody in this world had spoken for long enough that the speaking of it had been forgotten along with the meaning of the words.

The fire from the edges moved to the pages.

Not burning them. Tracing them — following the circles and the writing, the fire finding the lines that were already there and illuminating them, the four pages becoming four pages of fire-traced script in a language nobody could read.

The compound was quiet except for the fire that was still burning everything it had been burning all evening.

The three clerics looked at the book.

Elysia turned her hand.

The book turned with it.

Tobias had been loading — the water already gathering in his palm, the slash forming, his cowl feeding it, the next attack in the sequence he had been building all fight already in motion. He read the turn of her hand and he switched. The attack became a barrier — the water gathering differently, pulling inward rather than projecting outward, the shield of it building in front of him in the time between Elysia's hand turning and whatever came next arriving.

What came next arrived.

The fireball formed in front of the book.

Not from the book — not the way Elysia's fire came from her palms, not the way any mage's output emerged from their body as the expression of their nature and their cowl. The fireball didn't touch the book. It didn't look like it was coming from the book. It looked as if the book had asked the air to create fire and the air had simply done it — the fire appearing in the space in front of the cover the way things appeared when they had always been there and had simply been given permission to be visible.

It was the size of a fist when it formed.

By the time it moved it was larger.

Elysia pushed mana into the book. The page turned — on its own, the thick page moving without anyone touching it, finding the next configuration of circles and the thin writing between them. The runes on the open page changed — the fire-traced script shifting, the circles rearranging in the way that mechanisms rearranged when something upstream of them had been adjusted.

The fireball moved.

Fast — faster than Elysia's stream moved, faster than anything she had produced all evening, the speed of it wrong for something that size, the air around it distorting slightly as it crossed the distance between where it had formed and where Tobias was standing.

It hit his barrier.

The barrier held.

For a moment — the specific moment of something that was built to hold holding, the water of it absorbing the impact the way water absorbed impacts. And then the fireball didn't stop. It didn't dissipate the way mana-produced fire dissipated when it hit something that resisted it. It spread — outward from the point of impact, across the surface of the barrier, the fire moving over the water the way oil moved over water, finding every inch of the barrier's surface and covering it. Not burning through it. Covering it. Staying.

Tobias felt it.

The fire was consuming the mana of his barrier — not breaking it, not hitting it hard enough to shatter it, eating it. The barrier was still there but it was smaller than it had been a second ago and it was getting smaller, the fire clinging to its surface and taking what the surface was made of and not releasing it, not returning it to the ambient field the way mana was supposed to return when it was done doing what it was doing.

The fire surrounded him.

Not all at once — gradually, the spread of it moving around the edges of the barrier until he was inside it, the barrier between him and the fire on every side, the orange of it pressing in from all directions, the heat of it reaching him through the water in a way that communicated very clearly what would happen to the space he was occupying if the barrier stopped existing.

He knew he couldn't drop it.

He knew he couldn't maintain it indefinitely.

He knew both of these things simultaneously and they did not resolve into anything useful and he stood inside the fire that wasn't going away and kept the barrier up and kept the barrier up and kept the barrier up.

# 24 \- What The Tyrant Left Behind \- Part 3

**Chapter Twenty-Four — What The Tyrant Left Behind \- Part 3**

---

Tristan made the order when the ravens pulled back from what remained of Lucian.

One word. The men moved.

Berrick made the order to split and Tristan concurred with a gesture — the two of them arriving at the same decision from different positions at the same moment. The soldiers split into formation — not the rough split of people reacting but the clean split of people executing, two groups moving away from each other and away from Silas simultaneously, the distance between them calibrated rather than simply fast.

Above them the ravens split.

No order. No gesture from Silas. The flock divided itself — half following one group, half the other — with the immediacy of things that didn't need to be told because the telling happened somewhere nobody on the ground could hear. They were faster than the soldiers. They came from above, from angles that ground formations weren't built to account for.

The crossbow barrages came simultaneously from both groups.

Not in sequence — at the same moment, the two groups releasing together with the coordination of soldiers who had received the same training and were executing it at the same time without needing to see each other to do it. The bolts rose from both sides and met the ravens and the ravens came apart where the bolts passed and the darkness dispersed and the red eyes went out — and then reformed and kept coming.

They found one of Tristan's soldiers.

The darkness closed around him — the column of it forming before anyone could close the distance, the ravens working with the specific efficient brutality of things that had done this before and knew exactly how long it took. The soldiers nearest to him raised their crossbows and held them. Shooting into the column meant shooting into their own man. They held and watched and the column did what the column did and then it was over and the column was moving — already moving, already finding the next soldier who was close to where the first had been.

Tristan made the order.

Not loud. Not easy. Leave him.

The men around the second soldier scattered — breaking the proximity that made the ravens' jump worthwhile, the formation adjusting around the order, the gap where two men had been closing as the others moved through it. The ravens found the second soldier anyway — he hadn't moved fast enough, the distance between him and the first man not enough — and the column formed again and Tristan's order arrived too late for him and Tristan noted this and noted the cost and kept moving.

The crossbow barrages kept coming.

The ravens kept reforming.

---

Tristan's group went out of sight first.

The buildings swallowed them — the group pushing into the narrow gaps between structures, the angles available to Silas from the air closing one by one as they went deeper. The gaps were not empty. The civilians who had come out when the bell rang and stayed when the glow appeared to the north were here — in their doorways, in the alleys between buildings, pressed against walls with children pulled close, old men standing at the edges of their thresholds with nowhere useful to go. The soldiers moved through them and around them, the two groups occupying the same narrow spaces, the specific chaos of a military unit moving at speed through a civilian population that had nowhere to clear to. the soldiers pressed on doors as they passed — not asking, not explaining, the order delivered in the flat urgent tone of someone who needed the door closed immediately. Inside. Lock it. Stay away from the windows. The next door the same. And the next. The alleys filled with the sound of bolts sliding home and children being pulled away from windows and the specific frightened quiet of people who had understood that going inside was the only thing left available to them. 

Silas lost the group.

The ravens that had been following Tristan wheeled back toward him and reformed above the broom in their loose cloud. Below him Berrick's group was still visible — circling, using the time Tristan's disappearance had bought to move around the perimeter of Silas's position, the group spreading as they moved.

Berrick had the rifle.

Silas had been watching him since the split. He kept his eyes on Berrick and kept the broom moving — the continuous repositioning of someone who understood that stillness was the thing that killed you when the other side had what the other side had.

The ravens regrouped and went for Berrick.

All of them — converging on a single target, the darkness massing between Berrick and the open air above him. Berrick fired.

The bullet went through them.

The darkness parting around the bullet's path and the bullet continuing through and out the other side, leaving behind a black cloud where the mass of dispersed ravens hung in the air in the shape of the bullet's passage. Silas had already moved — the broom carrying him sideways in the moment the ravens covered Berrick's line of sight, faster than an air mage moving under their own power, the object going where it was directed at the speed it was capable of going.

Berrick looked at the cloud.

It was coming together. Slowly — the darkness pulling toward itself, the shapes of individual ravens emerging as suggestions before they became outlines. Taking longer than before. He had the number in his head — the duration of the reforming, how long it took, and this was longer than that number.

He made a gesture.

One hand, one motion. The soldiers received it and the barrage came at the cloud while it was still becoming ravens — bolts arriving before the reforming finished, interrupting it, the darkness coming apart again before it had finished coming together.

By the time the second barrage landed Tristan had circled around.

His men emerged from different positions — spread, each man finding his own angle on the air above the gate where Silas was moving. Tristan had the rifle up. He was waiting for Silas to be still.

---

Silas passed above Berrick's group and released the light.

The cowl had been building since before he passed over them — the brightness of it gathering in the specific way his nature gathered before it was released, and when it came it came the way it always came, everywhere at once, the condition of it arriving before the eyes below could process that it was arriving. Berrick's group went blind.

In the blindness the ravens reformed.

They split into two groups and each group found a target simultaneously — no hesitation, no transition between forming and attacking, the two soldiers simply being where the ravens needed them to be and the ravens being there. They moved fast. They were already moving to the next before the soldiers nearest to the first could raise their crossbows and find the angle.

Tristan had a clear shot from across the open ground.

He fired at one group while it was between soldiers — in transit, the darkness of it moving through the open air, the moment of it being neither on one man nor the next. The shot caught the edges. The darkness dispersed partially and Berrick's soldiers, their eyesight returning in the way eyesight returned after Silas's light — gradually, the shapes coming back before the details did — took care of what remained with the bolts they had left.

The other group reached another soldier.

Berrick looked at his man inside the column.

He was still fighting. Still swinging the sword, still on his feet, the ravens finding the gaps in what remained of his armor and the gaps finding what was underneath. He would not be on his feet much longer. The ravens would finish and move to the next man and the next man was close and Berrick had looked at the next man and made the calculation and the calculation had one answer.

He raised the rifle.

His man saw him.

They looked at each other through the darkness of the column — through the silhouettes and the red eyes and the dark flame trailing from the bodies of the things that were taking him apart. His man looked at the rifle and looked at Berrick and looked at the rifle again and something in his face settled, the screaming stooped as if the pain was no longer there. It wasn't acceptance — something past acceptance, the specific stillness of someone who had understood what was coming and had decided to meet it without the expression that made it harder for the person pulling the trigger.

He stopped swinging.

Berrick fired.

The column dispersed. The ravens came apart where the bullet passed through them and the darkness scattered and the red eyes went out and what was on the ground when the darkness cleared was not something Berrick looked at for longer than he had to.

---

Silas focused.

The evasion didn't stop — the broom kept moving, the bolts from Tristan's men kept passing through the spaces he had already vacated — but something behind the evasion changed, the attention that had been distributed across tracking and directing and moving pulling inward, narrowing, finding the thing it needed to find.

Above his head the rune circle appeared.

The light runes turning slowly, the script of them luminous, the circle complete. It turned once. It turned again.

Then it shattered.

Not broken — shattered, the specific disintegration of something made of light and structure being unmade at once, the pieces of it dispersing into the air around it. The circle simply ceased to exist.

The ravens ceased with it.

All of them at once — the darkness going out simultaneously across every silhouette, the red eyes going dark in the same instant, the shapes of them simply not there anymore in the space where they had been.

Berrick's men stopped releasing.

The quiet after the barrages was loud in the way quiet was loud when it replaced something sustained. Berrick assessed. Ravens gone. Silas above — the broom repositioning again, moving through the angles Tristan's men were holding with crossbows running low on bolts. His own men: the count arriving at a number that communicated clearly how many more barrages he had before that number was zero. No time to collect what had been fired. The bolts were on the ground somewhere in the street and the rooftops and the gaps between buildings and going to get them meant exposing the men who went to the thing they were trying not to be exposed to.

Tristan had run the same numbers. Berrick could see it in how Tristan was holding his position.

Neither of them moved.

They had both arrived at the same place: the next move belonged to Silas.

What neither of them had information to account for was that Silas had run his own numbers and arrived at the same place from the other direction. He could not summon without complete focus. Complete focus required stillness. Stillness — above two groups of soldiers with rifles and crossbows that were finite but not yet exhausted — produced a specific outcome, and that outcome did not resolve in his favor.

He kept moving.

---

*"Do you need help,"* Cedric said.

The smug quality of it arriving through the fight with the specific ease of someone who had enough capacity left over to be smug while conducting it. Vorne's greatsword descended at his shoulder and he moved — not far, just enough, the blade passing through the space his shoulder had been.

*"You're in no position to be arrogant,"* Silas said from above, dry.

*"I'm just getting warmed up,"* Cedric said.

The greatsword came again. The stone vambrace met it and Cedric's own sword caught the angle and redirected, the two movements happening as one — and then his fist was coming, the stone building around it in the instant before impact, covering his knuckles and the back of his hand in a layer that added mass and hardness to what was already behind the punch. It hit Vorne in the lower left torso. The stone launched off the fist on impact — not staying, releasing, the mass of it converting into additional force at the moment of contact, the push of it carrying Vorne back a step.

Cedric came after with the sword.

Vorne caught it on his own blade and kicked — the specific short sharp kick of someone who had identified the distance and used what the distance allowed. It hit Cedric in the chest. They both went back.

Cedric had not guarded the kick. He had taken it — the chest absorbing it with the specific quality of someone who had wanted to know what it felt like and had made room for the knowing.

*"You think this is a game,"* Vorne said.

*"You can't deny you love this,"* Cedric said. A stone projectile left his hand — not large, not the full investment of his magic, a question thrown at Vorne while the conversation continued. *"When was the last time you were in battle."*

Vorne moved around it. *"You flatter yourself."*

*"Admit it,"* Cedric said, coming back in — sword, then a stone vambrace check with the forearm, then the sword again from a different angle, then a palm strike with stone built into it, the variety of it continuous, no pattern repeated, each exchange beginning from wherever the last one ended without returning to a neutral position. *"You are enjoying this as much as I am."*

*Vorne said nothing to this. He moved — the greatsword moving with him,*  Finding the openings — they were there, Cedric's variety producing them the way variety always produced them, the unpredictability of the sequence creating gaps in the coverage that a precise fighter with enough experience could locate. Vorne found them and used them and kept moving.

He was reading something.

It had been building since the first exchange — the specific information that accumulated when you fought someone long enough to start receiving data beneath the surface of the individual attacks. The testing quality of it. The way each variety of attack communicated not the attack itself but the question behind the attack — what does this produce, how does he move here, what does he do when I come from this angle. Cedric had been building a picture since the first greatsword came down.

He had not been fighting.

He had been measuring.

Vorne understood this and stopped holding back.

What changed was not dramatic. It didn't look different from the outside — the same greatsword, the same movement, the same finding of openings. But the quality of the finding changed, the commitment behind each opening different from what it had been, the specific shift of someone who had been working levels below their level and had stopped working at that level.

Cedric felt it immediately.

Something moved in his face — not alarm, something closer to satisfaction. The measuring had produced a result and the result was that his opponent had been holding back too and had now stopped holding back and this was what Cedric had come here to find.

He was still smiling.

---

Berrick saw the opening.

Cedric occupied with Vorne — fully occupied now, the exchange between them producing the specific density of two people who had stopped testing and started fighting. Silas managing Tristan's men above. The angle between Berrick's position and Cedric's position was clear.

He raised the rifle.

Silas saw him raise it.

The pride arrived before the calculation did — the specific involuntary response of someone who had identified what was about to happen and had decided, independently of whether it was tactically sound, that it was not going to happen. Not in front of Cedric. Not while he was watching.

The light beam left his hand.

Not the blinding release — a directed beam, concentrated, aimed at Berrick specifically. Berrick had been waiting for Silas to commit to something, had been watching for exactly the moment when Silas would stop moving long enough to produce something directed. He had the rifle up and the angle and the window.

The beam arrived before the bullet did.

It hit Berrick at the chest — the armor receiving it, the force of it communicating itself through the armor and into the body underneath, the specific impact of something that carried enough force to matter even when the armor took the majority of it. Berrick went down. Not dead — the armor had done what armor was supposed to do — but down, the hit carrying a toll that the getting back up from would cost something.

The light spread above Berrick's men.

The group went blind — the temporary total blindness of Silas's release arriving in every direction at once. Silas descended. The broom carried him down through Berrick's blinded group, through the space between them, and his hand closed around the rifle that had been in Berrick's hand before Berrick went down.

He rose again.

Tristan's men — spread further out, the distance between them and Berrick's group having saved their eyesight — were tracking him. The angles between them covered the air above the gate. They didn't have a clean shot. Silas was surrounded by Berrick's blinded men and firing into that meant firing into their own.

Berrick got back up.

He stood. He assessed himself — the armor had taken most of it, the body underneath reporting its findings with the specific clarity of a body that had absorbed something significant and was communicating what the absorption had cost. More hits like this and the assessment would come back different.

He signaled to Tristan.

Tristan's men began leading Silas away from Berrick's position — drawing him north, creating the distance that would give Berrick's men room to recover their vision and Berrick room to move.

Berrick moved south.

Toward where Lucian had been.

He had not been able to reach it before — the ravens, the fight, the distance between him and the street where Lucian went down all making the reaching impossible. The path was clear now. He kept low and moved fast and did not look at what was on the ground when he arrived at where Lucian had been. He found what he came for with his hands rather than his eyes.

The rifle was still there.

Silas saw Berrick moving south.

He tracked him across the ground below — the specific direction of him, the destination of it, the street where Lucian had been and what was still there. He understood what Berrick was going for before Berrick had covered half the distance.

He sat down on the broom.

Not the standing position he had maintained all night — he sat, the broom between his legs, the specific adjustment of someone who needed stability for something that required stability. He had watched the knights with the rifles since the fight began. He had watched how they held them — the shoulder placement, the way the cheek came down against the stock, the specific geometry of a weapon that communicated through its design exactly how it wanted to be held. He had watched the thunder it made and the pushback that followed the thunder and he had filed both of these things.

He placed the rifle on his shoulder.

His cheek came down. He found the line of it — the barrel, the sight, the distance between where he was and where Berrick was moving. Tristan's men were still firing at him, the bolts passing through the spaces he kept vacating, and he kept the broom moving while he held the rifle up, the evasion and the aiming happening simultaneously, the broom carrying him in the slow arc toward Berrick's position.

The right moment arrived when Berrick stopped.

He had reached the site where Lucian had been. He had stopped — not for long, just the specific pause of someone who had arrived at a destination and was making themselves not look at what surrounded the thing they had come to collect. Silas held his breath the way he had seen the knights hold theirs before the trigger.

He fired.

Nothing.

The trigger moved and the mechanism responded and nothing came from the barrel — no thunder, no pushback, no result. He pushed his mana into it the way you pushed mana into an artifact, the way you fed the lantern or the broom, the way you activated anything that was supposed to respond to mana. Nothing. The rifle sat in his hands and received his mana and produced nothing with it and communicated through its silence that it had no interest in mana and never had.

He put it away.

The light beam left his hand a moment later — aimed at Berrick, aimed at the back of him, arriving before Berrick had finished processing that the rifle had not fired. It hit him between the shoulder blades and the force of it carried him forward and down, the ground receiving him with the specific impact of someone who had not seen it coming and had not prepared for it.

Berrick's men released immediately — the barrage going up at where Silas had been. Silas had already moved. The broom carried him north toward Tristan's position, the bolts passing through the space he had vacated, and behind him on the ground Berrick was not getting up.

Vorne saw it.

He was mid-exchange with Cedric — the greatsword already in motion, the arc of it committed — and he saw Berrick go down in the space between one movement and the next. Something shifted in his face. He wanted to move. He wanted to break away — to cover the distance between himself and Berrick, to do something about what had just happened to his man.

Cedric didn't give him the window.

Not a single exchange, not a single moment in the sequence of attacks that produced the gap Vorne needed to break away cleanly. He had not been giving Vorne gaps all night and he was not giving him one now. The attacks came — stone walls rising from the ground between Vorne and the direction he wanted to go, rock blasts from Cedric's palm forcing him to deal with what was in front of him before he could deal with anything else, sand at his eyes when he tried to find the angle that let him look at Berrick while keeping Cedric in his peripheral vision.

Vorne stopped looking at Berrick.

He stopped assessing Cedric. The specific step-by-step reading of an opponent — the pattern recognition, the filing, the gradual accumulation of information toward a complete picture — he stopped doing all of it. There was no time for it. There was no time for anything that wasn't ending this.

The shift was immediate.

Cedric felt it before he could account for it — the quality of what was coming at him changing, the commitment behind each attack different from what it had been, the specific force of someone who had removed a layer of restraint arriving in the space where the restrained version had been. He retreated. The stone vambraces caught what they could catch and the rest he moved around and the moving was working but the working was costing him more than it had been costing him and the cost was going up.

He escalated.

Walls of stone rising from the ground in front of him — his palms driving downward, the earth responding to the intention behind them, the walls erupting upward from where his hands directed rather than from where his feet stood. — not barriers, obstacles, the specific use of earth magic to change the terrain rather than simply defend against what was crossing it. Rock blasts from both hands while the sword came from a different angle simultaneously. Sand at Vorne's eyes — the stream of it hitting his face and going solid the way it had earlier, and Vorne took it and brushed it off with the specific brute practicality of someone who had decided that whatever the sand did was less important than what he was going to do while the sand was doing it. The sword heavier when Cedric needed gravity — the stone building around the blade in the moment before a downward strike and dissolving the moment after, the weight arriving and departing in the specific rhythm of someone who had been doing this long enough that the timing was no longer a calculation.

Vorne went through the walls.

Not around them. Through them — the greatsword meeting the stone and the stone communicating what stone communicated when a greatsword hit it with enough force and commitment, which was that stone had a limit and the limit had been reached. The walls came apart. He kept going.

---

Tristan was moving.

He had read the situation — Silas faster on the broom, the distance between them closing regardless of how fast the formation moved, the rifle in his hand the thing that made him the primary problem. He made the orders without stopping: his men follow, Berrick's men stay with Berrick's body, nobody separates from the group they're assigned to.

They moved. Silas was faster.

The broom closed the distance with the specific inevitability of something that didn't have to manage the ground it was crossing — no obstacles, no footing, no weight to carry except Silas's weight, the air offering less resistance than the street stones offered the soldiers' boots. Silas came directly above Tristan's group and Tristan made the call he thought he needed to make.

*"Cover your eyes."*

His men covered their eyes.

The flash didn't come.

The beam did — concentrated, directed, aimed at Tristan specifically, arriving at him before the order to cover eyes had finished leaving his mouth. It hit him and he went down and his horse went somewhere without him, the animal making its own assessment of the situation and acting on it with the speed that animals acted on assessments.

His men opened their eyes.

Four of them. They surrounded him and raised their crossbows and released — the barrage going up at the broom moving above them, the bolts passing through the spaces the broom had already left. The beams came back down. Not one — sequential, each one finding a target, each target going down before the next beam came, the four men falling in the time it took the broom to make two passes above them. Not dead — Silas wasn't ending them, just removing them from the equation, the beams carrying enough force to put a man on the ground without carrying enough to keep him there permanently.

Silas came down.

He held the broom in his hand — not riding it, holding it, the object at his side as he walked toward Tristan who was trying to get his arms under him and push himself up. Silas put his foot on Tristan's chest. He pushed him flat.

He looked at the rifle in Tristan's hand.

He stepped on the hand.

Not the rifle — the hand holding it, the fingers wrapped around the grip, the hand that was now between the metal of the rifle and the stone of the ground. He put his weight on it. All of it. Slowly — the weight arriving gradually, the pressure building the way pressure built when something was being committed to rather than done quickly. The fingers communicated what they communicated when they were being asked to occupy a space smaller than they could occupy.

The sound they made was covered by the sound Tristan was making.

Tristan was making very little sound. The contained scream of someone who had decided that the sound was a thing he could control even when everything else was not — compressed, held, arriving only at the edges of what the control could manage.

He examined Berrick's rifle — the one already in his hand. He turned it over. He looked at it the way he had looked at it from the air — with the attention of someone who had tried to use it and found that it refused to be used in any way he understood.

*"This is not an artifact,"* he said. *"What is it."* He turned it over again. *"I don't need to take a hit from this to know the devastation."*

---

Berrick's remaining six men were surrounding their leader's unresponsive body.

They were looking at Silas standing over Tristan and they were looking at each other and none of them knew what the next thing was supposed to be. One of them looked down. He looked at what was on the ground near him — at the street where Lucian had been and what the street contained beyond what Lucian had been. The rifle was there. Lucian had dropped it when the ravens took him and it had been there since, and none of them had been close enough or in a position to reach it until now.

He picked it up.

He had not fired one before. But Vorne had made sure his trusted soldiers understood the mechanism — the demonstration had reached further than just the knights. He knew the sequence. He opened the chamber, He opened the chamber. He found a bullet in Berrick's pouch — his hands steadier than they had any right to be. He slid the bullet in. He closed the chamber. He pulled the lever. He raised the rifle and pointed it at Silas standing over Tristan.

He fired. The recoil hit him before he understood what recoil was — the rifle driving back into his shoulder with a force that had no equivalent in anything he had fired before, pushing him off his feet and onto his back, the sky above him replacing the street in front of him between one moment and the next. 

Ten inches. The miss was ten inches — the bullet passing through the air beside Silas's head and continuing into the wall behind him and the wall receiving it without comment.

Silas kicked Tristan's rifle away from him.

He turned toward the soldier.

He started walking.

Not fast — the specific unhurried pace of someone who had assessed the distance and the situation and found neither of them urgent. The soldier looked at him walking and looked at the rifle in his hands and started reloading. His hands were less steady now. The bullet went in wrong the first time and he pulled it out and tried again, Silas getting closer with each attempt, The other five kept their crossbows up and releasing — the bolts coming at Silas continuously, Silas's barrier stopping them while he maintained the summoning ritual, the barrier adequate for crossbow bolts in a way it would not have been adequate for the rifle. 

---

Above the ground fight Silas raised his hands.

The language came — the same language that had produced the raven circle, the same syllables that nobody on the ground had a framework for, spoken with the flat purposeful delivery of someone reciting something that needed to be said rather than something they were choosing to say. The runes appeared above his head. But differently from before — more of them, smaller, the circles they were forming moving in a pattern that was not the pattern the raven circle had moved in, the specific geometry of a different configuration producing itself in the air above the street.

Cedric saw it from where he was fighting Vorne.

Cedric saw the circles and saw Silas — saw the specific quality of his comrade's focus, the way Silas moved when he was building toward something rather than maintaining something, the body language of someone who had committed to a conclusion and was executing it. 

*"It seems he wants to end things quickly,"* Cedric said. He was still moving — still in the fight with Vorne, still dodging and defending. *"I guess I must do the same."*

He stepped back from Vorne for a moment.

His cowl came. He removed the leather vambraces — the straps coming loose, the leather falling. What replaced them was not stone. Quartzite — denser, building around his forearms with the same rapid formation his magic had been producing all night but in a different material entirely. His neck covered. His head — not a helmet, a covering, the quartzite conforming to the shape of it rather than approximating a separate structure. The quartzite moved along the sword, finding the edge and extending it, adding length and a new edge that was harder than stone and would hold longer.

He looked at Vorne.

The fight shifted back in Cedric's favor.

Vorne felt it — the hits landing differently, the stone he had been breaking through requiring more force than the stone he had been breaking through before, the specific material communicating that it was not the same material even when it looked similar. He adjusted. He kept going.

---

Silas finished reciting.

The circles above his head stabilized — the movement of them slowing, the runes settling into their final configuration, the script of them holding its arrangement with the specific stillness of something that had found the position it was going to occupy and had stopped moving.

A new circle appeared on the ground.

In front of his feet — large, larger than the raven circle had been, the runes of it inscribed in the stone of the street the way light inscribed itself on surfaces when the light was strong enough, visible without being carved, present without being permanent. It turned. The script of it moving in the opposite direction from the circles above his head, the two rotating against each other with the specific mechanical quality of two parts of the same thing doing different work toward the same end.

Berrick's soldier had finished reloading.

He raised the rifle. He aimed at Silas standing beside the circle on the ground and he fired and the bullet left the barrel with the thunder that rifles made and crossed the distance between him and Silas and didn't reach Silas.

Something came out of the circle.

It came up from the ground the way things came through openings — not gradually, not tentatively, simply present in a space it had not been present in a moment before. A toad.
