The word arrived in every mind that was looking at it and immediately proved inadequate — the shape of a toad, the outline of a toad, the specific geometry of a creature that belonged to a category everyone present had a name for. But the category stopped being adequate when the size of it registered. Almost as tall as a man. The mass of it overwhelming in the way the mass of something that large was overwhelming when it arrived in a space that had not been built to contain it. Red at its surface — the color belonging to it completely, not the red of injury or corruption. It looked as though it was dripping, the surface of it giving the impression of something in slow motion without anything actually falling, the appearance of it communicating liquid without producing liquid. 

It had met the bullet.

The bullet that should have reached Silas was somewhere inside it or somewhere behind it and the toad was between Silas and the soldier and the soldier was looking at it with the specific expression of someone whose understanding of what was possible had just been revised in a direction they had not prepared for.

The sac under its chin inflated.

Slowly — the skin of it distending outward, filling, the specific biological preparation of something that was about to produce a sound. Everyone in the street was looking at it. Everyone in the street understood, from the size of the sac and the size of the creature and the relationship between those two measurements, that whatever came next was going to be loud.

It was louder than that.

The sound arrived everywhere simultaneously — not traveling, arriving, the specific quality of something at a volume that didn't require travel because it was already present at every point it was going to reach before the air had finished moving. Louder than the rifles. Louder than the wall coming down. louder than anything the night had produced in any of its locations simultaneously. It hit the buildings and the buildings returned it and it hit the street and the street returned it and it moved south and north and east and west through the district without losing anything on the way.

It reached the western gate.

The croaking ended.

The silence that replaced it was not the silence of something finishing — it was the silence of something that had finished and was now waiting for everyone who had heard it to understand what they had heard. The toad sat at the edge of the circle. Red, enormous. The street around it had changed — the sound having done something to the air that the air was still recovering from.

Everyone was looking at it.

Even Vorne.

*"Did you see that,"* Cedric said. He was looking at the toad with the expression of someone who had seen this before and was still impressed by it. *"It took the blast from your weapons and it's still standing."*

Vorne was thinking the same thing. The bullet had gone in. The body had absorbed it. No exit wound, no visible damage, no indication that the impact had produced anything worth noting in something that size.

*"I think he calls it sangui—"*

*"Sangui-batrachos,"* Silas said. His voice had changed — not louder, not more confident, just the quality of someone standing next to the completed version of something they had been building their entire life. *"My magnum opus. All my life's work has led to this."*

---

Silas turned his head toward the six soldiers staying with Berrick's unconscious body.

The toad turned with him.

No word. No gesture. The toad's head moving in the same direction as Silas's head, the two of them orienting toward the same point at the same moment with the specific synchronization of things connected by something that didn't require language to function.

It covered fifty yards in a single jump.

The ground shook when it landed — the weight of it arriving at the street stones with the impact of something that had no business being airborne and had been airborne anyway and was now letting the ground know about it. It stopped directly in front of the soldier carrying the rifle. The soldier who had loaded and fired and missed by ten inches and had been trying to reload when the summoning started.

The tongue came out.

It happened in the time between the soldier seeing it and the soldier understanding what he was seeing — the tongue crossing the distance between the toad's mouth and his body before his body had finished processing that the tongue was coming. He was off the ground. He was in the air. He was at the mouth.

He was being chewed.

The five soldiers around him released everything they had — the crossbow bolts hitting the toad's body and the toad's body receiving them the way it had received the bullet, without comment, without adjustment, the bolts going in and the body closing around them and continuing to do what it was doing. The soldier in its mouth was still alive. The sound he was making was the sound of someone being crushed by something that was not crushing him quickly — the sustained compression of a body inside a space that was getting smaller, the specific horrible patience of a creature whose mouth was designed to break things down gradually rather than all at once. The armor began to come out. Pieces of it — the shoulder plate first, then the vambrace, then the chest piece — pushed out from between the lips the way a frog pushed out the shell of a beetle, the specific mechanical rejection of the parts it didn't need.

The screaming stopped.

The bolts ran out.

The toad stopped chewing. It opened its mouth and what came out was not the soldier — it was what the soldier had become inside the mouth, the specific result of sustained compression and whatever else the mouth had been doing while it was closed. It spilled out onto the street in front of the remaining five men and Berrick's unconscious body. The substance of it reaching their boots before any of them moved.

---

The crack of thunder came from behind Silas.

He felt the bullet pass him — the heat and the velocity of it close enough to register against his skin, the specific near-miss that communicated everything about how close it had been. He saw where it hit the toad on its back — the impact visible, the body absorbing it, the red surface closing over the entry point the way it had closed over everything else that had entered it tonight.

He turned.

Tristan was sitting on the ground at the spot where Silas had kicked his rifle. His right hand was at his side — the fingers broken, the hand not participating in what the rest of him was doing. His left hand was on the rifle. He had set it on his knee — the barrel pointed at Silas, the stock braced against his thigh rather than his shoulder, the trigger operated by the wrong hand because the right hand no longer had the fingers to operate anything. He had loaded it and aimed it and fired it with one hand and broken fingers on the other and he had almost hit Silas from sixty feet away.

The toad was already at Silas's side.

Tristan loaded another bullet. Left hand — the chamber opening awkwardly, the bullet going in at an angle, the chamber closing. He aimed at Silas. The toad moved in front of it — the red mass of it occupying the space between the rifle's barrel and the man behind the toad.

The toad started walking toward Tristan.

Not jumping. Walking — the front limbs extending forward and the back limbs pushing, the body moving across the street at the pace of something that had decided pace was a choice and had chosen slowly. The sound of it was the sound of weight being transferred from one limb to the next, the street stones receiving each step individually.

It was more terrifying than the jumping.

The jumping had been fast — the speed of it removing the time required to be afraid during the jump. The walking gave the time back. The walking said there was no hurry. The walking said the destination was going to be reached regardless of how long it took to reach it and the thing being walked toward was welcome to use the remaining time however it wanted.

Tristan dropped the bullet he was loading.

It fell from his shaking hand and hit the ground and rolled and he watched it roll and he did not pick it up. He looked at the toad walking toward him and he looked at the bullet on the ground and the calculation between the two was a calculation that had one answer and the answer was that picking up the bullet would change nothing about what was walking toward him.

He dropped the rifle.

He forced himself to stand. His body communicated everything about what standing cost — the broken hand, the ribs that had taken Silas's beam, the legs that had been on the ground for too long and were now being asked to work again without adequate preparation for the asking.

He drew his sword.

The specific motion of a hand finding a grip it had found ten thousand times before — the thing he had known for most of his life, the thing that had gotten him where he was, the thing that had carried him through every situation his career had produced and had never failed to be the thing he reached for when everything else was gone. It came out of the scabbard with the sound swords made when they came out of scabbards and the sound was the most familiar sound in his life.

He was face to face with the beast.

The tongue came out.

The sword met it — the blade finding the surface of the tongue and cutting into it, the steel doing what steel did when it encountered flesh. But the man holding the steel was not a match for the force behind the tongue and the force communicated this immediately — the impact carrying through the blade and through the grip and through the arm and through the shoulder and Tristan went down.

The sword had left a cut.

The cut forced the tongue's muscles to tighten — the specific involuntary contraction of damaged tissue, the tongue unable to produce the adhesion it was designed to produce, the surface of it failing to stick to the metal the way it had stuck to the soldier it consumed moments before. The tongue retracted. The cut healed — in a single moment, the tissue closing over the damage, the surface returning to what it had been before the blade found it.

Silas felt the healing.

The cost of it arriving in the place where all the costs arrived — the place that was not mana, that was deeper than mana, that was already being drained by the toad's existence and was now being drained by the toad's maintenance. The toad was consuming his stamina by being present. The healing was consuming it additionally. The arithmetic of this was not favorable and Silas was aware of the arithmetic.

The toad stepped on Tristan before he got back up.

The front limb came down on his lower body — the weight of it pinning him to the street stones, the force of it not crushing but holding, the specific application of enough pressure to remove the option of movement without removing the option of continuing to be present for what came next.

---

Vorne was trying to reach his knight.

He could see it — Tristan on the ground, the toad's limb on him, the distance between where Vorne was and where Tristan was crossable in the time it would take to break away from the fight and cover the ground.

Cedric was not giving him the time.

Stone shards came from Cedric's palms — a barrage of them, sharp, the quartzite edges harder than anything the stone had produced earlier in the night. Vorne met them with his shoulder armor. The armor caught most of them. Not all. The cuts that had been accumulating on Vorne since the fight began — the scrape from the broken vambrace, the smaller cuts from the shards that got through, the places where the armor had gaps the shards found — were starting to show. Nothing critical. Nothing that slowed him. But present, and accumulating, and communicating that the accumulation had a ceiling.

*"He's toying with them,"* Cedric said. Releasing shards while speaking, the two operations happening simultaneously with the ease of someone who had more capacity than either operation required on its own. *"Can you imagine if that thing was let loose in the city."* Another barrage. *"Could you imagine the havoc."*

*"You underestimate this city,"* Vorne said.

Vorne drove his boot through the stone wall Cedric had raised between them — the wall coming apart at the point of impact, the stone communicating its limit. He thrust the greatsword through the gap before the dust settled. Cedric redirected — the quartzite-augmented sword meeting the greatsword and sending it sideways, the two weapons communicating through the contact what the two men behind them already knew about each other. 

*"What do you think is happening at the other gates,"* Cedric said. *"You can't be in all three places at once."*

Vorne looked to his left.

The toad's front limb was on Tristan's lower body. Tristan was not moving under it. Tristan was looking at Vorne across the distance between them with the expression of someone who had run out of things to do except be present.

The sound of horses echoed from the south.

The fireball came from the dark.

It hit the toad — not at the limb on Tristan, at the body, the mass of it, the fire finding the red surface and producing the first visible reaction the toad had shown to anything that had hit it tonight. It jumped. Not forward — backward, toward Silas, the limb leaving Tristan's body, the weight of it departing the street stones with the specific sudden lightness of pressure being removed.

Three figures appeared from the dark.

They came on horses — church robes, white, bright in the firelight that was still burning above the northern compound, the three of them arriving in the street at the southern gate with the controlled pace of people who had been riding hard and had slowed at the last moment because arriving in control was more useful than arriving fast.

Valerius. Hadrian. Mathias.

*"Do you think I'm the only one in this city,"* Vorne said. Still fighting. The greatsword still moving, Cedric still in front of him, the exchange between them continuing without pause while the words arrived through it.

Cedric looked at the white robes.

The look on his face changed. Not surprise — something older, something that didn't need a trigger because it was always there underneath, the same look that had arrived on Elysia and Severin's faces at the northern compound when they saw church robes in the firelight. The specific disgust of someone whose entire belief system was organized around the rejection of what those robes represented.

*"The signals you made,"* Vorne said. *"I'm assuming there should have been one from the western gate. Correct."*

Cedric said nothing.

The silence communicated everything the words would have communicated and more than the words would have communicated because silence was the thing people produced when the answer was something they didn't want to confirm.

*"Did you really think I would leave my post unprotected,"* Vorne said.

---

The ice sealed the hole where the gate had been.

Emmeline stood at the edge of it with the wand in her hand — the glacier behind her thick and white and smoking faintly in the night air, the compound on the other side of it gone from view, gone from sound, simply absent. She looked at Seris with the confidence of someone who had just changed the terms of the exchange and knew she had changed them.

Seris was not looking at her.

She was looking at the wand.

The expression on her face was not the expression Emmeline had expected to find there. Not anger, not concern, not the focused combat attention of someone whose students were on the wrong side of a glacier. Something else — something that sat uneasily on a face that did not usually produce it. Excitement. The specific barely-contained excitement of someone looking at the answer to a question they had been asking for twenty years, held in the hand of someone who had no idea what it was worth.

A smile was almost escaping her serious face.

Even Emmeline, who barely knew her, knew the look was unusual.

*"I take it you know what this is,"* Emmeline said.

Seris was still looking at it. The wand didn't seem to carry the weight of time — no decay, no missing sections, no evidence of the centuries that should have been visible on something this old. It looked new. It looked like something that had been made recently by someone who knew how to make it. 

*"Where did you get it,"* she said.

*"Maybe I did,"* Emmeline said.

Seris looked at her face.

*"You're lying,"* she said. *"Where did you get it."*

Emmeline saw what was on Seris's face and understood what it meant — the hunger of it, the twenty years behind it, the specific vulnerability of someone who wanted something badly enough that the wanting was visible. She understood what she could do with it.

*"Do you really want to know,"* she said. *"I can tell you everything about it. Everything. I'll even give it to you."*

Seris knew where this was going before the next sentence arrived.

*"All you have to do is step aside and wait for a while,"* Emmeline said. *"You're already outside the district."*

Seris's face returned to its normal state. The excitement gone — not suppressed, just replaced by the thing that usually occupied her face, the flat direct attention of someone who had arrived at a conclusion and was stating it.

*"I have a better proposition,"* she said. *"I will take both the information and the wand. With or without your permission."*

---

Emmeline released from the wand.

The ice wall erupted from the ground — not gradually, not the way magic usually built itself from intention to expression with the visible transition between the two. All at once. The entire wall arriving simultaneously from every point along its base, the ice already at full height before the eye could track the growing, as if the air had decided to stop being air and become a wall of ice and had done it without the courtesy of a transition.

Seris was already out of the way — the tentacles from her back carrying her sideways before the wall finished arriving. It erupted beside her. Close enough to feel the cold of it against her skin.

She stopped.

She looked at the wall.

She put her hand on it.

She felt the mana — it was there, present, the same ambient mana that every magical construct was made of. But there was also ice. And the ice left her hand wet. And the wetness felt real — not mana pretending to be water the way mana-produced elements pretended, not the temporary approximation that would dissipate back to the ambient field when the intention behind it stopped. Wet. Real. The moisture on her palm was actual moisture that did not feel like it was going anywhere.

The look on her face changed.

Not excitement this time. Something else — the expression of someone who had just put their hand on the thing they had been working toward for years and found that the thing was not what they expected it to be, that the framework they had built to understand it was wrong or incomplete or pointed in the wrong direction. For the first time, the flat certainty that Seris brought to everything she encountered was not there. What replaced it was the absence of that certainty — the expression of someone standing in a space where their understanding ended and the thing in front of them continued.

*"Fascinating, isn't it,"* Emmeline said. *"It breaks every fundamental rule we know about magic."*

Seris was thinking. How the ice had grown simultaneously from all places — not one point spreading outward but every point arriving at the same time, as if the air itself had received a single instruction and every particle of it had executed the instruction in the same instant.

*"Somehow this wand commands the mana surrounding us,"* she said.

She looked at the ice covering the branch. She looked at the gem.

*"Does it only create ice,"* she said. *"Or is it dependent on the user."*

She looked at the wall again.

*"What about its reach. Is it finite."*

The questions came fast — one after another, the specific cadence of a true scholar encountering something new, the twenty years of research behind each question giving each one a weight that a casual question would not have carried.

*"I thought you wanted to learn about it the difficult way,"* Emmeline said.

*"You flatter yourself,"* Seris said. *"I would not consider you difficult in any matter."*

The thin water stream came from her palm — pressurized, aimed at Emmeline directly. The glacier met it — Emmeline raising the wand, the ice growing where the water pressure cut, the glacier rebuilding itself faster than the water could carve through it. The ice kept pushing forward, growing from the glacier toward Seris, the mass of it advancing across the ground between them.

Seris moved out of the way.

*"How long can you keep this up,"* Emmeline said. *"Unlike you, the Wand of Rime does not get tired."*

*"The Wand of Rime,"* Seris said. *"Is that its original name. Or is it a translation."*

*"You ask so many questions,"* Emmeline said. *"My offer still stands. Step aside and I will tell you everything you want to know."* She looked at Seris. *"How long have you lived here anyway. Do you actually know anyone here."*

Seris looked behind her.

At the glacier covering where the gate had been. At the compound on the other side of it — not visible, not audible, the ice thick enough to remove both. Her students were behind it. Highmore was behind it. Whatever was happening behind it was happening without her.

*"Ah, of course,"* Emmeline said. *"Your students. They're quite lucky to have a teacher like you."* She looked at the glacier. *"You don't have to worry about them for now. They're in good hands."*

The ice on the gate hole was starting to thin — the mana bonds that held it together beginning to dissipate the way all magic eventually dissipated, the ice more resilient than ordinary mana constructs but still magic, still subject to the same rules even if it took longer to obey them. Emmeline raised the wand and the glacier thickened again — a fresh layer building over the thinning surface before it could finish failing. 

---

Behind the glacier the students were standing with their backs to the gate.

Highmore was still in front of them.

The compound interior stretched behind them — the training ground, the dormitory, the armory, all of it quiet in the way a place was quiet when the people who usually occupied it had ridden south with Vorne and the ones who had stayed had not yet arrived. The ice behind them blocked the sound of whatever was happening outside. They could hear nothing from beyond it — not Seris, not Emmeline, not the fight. Just the compound and the man in front of them and the quiet.

*"You are her students,"* Highmore said. *"Is that correct."*

*"Yes we are,"* Myre said.

She said it the way she said everything — directly, without softening, without the hesitation that might have been expected from someone standing in front of a man who had just cut a rider and his horse in half. The pride in it genuine and present.

Bael released a fireball.

It left his palm fast and hot and crossed the distance between him and Highmore in the time it took to leave his hand. Highmore moved his hand — a casual redirect of compressed air, the fireball going sideways and hitting the ground and dying against the stone without producing anything except a scorch mark.

He didn't look at the fireball while he was deflecting it. He was still looking at the students.

*"Can you behave yourself,"* he said. *"I'm trying to have a conversation."*

*"We have nothing to say to you, heretic,"* Bael said.

Highmore's face changed.

The scowl that arrived was not performed — the word landing on something real, something that lived underneath the calm, the specific involuntary response of someone who had heard a word enough times that the hearing of it had become the thing rather than the word itself.

*"I really hate that word,"* he said. *"Especially when it comes from a child."*

---

The soldiers arrived before the sentence finished settling.

Ten of them — the garrison staff who had stayed behind when Vorne rode south, emerging from the compound interior with the specific urgency of people who had heard what happened at the gate and had taken the time to organize rather than the time to arrive quickly. The commanding officer read the scene in the time it took him to cross the threshold — the man in dark robes, the students behind him, the glacier where the gate had been.

He ordered the students to move out of the way.

Five crossbow carriers dropped to one knee and raised their weapons. Five others moved forward with shields — heavy, metal-faced, the specific equipment of soldiers who were trained to absorb what the crossbows needed time to produce.

Solen looked at the others.

*"Move,"* Solen said.

They started moving south.

The air changed.

*The air changed in front of them. a wall, invisible, the pressure of it arriving before the evidence of it, the air between them and where they were going becoming something they could feel against their faces and their chests and their feet. The pressure of a hurricane compressed into a flat surface that communicated one thing: you are not going this way.*

*They looked at Highmore. His palm was extended toward them.*

*"Please stay put," he said. "I don't want you to miss what's about to take place."*

They stayed. Not because they agreed — because the hurricane communicated that not staying would produce consequences and the consequences would arrive before the not staying was completed.

He put both hands forward toward the soldiers.

*"Watch,"* he said.

The commanding officer made the order to release. The five crossbow carriers fired. The bolts crossed half the distance and met something — something that was already moving toward them, something invisible and faster than the bolts. The bolts came apart in the air. The wood splintering, the metal heads separating, the pieces of them scattering sideways as if they had been fed into something that chewed.

The something continued past the bolts and reached the soldiers.

The first row came apart at the waist. All five of them — simultaneously, the upper halves of their bodies separating from the lower halves with the clean finality of something that had passed through them without slowing. The shields fell. The crossbows fell. The upper halves fell. The lower halves stayed standing for a moment — the legs not yet understanding what the torso already knew — before they folded.

The second row had time to see the first row.

They did not have time to do anything with what they saw. The invisible edges found them where they stood — not at the waist this time, everywhere, the compressed air moving through them in multiple passes that arrived so close together they were indistinguishable from a single event. A man with a shield became the shield and the arm and the head and the legs arriving at the ground separately, each piece hitting the stone at a slightly different time, the sound of it the sound of several impacts rather than one. The man beside him became something the eyes refused to organize into a recognizable arrangement — the pieces too many, too scattered.

The students froze.

Highmore turned back to them.

*"Where were we,"* he said.

Iren's body made a decision her mind had not authorized — her stomach rejecting what her eyes had just delivered to it, the contents of it arriving at her throat before she could hold it, the specific involuntary response of a body that had received more than a body was meant to receive through the eyes alone. Solen stepped in front of her and turned her away from the scene and held her there while she finished and she held onto his arm and neither of them said anything about it.

The others were in shock — the specific stillness of people whose bodies had stopped producing the normal operations of standing and breathing at their usual rates and were instead producing the minimum of both while the mind behind them tried to process what it had just been given.

Sera looked at the scene. This wasn't her first time seeing something like this — but it was her first time seeing it inside the walls. The walls that were the sign of salvation for everyone inside, and everyone inside felt untouchable because they prayed in her profaned name and that was the only thing on Sera's mind. 

That was the only thing on Sera's mind.

---

Highmore snapped his fingers.

Twice. Three times. The specific sharp sound of someone calling attention back from wherever attention had gone.

*"Focus,"* he said. *"Don't get distracted."*

They looked at him. All of them — even Bael, who had released a fireball at this man minutes ago and had watched it be dismissed like a cinder, reluctantly brought his attention back to the face of the person requesting it.

*"My name is Aurelius Highmore,"* he said. *"Pleased to make your acquaintance."*

*"You're from House Highmore of Oakhaven,"* Myre said.

Her voice was afraid. She said it anyway — the words arriving through the fear rather than despite it, the specific reflex of someone whose training ran deeper than whatever was happening to the rest of her.

*"Correct,"* Highmore said. Something moved in his face — approval, or the cousin of approval. *"You're quite the scholar. What are your names."*

Myre introduced herself.

It was not a choice. The words came out of her the way certain words came out of people who had been trained to produce them before they were old enough to understand what training meant — the automated response of someone born into aristocracy, the specific reflex of etiquette overriding the situation that etiquette had no framework for.

*"My name is Myre Telvaris."*

*"House Telvaris,"* Highmore said. He received the name the way he received everything — with the attention of someone for whom information was a currency he never stopped collecting. *"The current head of House Telvaris is Percival the Third. Who is he to you."*

*"He's my grandfather."*

Her mouth answering again without permission. The words leaving before the decision to say them had been fully formed, the etiquette doing what etiquette did when confronted with a direct question from someone of standing — producing the answer because the answer was the thing it had been built to produce.

The others introduced themselves. One by one — each name arriving with the same automated quality, each response to Highmore's follow-up questions arriving with the same reluctant reflex. Even Iren, who had been vomiting thirty seconds ago, collected herself when Highmore addressed her directly and answered with the composure of someone for whom composure in the presence of authority was a deeper reflex than nausea.

Highmore turned to Sera.

He waited.

She didn't say anything. She didn't know what to say — the automated response that had carried the others through this exchange was not something she possessed, the etiquette of aristocratic introduction not being a thing you learned in a monastery where you weren't allowed to know anyone's name.

*"Did you lose your etiquette,"* Highmore said. The words didn't match the tone — the words were polite and the tone was firm and the gap between them communicated that the firmness was the real thing and the politeness was what covered it. *"Introduce yourself. Please."*

*"My name is Sera."*

He waited.

*"Sera—"*

*"Just Sera,"* she said.

*"A commoner,"* he said. He scanned the others — the noble names he had just collected, the houses he had just placed, the specific social geography of the group standing in front of him. *"Among all these noble names."*

He looked at her for a moment longer than he had looked at the others.

*"You must be quite the impressive mage,"* he said. *"After all, I doubt the sorceress of the northern valley would take you as a student if you were anything but."* He paused. *"Isn't that right, Mr. Astorel."*

Davan didn't understand why he was being addressed.

The others didn't understand either — the shift in Highmore's attention from Sera to Davan arriving without the transition that would have explained it.

*"House Astorel changed the view on air magic,"* Highmore said. He was looking at Davan now with something that the word fondness didn't quite fit but was adjacent to. *"Before your great uncle Balthazar, air was viewed as the weakest form of magic. The most common. But Balthazar was able to unlock its full potential."* A pause. *"It was a great honor to be his student."*

Davan looked at him.

The shock of this arriving in a different register from the shock of everything else — not the horror of what had just happened to the soldiers but the specific disorientation of hearing a man who had cut ten men apart in front of you say the name of someone in your family with the tenderness of someone who had loved them.

*"Why are you telling us all this,"* Davan said.

*"I don't know, really,"* Highmore said. He laughed — not the laugh of someone who found something funny, the laugh of someone who had surprised themselves by arriving somewhere they hadn't planned to go. *"I guess I just started reminiscing about my days as a student."*

The laugh faded.

*"It really broke my heart,"* he said, *"when I had to take his life."*

The six of them had nothing to say to this.

*"You probably were only an infant when he died,"* Highmore said.

Davan was quiet for a moment. He had not known Balthazar — not in the way you knew someone you had been alive at the same time as. But he had been taught the history of his house and the greatness of Balthazar was the centerpiece of that history and the statue of him stood at the entrance of the Astorel manor and every child who grew up in that manor grew up walking past it.

*"I didn't get the chance to know him,"* Davan said. *"But I know how great he is."*

He looked at Highmore.

*"And I know that he was stabbed in the back by a coward."*

The words left his mouth despite the fear. The fear was still there after they left — present and real and unchanged by the fact that the words had already gone and could not be taken back.

Highmore smiled.

*"For your information,"* he said, *"I wasn't the one who made the first move. All I wanted was to open his eyes. To show the truth to the person I respected most."* He looked at the training ground wall. *"But he wouldn't listen. He called me that word and threatened to out me and I just couldn't afford to be outed yet. I was too young."* He looked back at Davan. *"And he taught me too well."*

The six of them stood in their places and listened to him talk and every second standing in front of him felt like hours. They knew that if he wasn't talking he would be acting and they knew he was not going to talk all night.

*"Here I go talking too much again,"* he said.

It was the last thing they wanted to hear.

*"Unfortunately I have a job to do, so I cannot continue our conversation,"* Highmore said. *"I really hate killing young aspiring mages. So I would appreciate it if you got out of my path."*

All of them didn't know what to do. They were battling their thoughts — the specific internal war of people who had been told to move and couldn't decide whether moving was surrender or survival and couldn't afford to take the time to decide.

*"Everyone in my family knows who you are,"* Davan said.

He broke the silence the way he broke every silence — by walking into it without fully deciding to, the words arriving before the calculation behind them was complete.

*"You forgot to mention how you murdered his wife and children,"* he said. *"Did they also threaten you."*

*"In many ways, yes,"* Highmore said.

*"And yet you were exposed,"* Davan said. *"And all of it was for nothing."*

Highmore's jaw clenched.

The frustration on his face was not the calm he had been producing — not the measured conversational quality of someone who had been controlling the temperature of the exchange since it began. This was real. This had found something and Davan had found it and the finding was visible in the way the jaw moved and the way the eyes narrowed and the way the hands — the hands that had just cut ten men apart without changing expression — tightened at his sides.

Myre's hand pressed Davan's wrist.

Hard. The pressure of it communicating everything the words she wasn't saying would have communicated — stop, stop now, stop immediately, you are right and being right is going to get us killed. Davan looked at the others. They all looked at him. None of them said it. None of them wanted to diminish what he had said or the family trauma that had produced it.

But at that moment it was not the time.

Highmore's jaw unclenched.

The frustration that Davan's words had found settled back into whatever it had been before the finding — not gone, just returned to the place underneath the calm where it lived. He stepped forward. Slowly. The same deliberate pace he brought to everything. He walked until his face was a foot from Davan's.

Davan's knees were shaking.

He wanted to step back. He wanted to step back the way his body wanted to step back from things that were going to hurt it — automatically, involuntarily, the impulse arriving before the decision. But he couldn't move. Something about the proximity of Highmore's face — the black eyes that registered everything without appearing to move, the handsome features carrying the expression of someone who had just told a story about killing a man he loved and was now standing close enough for Davan to see the specific quality of calm that produced — held him where he was.

*"I'll say this only one more time,"* Highmore said. *"Go home."*

Davan's cowl started to build.

Slowly — the wind nature of it accumulating around his body without announcement, without the visible preparation that usually preceded a cowl's arrival. It gathered the way fear gathered — incrementally, in response to something the body understood before the mind finished processing it. He was still afraid. The cowl was not replacing the fear. It was happening alongside it.

Highmore looked at the cowl and something moved in his face. Surprise — not the performed version, the real kind, the kind that arrived before you decided whether to show it.

*"No,"* Davan said.

Behind him the others created their cowls.

Bael's fire nature flaring fast and hot. Solen's water building evenly around him. Myre's lightning crackling once and holding. Iren's earth slow and deliberate. Sera's — bright, warm, the quality of it that had no clean name among the four types.

Highmore looked at the six cowls in front of him.

*"How brave,"* he said.

He looked at them for a moment longer — the assessment of someone reading what was in front of him and arriving at his conclusion about it without needing additional information.

*"To be honest,"* he said, *"there was nowhere for you to run. Soon the entire district will be leveled."*

The words landed on all of them with the weight of something that was not a threat but a schedule — not what he intended to do but what was already being done, the district's future described as a fact rather than a warning. They stood inside the weight of it and none of them had the words to answer it.

The croaking arrived.

From the south — enormous, the volume of it reaching the compound from whatever had produced it at the southern gate, the sound traveling through the district without losing anything on the way. It hit the compound walls and the training ground and the dormitory and the glacier where the gate had been and it kept going.

Highmore looked toward the sound.

Something in his face changed — not the surprise of the cowls, something else, the expression of someone receiving information that confirmed a suspicion they had been carrying. Another sign. Another location where the plan was not going the way the plan was supposed to go.

---

Outside the wall Seris and Emmeline heard it.

The sound arrived between them without announcement — the same enormous volume reaching the space outside the glacier where the two of them had been fighting, the croak cutting through everything that had come before it in the evening's collection of sounds and announcing itself as the loudest and the strangest.

*"Look what you've done,"* Emmeline said. She was looking at Seris. *"You made us look incompetent."*

*"You've done that yourself,"* Seris said.

She moved.

The water whip came from her right hand — fast, coiling around Emmeline before the sentence had finished settling in the air between them. She swung her. Half circle — Emmeline's body leaving the ground and traveling through the arc of it with the force of someone who had decided that the conversation was over and the force was going to communicate the decision. She hit the wall.

Emmeline's barrier took it. The impact absorbed, the force distributed across the barrier's surface, the wall behind it receiving what got through the barrier and holding.

Seris put both hands forward.

The mana started to accumulate on her palms — not a stream, not the pressurized continuous output she had been producing all night. Something else. The mana gathering and not releasing, building and not going anywhere, the pressure of it increasing in her hands the way pressure increased in things that were being compressed and had not yet been allowed to decompress. She held it. The accumulation growing visible — the light of it present in the air around her palms, the water nature of it dense and concentrated in a way that communicated what was coming before it came.

She released.

The slash hit the glacier.

The ice exploded — not cracked, not broken, exploded, the entire mass of it coming apart at once, the dry ice and the real ice and the mana bonds holding them together all failing simultaneously under the force of something that had been built to make them fail. The fragments went everywhere — into the compound, into the street, into the air above both. The gate hole was open.

Highmore turned.

The students turned.

The gap where the glacier had been was empty and the night air outside was visible through it and the sound of the district at war was audible again through the opening.

Seris lunged.

The tentacles from her back carried her forward — fast, the water propelling her toward the gate with the speed of someone who had been separated from the thing she needed to reach and was no longer separated and was not going to be separated again. Emmeline raised the wand. The ice started forming at the gate's edges — the same simultaneous eruption, the air at the gate hole beginning to obey the instruction the wand was giving it.

Seris released again.

The slash came while she was still moving — the accumulated force of it hitting Emmeline's barrier before the ice finished closing. The barrier held. Barely — the surface of it showing the impact in a way barriers showed impacts when the impact was at the edge of what they could absorb, the visible distortion of something that had taken more than it was comfortable taking. The ice at the gate hole stopped growing.

Seris reached the gate.

She passed through it — the tentacles carrying her through the opening, and on her way through her right hand extended and the water whip found Emmeline again. Not the arm this time — the body, the whip wrapping around Emmeline's torso with the force of something that was not asking permission to take her where it was taking her. Seris carried her through the opening.

She slammed her on the ground in front of Highmore and the students.

Emmeline hit the compound stone on her back. Her barrier had given at some point between the wall and the ground — the damage showing in the way she landed, in the way she didn't immediately get up, in the specific quality of someone who had been absorbing impacts all night and had just received one that exceeded what the absorbing could handle.

The students looked at the woman on the ground.

Then they heard the footsteps.

The sound arrived before the person — the familiar sound, the shoes on stone, the same measured cadence they had heard every morning when she walked to the training ground and every afternoon when she walked to her office and every time she moved through the compound at the pace she always moved at. The pace that said she had decided where she was going and was going there.

They turned.

Seris was standing in the gate.

Unscathed. Her attire still clean — the deep structured fabric of it carrying no evidence of the fight that had been happening outside, the water nature of her magic having produced nothing that left a mark on the person who produced it. She looked the way she always looked. She looked the way she looked when she walked into the training ground in the morning and told them to begin.

Something in the six of them changed when they saw her.

Not relief exactly — relief was the word for when something bad stopped happening. This was different. This was the word for when you had been standing in the dark and the person who knew how to handle the dark arrived and you understood, without anyone saying it, that the dark was now someone else's problem.

# 25 \- What The Tyrant Left Behind \- Part 4

**Chapter Twenty-Five — What The Tyrant Left Behind \- Part 4**

---

The stone shards came from Mathias before the clerics had finished dismounting.

They flew at Silas — fast, sharp, the earth nature behind them concentrated into edges rather than mass. The toad was between them in an instant. The shards hit its body and the body received them the way it received everything — without reaction, without adjustment, the red surface closing over the points of impact before the sound of the impacts finished echoing.

Valerius's fireball came after.

It hit the toad full in the side — the fire spreading across the red surface, the heat of it visible in the distortion of the air around the point of contact. The toad didn't move. The fire sat on its skin for a moment and then the skin was the same as it had been before the fire arrived. Barely any effect.

The toad jumped.

One jump — the distance between where it had been and where the clerics were standing crossed in a single motion, the weight of it arriving at the ground in front of them with the impact that weight at that scale produced. Mathias raised both hands and the stone wall came up from the ground between them and the toad. The toad hit it. The wall stopped the lunge — for a moment, the stone holding what the stone could hold, and then the stone broke and the pieces of it went in every direction and the toad was through the gap.

The tongue came out.

Valerius's fire met it — the stream of it hitting the tongue before it reached anyone, the fire doing something to the muscle that the muscle responded to, the first reaction the toad had shown to anything that wasn't the greatsword. The tongue retracted. The toad pulled back.

The clerics split.

Hadrian stayed in front of the toad. He extended both hands and a stream of stone dust came from his palms — not shards, not projectiles, dust, the finest particulate his earth magic could produce, a cloud of it pouring from him and finding the toad's face and its eyes and filling the air around it until the toad could not see what was in front of it.

Hadrian moved.

From the left Valerius's fireball came. From the right Mathias's stone shards. Both hitting the toad simultaneously — the fire on one side, the shards on the other, the two attacks arriving at the same moment from opposite directions. The toad took both. The red surface absorbing both. Barely any visible damage.

But Silas felt it.

The toad drawing from him — the cost of the hits arriving not at the toad's body but at his, the life force that sustained the summoned creature being drawn in the amounts that sustaining required and the amounts increasing when the creature took damage. He felt the draw and he understood the arithmetic of the draw and the arithmetic was not going in the direction he wanted it to go.

He pushed his mana into the broom. It started to lose weight in his hand — the object responding to his mana the way it always responded, the interface between the artifact and the user activating, the broom becoming what it became when someone who knew how to use it told it to work. He jumped on it and flew.

Mathias released at him from below. Too slow — the broom carrying Silas through the angle before the shards arrived at it. Silas released a light beam at Hadrian from above. Hadrian's barrier took it — the light hitting the barrier and the barrier holding without breaking.

Silas circled around toward Mathias.

Below him the toad advanced on Hadrian. The tongue came out whenever the distance between the toad and Hadrian closed — the muscle extending and retracting, extending and retracting, each time testing the barrier Hadrian was maintaining, each time the barrier absorbing the impact and Hadrian absorbing the cost of the barrier absorbing the impact.

Valerius released at the toad's mouth whenever it opened — the fire finding the interior, the soft tissue that the exterior didn't have, the mouth being the one place the toad showed anything resembling a response to what was hitting it.

Silas made the toad target Valerius.

The distance closed in an instant.

One jump — the toad leaving the ground in front of Hadrian and arriving in front of Valerius before Valerius had finished processing that the toad was no longer in front of Hadrian. The toad descended on his barrier and the barrier held and the force of it pushed Valerius backward across the ground, his boots leaving marks in the stone.

Another jump. Closer. Valerius barely moved in time — the toad landing where he had been, the ground receiving the weight of it with the crack of stone being asked to hold more than stone wanted to hold.

He put his hand out.

The tongue met it.

Not the way he intended — not the way you met something with a barrier or a blast, the specific wrong way of a hand being in the wrong place at the wrong moment and the tongue finding it and the tongue doing what the tongue did to things it found. His hand was in the toad's mouth. His arm followed the hand. The toad flung him — the weight of his body nothing to the thing doing the flinging, his body going sideways and up and sideways again without the mouth releasing what it had, the motion of it the motion of something that was positioning its food before swallowing.

Valerius released fire from the hand that was inside the mouth.

Not controlled — the fire coming from his palm without the direction he usually gave it, the output arriving in every direction at once inside the toad's mouth, the interior receiving fire in a way the exterior had not been receiving fire. The mouth opened. The toad jumped back — a few feet, the mouth releasing what it had been holding.

The sound of a screaming man echoed across the street.

Valerius looked at his arm.

It was barely hanging. The bone — the bone that ran from his elbow to his wrist, the structure that made the forearm a forearm — was dust. The meat around where the bone had been was turning blue, the color arriving fast, the tissue communicating what had happened to it in the only language tissue had. The hand at the end of it was not a hand anymore in any functional sense.

He lifted his right arm.

The fire came from his right palm — concentrated, hot, a torch rather than a stream. He bit down on his folded cincture — the cloth between his teeth, the specific preparation of someone who had made a decision and needed something to bite on while the decision was executed. He brought the fire to the arm. The cut was not clean and it was not supposed to be clean — it was the severing of something that was no longer useful by something that was hot enough to sever and cauterize simultaneously, the fire doing both jobs at once, the smell of it arriving at everyone in the street before the sound of the screaming changed from the scream of someone being hurt to the scream of someone hurting themselves on purpose.

The arm fell.

The wound closed — not healed, closed, the cauterization sealing what needed to be sealed in the way fire sealed things, the specific brutal sufficiency of a method that worked without being the method anyone would choose if choice was available.

Hadrian released.

The dust stream came from both hands — continuous, sustained, the full output of his earth magic directed into producing the finest particulate he could produce and producing as much of it as he could produce at once. The cloud expanded. It covered Mathias. It covered Valerius. It covered the toad. It covered the space between all of them and made the space into something Silas could not see through from the air.

Inside the cloud Mathias released.

Stone shards — aimed at Silas above the cloud, the shards coming up through the dust and out of it and into the air where Silas was. Hadrian had allowed Mathias to see — a narrow lane through the dust, the two of them having trained this before, the coordination of two earth mages who had worked out how to use a dust screen offensively without blinding each other.

Silas dodged.

The broom carried him sideways before the shards arrived. The toad jumped to where the shards had come from — the origin of the attack being the information the toad used to find the person who had produced it. The dust cleared for a moment from the toad's momentum — the mass of it displacing the cloud as it passed through, the air around it going briefly transparent.

Mathias was not there. He had moved the moment he released — sideways, away from the origin point, the dust closing behind him.

The dust accumulated again. Mathias released again from the new position. Silas dodged. The toad didn't move this time — Silas had learned from the last jump that the origin of the attack and the location of the attacker were not the same thing.

Silas moved toward Hadrian.

Valerius's fireball came from somewhere in the cloud — weaker than before, the output of someone who was fighting with one arm and a cauterized stump and the diminishing reserves that fighting in that condition produced. The toad moved toward where the fire came from. Valerius wasn't there.

Silas got frustrated.

The toad started moving erratically — not the directed jumps it had been making, not the controlled advances toward targets Silas was identifying. Random. Fast. The mass of it dashing through the thinning dust cloud in directions that had no tactical logic, the randomness being the tactic, the unpredictability replacing the precision that the dust screen had made impossible.

A random dash caught Mathias.

He had been repositioning — moving between release points the way he and Hadrian had trained, the movement that was supposed to keep him ahead of the toad's responses. The toad came from a direction he was not moving away from. The collision was not the kind of collision a body survived — the mass of the toad hitting him at the speed the toad was moving and the wall of the house behind him receiving what the collision produced. He hit the wall. The wall held. He was planted in it — the stone of it closing around the shape of him, the impact having driven him into the material of the wall itself.

He did not come out of the wall.

Silas moved toward Hadrian again.

The beam hit Hadrian's barrier — the light finding it and pushing, the barrier holding but the dust stream stopping, Hadrian's attention split between maintaining the barrier against Silas's beam and maintaining the dust screen that had been protecting all of them.

The dust settled.

The toad lunged at Valerius.

Someone crossed between them.

Fast — the specific speed of someone who had been fighting in a different part of the same street and had covered the distance between that fight and this one in the time it took the toad to leave the ground. Cedric. The greatsword was behind him — not Cedric's greatsword, Vorne's, the weapon arriving after the person arriving after the person, the specific sequence of a man running to intercept and another man pursuing the man who was running.

The greatsword collided with the toad.

The blade went into the red surface — the first thing all night that had penetrated past the exterior, the steel finding purchase in the thick skin and going in and the toad's momentum almost yanking Vorne with it, the sword threatening to take the man holding it in the direction the toad was going. Vorne planted his left foot. The sword moved — one motion, the blade traveling through the skin with the effort of someone cutting through something that did not want to be cut through, the resistance of it enormous, the muscle in Vorne's arms and shoulders and back communicating what the resistance was costing them.

The slash opened the skin.

Silas turned from Hadrian to see why the toad was taking damage.

Vorne backed up from the beast. Its size was impressive even for him — the red mass of it occupying the street in a way that communicated scale beyond what the word large could carry. The sword in his hands had taken everything he had to move through that skin.

Valerius released at the wound — fire finding the opening Vorne had made, the interior tissue receiving the heat in a way the exterior had not.

Vorne lunged simultaneously — a stabbing form, the greatsword going in point first into what remained of the slash, the blade entering the wound and going deeper than the slash had reached. The toad pulled back. The sword was stuck — the skin closing around the blade, the muscle of the toad's body gripping it. Vorne was almost pulled with the beast, the weight of the toad against the weight of the man, and for a moment the question of who was going where was genuinely uncertain.

The sword came out with extreme effort.

"You can't handle one man," Silas said from the air.

"You're in my way," Cedric replied from the ground.

The toad moved away from Vorne. Vorne turned from the toad and lunged at Cedric — spinning his body to create momentum, the greatsword coming around in the arc that used the full rotation to produce its force. Cedric met the blade with a quartzite wall and the kick that followed with both forearms crossed.

"Fine," Silas said. "Let me get out of your way. I'm already finished."

The toad jumped at Hadrian.

The barrier broke. The tongue did what it did — fast, the muscle extending and finding him and the finding being the end of the exchange. Hadrian did not get up from what the tongue produced.

Valerius released at Silas.

The beam from his remaining hand — aimed at the broom, at the figure on it, the fire coming fast but coming from someone whose body had been doing this all night with two arms and was now doing it with one and a cauterized stump and the difference between those two conditions showing in the output. Silas closed the distance with the broom — fast, the artifact carrying him directly at Valerius, the evasion becoming approach, the approach becoming the offensive.

The beam hit Silas's barrier.

Once. Silas kept coming.

Twice. Closer now.

Three times. The barrier holding each time, the light nature of it absorbing what Valerius's fire could produce in his current state, the gap between what Valerius could give and what Silas could take widening with each exchange.

Valerius's condition gave out.

The barrier broke — not dramatically, just stopped being there, the mana behind it exhausted, the body behind the mana exhausted, the one arm and the cauterized stump and the fighting and the toad's mouth and the cauterization and everything the night had done to him arriving at their total simultaneously.

Valerius said a prayer.

Quiet. The words of it arriving in the space between him and the figure descending toward him on the broom with the quality of something said for the last time by someone who knew it was the last time.

The thunder came.

The sound of it enormous in the street — the crack of the rifle arriving before anything else, the echo of it bouncing off the walls and the rubble and the buildings still standing and coming back diminished but present. Everyone heard it. Silas heard it.

He stopped.

Cedric stopped.

Silas felt the numbness first. Not pain — the specific absence of something that should have been present, the body's report arriving as a negative rather than a positive, the thing that was supposed to be there not being there anymore. He turned.

Berrick was on his knees.

Holding Lucian's rifle. The man who had been unresponsive on the ground — who had taken two light beams to the body and had been lying in the street while the clerics fought and died around the toad — was on his knees with the rifle against his shoulder and the barrel still pointed at where Silas had been when the bullet left it.

Cedric looked at Silas.

He saw the look on his face. Not pain — the look that came before pain, the look of someone whose body was communicating something the mind had not yet finished receiving.

Silas started descending.

The broom carried him down — not the controlled descent of someone landing, the gradual uneven descent of someone who was no longer fully directing the object they were on. He collapsed before the broom reached the ground. The sound of his body hitting the street from ten feet was the sound of a body hitting stone without any of the things a body usually did to prepare for hitting stone — no bracing, no rolling, no attempt to distribute the impact. Just the arrival.

The broom hit the ground after him.

Cedric ran.

Vorne allowed it.

He reached Silas and knelt and turned him over onto his back. The stomach was bleeding — heavily, the blood coming from the entry point with the volume that communicated what the bullet had found inside and what it had done to what it found. The blood spreading outward from him across the street stones, reaching Cedric's knees where he knelt.

"Dismiss the batrachos," Cedric said.

Silas coughed. Blood came with the cough — the blood that was in his lungs now, the blood that had found its way there from the stomach, the body's internal geography rearranging itself around the damage the bullet had produced. He tried to speak. The speaking was not available to him in any form that produced words.

A circle appeared above his head.

The light runes — turning slowly, the script of them dim now, the luminosity that had been present when he summoned fading. The circle turned once and the toad stopped existing. Not gradually — completely, the red mass of it simply not present in the street anymore, the space it had been occupying returning to being ordinary air and ordinary ground, the absence of it immediate and total.

The strain on Silas's life force eased.

The damage did not.

"Fuck," Silas said. The word arriving with extreme effort, each letter costing something. "I can't believe you're going to outlive me."

Cedric looked at his face. At the pale of it — the pale that had been there before, the pale that was Silas's natural color, now becoming a different pale, the pale of someone whose body was losing what it needed to maintain color. He couldn't find the feeling to gloat. He looked for it — the thing that would have been there between them on any other night, the thing their dynamic was built on, the back and forth of two people who had known each other long enough to know exactly where to push. It wasn't there.

"Stop being so sensitive," Cedric said. "You're not dying from this."

The warm blood from Silas's abdomen reached Cedric's knees. He could feel it through the fabric — the temperature of it, the specific warmth of something that was supposed to be inside a person arriving at the outside of a different person, the warmth communicating what the words were not communicating.

The shivering started.

Violent — not the shivering of cold, the shivering of a body that had lost enough of what it needed that the systems maintaining temperature were failing, the involuntary response of something that was shutting down and was not going to stop shutting down. Cedric tried to hold him — his hands on Silas's shoulders, pressing down, trying to keep the body still. The blood came out faster. The pressure of the holding squeezing what was inside toward the opening. He released him.

The shivering continued.

Cedric watched.

He watched the consciousness go — the eyes losing the thing behind them that made them Silas's eyes, the focus that had been there even at the end, the dry flat attention that had made Silas who Silas was departing from behind the eyes without announcement. The shaking slowed. The shaking stopped.

Silas was still.

Cedric closed his eyes with two fingers.

"Let the deep void claim you, brother," he said. "We will meet again in the eldritch."

Cedric stepped back.

The stone came from beneath his feet — not a wall, not a barrier, a launch, the earth magic directing itself downward and producing upward, the force of it throwing him backward and into the air with a speed that covered the distance between where he had been standing and where Berrick was kneeling in a single arc. He rose high enough that the street below became a map of itself — the rubble at the gate, the bodies, the fire still burning at the northern compound in the distance, the broom on the ground where Silas had fallen — and at the top of the arc his hands were above his head and between them the stone was forming.

Not a wall. Not a barrier. A boulder.

It built from his palms outward — the earth magic producing mass at a scale he had not produced all night, the quartzite and the stone and the compressed earth accumulating into something that had weight beyond what a person should be able to hold above their head and he held it anyway. He was above Berrick. Above the remaining soldiers gathered around Berrick's kneeling body. Above all of them.

He brought it down.

The boulder descended with the force of its own weight and the force Cedric added to its weight and the distance it fell adding to both. It hit the ground where Berrick and the soldiers were and the ground received everything it received and when the boulder dissipated into mana — the stone returning to the ambient field, the mass becoming nothing, the air where the boulder had been becoming air again — what remained underneath was not something that could be looked at for long.

Cedric hit the ground.

He walked to the rifle. Lucian's rifle — the weapon that had been on the ground since the ravens took Lucian, the weapon Berrick had crawled to and used and aimed at Silas and fired and hit. The weapon that had ended the only person in this fight Cedric could not replace.

He lifted his foot. The quartzite covered it.

The rifle shattered under the impact — the metal and the wood and the mechanism that nobody in the Godless Hand understood coming apart under the concentrated force of quartzite meeting it, the pieces of it scattering across the stone in every direction, the specific destruction of something being made permanently unable to do what it had been built to do.

---

Vorne walked.

Slowly. Not the pace of someone who was tired — the pace of someone who was taking in what was around him and giving it the time it required. The rubble on the gate where the wall section had come down. The street between the gate and where Cedric was standing. The bodies — fifteen soldiers who had ridden south with him from the compound, men he had commanded, men he had trained beside, men whose names he knew. Tristan on the ground with broken fingers. Berrick under what the boulder had left. Lucian's remains on the street where the ravens had been. The fire still visible above the rooftops to the north.

He walked through it. He let himself see it. He arrived behind Cedric and stopped.

*"What message is this supposed to send,"* he said.

Cedric didn't turn.

*"Do you really think the people of this kingdom will fall into desperation because of you,"* Vorne said. *"I've been in countless battles with some of these men. We were brothers in many ways. But that's the life we lead. We lost so much and we grieved enough."* He looked at the rubble and the bodies and the street that had been a street and was now a record. *"You think you could come here and break our spirits."*

*"It's not about you,"* Cedric said. Still without turning. *"It's bigger than all of us. It's his will that we the enlightened must carry."*

*"Quite the burden you put on yourself,"* Vorne said.

*"Not a burden,"* Cedric said. *"An honor."*

Vorne's face changed. Something in the word honor finding something in him that the rest of the conversation had not found.

*"Honor,"* he said. *"How many innocents did the Hand murder in cold blood."*

Cedric turned.

*"Innocent,"* he said. His voice elevated — the first time his voice had been anything other than conversational all night. *"Ignorant you mean. All of you are scum who are unable to distinguish between good and evil without a doctrine."*

---

He jumped.

Vertically — the earth magic beneath his feet producing the force, his body going straight up, the quartzite-covered sword in his hand catching the firelight as he rose above Vorne's position. He reached the top of the jump and came down. Full force — the quartzite sword descending on Vorne with the weight of the fall and the weight of the quartzite and the weight of the arm driving it.

Vorne's greatsword met it.

The impact traveled through both weapons and both arms and both bodies and the ground beneath both of them received what traveled through and held.

*"The irony is lost on you,"* Vorne said.

Cedric came again — the quartzite sword from a different angle, the stone fist from another, the variety that had been his signature all night continuing to produce itself without repetition.

*"What is that name you call us,"* Cedric said between attacks. *"The Godless Hand,"*

*"We don't give ourselves a name really,"* Cedric said. He released a stone projectile that Vorne moved around. *"Why would we. After all we leave nothing behind but the rubble."*

*"How many of you are there,"* Vorne said. He didn't expect an answer.

*"We are many,"* Cedric said. *"Enough to attack three kingdoms in one night."*

The greatsword came at Cedric's torso and the quartzite caught it and the kick followed and the forearms guarded and both of them reset and both of them came again.

*"You should have brought more,"* Vorne said.

---

Vorne's attacks changed.

Not technique. Force. The greatsword hitting the quartzite with something behind it that had not been behind it earlier in the night — the physical strength of a body that was being pushed past where bodies were supposed to go, the life force beneath the muscle and the bone and the training communicating itself through the weapon in a way that the weapon transmitted to everything it hit. Each swing arriving faster. Each recovery shorter. The gap between one attack and the next shrinking until the attacks were not a sequence but a pressure, the greatsword becoming a continuous thing rather than a series of individual things.

Cedric's quartzite took the hits.

The hits were landing differently. The vibration of each impact traveling through the quartzite and into the body underneath — not cracking the armor, not yet, but communicating through the armor in a way the armor was not designed to prevent. The body underneath receiving the communication and filing it and continuing and filing the next one and continuing.

Cedric responded.

The quartzite thickened — the armor getting heavier, the coverage increasing, the earth magic producing more protection because more protection was what was being demanded. His attacks escalated with the protection — stone fist, sand, projectiles, walls rising from the ground in front of his hands, everything in his repertoire coming out now in the variety that had defined his fighting all night but at a higher output than the variety had been producing before. The output of someone who had realized that the man in front of him was doing the opposite of what opponents were supposed to do at this stage of a fight. Opponents were supposed to slow down. Vorne was speeding up.

Both of them were past what they had been producing at the start of the night.

Vorne's greatsword cracking quartzite that would have held without cracking an hour ago. Cedric's attacks finding places in Vorne's armor that would have been guarded an hour ago. Both of them accumulating damage — the cuts on Vorne deepening, the quartzite on Cedric showing fracture lines that hadn't been there before, the specific arithmetic of two people who were spending more than they were recovering and were both aware of this and were both continuing regardless.

---

The greatsword broke.

Not at the hilt — at the blade, the specific failure of steel that had been hitting stone and quartzite all night reaching the point where the hitting exceeded what the steel could sustain. The break arrived between one strike and the next — the blade meeting Cedric's quartzite wall and the wall holding and the blade not holding and the upper half of the blade separating from the lower half with the sound of something that had been reliable for two decades deciding it was done being reliable.

Vorne held what remained.

Half a greatsword. The grip and the guard and enough blade to be a weapon but not the weapon it had been — shorter, lighter, the balance different from the balance his body had spent years learning. He adjusted his grip without looking at it. The adjustment arriving from somewhere deeper than thought, the body making the change because the body had no time to consult the mind about the change.

Cedric saw the broken blade.

The quartzite sword came at Vorne — from the right, the full length and weight of it, the augmented edge coming at the space that the broken greatsword's shorter reach could not cover. Vorne brought the broken blade up and caught it — the quartzite meeting the remaining steel, the two weapons locking for a moment, Vorne's shorter blade holding the quartzite blade in place through force rather than leverage.

The block opened him up.

Both arms committed to holding the quartzite sword in place. The torso exposed. The broken greatsword's shorter reach keeping his arms closer to his body than the full greatsword would have kept them, the specific vulnerability of a shorter weapon against a longer one arriving in the geometry of the block.

Cedric's left arm moved.

The normal sword was there — behind his forearm, hidden by the quartzite vambrace, the unaugmented blade that he had been carrying all night behind the quartzite the way you carried a knife behind a shield. Not quartzite. Not stone. Just steel — lighter, faster, coming from the angle that the broken greatsword couldn't reach because both of Vorne's arms were holding the quartzite sword that wasn't the real attack.

The steel went into Vorne's gut.

It found the gap in the armor that the quartzite sword had drawn the guard away from — the specific gap that existed because the block required both arms and both arms being committed meant the torso was not guarded by anything except the armor and the armor had a gap and the gap was where the sword went. The blade going in. The feeling of it arriving at Vorne through the specific channel that a blade entering a body used to communicate what it was doing — not pain first, pressure first, the wrongness of something being inside that was not supposed to be inside.

Vorne's hand found Cedric's arm.

Not the sword — the arm. The arm connected to the hand connected to the grip connected to the blade that was inside him. His right hand released the broken greatsword and closed around Cedric's forearm with a grip that had nothing to do with technique and everything to do with what was underneath technique, the life force that had been pushing his body all night now pushing his grip past what grip was supposed to be capable of.

He broke it at the elbow.

The joint went in the direction the joint was not built to go — the specific sound of it arriving before Cedric's response, the bone and the ligaments and the structure of the elbow communicating their failure simultaneously, the sound of something that had been intact becoming something that was no longer intact.

Cedric made the sound he had not made all night.

He pulled back.

The sword came out of Vorne as Cedric retreated — the blade leaving the body through the same path it had entered, the withdrawal producing what withdrawals produced, the blood following the steel the way blood followed steel when steel left a body it had been inside.

Both of them stood.

Both of them paying for what they had just done to the other. Cedric's left arm hanging at an angle arms did not hang at. Vorne's left hand pressed to his gut where the blood was coming through his fingers. Both of them breathing the way people breathed when breathing had become something that required attention rather than something that happened on its own.

---

Something appeared in the sky to the west.

From the direction of the western gate — a beacon, visible, rising into the dark above the rooftops. Not fire — not the orange-red of Elysia's beacon at the northern compound. Air. The specific visible distortion of compressed air being directed upward at a scale that made it visible against the night sky, the air above the western gate moving in a way that communicated signal rather than weapon.

Cedric laughed.

Despite the arm. Despite the blood on the quartzite. Despite everything the night had produced and everything it had cost. He laughed — the laugh of someone who had just received the one piece of information that made everything else worth it. The western signal. The signal that was supposed to come from Highmore and Emmeline hours ago and hadn't. It was here now. Late and present and visible in the sky above the district.

Vorne's face changed.

The expression on it doing what expressions did when a calculation that had been running resolved in a direction that required a new calculation entirely.

Then something Cedric didn't expect happened.

The beacon stopped.

Abruptly — not fading, not dissipating the way signals dissipated when they were done. Stopping. The compressed air that had been rising ceasing to rise, the signal cutting off between one moment and the next as if someone had interrupted it.

It came back.

The beacon rising again — the same compressed air, the same visible distortion, the same signal. Present in the sky above the western gate for a moment.

It stopped again.

It came back again.

Three pulsations. Three distinct interruptions and three distinct returns, the signal appearing and disappearing and appearing and disappearing and appearing and disappearing with the specific regularity of something that was being done deliberately — not a malfunction, not an interruption, a message.

Cedric's smile faded.

The laughter was gone from his face. What replaced it was the expression of someone who had received information they had not expected to receive and were now sitting inside the receiving of it without knowing yet what it meant. But knowing — from the way the smile left and the way the eyes changed and the way the broken arm stopped being the thing he was most aware of — that whatever three pulses meant, it was not what one pulse meant.

Both of them stood in the street and looked at the sky above the western gate.
